What happens when an epoch arrives: the delta is computed against the FIRST snapshot, and a lossy schedule edit is refused
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31, on three calls put to him after the mechanism was measured rather than assumed. His original framing is preserved in the snapshot at `snap:epoch:arrival-delta:dec:arrival-delta`. WHAT ARRIVES, PER SCHEDULED ITEM — his three outcomes, the complement he did not name, and a FIFTH his four assume away: - DELIVERED — the plan held. Computed from the golden thread (`req:completion-computed`), never asserted. - DEFERRED — still intended, the date moved; the report names where it now points. - DISCONTINUED — no longer intended at all. Distinct from deferred the way `retire-from-design` distinguishes them: one is a date change, the other a withdrawal. - DELIVERED BUT NEVER PLANNED — reported as `added_after_baseline`, work scheduled here after the commitment was taken. A delta measured only against the plan cannot see the work that was not in it, and that is usually where the estimate went. - OUTSTANDING — still pointed at a moment that has arrived, and not delivered. THE FOUR ASSUME EVERY UNDELIVERED ITEM WAS CONSCIOUSLY MOVED OR DROPPED, and the commonest case is that nobody touched it and it did not happen. Calling that `discontinued` would put a withdrawal on the record nobody made; calling it `deferred` would invent a date nobody chose. It is exactly the question `req:plans-move-honestly` says must be ASKED and never defaulted — transferred or discontinued — so it is reported as its own outcome and put to the user. CALL 1 — THE BASELINE IS THE TARGET'S FIRST SNAPSHOT, with every later one returned as the movement trail. The brainstorm said the LAST snapshot, and that does not compute what he asked for: two replans leave epoch 3 holding {A,B,C} then {A,C}, so reading the last says the plan was always {A,C} and B's slip vanishes from the very report meant to show it. Where no snapshot exists the plan has never been recorded as moving, so the live edges ARE the original plan and are the baseline — stated as `BaselineSource`, not implied. ACCEPTED WRINKLE, named rather than hidden: the baseline is whenever a snapshot first happened to be taken, which may predate the plan being complete; where the baseline captured an empty plan the report says so in `notes` and the trail shows the growth. CALL 2 — `snapshot_node` EXCLUDES BY EDGE ROLE, NOT ENDPOINT TYPE. See `dec:commitment-edges-survive-snapshots`, minted for it. CALL 3 — A LOSSY SCHEDULE EDIT WITH NO RECORDED CHANGE IS REFUSED, mirroring `record_change` refusing a planned epoch. Removing a `SCHEDULED_FOR`, re-pointing it, or rewriting its modality all destroy a claim; each is refused while the plan is unrecorded, with the refusal naming the `record_change` that unblocks it. ADDING to a plan is deliberately NOT guarded — it destroys no earlier claim, and taxing it would punish correct work, which is the mistake this project keeps finding in detectors. `delete_node` is guarded from both directions too, because retiring a scheduled requirement is precisely how discontinuation happens and would otherwise walk straight past the refusal. WHAT IS COMPUTED VERSUS STORED, unchanged and load-bearing: NOTHING about the outcome is written down. The plan lives in the epoch's snapshots, delivery is computed from the thread, and storing the result would create a second source of truth able to disagree with the first — the same argument that keeps `achieved` out of the `modality` enum. WHAT FALLS OUT: `missed_obligations`, the `required` claims that did not land — computed violations rather than slips, and the scheduling face of a KPP. And once several epochs have arrived, the confidence `req:plans-move-honestly` wants a planned claim to carry can be MEASURED from arrival history rather than authored — Anthony's Black-Scholes analogy, answered with observation. DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT: delivery is not dated to an epoch, so 'delivered during this window but never scheduled anywhere' is not computable and is not claimed. `added_after_baseline` answers the narrower, answerable question, and `notes` says which one was answered.		MEASURED BEFORE DECIDED, and two of the three calls exist because the measuring found something the brainstorm had not. The mechanism claim held: `snapshot_node` really does chain incoming edges, so snapshotting the epoch captures every schedule edge pointing at it — the whole plan in one call. And `record_change`'s planned-epoch refusal keys on the epoch you FILE INTO, not the node you snapshot, so a replan files into the current arrived epoch with the planned epoch as its subject. That also answers the open question inside `cap:plan-movement-recorded`: filing in the arrived epoch is sufficient, and planned epochs need no revision chain of their own. But the trap was WORSE than the brainstorm stated, which is call 2. And 'the last snapshot' would have under-reported exactly the slip the report exists to show, which is call 1. Both were found by reading the code rather than reasoning about it — the same method that found the wrong-direction edge in `dec:epoch-pins-a-version-combination`. The fifth outcome came from asking what happens to an item nobody touches, which is the ordinary case and the one the four-outcome framing has no room for. Forcing it into `discontinued` or `deferred` would have made the report assert a decision that was never taken — the failure `dec:report-dont-judge` exists to prevent, arriving through a vocabulary that was simply too small. Mutation-checked, all three calls: empty the commitment-edge list and the snapshot test fails; take the baseline from the last snapshot instead of the first and the two-replan test fails; make the guard always allow and all three refusal tests fail.acceptedWhat was planned against what arrived, computed and never stored
Suspected duplicates are asked, never merged
possible_duplicate is a DETECT gap; HEAL merges only on a human-drawn DUPLICATES edge.		apply_heal deletes a node with no undo, so merge is safe only because the endpoints were asserted; a heuristic must not drive it. A gap can be acknowledged, a HEAL defect cannot be dismissed. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: 3dtictactoe trial, BL-27/BL-29.acceptedIngest a folder of specifications as one design, Detect gaps, Repair structure, DECIDED — a merge needs a discriminator, not a threshold: siblings are held apart by whole-word difference, Deleting a node is never mechanical, and never quiet on a shared graph
Attention is measured by what was READ, not by what a search scored — behavioural, not lexical
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-10: *'agreed on the 'behavioural rather than lexical' approach.'* SETTLED: if repeated attention to a node is ever used as a priority signal, the unit of evidence is that a search surfaced the node AND the agent then FETCHED IT IN FULL. Not the BM25 score, not the appearance in a ranked list. WHY THIS AXIS COULD BE SETTLED WHILE THE REST STAYS OPEN. The lexical route was measured and found unusable in the form anybody would reach for: `search_design` returns BM25, which is unbounded and query-dependent — the query 'export' scored its top hit at 4.48 and a longer query on the same subject scored 35.75, eight times higher for the same topic. Any accumulation of raw scores weights verbose queries over terse ones and would drift with whoever (or whatever model) writes the query. A behavioural unit needs no score at all, so it sidesteps comparability entirely and cannot be gamed by query length. ⭐ ANTHONY'S FRAMING, AND IT IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN DECORATIVE: *'this is a bit like a Q-table in reinforcement learning... the more that a search appears, the more that it is reinforced.'* Three consequences follow from taking that seriously, and none of them is obvious from the counter idea alone. (1) A Q-VALUE DECAYS AND A COUNTER DOES NOT. Reinforcement learning applies a learning rate precisely so that recent evidence outweighs old; a plain tally never forgets. Without decay, whatever was hot in a project's first month dominates its ranking forever, and a node read ten times in July and never since reads as more critical than one read three times this week. ⇒ IF THIS IS BUILT, RECENCY IS PART OF THE UPDATE RULE, NOT A LATER REFINEMENT. (2) VISIT COUNT IS NOT VALUE. In a Q-table the update is driven by REWARD; the visit count is exploration bookkeeping. 'Searched often' is a visit count. What Anthony actually wants is closer to Q — did going there PAY OFF — and that is the deeper argument for the behavioural unit he chose: choosing to read a node in full is a weak revealed preference, where appearing in a list is not even that. ⚠️ THE ANALOGY BREAKS HERE AND THE BREAK MUST BE RECORDED: THERE IS NO REWARD SIGNAL. Nothing observes whether reading a node helped. The agent's choice to read is a proxy for relevance, not a measurement of outcome, and treating it as reward would assert an observation nobody makes. The RL framing supplies STRUCTURE (decay, exploration) and does NOT supply the thing that makes Q-learning converge. (3) 🛑 THE EXPLORATION TRAP, AND IT IS `dec:bl-155` ARRIVING BY A NEW ROAD. A reinforcement scheme reinforces what has already been visited. A node nothing surfaces is never read, so it never accumulates, so it never rises — permanently. That is exactly bl-155's finding that reflow2 cannot tell 'unused' from 'unreachable', and `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content` already drew the consequence that counts may justify optimising and never, alone, justify cutting. THE RL FRAMING ADDS THE REMEDY SHAPE THAT THE EARLIER FRAMING LACKED: greedy exploitation of an under-explored table converges on a local optimum, and the standard answers are an exploration term or optimistic initialisation. ⇒ ANY ATTENTION RANKING NEEDS A DELIBERATE EXPLORATION COMPONENT — something that surfaces never-touched nodes on purpose — or it will bury exactly the material a discoverability problem is already hiding. Recorded as a REQUIRED PROPERTY of any such design, not as a nice-to-have. WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE, and `dec:idea-what-gets-searched-repeatedly-is-becoming-important` stays OPEN for all of it: whether attention should be tracked at all; where the record lives (`dec:how-should-reflow2-log-its-own-usage` holds that); how it composes with ranking by CONSEQUENCE (`dec:idea-a-critical-path-through-the-undecided`); and whether a bounded top-5 draws from one merged score or two lists. This decision closes one axis so the others can be argued without re-litigating it. STILL BINDING FROM THE OPEN NODE: the search history is LOCAL BY CONSTRUCTION and never enters a telemetry payload — `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content` governs what LEAVES a design and names search queries as the worst offender. And review records and bookkeeping must be excluded from any accumulation, per the exclusion list `fact:graph-analysis-covers-a-third-of-the-edge-types` had to learn the expensive way.		Recorded as its own accepted Decision rather than by editing the brainstorm node into an answer, per `dec:reopen-supersedes`' principle that the record should show both that a question was asked and how it was settled. It deliberately does NOT obsolete `dec:idea-what-gets-searched-repeatedly-is-becoming-important`: Anthony settled the lexical-versus-behavioural axis, not whether to build any of this, so superseding the whole question would claim more than he said. The Q-table framing is recorded as design content rather than as a metaphor because it produces three testable properties the counter idea did not have — decay, the visit-count-is-not-value distinction, and an exploration term — and because its BREAK is as informative as its fit: there is no reward signal here, and an implementation that pretended otherwise would be asserting an observation nobody makes. Consequence (3) is the one worth carrying forward. bl-155's unused-versus-unreachable finding has been restated three times in this design as a warning; the RL framing is the first time it has arrived with a known remedy shape attached.acceptedOPEN — should repeated, RELEVANCE-WEIGHTED search hits mark a node as becoming critical, when BM25 scores are not comparable across queries and the same data is named 'the worst offender' for telemetry?, PROPOSED — where-am-i shows four ranked open decisions and one deliberately UNRANKED, and a rough ranking is explicitly good enough
DECIDED — a merge needs a discriminator, not a threshold: siblings are held apart by whole-word difference
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-05, taking OPTION (c) from the options this node recorded while open. The measurement below is unchanged; what follows it is the choice and what it does not cover. ⭐ THE MEASUREMENT THAT FORCED IT, from the first real trial of cap:corpus-ingest over six dev_storyflow architecture documents. `dynograph_resolution::token_sort_ratio` against the auto-merge threshold of 90: 95 dynograph-vector vs dynograph-core <- SILENTLY MERGED, WRONG 94 dynograph-storage vs dynograph-core <- SILENTLY MERGED, WRONG 93 dynograph-extract vs dynograph-context <- SILENTLY MERGED, WRONG 91 dynograph-server vs dynograph-query <- SILENTLY MERGED, WRONG 84 Auth Service vs Authentication Service (NOT merged — and this is the case the feature EXISTS for) ONE DOCUMENT DECLARING NINE CRATES PRODUCED FIVE NODES. 44% of an architecture destroyed silently, and the survivors asserted something FALSE rather than merely being incomplete: `cmp:dynograph-core` carried the name 'dynograph-storage'. WHY NO THRESHOLD REPAIRS IT, which is the reason (a) was rejected: 95 was a sibling pair and 84 a true duplicate, so the ORDERING is inverted and no cutoff separates them. `docs/scope-corpus-ingest.md` asserted '90 on a token-sorted ratio is near-identity'; measured, that is false for the names real systems use. THE CHOICE — A DIFFERENT QUESTION, NOT A BETTER NUMBER. Before auto-merging, both names are tokenised on every non-alphanumeric (deliberately NOT `name_tokens`, which splits on whitespace and so cannot see inside `dynograph-core`). A merge is REFUSED when either side carries a whole word the other does not ABBREVIATE. 'core' and 'storage' are not spellings of each other; 'auth' and 'authentication' are, with a three-character minimum because below that almost anything prefixes anything. An unpaired extra word is distinguishing too, so `Auth Service` and `Auth Service v2` stay apart — the case the scope doc warned collapsing would lose. Reordered tokens still converge, so BL-186's ordering fix is untouched. AND THE REFUSAL SAYS WHICH WORD DID IT. `MergeCandidate.distinguished_by` carries e.g. '`storage` has no counterpart in \'dynograph-core\''. 'These two were not merged' is not something a person can rule on; naming the word is. `None` means the score simply fell short, which needs no explanation. THE SECOND FIX IN THE SAME CHANGE: `CorpusReport.fuzzy_merges` was a `usize` for one day and is now `Vec`, each entry carrying the DOCUMENT that caused it — which the single-document report structurally cannot know. A merge is the one thing an ingest does WITHOUT ASKING and cannot undo by re-running, and the aggregate had reduced it to a number at exactly the scale where that matters most. VERIFIED, AND MUTATION-CHECKED: `tests/sibling_merge.rs` pins nine crates staying nine, an abbreviation still merging, a version suffix staying apart, reordered tokens still converging, and the refusal naming its word. Disabling the discriminator returns 5-of-9 and fails exactly the three tests that name those properties while leaving the two that should be insensitive passing. Re-run against the real dev_storyflow document that found it: 9 of 9 crates survive, each with its own name. ⭐ WHAT THIS DOES NOT FIX, AND IT IS THE HALF THAT REMAINS: the destructive direction is handled; the MISSING direction is untouched. `Read Cache` ~ `Local Store` is still invisible — not a low score, no score at all — so two documents that RENAMED the same thing still produce two nodes. This decision makes the lexical pass safe, not sufficient. `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption` is where that half lives, and this trial is the strongest evidence yet for it: the lexical signal here was not merely weak, it was INVERTED, which is the argument a semantic tiebreaker has been waiting for. ALSO NOT SETTLED: the ask band is still noisy. The same trial's eleven merge candidates were ELEVEN OUT OF ELEVEN FALSE POSITIVES. The discriminator now labels the sibling ones, which should make them skimmable rather than gruelling, but nobody has measured the band again since. STILL NOT MEASURED, and it bounds every number above: what this does across the other 1,118 documents. The trial was SIX documents chosen for topical overlap; 44% is one document's crate list, not a corpus-wide rate.		Moved to accepted on Anthony's explicit instruction ('fix the fuzzy_merges regression, then the token discriminator'), which chose option (c) over the four alternatives this node had recorded. The measurement is kept in full rather than trimmed to the conclusion, because the numbers are what make the fix defensible and what would otherwise be re-derived: 'fuzzy matching is too aggressive' decays into folklore within a session, and '95 for a sibling pair, 84 for a true duplicate' does not. Two things are deliberately recorded as NOT fixed — the missing-convergence direction and the noisy ask band — so this does not read as having closed the resolution question. It closed the destructive half of it. The one that remains is the one that needs embeddings, and saying so here is what stops the next session treating lexical resolution as done.acceptednothing
The backlog is retired: every open row becomes the node type it already was, and docs/backlog.md is deleted rather than derived
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-07, verbatim: 'the backlog needs to be retired once and for all - I approve whatever decisions need to be made to make this action occur.' This settles dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph, open since 2026-08-04 with five options and no choice, and it supersedes it. THE CHOICE IS OPTION (a) — ROUTE EACH ROW TO THE TYPE IT ALREADY IS — and it is only available now because the one category that had no home was given one. dec:defects-are-temporal-facts (accepted 2026-08-06) closed it: a defect found by USING a built capability is a TemporalFact with fact_type 'defect'. So all four categories the 2026-08-04 taxonomy identified now have a destination: (i) a defect against a shipped capability -> TemporalFact, fact_type 'defect', basis 'measured', HAS_TEMPORAL_FACT from the node it indicts, VALID_TO set when fixed (ii) unbuilt work -> a Capability at `planned` behind a Requirement (iii) an open design question -> a `proposed` Decision (iv) a discovered limit -> a Constraint or a DesignRule OPTION (d) IS EXPLICITLY NOT TAKEN. Deriving a markdown backlog from the graph was the fallback that kept the file alive as a projection; 'retired once and for all' is a stronger instruction than that, and dec:views-are-projections already covers rendering if anyone later wants a view. The file is DELETED, and its history stays in git where deleted files live. THE MEASURED SCOPE, taken 2026-08-07 rather than carried from the 2026-08-04 note: docs/backlog.md is 3,356 lines / 589,326 bytes / 217 distinct BL ids. 129 open rows under 'Next up', 9 under 'Bigger threads', plus a 'Closed' section that is already only short pointers to the CHANGELOG and a 'Deliberate deferrals' section. 22 other files reference it, including AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, COORD.md and README.md, and CLAUDE.md names it as one of the three things to read at session start — so retiring the file is not finished until those pointers are too. ⭐ THE FAILURE MODE THIS DECISION MUST NOT PRODUCE, quoted from the decision it supersedes because it is the whole risk: 'A row moved in as one long `description` rebuilds backlog.md inside the graph with worse ergonomics and no gain — and that failure would be invisible, because it would look like progress.' So a row is migrated only when it becomes STRUCTURE: the node it bears on named by an EDGE, what was measured in a TYPED property, and whether it is still true carried by a status or a temporal bound. The prose hangs off that as explanation. A migration that produces 138 nodes of narrative and no edges has failed while appearing to succeed, and the honest test is whether the loop can see the result — not whether the file got shorter. WHAT IS STILL OWED AND IS NOT SOLVED BY THIS. dec:defects-are-temporal-facts says it in its own words: nothing in the LOOP reads defect facts yet. `statement` is fulltext so search_design finds them, but `loop_status` does not count open defects — measured again today, and it does not. So a migrated defect is DISCOVERABLE, not SURFACED. Retiring the file therefore trades a document nobody queries for nodes the loop does not yet count, and that reader is the next increment. Recorded here so the trade is a choice rather than a discovery. CLOSED ROWS ARE NOT MIGRATED. The 'Closed' section is already only stable-id pointers into the CHANGELOG, and a finished item's value is history that git holds. Migrating them would import 100+ nodes that indict nothing and are true of nothing.		Accepted rather than left `proposed` because Anthony's approval was explicit, unprompted and general ('whatever decisions need to be made'), which is the standard dec:three-party-checks sets — the human decides, and here they did, in advance and in writing. He had already stated the preference on 2026-08-04 ('I wanted to stop using the BL... instead, I wanted everything in the graph') and it sat unchosen for three days while the file grew. The cost of leaving it open is measured on the superseded node: 6 of 8 rows filed in one session referenced by zero graph nodes, and four things re-derived in that same session that were already written down. The falsifiable test from dec:what-lives-where applies to reflow2 itself and it has been failing it: if reflow2 works, reflow2 would not need a 589 KB markdown backlog.acceptedtools/migrate_backlog.py — the one-shot migration that executed dec:backlog-is-retired, and the record of which row became which node
Backing up a design is the consumer's job; what reflow2 owes is a documented update path and honest primitives
DECIDED by Anthony, 2026-08-06: 'the responsibility to backup the reflow2 graph is probably more the responsibility of the flo2 project? reflow2 only needs to provide the documentation on how to update reflow2 properly so that any graph data is persistent.' THE BOUNDARY, and it is cleaner than it first looked: BACKUP IS A PROPERTY OF WHERE THE DATA LIVES — the consumer's volume, their storage account, their retention window, their compliance rules. reflow2 knows none of those and cannot learn them. A design tool that shipped an opinionated backup would be wrong for most projects that installed it, and would be carrying operational burden that dec:multi-writer-architecture already rejected on exactly those grounds. WHAT REFLOW2 OWES INSTEAD, and this is the whole of it: (1) A DOCUMENTED UPDATE PATH — getting-started/UPDATING.md, which ships in the consumer kit rather than living in this repo's docs, per rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party. It states where the design actually lives, that the binary and the design are separate in every deployment shape, and the ONE mistake that looks like data loss: mounting the store directory instead of its parent leaves the identity sidecar behind, and a store opened without its identity PRESENTS AS AN EMPTY DESIGN while the data sits untouched on disk beside it. (2) HONEST PRIMITIVES a consumer can build a backup FROM: export_graph is a complete, deterministic, content-hashed snapshot; --import is a restore that preserves graph_id, so a restored design IS the same design rather than a copy sharing a name; and for the repo-file model the committed export means git is already an off-host backup, versioned and replicated for free. (3) NOT LYING when something is off. This is where the boundary stops being purely documentary, and it is the part that remains reflow2's problem: the version stamp reports an older store as 'additive only — everything in it still reads', and there is NO verdict at all for the reverse. See dec:idea-need-to-know-compartments and the downgrade gap. WHY THE ASYMMETRY BETWEEN THE TWO DEPLOYMENT SHAPES MATTERS HERE: under the repo-file model (dec:multi-writer-architecture, accepted) the export is committed, so backup is solved by git and nobody has to think about it. A HOSTED SERVER HAS NO REPO — the same asymmetry that makes --content-path's default wrong for a container — so the hosted case is the one that needs real backup work, and it is precisely the case that belongs to whoever runs the server. flo2 owns flo2's volume. WHAT WAS CONSIDERED AND NOT CHOSEN: reflow2 shipping snapshot/restore/off-host-push machinery, in the shape storyflow's scripts/ops already proves out (safe-deploy: snapshot, deploy, fingerprint node counts by type, alarm on any user-data decrease, off-host copy verified rather than assumed, receipts kept). Those concepts are sound and a consumer should borrow them — the doc points at the shape. They are not reflow2's to run, because every one of them is parameterised by facts only the consumer has. ⚠️ ONE THING THIS DECISION DOES NOT SETTLE, recorded so it is not read as settled: reflow2 gives a consumer a stronger fingerprint than node counts, because the export is content-hashed and deterministic. Whether a comparison helper belongs in the shipped kit — as reflow2_check.py's dependency reconciliation now does for pins — is a separate question from whether reflow2 runs backups, and it has not been asked.		Captured on Anthony's word, 2026-08-06, and it NARROWS a requirement rather than growing one: req:hosted-state-outlives-the-image already says designs must survive a container replacement, and this says who is responsible for the case where they do not. Scoping it down was his call and it is the right one — the alternative was reflow2 acquiring a backup subsystem parameterised by facts it cannot know. Recorded as a Decision rather than a Requirement because it says what reflow2 will NOT do, and the positive half it implies (the doc) is a deliverable that already exists rather than intent awaiting satisfaction. THE PART WORTH RE-READING LATER: the boundary holds for backup and does NOT hold for honesty. 'We do not back your data up' is a fair thing for a tool to say. 'We opened a store an older binary wrote and said nothing' is not, and no amount of documentation fixes it — which is why the downgrade gate stayed on the queue as work rather than being absorbed into this decision as prose.acceptednothing

Both are right, they answer different questions, and the recorded figure means directed. A bulk write is all-or-nothing AND reports every failure — the refusal-semantics question was a false choice
Every bulk form attempts every item, collects each failure with its index, and if any item failed discards the whole batch and returns the complete failure list. A rejected batch is returned as an ERROR carrying the failures in its data, never as a payload with applied:false.		BL-153 posed this as a choice — 'one refusal semantics to define (all-or-nothing, or per-item findings?)' — and the two were never exclusive. ALL-OR-NOTHING COSTS NOTHING HERE: the store already has an atomic batch (begin_batch/commit_batch/discard_batch) that HEAL's apply step and import_graph both use, and a partial bulk write leaves a design in a state nobody chose. PER-ITEM FINDINGS ARE SEPARATELY NECESSARY: BL-118 files exactly the opposite defect against import_graph — 'validation is fail-fast, one error per attempt' — and BL-139 records what it costs, that the adopt loop's corrective re-import is where it breaks. A bulk form surfacing one error per round trip would replace N writes with N retries and save nobody anything. The failure carries its INDEX as well as its id because an id alone cannot tell two identical entries apart, and a list an agent generated is exactly where a duplicate turns up. The error-not-payload choice follows the same rule as everywhere else: a tool result reads as success, so 'nothing was written' dressed as a result is the silent-failure shape this project forbids.acceptedOne call where the surface measured N
A bulk form collapses the round trip, never the judgement
Any bulk form over a tool that records a JUDGEMENT carries that judgement per item, never hoisted to a call-level argument: set_artifact_checksums takes a disposition per artifact, acknowledge_gaps a reason per gap, and gaps_to_prompts groups answers per gap. A shared timestamp is allowed because it is a fact about the call; a shared disposition is not, because it would be a shared decision.		BL-153 stated the trap before the build: 'a batch of 144 acknowledgements with one reason is exactly the erosion those decisions exist to prevent, so a bulk form needs per-item dispositions or it is worse than the loop.' This is the line that keeps dec:two-sided-accept ('silent drift-accept does not exist') and dec:ask-not-repair true under a bulk surface — 244 accepts now cost one call and still 244 decisions. It is also the distinction that let dec:manifest-derived-is-not-manifest-accepted go the other way and take no per-item disposition at all: a DERIVATION records no judgement, so there is none to preserve. For gaps_to_prompts the per-item grouping is additionally mechanical, not only doctrinal: grouping answers by gap is what stops two gaps' prompt ids colliding, so no gap is ever replayed against another's answers — and a half-answered batch is refused rather than half-served, because serving half would record some questions and silently drop the rest.acceptedOne call where the surface measured N
Circular validation is made structurally visible by a CALIBRATED_AGAINST edge, never detected analytically
A new CALIBRATED_AGAINST edge runs from a fitted node to the evidence its value was derived from (an Artifact or a Verification). A VERIFIES edge whose Verification IS, or PRODUCES, evidence its own target was calibrated against is reported as CONSUMED — a fit, not a test — and is excluded from the count of independent evidence. A capability whose only passing checks are consumed is reported as not independently verified.		Anthony's call, 2026-08-01. BL-136's closing evidence decides the shape and rules out the alternatives: the project that hit this built four independent internal diagnostics — a back-solve, a coefficient locus, a space-time frontier and a physical-floor proof — and every one narrowed the question correctly while none could have found the defect. Only the outside source could. So a circular check is not a weak check to be strengthened from inside; NO INTERNAL EVIDENCE CAN DETECT IT, BY CONSTRUCTION. That rules out any analytic detector and leaves exactly one move: record what a value was fitted to, and refuse to let that same evidence count as its validation. An edge rather than a provenance value because the detector is then a graph query rather than a scan, and because the relation carries WHAT was consumed, which a provenance enum cannot. The `calibrated` provenance value (BL-120(d), and what the originating project actually built) stays open and is not foreclosed — it answers HOW the value entered, a different question from WHAT it consumed. Stakes, from the same closing entry: a single-point fit does not merely get a number wrong, it can silently hold a wrong EQUATION in agreement with the data — the fitted coefficient absorbed a structural error in the functional form and agreed with the anchor anyway.acceptedRefuse to let evidence a value was fitted to count as its validation
CALIBRATED_AGAINST is a traceability edge — when the anchor moves, every value fitted to it is in the blast radius
CALIBRATED_AGAINST is entered in the structural direction table (nodes.rs structural_rule) as (forward: Upstream, backward: Downstream), the same shape as REALIZES and VERIFIES. From the fitted node you reach the evidence its authority rests on; from the evidence you reach every value that would be wrong if it were superseded.		Asked deliberately because the table's own comment says it is the question nobody asks: 'Twice now a new edge type has reached a Release without anyone asking whether the impact table should know about it, and nothing checks that question is asked' — INCLUDES and then SCHEDULED_FOR, each found only when disconnected_community fired on an island the new edge had failed to join. This is the third such edge and the question was put before the code was written rather than after a detector complained. The answer is yes on the merits: a calibration is a genuine dependency of a value on a piece of evidence, so when the anchor is corrected or superseded, every value fitted to it is exactly the blast radius propagate_change exists to compute — which is the payoff BL-136 asks for, since a wrong functional form absorbed into a fitted coefficient is only findable when the outside source arrives and someone can see what rested on the old one. Direction matches REALIZES because the evidence is the source of truth and the fitted value is downstream of it. Consequence accepted and stated rather than discovered: this puts CALIBRATED_AGAINST into design_network(), so it counts toward centrality, communities and single-point-of-failure — the surface BL-124 has just shown is sensitive to edge-set changes. On reflow2's own graph the effect is nil today because the design carries no fitted values, and that is a measurement, not an assumption.acceptedRefuse to let evidence a value was fitted to count as its validation
OPEN — does reflow2 gain a hosted surface (one MCP over HTTPS) alongside the repo file?
UNDECIDED. Raised by Anthony 2026-07-25 from his own situation: he is in Long Island, his brother is in Washington State, they want to work on one design at the same time and to see each other's projects. FOUR ROADS, and the middle ones are not the obvious winners. (a) GIT IS ALREADY THE CENTRAL SERVER — the design is a file in the repo, the repo already spans both coasts, and the claims layer that shipped 2026-07-25 already answers 'who has what in hand' the moment either side pulls. Nothing to host, nothing to secure, nothing to pay for, and no new place for the design to live. What it cannot do is tell you about a claim before the other person pushes. (b) A HOSTED MCP over HTTPS — one server process holding the graph, both people's agents connecting to it, so a claim is visible the moment it is made and a design is reachable by someone who never cloned the repo. Costs: reflow2-mcp serves stdio only today (rmcp's streamable-HTTP transport exists, the binary does not use it), authentication does not exist at all, and it puts the design on a machine — which weakens but does not erase dec:repo-file-embedded's objection, since the machine would be Anthony's own droplet rather than a vendor's. NOTE WHAT MAKES (b) CHEAPER THAN IT LOOKS: one server process with many clients is ALREADY compatible with the single-writer store, because there is still exactly one writer — the server. (c) HYBRID — host a read/publish surface for reaching and browsing designs, keep writes local and merge through git, so the durable record never moves. THE CHEAPEST FIRST CUT, worth naming because it needs almost no core work: one server process PER PROJECT, each with its own graph path and its own token, and project selection becomes which URL the agent points at — no graph_id plumbing, no multi-tenancy, and a per-project blast radius if one goes wrong. A private tailnet instead of public TLS removes the authentication problem for exactly two people, which is the population this actually has. (d) ONE LIVE SHARED WORKING TREE on a droplet — both people editing the same checkout simultaneously, seeing each other's edits, with a push to a 'true' git repo every so often for permanent storage (Anthony, 2026-07-25). THE DESIGN HALF OF THIS IS (b) AND IS SOUND; THE CODE HALF INVERTS THE PROPERTY IT IS REACHING FOR. A shared checkout does not remove conflicts, it removes conflict DETECTION: with one copy there is no common ancestor to merge against, so two agents doing read-modify-write on one file interleave into last-write-wins with no marker, no three-way merge and nothing to review — strictly less safe than what they have now. It also shares the things git assumes are private (one index, one HEAD, one branch: `git checkout` on his side changes files under her mid-edit), shares the build directory and the graph's single-writer lock, and makes the droplet a single point of failure for two people who can currently both work on a plane. The batched push is its own cost: history granularity, attribution and bisect all collapse into one commit, the gates that are supposed to gate a commit are replaced by a timer, and 'every so often' is precisely the size of the loss window when the droplet dies. ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ SHARPENED 2026-08-11 — THE PUBLISHING CASE ARRIVES WITH A NAME, AND IT BREAKS AN ASSUMPTION EVERY OPTION ABOVE SHARES ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony is thinking out loud; nothing here settles this decision, which stays `proposed`. ⭐ DELIBERATELY SHARPENED RATHER THAN OPENED AS A NEW NODE. This node's own rationale already named the gap it is being filled with — 'what it does NOT deliver is the publishing case, and that is the strongest argument on the hosted side' — so a second node would have been the near-duplicate the search-first rule exists to prevent. What follows is new EVIDENCE on the same question, not a new question. HIS WORDS, 2026-08-11: 'I want to use reflow2 within flo2. it is purposefully designed to allow collaboration on projects via a web app. if one user posts some brainstorm idea or identifies gaps, the other user shouldn't have to run some terminal commands in order to see that (especially non technical people using web app where no CLI exists).' ⭐⭐ THE ASSUMPTION THAT JUST BROKE, and it is the reason this is worth re-weighing rather than merely noting. EVERY option above was weighed for TWO TECHNICAL PEOPLE WITH TERMINALS. Option (a) — 'git is already the central server' — is only free if both parties can run git. The moment one participant is a non-technical user of a web app, (a) stops being free and starts being impossible: there is no shell to run `git pull` in, no checkout to pull into, and no way to run the import that makes a pulled file readable by the tools. THE CONCRETE FRICTION HE IS OBJECTING TO, measured today rather than supposed: for a second person to SEE a brainstormed idea in a form the tools can answer questions about, they must today (1) `git pull`, (2) run `reflow2-mcp --graph-path .reflow2/graph --import docs/design/reflow2.json`, and (3) have a merge driver configured per-clone or meet a raw text conflict in a 4 MB JSON file. That is three technical steps between one person recording a thought and another person seeing it. For an agent-driven CLI user it is friction; for a web-app user it is a wall. WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT CHANGE, stated separately so neither is overclaimed: - It does NOT re-open `dec:multi-writer-architecture` (accepted 2026-07-25, 'no hosted service'). That decision answered how two WRITERS avoid clobbering each other, and its rejection of hosting rested on `req:persistence` and `req:invocation` — both of which describe where a design DURABLY LIVES. A read/publish surface does not move the durable record, which is exactly why option (c) exists here. - It DOES weaken option (a) as a general answer, because (a)'s cheapness was priced for participants who all have a shell. - ⚠️ It sits against `dec:one-process-many-stores` (ACCEPTED, conditional) and `rule:per-design-state-is-never-a-process-global`, which already contemplate a hosted reflow2 holding N single-writer stores. So the hosted direction is NOT unexplored ground — it is partly built toward, and `req:a-session-cannot-address-another-design` is the guard that must be proven before it ships. - `fact:the-hosted-case-breaks-the-git-transport-and-the-access-topology-is-now-stated` already recorded the same collision from the other side, on 2026-08-09. THE NEW QUESTION THIS RAISES, which none of (a)–(d) answers: WHO IS THE WRITER when the participant is a web-app user? reflow2's loop is ask-the-human-and-record-an-ATTRIBUTABLE-answer. Today attribution comes from a Contributor a local agent names. Through a web app, the app is the MCP client and the human is behind it — so either flo2 passes identity through to reflow2 on every write, or every contribution from that surface is attributed to 'flo2' and the confirmation ledger stops meaning what it says. ⭐ THAT IS A HARDER PROBLEM THAN THE TRANSPORT, and it is the one most likely to be discovered late. ⚠️ A REPO-BOUNDARY NOTE, so nobody skips it: flo2 is a SEPARATE PROJECT with its own design graph and its own owners. Nothing here may be built into flo2 from this repo without Anthony's word (AGENTS.md rule 6). What reflow2 can decide alone is whether it OFFERS a surface flo2 could consume; whether flo2 consumes it is flo2's decision to record. NOT DECIDED, and deliberately not ranked. Option (c) — publish/read hosted, writes stay local — is the one this evidence pushes hardest on, but it is also the one whose attribution story is least worked out.		Held proposed, not built, because it sits against a decision made HOURS earlier on 2026-07-25 (dec:multi-writer-architecture: repo file plus merge on pull, no hosted service) and it must not be drifted into. Per dec:reopen-supersedes, the move is a NEW decision point rather than flipping that one back to proposed. What is genuinely new, and the reason this is not a rerun of the same argument: that decision answered 'how do two writers avoid clobbering each other', and its rationale turned on concurrency being hypothetical and on not putting the user's design on someone else's machine. Neither objection addresses what was raised now — two machines that never share a filesystem, several projects per person, and wanting to READ and contribute to a design without cloning its repo. It is also the second field-sourced trigger in two days on the same seam, which is what cap:revise-trigger exists to notice; that it arrived by conversation rather than by detector is a finding about the detector, not about the trigger. THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded so nobody has to rediscover it: reflow2's loop is ask-the-human-and-record-the-decision, which is deliberate, attributable and slow — a shared live server optimises for simultaneity, which this tool does not need and may be harmed by. The thing the two of them described wanting is mostly non-colliding parallel work plus visibility, and git plus the claims layer already delivers most of that. What it does NOT deliver is the publishing case, and that is the strongest argument on the hosted side. WHAT OPTION (d) CLARIFIED, and it is the useful split: the appeal is real-time VISIBILITY, and visibility does not require a shared working tree. The graph is the artefact where simultaneity genuinely pays and where a single writer already exists to serialise it; source code is the artefact where the distributed copy is doing load-bearing work that a shared tree would silently undo. So the two halves of 'host it' should be decided separately rather than together. THIRD FIELD TRIGGER, 2026-08-11: the publishing case named in this rationale arrived concretely as flo2 — a web app whose users have no CLI at all — which breaks the shared assumption that every participant can run git. Sharpened in place rather than forked, because this node had already named the gap.proposedReachable from another machine, but only on purpose, Several sessions work one design at once, through one server, ACCEPTED 2026-08-06 (conditional) — a hosted reflow2 holds N single-writer stores in one process, one lock each; the directory stays the unit of a design, Someone without the repo can reach a design, read it, and contribute to it, One reflow2 can hold several designs, and a session says which one it is working on
A Requirement's certainty is derived from status × provenance; every move off proposed is the user's word
Requirement certainty is a computed reading, never a stored third axis: status accepted/met → user-confirmed; status deferred/dropped → settled out (also the user's word); status proposed → asserted (provenance authored/planned/imported) or recovered (provenance inferred/reconciled/healed). The load-bearing doctrine: an agent captures requirements at proposed and ONLY the user's answer moves the status — accepted, met, deferred and dropped are all user-only verbs. Reports render the certainty breakdown directly so no session reconstructs it in prose.		User decided all three axes 2026-07-22 (BL-75 vocabulary session, from their fleet trial: where-am-i had to caveat user-confirmed vs recovered in prose every session). Derived over stored for the BL-73 reason — a third stored property can contradict the two axes that already span the space, and the backlog's own warning was 'decide deliberately, not additively'. Every-move-off-proposed rather than accepted-only because an agent dropping a requirement on its own judgment is exactly the silent decision the loop exists to prevent — and this is BL-12 sketch idea 2's example made real ('a requirement moves to accepted only on the human's say-so'), enforced culturally in the skills and the tool description today; the mechanical half stays with BL-41. 'Recovered' over the trial's 'adopted' because it matches the graph's own vocabulary (cap:adopt: 'Recover a design from an existing system') and names the fact, not the workflow. No schema change: the whole defect was the read side — the second time this week (BL-73) the vocabulary was already sufficient and unread.acceptedCompute what is delivered, and expose the requirement lifecycle that is currently unused, Say where the design stands
`change_type` answers WHY; a new `subject` answers WHICH AXIS — the system changed, or only the design's knowledge of it did
SETTLED ON ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-15: option (c), split the axis. He was shown four options and chose the one that addresses the pattern rather than the loudest instance. DISTINCT FROM its two neighbours by design: the FACT measures the problem and counts its occurrences; the IDEA held the four unmade options; THIS records the choice and what was built. WHAT WAS BUILT, the same day: · `ChangeSubject { System, Record }` — a new OPTIONAL property on ChangeEvent. Absent means nobody said and is NEVER inferred from `change_type`, because the mapping is not total: a `resync` can be either. · `ChangeType::DefectFix` — 'the design was right and the code was wrong', distinct from `TestFailureFix`, which is the same repair with different PROVENANCE (a check caught it). That difference is one this project already cares about everywhere else. · Both reachable from `add_change_event`, and the tool description now says the two questions are two questions. · The two internal call sites now STATE their axis: a `design_holds` accept is `system` (the file moved; the move carried no design meaning), and a first baseline is `record` — the case the axis was named for. `record_change` passes None on purpose: the generic path cannot know, and a guess would be a claim nobody made. ⭐ THE SPLIT WAS ALREADY NAMED IN THE CODE AND LEFT UNUSABLE, which is the whole argument. `BaselineEstablished`'s own doc comment reads: 'the odd one out, and deliberately so. Every other variant answers why the THING changed; this one says the thing did not change and only the design's KNOWLEDGE of it did.' An axis with exactly one member, reserved so nobody could reach it — and five forced choices followed. THE EVIDENCE, and the count is the argument: five sessions, four people, three projects, two independent tool surfaces. `chg:duplicate-merge-needs-a-human-20260808` and `chg:accept-acb06c45b63a7b6d` used `test_failure_fix` where no test existed; `chg:arrival-delta-decided` used `scope_change` to mean 'an open question was settled'; Alex tried `bugfix`, was refused, and wrote 'the enum forces a lie'; and the edit recording his report used `resync` to mean 'our knowledge moved and the thing did not'. THE SAME MISSING MEANING WAS ABSENT FROM `set_artifact_checksum`'s DISPOSITION TOO — one absence is a wording gap, two independent absences of one category is a category the vocabulary did not have. PROVEN: 5 tests, MUTATION-CHECKED TWICE, each killing exactly one counterweight. Defaulting an unstated axis to `system` kills only `an_unstated_axis_stays_unstated`. Deriving the axis from `change_type` kills only `one_change_type_appears_on_both_axes` — the test that pins `Resync` appearing on BOTH axes, which is why the mapping cannot be inferred. The reserved-value counterweight holds throughout: `baseline_established` is still `set_artifact_checksum`'s alone. 📌 THE STAMP DOES NOT MOVE, verified rather than assumed: `GraphStamp` carries type NAMES and COUNTS only — no properties, no enum values — so both halves are invisible to it and NO UPGRADE DOC IS OWED. The flip side is worth knowing and is the stamp's blind spot again: a consumer cannot learn from the stamp that a property appeared. NOT SETTLED: whether anything should READ `subject` — it is expressible now and nothing computes from it, which is this project's own recurring 'declared and read by nothing' risk, taken knowingly. And 'an open question was settled' still has no `change_type` value; the axis now lets `resync`+`record` say it honestly, which may be enough or may not.		Recorded as his ruling with what was built attached, so a later reader sees the choice and its consequence in one place. He chose (c) over (a) after the evidence showed at least three missing meanings rather than one — adding a single value would have fixed the loudest case and left the mechanism that produced all five.acceptednothing
Slash commands ship with the kit — the one narrow exception to serving everything
🔄 **WIDENED 2026-08-14 to ALL TWENTY SERVED SKILLS** by `dec:idea-does-every-served-skill-get-a-command` (accepted, option A). The exception below still stands exactly as reasoned — skills, working instructions and everything else remain SERVED, and only commands are installed — but the SET is no longer eight. **Twenty-two command files now ship** (twenty fronting a skill, plus `debt.md` and `decisions.md` which front tools), and `skill_lint` now fails a skill that no command names, so the number cannot silently fall behind again. The original ruling, and its reasoning, is kept below unedited. ════════ AS RULED 2026-07-28 ════════ The eight slash commands (`/gaps`, `/health`, `/where`, `/req`, `/decisions`, `/debt`, `/brainstorm`, `/kpp`) are INSTALLED into a consumer project's `.claude/commands/`. Skills, working instructions and everything else remain SERVED. Anthony's call, 2026-07-28.		QUALIFIES `dec:skills-served` rather than overturning it, and the distinction is what makes the exception safe. WHY THAT DECISION EXISTS: a copied skill goes stale, and the agent then loads last release's content in preference to what the server would serve. That happened here for four releases running without anything noticing, which is why nothing is copied. WHY A COMMAND IS DIFFERENT: each is four lines that name a skill and say how to report the answer. There is no version-coupled content in it. When the skill behind it changes, the command is still correct, because the skill is fetched fresh at use time — the command is a pointer, and the thing it points at is the thing that moves. THE ONE WAY IT CAN ROT, and it is now closed: a command could name a skill that no longer exists. `skill_lint` fails on exactly that, so the failure is caught in this repo rather than discovered in a consumer's, where the symptom would be an agent reporting it cannot find a skill the user was told to use. The mirror is byte-checked too, so `.claude/commands` cannot drift from the kit source. WHAT IT COSTS IF WE ARE WRONG: eight small files in a consumer repo, each independently deletable, none of which changes behaviour when stale. Compare the cost of a stale skill, which silently answers with last release's method. WHY IT WAS WORTH DOING AT ALL: without them a consumer install is experienced as BROKEN rather than thin — the skills are reachable and nothing tells you they are. That is the same invisibility `req:kit-reaches-the-agent` was raised for, one layer up: the pointer now reaches the agent, and the commands are what make the reachable thing usable.acceptedThe install lands where the agent will actually read it, OPEN — does every served skill get a slash command, or is the shortfall the wrong thing to fix?
A snapshot excludes by edge ROLE, not by endpoint type — a commitment to an epoch is design content
`snapshot_node` skips edges whose other endpoint is a bookkeeping node type, and `DesignEpoch` is on that list. Anthony's call 2026-07-31, of three offered: FIX IT by excluding on the edge's own role — a named `COMMITMENT_EDGES` list holding `SCHEDULED_FOR` — rather than leaving the epoch as the only route or deferring it to separate work. THE PROXY WAS EXACT WHEN IT WAS WRITTEN AND STOPPED BEING SO. Every edge to a `DesignEpoch` used to be audit trail (`AT_EPOCH`, `OCCURS_DURING`), so excluding the endpoint type excluded the role, and the rule read as correct because it WAS correct. `SCHEDULED_FOR` broke it: an edge to an epoch is now a COMMITMENT — when this was due — which is design content by any reading, and `req:intent-preserved` says the past is never overwritten. WHAT IT COST WHILE IT HELD, and why this is a defect rather than a preference: `record_change` on a scheduled requirement — the obvious, natural way to record 'this slipped' — captured a snapshot with the schedule edge silently dropped. The old due date was destroyed by the very call whose entire job is preserving it, and the call REPORTED SUCCESS. Only the epoch-side snapshot preserved it, and nothing said so. The trap `dec:arrival-delta` named was therefore worse than stated: it is not merely that re-pointing an edge loses the slip, it is that the correct-looking remedy lost it too. The audit trail it travels with is still excluded, and a test pins that: `AT_EPOCH` on the same node stays out. Role, not endpoint. REJECTED: leaving it, with the epoch-side snapshot documented as the only route — the obvious wrong route would stay silently lossy, and a convention that has to be known is not a property. REJECTED: taking it as separate work — it is the substrate the arrival delta reads, so building the delta on a lossy capture would have shipped a report whose inputs quietly disagreed with each other.		FOUND BY READING THE CODE THE DECISION DEPENDED ON, not by a detector — and nothing could have flagged it. A snapshot that drops an edge is indistinguishable from a snapshot of a node that never had one: there is no second, contradicting fact to make the loss computable. That is the same blind spot recorded in `dec:epoch-pins-a-version-combination` ('a single edge pointing the wrong way creates no cycle and trips no detector'), one layer down — here it is an edge's ABSENCE from a record, which is even quieter than a wrong edge's presence. The general shape is worth keeping, because this project keeps meeting it: a rule that was exactly right for the vocabulary existing when it was written, and became wrong when the vocabulary grew, WITHOUT anything changing at the site of the rule. `BOOKKEEPING_TYPES` was never edited; `SCHEDULED_FOR` was added somewhere else entirely. Proxies decay silently when the thing they proxy for moves. Mutation-checked: empty `COMMITMENT_EDGES` and `a_schedule_edge_survives_a_snapshot_of_the_item` fails, while the epoch-side test keeps passing — which is also the evidence that the two routes were genuinely asymmetric before this.acceptednothing
Component-granularity verification is a computed third state, one question per component
A capability's verification state is three-valued: verified (a passing check of its own), component_verified (no check of its own, but a component it is allocated to carries a passing one — computed at read time, never written), and unchecked. The coverage line reports the third state as its own clause; detect_gaps replaces the N per-capability unverified alarms with ONE component_granularity_verification gap per carrying component at 0.35 — listing the riding capabilities, acknowledgeable once; status_contradiction accepts component-granularity proof for a verified status claim; loop_status counts component_verified as proven. A failing component suite carries nothing: passing-is-verified holds at every granularity.		User decided all three axes 2026-07-22 (BL-73 vocabulary session, from their own fleet's field trial): a brownfield adopt with real per-service suites plus a 137-file integration suite read as '0/20 capabilities verified' and cost 21 near-identical acknowledge writes. Computed state over a bulk-attest write because the graph should record exactly what was checked — the component — and derive what that means one hop away; manufactured capability-level VERIFIES edges would be indistinguishable from direct checks forever after. The word component_verified because it says where the check lives. One gap per component because the residual question ('is component granularity enough for these?') is genuinely per-component and deserves to be asked once, not N times — the BL-42 lesson again: a loud detector needs a different question, not a tuned number. The write side needed nothing: VERIFIES accepts any target and even carries an unused coverage enum — the whole defect was the read side.acceptedDetect gaps, Say where the design stands
OPEN — how are two people's simultaneous edits kept apart: worktrees, temporary repos, or a live channel?
UNDECIDED, and recorded as BRAINSTORMING rather than as a proposal — Anthony's own framing, 2026-07-25, thinking out loud. His starting doubt is the right one and had not been written down: claiming a cluster of nodes says nothing about the REPOSITORY, and if the design and the code share one repo, two people working different clusters still collide in git even when they never touch the same node. FOUR IDEAS AS HE PUT THEM. (1) reflow2 REPLACES git — the graph defines who may touch what, and git becomes an internal implementation detail. (2) The graph is a set of TEMPORARY LOCAL repos, pushed upstream only once work is done and no conflicts exist. (3) Each session opens a TEMPORARY WORKTREE BRANCH holding an identical copy of the graph; the person works there, then reflow2's own merge reconciles the copy back and the temporary is deleted. (4) A WEBSOCKET pushing every change to every user, giving live simultaneous collaboration. WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, and it matters for ranking them: the collision is in the export FILE, not in the graph, and reflow2 already answers file-level collision semantically — BL-80's three-way merge compares per node and per property against the common ancestor and mints each real conflict as a Question with a deterministic id, and `--merge`/`--merge-apply` run it without a server. So idea 3 is not new machinery; it is mostly a PROCEDURE over machinery that exists, and a git worktree already gives each person their own checkout with its own `.reflow2/graph` (the store lock is per-directory). The missing piece is small and specific: git supports per-path merge drivers — this repo already uses `merge=union` for COORD.md — so registering the design export with a driver that calls reflow2's own merge would make two people working different clusters merge automatically, and make a genuine overlap arrive as a Question instead of as conflict markers in a 500KB JSON file. Idea 2 is idea 3 with extra steps, since git branches are already local until pushed. Idea 1 would make reflow2 a version-control system, contradicts dec:repo-file-embedded and req:persistence, and would have to reinvent what it currently inherits for free. Idea 4 is the simultaneity road already held open by dec:central-host and BL-99, with the counter-argument recorded there: this tool's loop is deliberate and attributable rather than live.		Held as brainstorming on purpose. Anthony called it thinking out loud, and the first honest thing to do with four ideas is to write them down as four ideas rather than pick one and start building — which is precisely the practice dec:exploratory-staging is about. Two notes for whoever takes it up. The ranking above is a finding, not a decision: it says which ideas are cheap and which are large, and the cheap one is testable this week by two people on one design without a line of new Rust. And the doubt that started it should survive into whatever gets built — a claim on a cluster of nodes is not a claim on a repository, so any answer here has to say what happens to the CODE two people are writing beside the design, not only what happens to the graph.proposedSeveral people can plan against one design without colliding
What bounds the store is WHAT gets stored, not how big it is — transcripts by exception, a cap only for the catastrophic case
Anthony's call 2026-07-31, on a measurement that inverted the assumption the earlier decisions were written under. MEASURED FIRST, on reflow2's own material: its entire design prose is 3.5 MB across 64 markdown files; the design export is 1.7 MB; the whole `.git` history is 81 MB. AND 29 SESSION TRANSCRIPTS COME TO 115.8 MB, A MEAN OF 4.0 MB EACH — already 1.4× the entire repository history, accumulated in a couple of weeks. THE CORRECTION THIS FORCES. `dec:content-manifest` states that 'raster images are the real risk and are the thing to watch first'. THAT IS WRONG, and it is recorded here rather than edited into his accepted text. Documents are noise and images are occasional; TRANSCRIPTS ARE THE GROWTH, by an order of magnitude, and they recur every session forever. WHY A SIZE CAP IS THE WRONG LEVER, which is the whole point. A 4 MB file passes any sane per-file threshold. What ends a repository is not one large object but 4 MB × EVERY SESSION, PERMANENTLY, UNPRUNABLE — git history cannot be trimmed without rewriting it and breaking every clone. Even assuming JSONL compresses to roughly a third, 500 sessions is a repository of several hundred megabytes, and 'clone and you have everything' stops being a feature. SO THE CONTROL IS WHAT GETS STORED. Session transcripts go in BY EXCEPTION, not by default — kept when a specific claim needs its receipt, not routinely. This is not a new position, only a newly-connected one: `cap:session-memory` already says 'a pointer to a 3 MB transcript is a RECEIPT, not documentation: leaning on it recreates the markdown problem one level down.' It named the size and named the danger; nobody had joined that to repository growth. A SIZE GUARD STILL, AND HONESTLY SCOPED. `put` refuses above a threshold with an EXPLICIT, RECORDED OVERRIDE — the idiom this project already uses everywhere: `export_graph`'s `accept_divergence`, `set_artifact_checksum`'s required disposition, `record_change` refusing a planned epoch, the schedule-loss guard. Refuse loudly, allow deliberately, record the choice. It catches the catastrophic accident — a video, a dataset — and NOT the real risk, which is stated so nobody mistakes it for the answer. The threshold is anchored to GitHub's 100 MB hard block rather than a number invented to feel safe (`req:defaults-do-not-assert`): past that the problem stops being local and becomes a failed push someone else has to understand. AND THE MANIFEST REPORTS TOTAL BYTES AND THE LARGEST ENTRIES. Report, never judge (`dec:report-dont-judge`): no threshold, just visibility on every check. This is the piece that would have surfaced the finding without anyone measuring by hand, which is the argument for it. NOT GIT LFS. It reintroduces the second distribution channel `dec:where-content-lives` chose committed blobs to avoid, and breaks the clone-and-you-have-everything property that decision was made for. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS, stated so it is a condition rather than a hedge: if distillation keeps proving insufficient — if people genuinely reach for raw transcripts often — then storing them routinely is correct, and the answer becomes LFS or an external store. That REOPENS `dec:where-content-lives` rather than patching around it.		The recommendation changed shape when it was measured, which is the part worth keeping. The obvious answer to 'nothing bounds repo growth' is a size cap, and a size cap would not have caught the thing that is actually growing — it would have shipped, looked prudent, and left the repository on the same trajectory. Anthony asked for the recommendation rather than taking his own earlier 'committed, no cap' as settled, which is what created room for the measurement. Worth noting because the useful move was cheap: four `du` and `ls` calls against real material, rather than reasoning about what a content store might contain. The correction to `dec:content-manifest` is recorded here rather than edited into it, per `dec:reopen-supersedes` — the earlier claim was reasonable when written and is simply wrong, and overwriting it would erase the fact that the project believed something else on the evidence it had.acceptedSay what content the design depends on, in names a person can read, Store bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash
A committed manifest — hash to filename to referenced-by — plus .gitattributes marking blobs binary
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31, delivering `req:export-says-what-it-cannot-carry` and closing the last open question under `cap:content-store`. A COMMITTED MANIFEST, plain text, mapping CONTENT HASH → ORIGINAL FILENAME → WHAT REFERENCES IT. One artefact, two jobs, which is why it was chosen over either job's narrower answer: 1. COMPLETENESS. Once content exists, the export document holds only pointers, so handing someone `reflow2.json` alone gives them a design whose diagrams silently fail to resolve. The manifest makes 'do I have everything?' a set comparison — hashes listed against hashes present — rather than a discovery made when a picture does not open. That is `req:content-reaches-every-seat`'s fail-loud requirement made checkable by a person, not only by the tool. 2. LEGIBILITY IN GIT. A content-addressed blob lands as `blobs/ab/cdef…` and git reports it as an added file with a hex name that tells a reviewer nothing. The manifest is text, so the same change also appears in a diff as a readable line — `architecture-sketch.png` added, referencing `dec:x` — which is what a human actually reads in `git log -p`. `.gitattributes` MARKS THE BLOB DIRECTORY `binary`. Two concrete effects, and the second is the one that matters: git stops attempting diffs it cannot produce, and — critically — stops applying line-ending conversion, which would CORRUPT a PNG on a checkout configured for CRLF. That is silent data loss on someone else's machine, and one line prevents it. WHY THE BINARY WORRY WAS SMALLER THAN IT LOOKED, recorded because the reasoning nearly went the other way. Git's weaknesses with binaries are poor diffs, poor delta compression, and unresolvable merge conflicts. IMMUTABLE CONTENT ADDRESSING removes two of the three outright: a blob is never updated, so an 'edit' is a NEW FILE with a new name — git sees an addition, which is the clearest possible signal — and two people adding different blobs add different files, so a binary merge conflict cannot arise. The only conflict is on the pointer inside the export, which the `merge.reflow2` driver already handles. WHAT REMAINS IS GROWTH: every version is a new file that stays forever, and that is the size-cap question `dec:where-content-lives` deliberately left open. DELIBERATELY NOT DECIDED HERE: whether the manifest lives inside the export document or beside it as its own committed file. Both satisfy the requirement; the second keeps the export byte-stable diff properties simpler and is the likelier answer, but it is an implementation choice for build time rather than a design commitment.		Taken because one artefact answered two questions that arrived independently — the export-completeness gap found by an impact-check, and Anthony's worry about git legibility for binaries. When a single small thing satisfies two unrelated needs, that is usually the right shape rather than a coincidence. The `.gitattributes` line is the part with a real failure behind it rather than an inconvenience: line-ending conversion silently corrupting a binary on a differently-configured checkout is the kind of fault that appears as 'the diagram is broken on my machine' weeks later, with nothing in the history to point at. The binary-churn analysis is recorded because the initial framing — mine — overstated the problem, and correcting it is what made the manifest a legibility feature rather than a workaround. Content addressing had already solved most of what was being worried about; naming which part it did NOT solve (growth) is what keeps the remaining risk visible instead of assumed handled.acceptedSay what content the design depends on, in names a person can read
Hand-rolled synchronous content store in reflow2-core, zero new dependencies; object_store is the documented upgrade path
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31, refining `dec:where-content-lives` (accepted) per `dec:reopen-supersedes`. The proposal and its measurement are preserved in the snapshot taken before this edit. THE STORE IS HAND-ROLLED, SYNCHRONOUS, AND LIVES IN `reflow2-core`. Three operations — `put(bytes) -> hash`, `get(hash) -> bytes`, `exists(hash)` — over `sha2` (already a core dependency) and `std::fs`, with write-to-temp-then-rename for atomicity. Zero new crates. WHY, MEASURED RATHER THAN REASONED. `object_store` 0.14.1 with `default-features = false, features = ('fs')` resolves 68 crates, **36 of them new to reflow2**. About 24 arrive through `url`'s internationalised-domain-name machinery — the whole ICU4X stack, `zerovec`/`yoke`/`tinystr`, `idna`, `percent-encoding` — which a local content-addressed store never calls. The accepted decision's note that cloud features off 'avoids reqwest and the crypto providers' was true and did not describe the tree. AND IT UN-DOES A COMPLICATION RATHER THAN ADDING ONE. `dec:where-content-lives` split hash-in-core from store-in-mcp ONLY because `object_store` is async and `fs` pulls tokio. A synchronous `std::fs` store keeps `reflow2-core` free of a runtime — measured, its entire dependency list is dynograph-{core,storage,graph,resolution,vector}, serde, serde_json, sha2 — and keeps the store deterministic and in-memory-testable alongside everything else in the core. THAT PART OF `dec:where-content-lives` IS SUPERSEDED; its other two parts (blobs committed to the repo; content-addressed, immutable, fail-loud pointers) STAND UNCHANGED. `object_store` IS THE DOCUMENTED UPGRADE PATH, recorded rather than discarded. It is the right crate for multi-cloud object storage and remains the answer if a cloud backend is ever wanted: it presents one trait over local filesystem, in-memory, S3, GCS, Azure and HTTP/WebDAV, so the backend becomes runtime configuration. The three-function interface above is deliberately the shape it slots behind — content addressing is what makes the swap safe, because a blob fetched from anywhere verifies against its own hash. Adopting it later changes how bytes are fetched and nothing about what the graph says. WHEN THAT DAY COMES, the costs already measured apply: 36 new crates, an async runtime reaching the core (or the hash/store split reinstated), and a declaration per `dec:design-dependencies-declared`. WHAT WE GIVE UP TODAY, stated so nobody rediscovers it: multipart uploads, conditional writes, listing and prefix semantics, and cloud backends. Immutable content-addressed blobs need none of them — there are no paths to list, no partial writes to resume, and no update-in-place to make conditional.		Anthony's call on a measurement the accepted decision had itself demanded before adoption. That clause — 'STILL TO CHECK BEFORE ADOPTING: its transitive tree with cloud features off MEASURED rather than assumed' — is the only reason this surfaced before code rather than after, and it is worth noting as a habit: a decision that names what it has NOT verified does work a confident decision would not. The deciding argument was not dependency count for its own sake. It was that `object_store`'s value is uniformity across backends, and the feature set it exists to provide — paths, prefixes, listing, multipart, conditional writes — is precisely the set an immutable content-addressed store does not have. Paying 36 crates and an async runtime for capabilities the use case forecloses is the wrong trade at this size, and the trade reverses the moment a cloud backend is real. Recorded as an upgrade path rather than a rejection, because the alternative to a hand-rolled store is not 'no library forever' — it is 'no library until there is something a library does better'. Writing that down is what stops the next session re-running the same evaluation from scratch.acceptedStore bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash
DECIDED — the claim board moves into the graph; COORD.md keeps the conventions and the conflict doctrine
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-04, taking the split this node had already written down while it was open: CLAIMS IN THE GRAPH for who has what, COORD.md RETAINED for the conventions and the merge-conflict doctrine, and the IN-PROGRESS TABLE DELETED rather than maintained in two places — because two places for the same fact is the failure the whole documents-into-the-graph move exists to end. THE STATED BLOCKER DISSOLVED RATHER THAN BEING OVERRULED, which is worth recording precisely because this node held itself open on it since 2026-07-25. The rationale read: 'a claim board is a coordination mechanism between two people, and switching it unilaterally would mean one of them silently changing where the other must look; that is Anthony's brother's call as much as his.' Anthony, 2026-08-04: 'my brother hasn't actively developed any of this apart from offering feedback.' So there is no second writer to strand — the premise was that two people coordinate through this board, and only one of them has ever written to it. The caution was correct when written and the fact it was resting on turned out not to hold. THE CONSEQUENCE IS NARROWER THAN THE DECISION LOOKS: reflow2 still has no live multi-writer case, so the claims layer remains UNPROVEN under contention. This move proves it under a single writer only, and that limit should not be quietly forgotten the first time a second person appears. ⭐ THE PREREQUISITE WAS RUN, AND IT PASSED ON A CAPABILITY THE MARKDOWN STRUCTURALLY CANNOT HAVE. This node named its own gate — 'nobody has used claim_region for real yet, so the first move is to run it on one real piece of work and see whether claim_report says something a person would have said.' Run 2026-08-04 on the live work: `claim_region` with seed `cap:corpus-ingest`, depth 2, contributor `who:ajs`, carrying BL-186's note. `claim_report` returned the claim, zero overlaps, zero stale — and `liveness: 'live'`, COMPUTED from the claiming seat's host and pid rather than stored. Its own advisory states the payoff: '`gone` means that session has exited and the claim is a ghost (excluded from overlaps), `unknown` means it was made on another machine or before seats were recorded — unknown is never read as free, because taking work somebody is actively doing is the expensive mistake.' THAT IS THE DIRECT FIX FOR THE FAILURE THAT PROMPTED THIS, and it is not the reason first given. This node argued the gain was that a computed region FOLLOWS THE DESIGN instead of going stale as a hand-typed file list. True, but secondary. The measured failure is different: on 2026-08-04 COORD.md was carrying BL-186 as in-progress after #73 had landed it, and the file itself contains a note recording that this was the THIRD STALE CLAIM FOUND IN ONE SWEEP. A markdown line cannot know its author walked away — a claim is only ever retired by someone remembering to retire it, which is exactly the class of thing people forget. Liveness computed from the session means an abandoned claim reads `gone` on its own, with nobody remembering anything. The markdown board was not merely going stale; IT HAD NO MECHANISM BY WHICH IT COULD EVER NOT. WHAT IS KNOWINGLY GIVEN UP, restated at the point of deciding rather than left in the open-question text where it would read as unresolved: COORD.md's in-progress table was readable by a human with no reflow2 and no binary, and it appeared as a diff in every pull request. A graph claim does neither — it travels in the committed export, so it is visible, but reading it needs the tool. That is accepted deliberately. The conventions, the handles table and the merge-conflict doctrine STAY in COORD.md for exactly that reason: they are addressed to someone who may not have reflow2 running, and they are prose about practice rather than facts about state. THE STANDING RULE THIS SETS, and it is the general form: A DOCUMENT SHOULD HOLD WHAT IS ADDRESSED TO SOMEONE WITHOUT THE TOOL, AND THE GRAPH SHOULD HOLD WHAT THE TOOL CAN COMPUTE. COORD.md splits cleanly along that line — practice stays, state goes. It is the same test as `dec:the-transition-is-two-halves-and-reads-are-the-unscheduled-one` ('can you delete this document and regenerate it from the graph?'), and the in-progress table is the first thing in this repo to pass it by being deleted rather than by already having been derived.		Raised as a dogfooding question, which is how most of this project's real findings have arrived — and it was a genuinely good test of the claims layer. MOVED TO ACCEPTED 2026-08-04 on Anthony's explicit word, after its own stated prerequisite was run for the first time. Two things are recorded here that a later reader would otherwise have to reconstruct. FIRST, the decision did not overrule its objection — the objection's premise (two people coordinating) turned out to be false, and saying so is different from deciding against it, because if a second writer ever appears the caution becomes live again rather than having been settled. SECOND, the reason for the move is not the reason originally given: computed-region-follows-the-design was the argument, and computed LIVENESS turned out to be what actually fixes the observed failure. The original argument was not wrong, it was aimed at the wrong half — worth keeping, because it is the second time in this project a fork resolved on something outside the recorded options (see the method finding on dec:agent-navigates-content). The unproven-under-contention limit is stated on the node rather than left implicit: a single-writer proof is what was obtained, and the claims layer's real case is still ahead of it.acceptedClaim a region of the design so two people do not collide in it, claims, OPEN — a claim in the graph cannot be announced before the work, because the export it rides in may only be written once per PR
The DesignGraph API is an accepted single point of failure
