ifc:core-api — the DesignGraph API cmp:graph provides and the MCP service consumes — is the sole operational path between the Design Store and the Agent Surface subsystems. Accepted as a SPOF, like dec:graph-spof-accepted and dec:service-spof-accepted.		One store, one surface over it (req:agent-native, single-writer storage): the bridge between them is inherently single. Surfaced when BL-83a retired cmp:core and moved the API's provider to cmp:graph; the topology is honest, not a defect to engineer away.acceptedDesignGraph API
A folder of documents goes through the ingest handshake, not a skill
DECIDED (b) THE SP-3b HANDSHAKE, on Anthony's word 2026-07-27. `ingest` goes on the MCP surface with the AGENT as the backend: reflow2 returns the extraction prompts and the agent returns the JSON. No LLM provider dependency is added, so the agent-native deferral stands. (a) an agent-driven skill walking the folder was rejected, not unconsidered: it is cheaper and consistent with every other reflow2 skill, but it moves the disciplines ingest.rs enforces IN CODE — never cascade-fail, no phantom edges, provenance on everything, time-aware resolution, and now the resolution bands and the structural subset pass — into prose an agent is asked to follow. An instruction is weaker than a type system, and docs/sharpening.md names that exact failure: shaping the model until the tool goes quiet. THE DECIDING CONSEQUENCE is what it does to the missing extraction passes: a pass written in Rust behind the handshake is reusable by every future ingest and testable without a model, while the same pass written into a skill is prose that cannot be regression-tested at all. Since Decision and Verification passes are the two-thirds of the requester's ask that reflow2 cannot currently see, the option that makes those passes worth writing is the option that delivers the feature.		Scoped 2026-07-26 by reading ingest.rs, graph.rs and the schema after Anthony asked whether reflow2 could take a colleague's years of markdown. The reading moved the work in BOTH directions. (1) BL-97 called cross-document identity the hard part; it is largely BUILT — fuzzy_match resolves each extracted node against every existing node of that type in the whole graph, so ingesting forty specs already converges, with the merges reported and prior states snapshotted rather than clobbered. What is missing there is COST, not capability: scan_nodes is a full type scan run once per extracted node, so a corpus is quadratic. (2) The gap nobody had named is COVERAGE OF THE ASK: ingest creates exactly eight node types, and Verification and Decision are not among them. The request was 'requirements, test results, designer intent' — reflow2 extracts the first and neither of the others, so a corpus run today would return a design with no test evidence and no rationale, from documents containing both, and nothing would say so. Full write-up in docs/scope-corpus-ingest.md, including the auto-merge-at-90 tension with dec:ask-not-repair at corpus scale, and the fifth instance of this project's recurring shape: the schema's per-type resolution thresholds are declared and read by nothing.acceptedIngest a folder of specifications as one design
Coverage scope is DERIVED from version control — because a sweep covers the design's artifacts, never the subject system
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-02, option 3 of three: the sweep is everything the version-control system tracks, minus NAMED exclusions echoed back with the rule that excluded them. No vocabulary change, no new property, no new node type — so the schema stamp does not move, which on this project is what locks out older binaries. (The node id says `declared` because that was the QUESTION; the answer is `derived`. Kept as a stable handle rather than re-minted, since `cap:coverage` is already GOVERNED_BY it.) WHAT IS IN THE REPOSITORY, in his own decomposition — this is the load-bearing part, because getting it wrong is what produced the objection this decision had to overturn. A NON-CODE PROJECT puts TWO things under version control: the reflow2 design graph, and the design artifacts. A CODE PROJECT puts THREE: the reflow2 design graph, the design artifacts, and the actual implemented code. THE FIRST TWO ARE THE CONSTANT. The implemented system is the only term that varies, and it is present in exactly one of the two cases. THE OBJECTION THIS OVERTURNS, which was mine and not his: the weakness recorded against this option said deriving from a repo 'says nothing for a design whose subject is a fleet, a document set, or hardware', against `req:design-anything`. It conflated the SUBJECT SYSTEM with the DESIGN'S ARTIFACTS, and a sweep only ever covers what is in the repository. A satellite, a building, a fleet cannot live in a repo — but its drawings, specs, models, analyses and requirement documents can, and normally do. In his words: 'while a hardware system, for example, can't live within a git repo, its design artifacts can. obviously, for all non-code projects, this is the case.' So a derived scope is not a code-only convenience. It is the general case, and it is MORE clearly right for a non-code project than for software, because there the tracked artifacts are the whole of what a coverage question could ever have been asking about. CODE IS THE SPECIAL CASE, AND SPECIAL BY BEING MORE THAN THE NORM, NOT LESS — 'code based projects are the system and can be inspected by the agent as well as the design'. It is the one case where the third term exists, so one sweep sees the implemented system alongside the graph and the artifacts. He also expects that exceptional case to be the majority of reflow2's use, which is exactly why it must not be mistaken for the rule the design is built on: a default inferred from the common case would quietly assume an implemented system that most subjects do not have. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE SWEEP ITSELF. Of the three tracked things, the design GRAPH is the one that must be excluded — a design cannot be its own subject, and `docs/design` is a named exclusion in reflow2's own sweep for exactly that reason. The other two are swept: the artifacts always, the implemented code when there is any. WHAT THIS GENUINELY CANNOT DO, which is a different limitation from the one it was charged with: a design artifact that is NOT under version control — a CAD file on someone's machine, a spec in a wiki, a drawing inside a PLM system — is invisible to a derived sweep. That is not fatal, because the seam already answers it: `coverage_report` takes caller-supplied observations, so an agent that can reach a PLM or a document store sweeps it and hands the paths over exactly as it hands over a repo listing. Derivation is the DEFAULT, not a restriction on what may be observed. WHAT IS STILL OPEN AND WAS NEVER THIS: `cap:coverage` records that the sweep is not persisted, so `detect_gaps` cannot raise coverage from graph state the way `unresolved_drift` is raised from a recorded `DriftEvent`. That deferral survives this decision untouched — it was never the fix for the blind quadrant, and it still needs a node to record a sweep in and a staleness rule (the `cap:freshness` precedent).		Anthony's word, given 2026-08-02 in answer to the three shapes put to him. Recorded with his argument rather than just his choice, because the argument is the part that would otherwise be lost: it is not merely a preference between three costs, it identifies an ERROR in how option 3 was described to him — the artifact/subject conflation — and that error is what would have made a later reader re-open a settled question. The two rejected shapes are kept in the record deliberately (ADR discipline): (1) a scope property on Project/Component, cheap but with no history and nowhere to date a sweep; (2) a first-class node recording a sweep and its scope, which would have closed the persistence deferral in the same move but costs a schema change and pulls in the staleness decision. Both remain available as an OVERRIDE for a subject version control cannot enumerate — this decision fixes the default, not the ceiling.acceptedSay what the design has never heard of
A defect found by USING a built capability is a TemporalFact with fact_type 'defect' — no new vocabulary, and the lifecycle comes free
Answers option (b) of dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph WITHOUT adding a node type, which was that option's strongest objection. THE MECHANISM. A defect found by use is recorded as a `TemporalFact`: `subject_id` = the node it indicts, `fact_type` = 'defect', `statement` = the claim (FULLTEXT-INDEXED, so search_design finds it), `value` = JSON carrying the measurement, `basis` = 'measured' (never 'forecast' — a defect is observed), `confidence` = how sure the observer is. Edges: HAS_TEMPORAL_FACT from the indicted node, ABOUT_ENTITY back to it, VALID_FROM the epoch it was observed. VALID_TO is set WHEN IT IS FIXED — absent means still true. WHY THIS TYPE AND NOT A NEW ONE. Four reasons, each checked rather than assumed. (1) TemporalFact's own extraction_hint already says 'a time-bounded assertion true only between two epochs', and a defect is exactly that: true of the build from the epoch it was found until the epoch it was fixed. (2) `fact_type` is `{ type: string, indexed: true }` — free-form and INDEXED, not an enum, so 'defect' needs no schema change. (3) THERE IS A SHIPPING PRECEDENT for using fact_type as a discriminator a reader queries: crates/reflow2-core/src/readiness.rs:57 marks readiness assertions this way and reads them back. This is not a new convention, it is an existing one applied to a second case. (4) The prior against new vocabulary is heavy and documented — this project proposed and WITHDREW two node types in one week (Attestation to TemporalFact, Hazard to DesignRule + CONSTRAINS) — and dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph itself flagged TemporalFact as probably already the shape. WHAT THIS FIXES, precisely. The graph had no way to say 'this capability is BUILT, VERIFIED, and does not do what it claims'. Verification answers whether a check PASSES, and every defect of this kind sat under a passing check. DriftEvent answers whether code moved away from the design, and in these cases code and design AGREED and both were wrong. HEAL's issues are computed from graph shape and vanish between runs. So the largest category of backlog row had nowhere to go, which is why it went to markdown. THE LIFECYCLE IS THE PART MARKDOWN DID BY HAND. A row today is annotated 'DONE 2026-08-05' in prose. Here, fixing a defect means setting VALID_TO to the epoch that fixed it, so 'is this still broken?' is a graph question rather than a reading-comprehension one — and the history survives instead of being overwritten. MEASURED STARTING POINT: reflow2's own graph contained ZERO TemporalFacts before this decision, despite BL-68 building the measured/forecast distinction for them. The type was built, correct, and unused. WHAT IS STILL OWED, AND IT IS THE HALF THAT MATTERS. Nothing in the LOOP reads these yet. `statement` is fulltext so search_design finds them today — genuinely better than grepping a 592 KB file, and the reason this is worth doing before the reader exists — but loop_status does not count open defects, and until it does, a defect recorded here is discoverable rather than SURFACED. That reader is the next increment and it is a Rust change. Recorded so the gap is on the record rather than discovered later: writing facts nothing reads is this project's own recurring declared-and-read-by-nothing failure, and doing it knowingly with the reader scheduled is different from doing it by accident. NOT CLAIMED: that this retires docs/backlog.md. Three of the four backlog categories already had homes (unbuilt work is a planned Capability, an open question is a proposed Decision, a discovered limit is a Constraint or DesignRule) and were not being used either. This decision closes the one category that had NO home. Deriving the markdown from the graph is option (d) and remains open.		Chosen rather than left open because dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph has held five options and no choice since 2026-08-04, and the cost of that is measured: 218 backlog rows, 592 KB, and an accepted decision (dec:export-once-per-pr) violated and re-derived for the third time in the very session that asked for the fix. Anthony called it embarrassing and asked for it as first priority; the conservative option — reuse an existing type with an existing reader precedent — is the one that can ship now. Left `proposed` with him as approver rather than accepted: dec:three-party-checks says the human decides, and this changes how the project records its own learning.acceptednothing
DECIDED — discovery is a pair: the agent walks the tree, and reflow2 describes the design at a path without binding to it
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-05: 'I like and approve: a tool that describes the design at a given path — id, label, node counts, mint stamp — without binding to it. Your agent walks the tree (which it can, as you said); reflow2 says what's in each .reflow2 it finds. That splits cleanly along the no-file-I/O rule.' THE SHAPE. Two responsibilities, split along the line this project already draws. THE AGENT FINDS THE DIRECTORIES — walking a tree for `.reflow2` is file IO, which reflow2 does not do and does not need to, because the ambient agent does it well (`dec:agent-navigates-content`, and its parent `dec:three-party-checks`: 'the LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides'). REFLOW2 SAYS WHAT IS IN ONE — given a path, it reports the design's identity: graph id, label, how many nodes of what kind, the stamp it was minted under. Neither half can do the other's job, and the split is the same one that already governs content navigation and coverage sweeps. ⭐ WHAT IT REPLACES, AND WHY THE OBVIOUS ASK WAS THE WRONG ONE. Anthony first asked for 'a reflow2 tool to simply return all graph_ids'. Measured before answering: that returns ONE PER STORE. Storage keys are `{graph_id}\x00{type}\x00{id}` and `dynograph_storage::keys::graph_prefix` exists, so the FOUNDATION supports many graphs per store — but reflow2 opens one graph per store by convention (`DEFAULT_GRAPH_ID`, one `.reflow2` per project), and the three graphs in the hxm_program field report are three separate STORES. Enumerating within a store is therefore a true answer to a question nobody has. Describing a store found on disk is the question that was actually being asked. WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SETTLE. It settles the DISCOVERY half of `req:a-session-chooses-its-design` — how an agent learns what designs exist before anything is created, which is what would have prevented the accidental third graph (`dec:no-design-here-never-looked`). It does NOT settle how a session is then POINTED at the chosen design: editing `.mcp.json` and reconnecting, versus a graph reference carried per call, remains open at `dec:how-a-session-is-pointed-at-a-design`, where Anthony has expressed a lean toward the first and the counter ((BL-123) — the `/mcp` reconnect is the one step an autonomous agent cannot take) is recorded against it. ⚠️ THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES THE BUILD, and it must not be discovered in the field: A ROCKSDB STORE HELD BY A RUNNING SERVER IS EXCLUSIVELY LOCKED. Describing a design at a path while another session holds it needs a shared or read-only open. `--shared` exists and this repo's own `.mcp.json` does not pass it — which is separately why the stale-server export replay is needed at every release cut. THE TOOL MUST SAY 'BUSY' RATHER THAN FAILING OPAQUELY OR, WORSE, REPORTING NOTHING FOUND: a describe that answers 'no design' because the store was locked would be the same defect this whole thread began with, in a new place. AND THE RULE THIS SERVES, which survives whatever the pointing mechanism turns out to be: DEFAULT WHEN EXACTLY ONE DESIGN IS REACHABLE; REFUSE AND LIST THEM WHEN SEVERAL ARE. Discovery is what makes the second half of that sentence possible — you cannot list what you never looked for. NOT CHECKED, and it decides whether this is a new tool or a parameter: whether `design_identity` could take an optional path and answer for a store it is not bound to.		Anthony's explicit approval of a shape that was offered as a CORRECTION to his own proposal, which is worth recording as the sequence rather than just the outcome: he asked for graph-id enumeration, the enumeration was measured and found to answer a different question, the inverse was offered, and he took it. Checking the ask before building it is what made the difference, and it took one grep. Recorded as accepted while `req:a-session-chooses-its-design` stays proposed. That is deliberate: he approved a MECHANISM, and the requirement's wording — particularly its second half about being pointed at a design — has not been read back to him. Promoting the requirement on the strength of approval for one half of it would be exactly the signature-forging `dec:certainty-derived` forbids. The locking constraint is on the node rather than left for the build because a describe-tool that reports 'no design' when the store is merely busy would reproduce `dec:no-design-here-never-looked` in a new place, and that is a cheap mistake to make.acceptedSay what design lives at a path, without binding to it
Design-authorship is a Contributor, distinct from an Actor; the seed is AUTHORED_BY
The design's authorship identity is a new first-class Contributor node type (kind: person / automated_agent / organization), kept separate from the existing Actor. Actor is who the designed system SERVES (boundary-facing domain content); Contributor is who authors and decides the design ITSELF. The first rung is the authorship seed: an AUTHORED_BY edge (any design node → Contributor, role author/reviewer/approver) — the structured 'who' behind provenance's 'how', replacing the free-text Requirement.source. AUTHORED_BY is deliberately NOT a traceability edge (absent from nodes.rs structural_rule), so authorship is metadata and never enlarges a blast radius. Later rungs, each needing the user on vocabulary: CLAIMS (BL-44 node/cluster claims, advisory-first), ACTS_FOR (agent-acts-for-person, git's author/committer split), alternative-authorship (BL-70), and signing the export content_hash with a Contributor key (BL-41 mechanical half). No 'unauthored node' detector yet — it would N-alarm on every existing node.		User chose the identity keystone as the next most important work (2026-07-22), and decided both axes: a new type over overloading Actor, and authorship-first over jumping to claims. First-class node over a bare property because a claim expires and authorship belongs on axis-Z — a property is invisible to history. One identity mechanism because the backlog's own warning is that building it for claims alone would be 'the recurring lesson in reverse': the same who-is-this is needed by BL-44 (claims), BL-70 (alternative authorship), BL-41 (the mechanical half of requirement-certainty, cultural today), and BL-12 sketch 2 (who may assert what). Contributor separate from Actor because they have different lifecycles — a UAF model keeps who-serves and who-makes apart. The git exploration (2026-07-22) independently ratified the shape: git's author-vs-committer split is exactly the deferred ACTS_FOR rung, and signing the record hash is BL-41's mechanical half. Additive schema change (28 node / 55 edge types); a new-binary graph is refused loudly by a pre-Contributor binary via the count-based provenance check (BL-19), so no schema_version bump.acceptednothing
Design-vs-design comparison is directional, banded, and lives in the core
A design-vs-design diff (compare_designs) exists as a core op exposed as both an MCP tool and a CLI flag. It compares two export documents, or the live graph against one document. Findings are directional — added / removed / changed relative to an explicitly named base — with property-level detail on changed nodes, grouped into two bands: design content vs the supporting/bookkeeping layer (ChangeEvents, DriftEvents, Fragments, Questions). It reports divergence between two as-designed records and never judges which side is right; the word 'drift' stays reserved for design-vs-reality.		User decided all four axes 2026-07-21 (BL-71 rung c vocabulary session). Directional because all three consumers have a real base — the committed record (the BL-71 clobber tripwire), the main branch (BL-70 branch-by-file comparison), the state a claim was made against (BL-12 merge) — while AoA can still read the report neutrally or run it both ways. Banded because the real 2026-07-21 divergence was 3 Decisions and 8 Requirements buried under ~20 bookkeeping nodes; a flat list hides exactly what matters. Core op (not a kit script) because deterministic design computation belongs in the tested core; CLI flag so CI and no-server contexts reach it, like --import/--export. It is the read side of the rung a+b upsert-layering, the sibling of the reconcile family — which compares design against reality, hence the separate word: divergence, not drift.acceptedCompare two as-designed records
Documentation is part of the product but has no operational coupling, so its island is accepted — and the detector should learn this
The Documentation subsystem, its docs component, the capability of explaining reflow2 to a newcomer, and the README/SETUP artifacts read as a disconnected community to `detect_defects`, and that reading is ACCEPTED rather than bridged. The cluster is correctly modelled: the project contains the subsystem, the subsystem contains the component, the component owns the capability, and the artifacts both REALIZE the capability and DOCUMENT the project, the installer and the service. Those DOCUMENTS edges are true and are kept on their own merit — the tool's own guidance is to record a file that way when something would be wrong if it drifted out of step with the design, which is exactly the property the user asserted when he said documentation is part of the deliverable. They simply do not attach the cluster, because the structural network is built from DEPENDENCY relations only (a direct DEPENDS_ON, or a CONSUMES/PROVIDES contract collapsed through its Interface), and documenting a thing is not depending on it. No further edge can fix this without being a lie: documentation genuinely does not participate in the operational dependency graph.		Decided 2026-07-24, immediately after the user answered that documentation belongs to reflow2 rather than sitting outside it ('it'd be like if I designed a fighter jet using reflow2, but then didn't deliver any documentation on it to the user'). Three bridges were attempted before accepting: project containment, which is how every other subsystem attaches; then DOCUMENTS edges to the project, the installer and the service. The detector still fired, and reading structure.rs explains why — the design network admits a defined TRACEABILITY set (SATISFIES, ALLOCATED_TO, REALIZES, VERIFIES, GOVERNED_BY, PROVIDES/CONSUMES, DEPENDS_ON, INCLUDES) and DOCUMENTS is simply not in it, while CONTAINS is deliberately excluded. That selectivity is correct and should not be weakened to silence this. THE GENERAL PRINCIPLE, which is why this is worth recording rather than shrugging at: dec:operational-spof already established that only things which OPERATE can be single points of failure, because the suggested fix — add redundancy — is meaningless for intent. The identical argument applies one category over. Only things that operate can be meaningfully disconnected FROM the operational network; a documentation subsystem has no operational coupling by its nature, so flagging it is a false positive of the BL-84 family, and the fix belongs in the detector rather than in the design. RESOLVED 2026-07-25, and NOT by the fix this decision anticipated — recorded because a decision that goes on claiming to accept something that no longer happens is exactly the drift this project exists to catch. The island dissolved on its own when cap:session-memory turned out to belong to BOTH cmp:docs and cmp:temporal: the user's point that a session's context is itself documentation gave documentation a genuine, non-cosmetic tie to the rest of the design, through ALLOCATED_TO edges that are true rather than manufactured. So the detector was never wrong about the topology — the topology changed, because the design gained a real connection it had been missing. The PRINCIPLE above stands unaltered and still applies to any future documentation-only cluster; only the specific defect it dispositioned has gone. Worth keeping as evidence for the detector fix: an island can be legitimate AND later dissolve legitimately, so the exemption must not be written in a way that hides a genuine disconnection.acceptedDocumentation
A rule's power is stated, never defaulted: `enforced` is true / false / unstated, and absence is reported rather than read as either
DECIDED 2026-08-08, Anthony's word: REMOVE THE DEFAULT. `DesignRule.enforced` becomes three-state — `true` (gate-blocking, and owes a detector), `false` (advisory, owes nothing), and ABSENT, which means nobody has said and is REPORTED as unstated rather than read as either answer. None of the three options originally written here was taken; this is a fourth. WHAT IT CHANGES IN THE COMPUTATION: `unverified_enforced_rule` (0.6) now fires only on an EXPLICIT `true`, and a new `unstated_rule_enforcement` (0.4) asks an unstated rule which it is. Two findings rather than one, deliberately, because deciding what a rule IS costs a word while PROVING one costs a detector — and collapsing those two questions is exactly what the old default got wrong. NO MIGRATION, and that is the point: nothing is reinterpreted, so the five existing values stay exactly as stored. WHY OPTION B (flip the default to false) WAS REFUSED, and this is the part that decided it: the value is MATERIALIZED INTO THE STORE AT WRITE TIME, so an inherited `true` is indistinguishable from a chosen one. Confirmed rather than assumed — `enforced: true` is present on all four rules even in a 0.24.0-written export, which omits unset properties. Any migration would therefore either silently downgrade rules somebody meant or preserve rules nobody chose, and neither would be detectable afterwards. THE CONSEQUENCE ACCEPTED WITH IT: reflow2's own four rules keep their `true` and keep owing detectors, because the graph genuinely cannot tell they were never chosen. The remedy is Anthony restating the ones he actually meant, one call each — not a migration that guesses. THE PRECEDENT THIS RESTORES: absence-is-reported-as-absence is this schema's most consistent rule — VERIFIES.pinned ('unset means the scope was never stated, which is reported as unscoped and never read as full coverage'), Constraint.objective ('unset is a true answer'), DEPENDS_ON.weight_basis, DUPLICATES.basis — and `enforced` was the single place it was broken, in the dangerous direction. It also matches GATED_ON.min_level, required and never defaulted because a threshold encoding risk appetite is the user's to state (dec:readiness-is-an-observation-the-threshold-is-the-judgement); whether breaking a rule should stop somebody's build is the same kind of claim one layer along. WHY REQUIRED (option C) WAS NOT TAKEN EITHER: an ingest pass reading a folder of documents genuinely does not know whether a convention should be gate-blocking, and refusing the write would either block bulk ingest or force an extractor to invent a policy. Unstated exists so that case can be recorded honestly.		The deciding argument was not this field's own merits but a pattern: THIS IS THE THIRD TIME IN ONE DAY that a value which could not distinguish a choice from a default caused real harm. `DUPLICATES.basis` could not tell asserted from suspected and cost dev_storyflow ten proposed node deletions, fixed by making provenance explicit and defaulting to the safe value. Serialized defaults in the export could not tell a default from a decision, produced 108 phantom property changes between two builds one release apart, and led an agent (me) to file a false data-loss defect and block a PR on it. And `enforced` cannot tell chosen from inherited, which is how four rules acquired detector obligations nobody agreed to. Each time the fix that worked was MAKING THE CHOICE EXPLICIT rather than picking a safer default — tuning which default is less harmful is the move that keeps producing this class of bug. Recorded here because the next person tempted to add a convenient default should meet this argument first. Audited before implementing rather than after: `enforced` had exactly ONE production reader (detect.rs), so the change is contained; everything else naming it is a test or the skill-lint allowlist.acceptedA rule the project follows is captured with its consequence stated, not inherited from a default
A vocabulary distinction earns its keep only if a computation reads it; retire VALIDATES + ENABLES edges
Standing rule for the edge vocabulary: two edge types must be orthogonal, because an LLM asked to choose between near-synonyms picks inconsistently (storyflow's lesson). The test for keeping any distinction is not 'is it true?' but 'does a computation — a detector, a report, a propagation rule — read the two sides differently?' If nothing reads it, the distinction is descriptive decoration that costs extraction consistency for no gain (the 'read side was blind' lesson turned on the vocabulary itself). Applied 2026-07-22: (1) RETIRE the VALIDATES edge — it was orthogonal-in-name-only with VERIFIES (both land Verification->Capability, the canonical V&V confusion) AND orphan (no core code ever referenced it). The verify-vs-validate distinction is real and worth keeping, so it moves to a Verification.kind property (verification | validation) — a property of the check, not a rival relationship, which removes the edge-choice ambiguity entirely — and it earns its keep via a new unvalidated_capability DETECT gap that reads it (a capability verified against spec but with no validation check confirming it meets intent). (2) FOLD ENABLES into CAUSES — same causal axis, differ only by degree (brings-about vs makes-possible), both wildcard-typed, and neither read by any computation; CAUSES's hint now covers the enabling case. (3) KEEP TRIGGERS — it is not a causal-degree variant: it carries a role property and drives the Flow/process-feedback model (flow_report, BL-37), so a computation reads it. Net: 55 -> 53 edge types; the 'does a computation read it?' test is the standing rule for any future edge.		User raised it from the storyflow lesson that edge types an agent chooses between must be completely orthogonal, and reasoned each case by cost/benefit: keeping a distinction buys nothing over collapsing unless a computation reads it, and sharpening extraction hints only lowers the error rate on a distinction that still has no reader — it cannot make a same-axis distinction orthogonal. VALIDATES was the clearest case: confusable AND orphan (the engine runs entirely on VERIFIES). Moving it to Verification.kind is strictly better than a rival edge because verify-vs-validate is an attribute of one check, not two relationships — as an edge it forces the confusable choice every time; as a kind there is always exactly one edge (VERIFIES). But a kind with no reader is the same orphan relocated, so it is kept only because the unvalidated_capability gap reads it — the mission-assurance question 'built to spec, but is it the right thing?', which the user's domain cares about. ENABLES vs CAUSES had no reader (0 core files each), so sharpening hints bought only cleaner extraction of a distinction nothing uses; collapsing removes the error class. TRIGGERS was rescued from the trio because it genuinely has a reader (its process role). The gap follows the BL-73 anti-flood lesson: one project-level rollup ('N verified capabilities have no validation check'), acknowledgeable once, not N per-capability alarms.acceptedHold inviolable intent (KPPs) and compute when the design breaks one, OPEN — a finding that corroborates another has to say CONTRADICTS to do it, and two code paths then filter that back out. Leave it, widen an unused edge, or make corroboration something reflow2 computes?, A recorded risk reaches someone — RISKS is a finding source, not an edge only propagation can see, The rule that a vocabulary distinction must be read by a computation is itself computed, not applied by hand
A planned epoch depends on a version combination, not the other way round
`req:epochs-can-be-planned` DEPENDS_ON `req:version-combination-is-an-object`. The reverse edge, which had been in the graph, is RETRACTED as mis-drawn. The direction is settled by the requirements' own words. `req:epochs-can-be-planned`: 'an epoch or increment must PIN THE SET of per-repo design versions it means, or the question 'which epoch are we talking about?' has no answer' — a planned epoch needs a named version set to be about anything. `req:version-combination-is-an-object` needs nothing from planning: 'does THIS SET of versions hold together?' is answerable about what is deployed today, with no epochs, no plan and no forward axis. One is built on the other, and only one way round. RETRACTED, NOT RECORDED AS HISTORY. The old edge asserted a dependency that was never true, which is a modelling error rather than something that stopped being so — retire-from-design's Path B. It also carried `weight_basis: estimated` with no `evidence` property, i.e. it was drawn without a stated reason, which is what `req:defaults-do-not-assert` describes one layer down. Both replacement edges carry `weight_basis: evidence`.		FOUND BY WIRING, and it is the point worth keeping. These four requirements sat in `disconnected_community` islands for two days. Adding the true dependency closed a cycle with the existing edge, and `detect_defects` reported it as `circular_dependency` at severity critical — so the wrong edge became visible only when a right one was drawn next to it. That is a blind spot worth naming: a SINGLE edge pointing the wrong way creates no cycle, trips no detector, and reads exactly like a correct one. Nothing in the design could have caught it in isolation. It took a second, contradicting edge to make the first one's error computable — which means an island is not merely unanalysed, it is a place where wrong edges are structurally undetectable. Disconnection hides more than it looks like it hides. One process note, stated rather than glossed: the prior edge state was not snapshotted before the deletion, so the retraction is recoverable from the committed export at `8eb70c8` rather than from the graph's own history. A `record_change` on `req:version-combination-is-an-object` before the delete would have captured it in-graph, per BL-63. Cheap to have done and worth doing next time an edge is retracted.acceptedAn epoch can be planned, not only recorded
Where does a planned epoch live — a git branch, the graph, or both?
OPEN (proposed): the storage mechanism for planned epochs is undecided, and deciding it by drift would repeat the mistake BL-100 names. Three candidates are on the table, none chosen.		(a) EPOCH BRANCHES, Anthony's first framing: a git branch per planned epoch holding the expected export — full-document snapshots, diffable with the delta machinery, zero schema change; cost: the roadmap lives outside the graph, invisible to detectors, and n branches of a mutable file invite the lineage problems BL-107 closed. (b) IN-GRAPH FUTURE EPOCHS: Epoch nodes with future sequences, planned nodes pinned AT_EPOCH, the unused ANTICIPATES edge (confidence property) finally reached; roadmap visible to detect_gaps and propagate; cost: no single handable document, and axis-Z was built pointing backward. (c) HYBRID: roadmap in-graph, planned epochs exported to refs on demand; cost: two representations that can drift. AMENDED 2026-07-28, same day, after Anthony's second pass: git already does versions/tags/releases well (industry ships small increments fast — his brother's project, ~2 minors/week), which strengthens git as the SNAPSHOT STORE — but his bottom line reframes the choice: the graph must be the INDEX (see req:graph-indexes-snapshots), so the real shape is likely (c-refined): git stores snapshots under refs it is already good at, the graph owns the map from epoch_n/increment_n to ref plus the planned content, and a user never remembers a branch name. The rel:v0180 <-> tag v0.18.0 pattern is this exact division of labor, already shipping, pointed backward. Still OPEN: whether (b)'s in-graph planned content is required for detectors to reason about the roadmap, or whether the index alone suffices. THIRD AMENDMENT, same day: Anthony's satisfaction-schedule distillation shrinks what a planned epoch has to BE. If the roadmap's atom is 'requirement X expected/required satisfied at epoch_n' — a dated pin with a modality and a confidence — then the plan's content is a set of edges the graph holds natively (AT_EPOCH / ANTICIPATES with confidence), NOT a full expected-graph snapshot per epoch; the full snapshot becomes a DERIVED view (render the graph as of the pins that hold at epoch_n), which further strengthens (c-refined): the graph owns pins and index, git stores any rendered snapshot a human wants to hold in their hands, and nothing stores the same truth twice.proposednothing
A check's input scope is a fact about the CLAIM, so it lives on the VERIFIES edge
What a check SWEPT and what it PINNED is recorded on the VERIFIES edge, as two comma-separated lists of parameter names, not as properties of the Verification node. A capability is reported as narrowly proven when every passing check that verifies it pins a parameter and none sweeps it.		Anthony's call, 2026-08-01, from three options. Scope is a property of the relationship between a check and a claim, not of the check: one suite can cover capability A across the whole input space and touch capability B at a single point, and a per-node property has to average that away — it would report the same narrowness for every target, so the detector could not say WHICH claim is thin. Placing it on the edge mirrors PERFORMED_IN's placement of WHERE, which is the same sentence rotated (BL-126's own framing). The existing VERIFIES.coverage enum (full/partial/smoke) was considered and rejected as the vehicle: it is a self-assessed adjective set by the person who wrote the check, and BL-126's founding case was a guard written by an author to protect a belief they had formed an hour earlier — they would have labelled it `full`. Named parameters are checkable against what the design says the capability is independent of; an adjective is not. Storage is a comma-separated string because the schema has no list type (the QualityGate.criteria precedent); the MCP surface takes and returns proper lists, so only the encoding is flat.acceptedSay what a check held fixed and what it varied, per claim
OPEN — do half-formed ideas get a place in the graph, distinct from things the design asserts?
UNDECIDED as a vocabulary question, but MUCH SMALLER than it looked, and the skill that tests it is BUILT (2026-07-25, the brainstorm skill). REFRAMED by Anthony the same day, and the reframe was the useful part: what he and his brother were asking for is not a staging GATE, it is a KIND. 'I think I now realize what my brother's idea was trying to say — it is like a brainstorming session where you can work through ideas without committing to anything yet. These would be more like 'ideas' not yet fleshed out and could be held in the graph as just that, 'brainstorming ideas'.' That dissolves the contradiction this decision was opened over: the git study rejected the index because a gate between every edit and the graph is where intent goes to be forgotten, whereas a brainstorm is the opposite move — the idea DOES enter the graph, immediately, labelled as what it is. Nothing waits outside, so nothing is lost, and the design still never claims a half-formed thought as intent. THE FINDING THAT SHRANK THE QUESTION, from reading the detector while building the skill: the existing vocabulary ALREADY tells a musing from a choice, and a computation already reads the difference. `detect_gaps` raises `undecided_decision_point` only on a proposed Decision holding TWO OR MORE REGISTERED ALTERNATIVES — a fork with a real design export behind each branch (detect.rs: `alts.len() < 2 { continue }`). A proposed Decision whose options live in its prose therefore raises NO gap at all. So brainstormed ideas are silent by construction, and the nudge to choose arrives exactly when the ideas stop being ideas: register_alternative turns an option into a fork, and being asked to decide a fork is correct. Nobody has to remember which is which, and no label was needed to get it. WHAT A `brainstorm` KIND WOULD STILL BUY, and it is now a short list rather than the four-item one recorded yesterday: (a) delivery and certainty counts already exclude Decisions, so nothing is owed there; (b) gap silence is already delivered, per the finding above; (c) what remains is RETIREMENT — an idea nobody has touched in months could be surfaced as a candidate for tidying rather than sitting in the decision list forever, which is a real computation and the only one left standing; and (d) READABILITY — a person scanning 70-odd Decisions cannot tell at a glance which were choices and which were musings, which the skill currently answers with a sentence of prose inside the node rather than with a queryable property. PRIOR FRAMING, KEPT because it was true when written: the ask read as an opt-in 'think first, commit later' mode; a session making no write calls IS rubber-ducking and the read tools are the ducking aids; and the narrow question was what happens at the END — which the skill now answers as a PROMOTION step, not a commit step. ===================================================================== ADDED 2026-08-10 — THE CAPABILITY HALF, AND IT IS NOT SILENT. Anthony re-opened this by asking, of 34 stuck gaps: 'what a not-yet-agreed wish should be in this graph?' RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. ===================================================================== THE FINDING ABOVE HOLDS FOR DECISIONS AND FAILS FOR CAPABILITIES. 'Silent by construction' rests on detect.rs skipping a proposed Decision with fewer than two REGISTERED alternatives. Nothing analogous protects a Capability: one at `planned` with no Requirement behind it raises `unmotivated_capability`, with no Artifact `unrealized_capability`, with no Verification `unverified_capability`. THREE GAPS EACH, FOREVER, BY CONSTRUCTION. MEASURED 2026-08-10: 34 of 73 open gaps — 47% — are the (BL-nnn) rows, and they have sat unanswerable since 2026-08-07. The cost of the wrong home for a wish is not theoretical; it is half the gap list. ⭐ TWO ACCEPTED DECISIONS COLLIDE HERE AND NEITHER KNEW IT. `dec:backlog-is-retired` routes unbuilt work to 'a Capability at `planned` BEHIND A REQUIREMENT'. Read strictly it is coherent — the Requirement is what makes the Capability motivated. But the migration wrote the Capability half and not the Requirement half, and the reason it did is the interesting part: A BACKLOG ROW USUALLY HAS NO REQUIREMENT TO WRITE. 'Advanced testing tiers' is a wish nobody has agreed to; inventing a Requirement to motivate it would manufacture intent, which is precisely what this project forbids everywhere else. ⇒ SO THE ROUTING IS NOT WRONG, IT IS INCOMPLETE FOR A SUBSET: work somebody INTENDS is a Capability behind a Requirement; a wish nobody has agreed to has no home, and got the Capability anyway. THE OPTIONS. (a) FINISH THE PRESCRIBED SHAPE — write the missing Requirements. Counter: for most of the 34 there is no requirement anybody stated, so this manufactures intent to silence a detector, and `graph_report`'s certainty line would count 18 new `asserted` requirements nobody confirmed. (b) A CAPABILITY GAINS A `proposed` STATUS. Requirement status models the INTENT lifecycle (proposed / accepted / deferred / dropped / met); Capability status models the BUILD lifecycle (planned / in_progress / realized / verified) and has no way to say 'wished for, not agreed'. Adding it lets the detectors stay quiet honestly. ⭐ THIS IS THE SAME ROOT AS `dec:idea-does-a-capability-need-a-cancelled-state`, already open and ALREADY ASSIGNED TO ANTHONY — that one asks for the other end of the same missing axis. They should be decided together or one will foreclose the other. Counter: it MOVES THE SCHEMA STAMP, and two statuses on one type meaning two different lifecycles is a modelling smell in itself. (c) A WISH IS NOT A CAPABILITY AT ALL. Route it to a `proposed` Decision — which IS silent by construction, per this node's own finding — phrased as 'should we build X?'. Cheapest by far and needs no schema change. Counter: a Decision is a CHOICE somebody faces, and 'advanced testing tiers' is not a choice, it is an item; collapsing wishes into decisions makes the decision pile the backlog again, which is the thing Anthony already said is unwieldy at 85. (d) DROP THEM. If nobody has agreed to a wish in the months it has sat there, the honest record may be that it is not wanted. Counter: `dec:bl-155` measured that reflow2 cannot tell 'unused' from 'unreachable', and the same applies to a wish nobody has looked at — dropping on silence deletes exactly what was never surfaced. (e) ACKNOWLEDGE EACH, INDIVIDUALLY AND HONESTLY. The tool already refuses the lazy form: `acknowledge_gaps` demands a reason PER GAP because 'a batch under one shared reason is exactly the erosion the ask-don't-repair rule exists to prevent'. Counter, and it is why this node exists rather than 34 acknowledgements: acknowledging is treating the symptom. The detector is correctly reporting that a wish is wearing the wrong type. WHAT IS NOT AN OPTION: 34 acknowledgements sharing one rationale with the subject swapped. That satisfies the letter of the tool's contract and defeats its purpose. THE QUESTION THIS ACTUALLY TURNS ON, and it is the one to put to the user: DOES A NOT-YET-AGREED WISH BELONG IN THE DESIGN AT ALL? If yes, it needs a home that is silent until somebody agrees to it — (b) or (c). If no, the backlog was retired into the wrong place and (d) is the honest answer for most of the 34.		Raised by Anthony and his brother 2026-07-24, reframed by Anthony 2026-07-25, and the skill built the same day on his word ('go ahead with the brainstorm skill'). Built as a SKILL and not a schema change deliberately: it tests the practice at the cost of prose, and if the practice sticks the vocabulary question can be answered with evidence instead of taste — whereas a new node type or an enum value would have bought an upgrade doc and a foundation-migration checklist for a noun nobody had used yet. The evidence for the feature is this session itself: Anthony produced four isolation ideas he explicitly did not want to commit to, and the only home for them was a proposed Decision. That worked (dec:concurrent-work-isolation), which is why this is not urgent; it is also a slightly wrong fit, since a Decision node is meant for a choice someone is actually facing, and knowing exactly which part of the fit is wrong is what the finding above now pins down. Left PROPOSED because two of the four original arguments for a kind have dissolved and the remaining two (retirement candidates, at-a-glance readability) are real but small — and whether they are worth a schema change is Anthony's call, not a judgement to be made by the agent that just wrote the skill.proposedWork an idea through without committing to it, on the record
The export document is an accepted single door, so its chain is an accepted SPOF
cmp:export and ifc:graph-export are the only route from a design to the kit converter (cmp:init) and to any other machine or reflow2 version, and they stay that way. Both single_point_of_failure warnings are accepted as intentional, not resolved by adding a second export path.		dec:repo-file-embedded made the deterministic export the durable, diffable record, and req:survives-upgrade makes export-with-the-old-build / import-with-the-new THE migration mechanism — a single door is the feature, because a second export path would be a second source of truth for what the design is, and byte-identical determinism (req:persistence: a backup under git shows what actually changed) is only a meaningful promise about one format. The detector is right that severing this chain cuts cmp:init off from the design; that fragility is the price of one canonical portability format, knowingly paid. Accepted 2026-07-21 while dispositioning BL-69's corrected findings; sibling of dec:service-spof-accepted and dec:graph-spof-accepted.acceptedexport, Design export document
The export proves itself: content hash + file-lineage chain, from AT proto's self-authenticating repos
Every export carries a content_hash — sha256 over the canonical sorted JSON of the design content only (graph_id, nodes, edges), excluding the stamp and chain fields, so the same design hashes identically whichever build wrote it. A prev_content_hash records file lineage: when an export overwrites an existing export file, the chain advances to the old file's content hash — but only when content actually changed, so two exports of an unchanged design stay byte-identical. The full hash is carried (not truncated like display checksums) because this is tamper evidence. compare_designs reports ancestry from the chain (other succeeds base / base succeeds other / siblings of a common parent / unknown); import reports an integrity mismatch loudly; the CI gate fails on a committed export that does not match its own hash. Documents predating the hash stay importable and comparable — absence is reported, never an error.		User directed 2026-07-21 after the AT Protocol comparison: atproto repos are self-authenticating (signed commits over a content-addressed root), and reflow2's export was already deterministic — the hash was well-defined and simply never computed. Content-only hashing (stamp excluded) was proven necessary the same day: the committed export and the live export had identical content but different writers (0.8.0 script vs 0.7.0-era session server), and they must fingerprint the same. The chain lives at the file-write seam because the committed export file IS the durable record whose lineage matters; the graph itself must not be mutated by a read-only export. Ancestry is what turns compare_designs from 'what diverged' into 'was the divergence made in ignorance of the base or in defiance of it' — BL-12 sketch idea 1's question, computable for the one-step case. Signing (identity) is deliberately deferred until a second writer is real; a hash chain without keys is already tamper-evident against accident and hand-editing, which is today's actual threat model.acceptedCompare two as-designed records, Export and import a design, Publish just the boundary — the contracts others may rely on, and nothing internal
The design is exported once per PULL REQUEST, not once per commit — squash-merge collapses the chain
A branch may hold as many commits as it likes; exactly ONE of them may write docs/design/reflow2.json, and it should be the last. The COORD claim commit goes first, since it carries no export.		Forced by the gate on 2026-08-01, immediately after merging PR #21 — the first PR in this project to carry two EXPORTING commits. AGENTS.md said 'export EXACTLY ONCE per commit' and that rule was followed exactly; it is still insufficient, because this project merges by SQUASH. N commits become one on main, and only the last export's prev_content_hash survives, so the surviving link points at a branch intermediate main never saw. main's chain now reads cd6e6c8:799b06d9 then 56bc698:prev=da60a633 — a hole. THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART: PRs #18 and #19 also carried two commits and were fine, because their first commit was the COORD claim, which touches no export. They complied BY ACCIDENT. The rule has been insufficient for every multi-commit PR this project has merged; it had simply never met one where two commits both exported. This is the req:schema-prose-is-checked family in the PROCESS layer — an instruction correct as written and wrong in the workflow it is embedded in, the same shape as BL-114's finding prose and BL-152's skill prose. Four surfaces now: schema, findings, skills, process. REPAIRED FORWARD, NOT BACKWARD. Re-exporting makes every future link sound; the hole at 56bc698 stays on the record. main is pushed and shared, and rewriting history to hide a break in a history-integrity chain would be its own kind of lie. Also learned in the repair: an unchanged graph re-exports byte-identically and the chain deliberately does NOT advance, so a lineage break cannot be papered over by re-running the export — it takes a real design change to move the chain on, which is the property working as intended. NOT ENFORCED, and that is the open half (BL-156): the gate catches this AFTER the merge, on main, where it is expensive. `git log --name-only origin/main..HEAD` would catch it on the pull-request trigger while it is still free.acceptedExport and import a design, OPEN — a claim in the graph cannot be announced before the work, because the export it rides in may only be written once per PR, OPEN — reflow2's own rules are tracked by hand while reflow2 has a governance layer built to track them. Should they be wired into it?, A rule states the scope it binds in, and a conflict between two rules is surfaced — because a rule conflict selects against the careful, Exactly one commit on a branch writes the design export, and it should be the last
A second exporting commit is caught by the CI gate, not by the server
Implement req:the-export-is-serialised-rather-than-socially-enforced in reflow2_check.py (the CI gate), which already reads the committed export, rather than by adding serialisation or refusal to the MCP server.		Anthony's word, 2026-08-08, when accepting the requirement; the fleet's own framing ('the tool could refuse or serialise') deliberately left the location open. THE GATE IS WHERE THE EVIDENCE ALREADY IS: the lineage chain lives in the committed export document and its prev_content_hash, which is a property of the COMMIT HISTORY rather than of any live server session — so the server would have to be told about git to enforce it, while the gate already reads exactly the artifact in question. IT ALSO MATCHES WHERE THE FAILURE HAPPENS: two exporting commits break the chain at merge time, not at write time, and both projects that hit this hit it in a pull request. A server-side lock would additionally have to survive the case reflow2's own release procedure records, where a fold rewrites history after the exports were made — which no live serialisation can see. NOTE THE HONEST LIMIT: the gate catches it at CI rather than preventing it at authoring time, so a session still learns about the collision late. That is accepted as the cost of putting the check where the data is.acceptedTwo exporting commits cannot silently break the lineage chain
OPEN — a recorded pressure on committed blobs: the real argument is not size relief, it is not having to ration
OPEN, and deliberately NOT a reopening of `dec:where-content-lives`. Anthony confirmed 2026-07-31 to proceed with the committed-blob recommendation 'for now and we can reconsider when or if we do the full object_store implementation' — so this records a live pressure and the condition under which it becomes a fork again. THE ARGUMENT, IN HIS SHARPER FORM. The first version of this note said the appeal of an external store was size relief. That undersells it. His framing: 'going with an external storage allows for ALL documentation to be stored and referenced.' The point is not that the repository gets smaller — it is that THE NEED TO BE SELECTIVE DISAPPEARS. `dec:content-growth-is-bounded-by-what-not-by-size` solves the measured problem by rationing: transcripts by exception, judgement exercised every time. That works, and it is a STANDING TAX ON JUDGEMENT rather than a one-off cost. An external store removes the question instead of answering it. WHICH CHANGES WHAT WOULD REOPEN THIS. The original condition was 'total grows past what a clone should reasonably carry, with the by-exception rule followed'. Keep it, and add the one his framing implies: IF THE RATIONING ITSELF PROVES COSTLY — if sessions routinely spend judgement deciding what is worth keeping, or if things that should have been kept were not — then the tax is real and the fork is back, whatever the byte count says. A discipline that works only because someone is paying attention every time is a discipline with a running cost, and that cost is the thing to watch, not only the total. WHY NOT NOW, unchanged: the policy addresses the measured problem directly, and reflow2's entire design prose is 3.5 MB. Reopening an architectural choice to solve something a policy already solves is the wrong order, and the no-service property — clone and you have everything, nothing to configure, nothing to be down — is worth more than the convenience. WHAT IS ALREADY UNDERSTOOD, so the reopening starts from evidence rather than from scratch. `object_store` (Apache Arrow) is recorded as the documented upgrade path in `dec:content-store-implementation`, WITH ITS COST MEASURED: 36 crates new to this workspace, ~24 of them URL/ICU machinery, and an async runtime reaching a core deliberately kept synchronous. Its unified API over S3, Azure, GCS, local files and memory is exactly what makes the backend a runtime detail — and content addressing is what makes the swap safe, because a blob verifies wherever it came from. The migration is understood; only its warrant is open. THE PROPERTY THAT WOULD BE SPENT: a second thing to configure, be down, and fall out of step — and a consumer who skips it sees a design with holes and cannot tell. `req:content-reaches-every-seat` is the requirement under pressure, not merely a preference. An answer must say what happens to the person who has the repo and not the credentials.		Amended rather than left, because the first version had the argument slightly wrong and a wrong argument on the record is worse than none — it would have set up the reopening as a size question when the better case is about recurring judgement cost. Recorded at all for the reason the same day already demonstrated twice: `cap:what-next` carried its blocker in prose and nothing noticed when the condition cleared. A lean stated in passing has that shape exactly. Writing the condition down is what makes it a trigger rather than a mood. This is the THIRD pressure on the no-service family, after `dec:central-host` and the content store itself. Three from unrelated directions is a fact about the decision worth having on the record — not an argument to change it, and not something to keep rediscovering from first principles.proposednothing
Fix the comparison before pointing it earlier — stop serializing defaults, then disclose build skew, then report distribution debt
ANTHONY'S CHOICE, 2026-08-10: 'let's go with D, then a small addition, then B.' Three steps in order, and the ordering is the substance — each one is cheap only because the one before it has landed. STEP 1 — STOP SERIALIZING DEFAULTS (option D, `fact:bl-198`). Do not write a property value equal to the schema default, so an ABSENT property honestly means 'nobody said'. Partly landed already: 0.25.0 wrote defaults into the export and 0.27.0 does not, while BL-198 is still listed PLANNED in `epoch:planned-one-write-surface` — so part of this step is reconciling the plan with what shipped rather than building. THE REASON THIS ORDERING PUTS D FIRST AND DROPS C, and it is the load-bearing argument: D DELIVERS C'S SEMANTICS DERIVATIONALLY. Option C was 'give a property difference provenance so a default never reads as a change'. BL-198's own fix shape already produces exactly that — presence means somebody said it, absence means nobody did — without storing a second provenance field, which is the form `dec:certainty-derived` insists on for requirement certainty and the same argument applies here. C is therefore NOT rejected on merit; it is rendered unnecessary by D, and stays on `dec:idea-does-a-session-open-by-comparing-the-record` in case something after D still cannot be answered. STEP 2 — A COMPARISON DISCLOSES ITS OWN CONFOUND (the addition, not among the five options). Every export carries `reflow2_version` in its stamp. When two records being compared were written by different builds, the comparison SAYS SO and says that property-only differences may be attributable to that. This is the one change that would have prevented both false claims: 2026-08-08 and 2026-08-10 were both cross-build comparisons, and neither reader could see the confound. It is DISCLOSURE, not a threshold — the same move `propose_heal` makes when it says 'the alphabet chose the victim', and deliberately NOT the rejected option of tuning severity until phantoms fall below it, which silences true and false findings at the same rate. IT IS ALSO WHAT D DOES NOT FIX. Suppressing defaults cleans the steady state and MOVES the disagreement to the version transition — every upgrading consumer meets it once. Step 2 is what makes that meeting survivable, which is why it follows D rather than replacing it. STEP 3 — THE LOOP SAYS WHAT DISTRIBUTION IS OWED (option B, flo2's F5). Extend the read-side hint chosen in `dec:read-hint-shape` (state-derived, riding orientation reads, fire-on-change) to carry 'the live graph and the committed record disagree' alongside coherence debt. LAST ON PURPOSE: a hint that fires on phantom findings teaches the agent to skim it, which would damage the one mechanism that currently earns attention — the exact failure `dec:read-hint-shape` rejected option B for. Its value is entirely downstream of the finding deserving belief. WHAT WAS NOT CHOSEN. (A) do nothing — the null option, and it was a real candidate: `where-am-i` already prescribes the comparison and what failed was belief, not compliance. Rejected because the record was wrong on main for an unknown number of PRs and `reflow2_check` structurally cannot notice, reading checksums and anchored gaps and never properties. (E) move the trigger to publish time — not rejected on merit, merely not now: it cannot catch what is already committed and wrong, which was the observed case, and it inherits the same confound until step 2 lands. It becomes nearly free afterwards. THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS was NOT 'when should the comparison run'. It was 'what has to be true before running it earlier makes anyone better off', and all three steps are about making the instrument believable rather than about scheduling it. Whether it then becomes a session's opening move is left genuinely open on the superseded idea node.		Recorded as a decision rather than left on the brainstorm node because Anthony chose, and `dec:governance-integrates-not-splits` set the precedent two days earlier for exactly this shape: a new accepted Decision OBSOLETES the brainstormed one, which goes `superseded` with all its options intact rather than being edited into an answer. The roads not taken keep their reasoning that way, and C in particular is worth being able to find again — it is superseded by an argument (D subsumes it) rather than by a judgement, and if that argument fails C is still there. The measurements this rests on are recorded separately and independently: `fact:bl-198-cost-measured-twice-in-both-directions` (why the instrument is not believable) and `fact:orphan-decision-is-silenced-by-an-edge-that-does-not-reach-it` (found while checking this session's own work). Both carry their own counter-arguments, so a later session can attack the evidence without having to attack the decision. Step 2 is mine rather than Anthony's and is marked as such: it was not one of the five options put to him, and he adopted it on the argument that it is the smallest change that would have caught both incidents.acceptedA comparison says when its two sides were written by different builds, An absent property means nobody said it — a value equal to the schema default is not written, The loop says what DISTRIBUTION is owed, not only what coherence is owed
The deterministic-id hash is a foundational primitive in nodes, not a detection concern — break the detect↔verify cycle by relocating it
The FNV-1a id hash (fnv1a) moves from cmp:detect (detect.rs) to cmp:nodes (nodes.rs), the vocabulary/identity leaf everything already sits above. This breaks the critical detect↔verify circular dependency: detect→verify is a genuine domain dependency (gap detection reads a capability's verification state, crate::verify::CapabilityVerification), but verify→detect existed ONLY because verify borrowed crate::detect::fnv1a to mint a deterministic id — not a domain dependency at all. Relocating the primitive removes that false edge (cycle broken, one-way detect→verify remains) and, as the same true consequence, removes five more fnv1a-only false couplings on cmp:detect (agent, artifact, drift, fielded, heal → detect all had no other detect reference); cmp:report keeps its real detect dependency (crate::detect::GapCandidate). Net self-model reconciliation: −6 DEPENDS_ON→cmp:detect, +1 cmp:agent→cmp:nodes (agent's new, real dependency on the primitive's home).		User directed fixing the critical cycle (2026-07-23). BREAK over ACCEPT because the cycle was not a genuine mutual dependency to live with — it was an artifact of a homeless utility: fnv1a began in detect.rs (where gap-id hashing first needed it) and eight modules reached through crate::detect::fnv1a, so the graph asserted a dependency on the detect DOMAIN that the code did not really have. Accepting it would embalm that lie; the honest move is to put the primitive where it belongs. RELOCATE-to-nodes over introduce-an-interface or invert-a-dependency because minting a derived node's id (gaps, heal issues, merge conflicts, prompts, drift/artifact keys) is an identity concern, and nodes is the vocabulary/identity module that is already a dependency leaf (depends on nothing), so the primitive gains no new coupling and creates no new cycle — the minimal, truthful home. The build script derives DEPENDS_ON from source (never prose), so a future rebuild reproduces exactly this shape; the committed self-model was reconciled by hand this session because it carries live-only nodes (req:nudge-covers-bypass, req:read-surfaces-debt) that block a full rebuild. Sibling in spirit to dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition (structure follows function/reality, not the file tree's accidents). The remaining structural defects are all accepted SPOFs and genuinely-disconnected intent clusters; this was the one critical one.acceptednodes
A fork point is a coordinate (decision → epoch → export hash), not a stored copy or a native ref layer
'The design as it stood at decision D' resolves by a three-step address: the Decision is pinned AT_EPOCH to a DesignEpoch, that epoch's existing `checksum` property carries the content_hash of the export cut there, and the document itself lives where it already lives — a git-committed reflow2.json. reflow2 supplies the coordinate; git supplies the bytes. No new node type, no mutable pointers, no reflow2-native DAG. Re-taking a road home is then the three-way merge already built (dec:merge-three-way), with the fork point as the base — which is precisely the merge-base reflow2 currently borrows from git, now derivable from its own epoch chain.		User decided 2026-07-24, choosing the coordinate over a native ref/branch layer. THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVE: branch names as graph nodes — mutable pointers to epochs, a real DAG, so reflow2 finds its own merge-base without git. Rejected on two grounds. (1) It duplicates machinery git already provides, and dec:repo-file-embedded already put the design in the repo as a file precisely so the repo's tooling carries the file-shaped concerns; dec:merge-three-way already chose explicit inputs over git's DAG for the same reason. (2) A mutable pointer is a foreign object in this graph: the whole doctrine of axis Z is that history is never overwritten (req:intent-preserved, req:roads-not-taken), and a ref that moves is by construction a thing whose past value is lost unless separately recorded — reintroducing the erosion the epoch chain exists to prevent. The coordinate has the further virtue of costing nothing: DesignEpoch.checksum already existed in the schema, described as 'a hash over the anchored spec set at this epoch', which is exactly this use. Honest limit: only exports from v0.9.0 on carry an embedded content_hash (dec:export-hash-chain shipped then), so epochs before it are addressed by git tag alone and claim no checksum rather than inventing one.acceptedHold and re-fork a decision's unchosen alternatives, alternatives
A dependency cycle running only through file and library contracts is a Warning, not a Critical
circular_dependency drops from Critical to Warning when BOTH hold: no hop of the loop is a real DEPENDS_ON edge, and every Interface it runs through carries a foundation medium (`library` or `data`). Any real DEPENDS_ON edge anywhere in the loop keeps the whole cycle Critical, and an `unspecified` medium never earns the downgrade.		Anthony's call, 2026-08-01, from three options. `Critical` means MUST FIX, and a loop that exists only because two parts read and write the same file formats has nothing to fix — a renderer that reads MIDI and writes WAV against a transcriber doing the reverse has no runtime dependency in either direction, and either runs on a machine where the other does not exist. Four such loops were reported `critical` in a single adopt pass over an ~11k-LOC repo and NONE was real, on the detector the adopt skill sells as the payoff of a brownfield pass. DOWNGRADED, NOT SILENCED, and that distinction was the decision. Option (c), suppressing the case entirely, was rejected because shared-data coupling is sometimes genuine — two services over one table can be truly entangled, since a schema change in one breaks the other — so the finding keeps its place, its affected set, its suggested fix and its explanation, and loses only the claim that it is an emergency. Option (a), leaving Critical and relying on the improved message from BL-141(a), was rejected because a severity is a claim about what the reader should DO: prose cannot repair a wrong word, and a severity cannot be filtered on if it is wrong four times out of four. TWO GUARDS MAKE THIS SAFE RATHER THAN QUIET. `contracts_only` is the load-bearing one — a single genuine DEPENDS_ON edge in the loop is a real dependency and does not stop being one by sharing a loop with a data contract. And `Interface.medium` defaults to `unspecified`, which is NOT a foundation medium, so silence about the medium keeps the louder answer; a design that never classified its boundaries is not quietly excused. Both are pinned by their own cases and both mutations are caught: dropping the contracts_only guard fails exactly the mixed-cycle test, and downgrading every cycle fails FOUR tests including the pre-existing one that has asserted Critical since the detector was written. THE PRECEDENT WAS NOT LEANED ON. `is_foundation_medium` already exempts library/data from single_point_of_failure, but on grounds that do not transfer — 'you cannot run a second copy of it, so add_redundancy is incoherent' is an argument about whether a FIX is possible, not about whether a DEPENDENCY exists. This decision stands on its own reasoning. VERIFIED ON THE ORIGINATING PROJECT'S REAL DATA: their reported loop, cmp:fundamental-detection → cmp:midi-renderer → cmp:fundamental-detection through ifc:midi-file and ifc:wav-audio (both `data`), now reports WARNING with its explanation intact.acceptedA dependency cycle says which edge kinds it walked, and through which contracts
OPEN — how should gap reporting behave when most requirements are legitimately unbuilt, as a captured corpus makes normal?
RECORDED AS A FINDING PLUS AN OPEN QUESTION, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised 2026-08-04 while answering Anthony's dev_storyflow question (req:no-idea-goes-quiet). Nothing here is settled. THE FINDING, VERIFIED IN CODE RATHER THAN SUPPOSED. `unsatisfied_requirement` fires per Requirement with no incoming SATISFIES, and it is NOT an aggregate gap — checked in `GapSource::is_aggregate()` (crates/reflow2-core/src/detect.rs), where `UnvalidatedCapability` is the sole `true` arm and `UnsatisfiedRequirement` is listed exhaustively among the `false` ones, with the comment that per-node keying is deliberate so a change to the named set expires the judgement. CONSEQUENCE: ingesting a corpus of 300 ideas that nothing yet implements produces 300 gaps that all say the same thing, burying every distinct finding beneath them. THIS IS (BL-145) AT AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE. That row reads: 'One detector produced 27 of 49 gaps saying the same thing, and buried every distinct finding below the fold' — found 2026-08-01 by an /adopt pass over music_graph. It was filed at 27 against 49. A captured corpus is where it stops being a presentation annoyance: at 300 it is not noise, it is a wall, and it lands on exactly the user whose whole reason for ingesting was to stop losing track of things. ⭐ WHY THIS IS NOT SIMPLY BL-145 RESTATED, AND IT IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Every existing detector was designed against a design that is MOSTLY BUILT, where an unsatisfied requirement is an exception worth naming one at a time. A captured corpus inverts the base rate: unbuilt is the NORMAL state, unbuilt is CORRECT, and req:accreted-intent-becomes-a-design already says so explicitly — 'every capability is `planned`, every requirement `proposed`, and the as-built half of the loop has no subject — which is honest and must not read as catastrophic.' So the defect is not that the detector is chatty. It is that the detector's severity model encodes an assumption about the design's phase that the corpus case falsifies. The same suspicion should be carried to `unrealized_capability`, `unallocated_capability`, `design_without_build` and `build_without_verification`, none of which were checked here. OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) MAKE IT AGGREGATE when the count crosses a bar — one gap saying '300 requirements are unsatisfied', drilling down on request. Cheapest, and `is_aggregate` is the existing seam. Counter, and the code comment states it directly: aggregate keying means a standing judgement does not expire when the set changes, so a requirement added later is silently covered by a judgement made before it existed — which is the right trade for a rollup and the wrong one for a finding that names nodes. (b) BAND BY PHASE — read the project's mode or the design's position on the maturity trajectory, and let a design with nothing built report this as a reading rather than as gaps. Fits maturity_report's existing frontier computation and dec:orientation-is-computed-not-written. Counter: it makes gap severity depend on a computed phase, and reflow2 has been careful that 'where this design SHOULD be is deliberately not stated'. (c) SCOPE IT — detect_gaps already takes a `scope` seed, so the corpus user asks per region rather than globally. Counter: it requires the user to already know which region to ask about, which is precisely what someone who just ingested 1,124 documents does not know. (d) DO NOTHING TO THE DETECTOR AND FIX THE PRESENTATION — group identical gap_sources in the report and lead with the distinct ones. Counter: `detect_gaps` is consumed by agents and by CI, not only by the report, so a presentation-only fix leaves both other consumers buried. WHAT THIS REPRIORITISES, offered as an observation and not as a plan. `epoch:v0240-planned` sequences the corpus increment as ingest-then-know-where-you-stopped. This finding says a fifth thing sits between them: a corpus that ingests correctly and then buries its own findings has not delivered req:no-idea-goes-quiet, whose whole content is that an unbuilt idea must stay LOUD. Loud and unreadable are not the same state, and 300 identical gaps is the second one. Whether that makes it a v0.24.0 obligation or a v0.25.0 one is Anthony's call — (BL-205) and (BL-194), both already scheduled for v0.25.0 as 'the loop tells the truth about what it is owed', are the same family and may want to travel together. NOT VERIFIED HERE, and it bears on which option is right: whether `acknowledge_gaps` (the bulk form) already makes 300 gaps tractable by letting one reason dispose of many at once. If it does, the wall is lower than stated and (d) rises. Nobody checked.		Recorded now rather than as a backlog row because it is a defect against a shipped capability with a real fork behind it, and this session has just spent an hour establishing that the backlog is where such things go to be re-derived. The measurement (is_aggregate checked in source, BL-145's 27-of-49 as the prior instance) is written down so the next session argues from the code rather than from the impression that gap output is noisy. Kept separate from req:no-idea-goes-quiet because that node states what the user needs and this one asks how the machine should behave — one node holding both could only ever be half-answered. The unchecked item (bulk acknowledge) is named explicitly so its absence is visible as a hole rather than passing as a completed analysis.acceptednothing
OPEN — does reflow2 run in tandem with GitHub's MCP server, and where would the pairing pay?
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-07-25: 'what if reflow2 was paired with github's mcp and two worked in tandem?' THE ARCHITECTURAL POINT FIRST, because it decides how expensive any of this is: MCP composes AT THE AGENT, not in the code. An agent can hold both servers at once, so reflow2 would never call GitHub and would never learn what a pull request is — the integration would live entirely in a SKILL that knows both surfaces exist. Zero coupling, no dependency, nothing in the core. Skills are now served from the binary, so such a skill costs a consumer project nothing. SIX PAIRINGS, strongest first. (1) THE PUBLISHING CASE — dec:nested-graphs says a design is its own graph per ownership boundary and designs link by mirroring a published surface, and the open question underneath dec:central-host was always 'how does the other team REACH my surface without cloning my repo'. GitHub is already that distribution network: an agent with github-mcp fetches another repo's committed export, and mirror_surface imports its published boundary with the coordinate. That is federation with no server, no hosting and no account beyond the one they already have — it may answer the strongest argument for hosting. (2) NOTIFICATION reflow2 structurally lacks — reflow2 can only nudge an agent that is already running, which is exactly req:nudge-path-proven's weakness; an unacknowledged gap posted as a GitHub issue reaches a PERSON who is not at a terminal, and closing that issue with an answer writes back through answer_question. (3) THE GATE EXPLAINS ITSELF IN REVIEW — today the coherence gate fails a build; with github-mcp the same finding becomes a review comment naming the thread ('this moves art:X, which realizes cap:Y, which satisfies req:Z — and req:Z has no verification'), landing where humans actually decide. (4) TRACEABILITY IN THE PR BODY — the golden thread from requirement to artifact, written where a reviewer sees WHY and not only what.
