The bounded reading is probably right and is how every package ecosystem already behaves; the cost is that transitive needs travel at the speed of humans, which is exactly the friction Anthony opened this whole thread wanting to remove. AND IT SHARPENS THE AUTHORITY QUESTION NEXT DOOR: the boundary of authority is EXACTLY the shared graph. Everything dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency asks — who may write intent into a design they do not own — is now localised to the overlap, C. It is not a question about the federation; it is a question about each seam in it, asked once per seam, between two named people. IT ALSO MAKES OPTION (c) NEXT DOOR ACTUALLY WORK AT SCALE. 'The upstream pulls rather than the downstream pushes' needs a reverse index — who declares a dependency on me — which today does not exist because req:design-dependencies-declared points downward only. Under this federation the reverse index is small and local: C's owner asks who declares a dependency on C and finds exactly user2's D, never the whole world. RELATED AND ALREADY OPEN: dec:idea-cross-org-federation asks whether reflow2 should federate heterogeneous designs across ORGANISATIONS the way OpenMBEE does, rather than composing exports. Anthony's example is the same shape one scale down — across PEOPLE rather than organisations — which is useful, because it means the mechanism can be tried on two brothers and three repos before it has to survive two companies. ⚠️ IT ALSO PULLS AGAINST A DECISION MADE TWELVE HOURS EARLIER. dec:one-process-many-stores (proposed, 2026-08-05) has each client session ATTACHED TO EXACTLY ONE graph, and carries req:a-session-cannot-reach-another-designs-graph as a SECURITY property for flo2: project A's design must be unreachable from project B's session. Both can be true, but only if the distinction is stated rather than discovered later: MULTI-TENANT ISOLATION (strangers' projects on a hosted server, must not see each other) is not the same as COMPOSITION (one author's own interdependent designs, useless apart). The federation above makes the split cleaner than it first looked — isolation is between TENANTS, composition is within one tenant's declared neighbourhood — but nothing in the design says so yet. IT LANDS ON AN OPEN QUESTION HE HAS ALREADY LEANED ON. dec:how-a-session-is-pointed-at-a-design (proposed) records his 2026-08-05 preference — 'I like this approach of just pointing .mcp.json at the graph_id' — and the counter beside it: (BL-123) holds that the /mcp reconnect is the one step an autonomous agent cannot take, so config-file selection is the option an agent cannot exercise for itself. A multi-graph .mcp.json inherits that counter unchanged. WHAT IS ALREADY BUILT, so the gap is smaller than the question sounds. cap:composed-analysis is REALIZED: two designs analysed together without either being written to, the other's ids namespaced into an in-memory graph, every finding attributed ours / theirs / seam. describe_designs (shipped 2026-08-05) answers what design lives at a path without opening it. So 'reason across several graphs' is a call you can make today; what a config would add is that it happens BY DEFAULT and WITHOUT BEING ASKED. OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) A FLAT LIST OF graph_ids, ALL EQUAL. Closest to the first phrasing. Now the weakest, because the federation example shows the entries are NOT equal and this is the only option that must then answer 'which one does a write land in' at every call site. (b) ROLES PER ENTRY — owned/writable versus depended-on/readable, which is what Anthony's own example describes. Preserves single-writer per graph, preserves the isolation property's shape, matches how every dependency manifest already works, and degenerates gracefully for the one-project case. Counter: it does not by itself serve the flo2 case, because flo2's need is for something to be written INTO reflow2 — that is dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency, not this node. (c) NOTHING IN CONFIG — composition stays an explicit call against a dependency declared in the manifest, where req:design-dependencies-declared already puts it. Cheapest and already built. Counter: an explicit call is one somebody has to remember to make, which is the failure req:no-idea-goes-quiet exists to reject. (d) THE MANIFEST, NOT .mcp.json, IS THE RIGHT FILE — and the federation strengthens this considerably. reflow2 ALREADY declares its dynograph-foundation dependency this way, pinned and version-checked, with ver:design-dependencies-declared passing against the real thing. A DEPENDENCY IS A PROPERTY OF THE DESIGN, NOT OF THE MACHINE SOMEBODY READS IT ON: projectD depends on projectC no matter whose laptop is open, so putting it in .mcp.json — per-machine, and gitignored in this very repo — means every clone and every teammate re-states it, which is the shadow-list failure in a new costume. The counter, and it is real: the manifest says what the DESIGN depends on, while .mcp.json says what THIS PERSON is working on, and Anthony's user1/user2 split is genuinely about people. Those may both be needed — a committed manifest for the dependency edges, a per-user config for which subtree you have in hand. ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ SHARPENED 2026-08-12 — THE UNION FRAMING, AND THE FIRST TRIAL EVIDENCE ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, thinking out loud, and he said 'it is just an idea'. HIS WORDS: 'as I own both reflow2 and flo2, I'd like to get to the point I can work in either project and changes I make in one project are automatically related to one another (maybe like there are external interface nodes that for a given session, allows you to treat the union of 2+ reflow2 graphs as one graph for that reflow2 session).' ⭐ DELIBERATELY SHARPENED RATHER THAN FORKED. This is the same question this node already holds; forking would be the near-duplicate the search-first rule exists to prevent. THREE THINGS ARE GENUINELY NEW in his framing: 1. **UNION, not read-across.** Everything above is about REASONING across graphs — compose, analyse, attribute ours/theirs/seam. He is asking for the graphs to BE one graph for the duration of a session, which is a stronger claim: not 'I can see both' but 'there is no seam to see'. 2. **EXTERNAL INTERFACE NODES as the mechanism.** A named thing in each graph that says 'this is where I join'. The federation model above has roles per graph but no vocabulary for the join itself. 3. **AUTOMATIC RELATING ON WRITE.** 'changes I make in one project are automatically related to one another' — the existing text is read-side. This is the write side, and it is where the cost lives. ═══ THE TRIAL EVIDENCE, 2026-08-12 — the first time pairing actually computed on this pair ═══ `pair_designs` was run for real, reflow2 against flo2's committed export. Result: **paired 0, conflicts 10, unmet_needs 5, dead_surface 2, candidates 1, unclassified 2 ours / 1 theirs.** Three findings, and all three argue FOR the union rather than against it. ⭐⭐ (A) THE SEAM COULD NOT COMPUTE, AND NOT FOR A FIXABLE REASON. Zero pairs — because flo2 models `cmp:reflow2-service` as a component it CONTAINS, providing `ifc:reflow2-design-api` to its own `cmp:tool-loop`. Pairing matches complements ACROSS a boundary; flo2 drew reflow2 INSIDE its boundary, so there is no boundary. That is a legitimate model (Anthony builds that half) and it makes the seam permanently uncomputable. **A UNION DISSOLVES THIS ENTIRELY** — if the two graphs are one for the session, containment is just containment and needs no complement. ⭐⭐⭐ (B) THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT FOR THE UNION, FOUND BY ACCIDENT: TWO GRAPHS CAN AGREE BY BEING IDENTICALLY WRONG. Both designs label the reflow2 boundary `medium: REST`; both MEAN MCP, and both say so in `spec` prose where nothing computes. Had the roles been complementary they would have PAIRED — on a shared falsehood — and reported a clean seam. The tool defends against `unspecified` reading as agreement; it has no defence against both sides stating the same wrong value. **A SHARED NODE CANNOT DISAGREE WITH ITSELF.** The entire class of seam-mismatch defects (medium, auth, transport_security, payload) exists only because the contract is TWO nodes that must be kept in agreement. One node has no agreement to maintain. That is the real argument for external interface nodes, and it is stronger than the convenience one Anthony opened with. 🛑 (C) BUT THE SUBSTRATE HE WOULD BE UNIONING IS THE WRONG ONE FOR THIS CONSUMER. A backtest replayed reflow2's history against the two places flo2's hand-written tracker went stale, and measured which signal would have caught them: - The TOOLSNAP diff caught both input-contract changes decisively and mechanically (`inputSchema.properties` {} → {contributor_id}). - The DESIGN EXPORT diff buried them: 1 relevant node in 70 changes, then 12 in 103. - NEITHER caught the result-shape change (`suggested_fix_type` → Option) — toolsnaps record `annotations, description, inputSchema, name` and NO output schema at all. - ⚠️ AND THE DESIGN EXPORT ACTIVELY LIED: `cap:owed-to-a-contributor` reads `in_progress` at v0.26.1, v0.27.0 AND v0.28.0, three releases after the capability shipped, because status moves only on the owner's word and nobody went back. A subscription built on it would have told flo2 'still in progress' about working code — worse than silence. ⇒ **flo2 consumes reflow2's TOOL SURFACE, not its DESIGN.** Unioning the design graphs joins the wrong two things for that dependency. It would be right for a sibling consuming reflow2's INTENT. So 'link two projects' is at least two different links, and the union answers one of them. ═══ WHAT THE UNION NEWLY COSTS, which the read-side framing above never had to answer ═══ - **WHICH GRAPH DOES A WRITE LAND IN?** Option (a) above was already noted as the one that must answer this; the union makes it unavoidable rather than optional. A new node created 'in the union' has no home until someone says which. - **TWO STORES, TWO LOCKS.** `req:single-writer-graph` gives each directory an exclusive RocksDB lock. A session writing across a union holds two, and lock ordering between them is a real concurrency design, not a detail. - **WHOSE EXPORT CARRIES A SHARED NODE?** If an external interface node is genuinely one node, both repos' exports either carry it (and now disagree on every unrelated commit) or neither does (and it lives nowhere durable). This is the phantom-drift problem at repo scale, and `dec:export-once-per-pr` exists because that problem is already hard within ONE repo. - **WHO ACCEPTS INTENT IN THE OVERLAP?** `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` is unambiguous with one owner per graph. In a union owned by one person it stays simple — which is exactly why Anthony's own case is the right first trial — and it is undefined the moment the union spans two people. ═══ WHAT IS ALREADY BUILT TOWARD IT ═══ `compose_and_analyse` is REALIZED and does the READ-ONLY union today: it imports the other design into an in-memory graph, NAMESPACES their ids so nothing overwrites, throws it away, and attributes every finding ours / theirs / seam. So the union already exists for reads and is thrown away; his idea is that it persists for a session and accepts writes. The namespacing is the part that would have to change, because a shared node is precisely one that must NOT be namespaced apart. NOT DECIDED. ⭐ THE CHEAPEST NEXT TRIAL, since it needs no new vocabulary: take the ONE boundary that should be shared (reflow2's `ifc:mcp-tools` and flo2's `ifc:reflow2-design-api`), and see what breaks if it is treated as one node rather than two — which export carries it, what happens when one side edits it, and whether the medium disagreement becomes impossible or merely relocated. ═══ SHARPENED AGAIN 2026-08-12 — MUTABLE / IMMUTABLE, AND THE TOOL THAT ALREADY DOES IT ═══ RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING. Anthony, on what happens when he does NOT own the other project: 'maybe I can still import, just all changes have to be in one side of the graph. basically, treat one side as unchangeable. this is like: mutable objects can change their internal state or value after creation, while immutable objects cannot be altered once they are created.' ⭐ THE FRAMING COLLAPSES THREE OF THE FOUR COSTS THE UNION SECTION ABOVE RAISED, and that is why it is worth recording rather than merely noting: - WHICH GRAPH DOES A WRITE LAND IN? — gone. Only one side accepts writes. - TWO STORES, TWO LOCKS — gone. You hold one write lock; the other side is a document. - WHOSE EXPORT CARRIES A SHARED NODE? — gone. Yours does, marked foreign. - WHO MAY ACCEPT INTENT IN THE OVERLAP? — gone, and elegantly: you CANNOT move intent in a design you are structurally unable to write. `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` stops being a discipline someone must remember and becomes enforced by construction. 🛑🛑 AND IT IS ALREADY BUILT. `mirror_surface` (dec:nested-graphs option (c)) mirrors another design's published surface in as FOREIGN NODES stamped with the coordinate — `mirror_of`, `mirror_content_hash`, `mirrored_at`, `provenance: imported`. Its own description states the design choice that makes the union work: 'foreignness is a property of the node rather than of the link', so local components provides/consumes the mirrored Interface with ORDINARY edges and the golden thread, propagate and every detector work unchanged. `mirrors` reads the coordinate back as 'a dated claim about a VERSION of another design, never a live truth'. COLLISIONS ARE REFUSED rather than merged. ⇒ Under Anthony's standing triage rule this half is SATISFIED and needs nothing new. 🛑 THE MEASUREMENT THAT REFRAMES THIS WHOLE THREAD, taken 2026-08-12: **ZERO MIRRORED NODES EXIST IN EITHER GRAPH.** No node in reflow2's design or flo2's carries `mirror_of`. `mirror_surface`, `export_surface`, `pair_designs`, `seam_report` and `mirrors` are all built, shipped, and have never once been run on a real pair and kept. That is precisely `cap:built-and-consumed-by-nothing`'s shape — built, correct, consumed by nothing — found on the linking layer the same day that detector shipped. ⇒ **SO THE CONCEPT WORK HERE IS NOT SPECIFYING SOMETHING TO BUILD. IT IS DISCOVERING WHY SOMETHING ALREADY BUILT WAS NEVER PICKED UP.** On today's evidence the answer is the bilateral precondition: mirroring needs the far side to have declared a published surface, and reflow2 declared no `required` interface at all until PR #130. Neither party gets value until both have paid. ⚠️ WHAT IMMUTABILITY DOES NOT SOLVE — it RELOCATES staleness into a refresh, and refresh is where the sharp edges are: - A mirror is a SNAPSHOT. Immutable means you cannot edit it; it does not mean it is current. - REFRESH REPLACES THE IMMUTABLE SIDE WHOLESALE — clean, like updating a lockfile. - BUT YOUR EDGES POINT INTO THEIR NODES. If they delete or rename something you consume, a refresh leaves your edges dangling — and reflow2 now REFUSES dangling edges outright. So a refresh can fail on referential integrity. Whether that is a refusal, a report or a gap is undecided and is the first thing a trial should exercise. - VENDOR OR REFERENCE? Does your committed export CARRY their mirrored nodes (self-contained and reproducible, but their churn appears in your diffs) or merely NAME them by `mirror_of` + `mirror_content_hash` (small, but your export alone is unreadable)? This is the vendoring-versus-lockfile question every package ecosystem faces. `mirror_content_hash` suggests the design already leans to the first with the second's guarantee. THE CHEAPEST TRIAL, needing no new vocabulary and nothing enduring: mirror flo2's published surface into a SCRATCH reflow2 graph and run the tool that exists. Learn what the coordinate supports, then mirror a SECOND time with the far side moved, and see what happens to edges pointing at a node that changed. ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ THE TRIAL PROPOSED ABOVE WAS RUN, 2026-08-12 — AND IT FOUND A DEFECT ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ The section above ended: 'mirror flo2's published surface into a SCRATCH reflow2 graph and run the tool that exists. Learn what the coordinate supports, then mirror a SECOND time with the far side moved.' Done. Read-only against both real stores — flo2's graph was NEVER OPENED, because opening a store writes a schema stamp and would have silently upgraded his other project from 0.27.0; its committed export was imported into a scratch graph instead. ⭐ THE FIRST MIRROR IS CLEAN, AND THE BLACK BOX IS REAL. `export_surface` on flo2 gave 5 boundaries / 13 nodes exposed, 93 nodes and 201 edges WITHHELD as internal. `mirror_surface` took it: **13 nodes, 19 edges, ZERO collisions**, pinned to `mirror_content_hash sha256:0463d397…`. What arrived was 1 Project, 6 Components, 5 Interfaces, 1 Artifact, with **5 CONTAINS edges from `proj:flo2`** plus PROVIDES/CONSUMES/SPECIFIES — i.e. A PROJECT NODE CONTAINING ITS PARTS, with its published interfaces as ports. Then `cmp:service CONSUMES ifc:reflow2-design-api` was drawn as an ORDINARY local edge into a foreign node and worked exactly as the tool's description promises. 📌 TWO DETAILS THE DESCRIPTION DOES NOT SAY. Mirrored ids are NOT NAMESPACED — `ifc:reflow2-design-api` sits beside reflow2's own ids, and safety comes from collisions being REFUSED rather than from prefixing (unlike `compose_and_analyse`, which namespaces). And the COORDINATE IS NOT ON THE NODE: a mirrored node carries only `provenance: imported`; `mirror_of` / `mirror_content_hash` / `mirrored_at` live on the mirrored PROJECT, read back by `mirrors`. So a node cannot say whose it is without tracing to its Project, and `imported` is the same value a plain restore-from-backup sets — the two are indistinguishable at the node. 🛑🛑 THE SECOND MIRROR IS THE FINDING: **`mirror_surface` HAS NO REFRESH.** The far side was moved the way a real partner moves — `ifc:reflow2-design-api` renamed to `ifc:reflow2-tool-surface`, `medium` corrected REST → unspecified — and mirrored again: mirrored_nodes 1 mirrored_edges 0 collisions 12 <- everything from the first mirror mirror_content_hash null **Twelve of thirteen ids were refused as collisions WITH THE PREVIOUS MIRROR OF THE SAME DESIGN.** The refusal is correct and protective for a genuine cross-design clash, and its message says exactly that — 'Two designs using one id for different things is a naming conversation between their owners' — but that is not what happened, and the guard cannot tell the two cases apart. THE RESULTING STATE IS QUIETLY WRONG, which is what makes this worse than a plain failure: - the STALE `ifc:reflow2-design-api` is still present, still `medium: REST`, still the old name; - the renamed `ifc:reflow2-tool-surface` also arrived, with ZERO edges (`mirrored_edges: 0`), so it is orphaned; - the host's own `CONSUMES` edge STILL POINTS AT THE STALE NODE, and nothing said it moved; - **`mirrors` still reports the FIRST hash and `mirrored_at: 2026-08-12`** — so after a failed refresh the staleness register READS FRESH. The whole value of `mirror_content_hash` is the tool's own claim that 'a newer surface with a different hash means this mirror is stale', and a silent no-op leaves the consumer believing they are current when they are two changes behind. ⇒ **RE-MIRRORING ONE `mirror_of` IS A DIFFERENT OPERATION FROM MIRRORING A NEW DESIGN.** One is 'replace what I hold of theirs, at a new pin'; the other is 'add a stranger, and refuse anything that clashes'. Only the second is implemented, and the first is what a standing subscription is made of. This is the sharp edge the mutable/immutable framing predicted — immutability makes the first import clean and relocates the whole problem into refresh — and it is worse than predicted, because refresh is not awkward, it is absent. 📌 AND IT EXPLAINS THE ZERO-INSTANCE FINDING. The layer was built, exercised on a FIRST mirror, and never run twice — so the missing half was never visible. `cap:built-and-consumed-by-nothing` finds things nothing consumes; this is the adjacent failure, a capability consumed exactly once and therefore only half-tested. ⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED BY THIS TRIAL, so the result is not read wider than it is: whether a refresh SHOULD replace, merge, or refuse-and-report; what should happen to a host edge whose foreign target was renamed or withdrawn (reflow2 now refuses dangling edges outright, so a replace-style refresh has to answer this); and whether the host's committed export should CARRY mirrored nodes or merely NAME them by pin. All three are open.		Captured under the brainstorm skill, 2026-08-06, and EXTENDED the same day when Anthony generalised his own example from three graphs to an arbitrary federation with per-user scopes. The extension was folded into this node rather than minted as a new one because it answers the SAME question — which graphs a session can see — at a larger scale; the skill's 'several unrelated ideas mean several Decisions' does not apply to one idea getting sharper. Kept SEPARATE from dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency deliberately, even though Anthony raised both in one breath: this is ACCESS (which graphs a session can see), that is AUTHORITY (who may write intent into a design they do not own). They have different right answers, and one node holding both could only ever be half-answered. The federation makes the split sharper rather than blurrier — it localises the authority question to each ownership seam. The collaboration fact that bears on it and is new to the design: Anthony and his brother are split BY LAYER, not by project — Anthony on reflow2 core, his brother on the flo2 web app around it. That is not 'many people on one project' (req:sessions-share-a-graph) nor 'many projects at once' (req:many-designs-one-service); it is one owner per graph with the dependency running BETWEEN the owners, so the seam is simultaneously a technical boundary and a human one. req:many-people-and-many-projects-compose was written hours earlier assuming several people on one project and does not cover this shape. Anthony's user1/user2 example is the general form of the same thing. What is NOT recorded here, because he has not said it: whether the per-user scope is meant to be a PERMISSION (user2 may not reach A and B) or merely a CONVENIENCE (user2 has no reason to load them). Those differ the moment anything is hosted, and reflow2 has no authentication to enforce the former. SHARPENED 2026-08-12 with Anthony's union framing and the first trial evidence. The trial argues FOR it from an unexpected direction: two graphs agreed by being identically wrong about a shared boundary, and a shared node cannot disagree with itself. It also found the substrate objection — flo2 consumes reflow2's tool surface rather than its design, so unioning the design graphs joins the wrong two things for that particular dependency. SHARPENED AGAIN 2026-08-12 with the mutable/immutable framing, which collapses three of the four costs the union framing raised and makes the authority rule enforced by construction rather than by discipline. The load-bearing finding is that `mirror_surface` already implements it and has ZERO instances in either graph — so this thread is diagnosing an unused capability, not specifying a new one. THE TRIAL WAS RUN 2026-08-12 and found that mirror_surface has no refresh: a second mirror of the same design collides with itself, leaves the stale node and the host's edge to it in place, and leaves `mirrors` reporting the old pin — so the staleness register reads fresh after a failed refresh. That is the concrete blocker under every option in this node, because a federation of independently-moving projects is made of refreshes.proposedA dependency that is itself a reflow2 design can say so, and one that is not stays silent (crates/reflow2-core/tests/depends.rs, 2 cases added, 12 passing in the file). LINKED: graph_id round-trips through the store and appears in reflow2.toml as `graph_id = \'dynograph-foundation\'`. UNLINKED, which is the case that carries the doctrine: a second declaration without one round-trips as None AND its manifest entry contains no graph_id line at all — absence is stored as absence, so a reader can tell \'this dependency has no reflow2 design\' from \'nobody recorded whether it does\'. BLANK IS NOT A VALUE: a whitespace-only graph_id is treated as unstated rather than as a design whose id happens to be blank. A TEST-AUTHORING SLIP WORTH KEEPING: the first version of the blank case asserted the whole manifest contained no \'graph_id =\', which passed for the wrong reason and then failed for the right one — the (reflow2) header always emits the design's OWN graph_id, so the assertion had to be scoped to the dependency entry. The test caught the test.
OPEN — when a served skill's text depends on a served tool's DEFAULT, should that dependency be asserted so the build breaks when the default moves?
UNSETTLED. The instance is fixed; the class is not. Two dev_storyflow seats independently measured that the `brainstorm` skill instructed them to call `set_decision_status(proposed)` because 'add_decision defaults to accepted' — behaviour that changed on 2026-07-25 and is dated in add_decision's own description — so a conscientious agent made a redundant write on every brainstormed idea. PR #102 corrected the text on 2026-08-08. WHAT REMAINS OPEN IS THE SHAPE OF THE GUARD, and three were offered: (a) let a skill ASSERT the defaults it relies on, so skill_lint fails loudly at the moment the default changes rather than the text aging quietly; (b) GENERATE the sentence from the tool's actual default at build time, so it cannot disagree; (c) forbid a skill from naming a default at all and require it to state the RELATION instead — 'confirm the returned status is `proposed`' — which stays true across any default change and needs no new machinery. THERE IS AN OBVIOUS HOME: skill_lint.py already enforces that every tool a skill NAMES is served, and is run in CI on every push; asserting a default is the same kind of contract one field deeper.		Worth a decision rather than a fix note because of what the reporters said about it, which generalises past this skill: a served skill and a served tool ship from the SAME BINARY and disagreed about that binary's behaviour — the one place this class of drift should be impossible. And the skill is the half a session reads BEFORE acting, so it is the half that silently teaches the wrong model; here it taught it with emphasis ('This call is not optional'), which is exactly the wording that survives a skim. Their formulation is the reusable one: A RULE PINNED TO A BEHAVIOUR MUST NAME HOW TO RE-CHECK IT, NEVER JUST ITS VERDICT. Reported 2026-08-08 by dragon Boss f96eccd3 and api-boss 5d608b85, both by RUNNING it and reading the echo; api-boss stated their own bound honestly, that they did not test whether the redundant call is harmful, only that it is unnecessary.proposednothing
DEFERRED, SHAPE ONLY — vertical (tier-to-tier) linking: Alex means A GRAPH PER TIER linked vertically (option b), and the FORM waits behind the decomposition coverage check
🕐 DEFERRED 2026-08-14 BY ANTHONY — THE SHAPE ONLY, AND DEFERRED IS NOT DECLINED. Asked which form vertical linking should take, he chose to **fix `req:decomposition-covers-its-parent` FIRST and decide the shape after**: every option below makes decomposition more load-bearing, the coverage hole is already measured with a field instance, and settling a tier shape on top of a broken roll-up would bake the defect into precisely the boundary where nobody can see it. ⭐ **AND THE ASK IS NARROWER THAN 'OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN' SUGGESTS — ANTHONY CLARIFIED WHAT ALEX MEANS:** *'I think my brother is more indicating that each tier is its own reflow2 graph that others are linked to vertically.'* ⇒ **ALEX IS ASKING FOR OPTION (b): A GRAPH PER TIER, WITH VERTICAL LINKS BETWEEN THEM.** Not one graph with levels, and not a rendering. When this re-opens, (b) is the stated starting position rather than an open field — the others stay on the record as roads, not as equals. ⇒ WHAT IS SETTLED: nothing about the shape. ⇒ WHAT IS NOW LIVE WORK: `req:decomposition-covers-its-parent` (moved to **accepted** on his word) → `cap:decomposition-coverage-is-asked` (planned, `cmp:detect`). ⚠️ Its gap acknowledgement `decision:ack:1947285897ace4dc` — *'deferred on Anthony's word 2026-07-28… a handshake to design rather than a check to write'* — was WITHDRAWN, since a parked gap and a planned capability cannot both describe the same work. 🎯 **RE-ASK TRIGGER, NAMED SO THIS CANNOT DEGRADE INTO NEVER ASKED AGAIN** (the shape `dec:the-other-uaf-domains-wait-for-a-project-that-needs-them` set): re-open when the coverage check is BUILT and one of — (i) a real design is split across an authority boundary and someone needs a parent's number to mean something, (ii) `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs` is settled, since binding-versus-visible is this question in disguise, or (iii) a second user asks for tiers. ⚠️ WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS DEFERRAL WRONG: someone building a tier hierarchy in prose or file layout while waiting — the workaround that looks like patience and costs exactly what the deferral was meant to avoid. 📌 NOT ANSWERED BY THE RENDERING ROUTE: `dec:idea-a-view-can-slice-by-altitude-not-only-by-aspect` covers what a reader is SHOWN. It composes with this and does not substitute for it — a first version of that node claimed otherwise and was corrected. ═══════════════════════════════════════════════ RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Alex (`who:alex`) 2026-08-14, sharpened by Anthony's framing. ALEX'S WORDS: *'I found myself wanting a top level graph and then graphs for the different components. The top level graph could hold information about the project as a whole and be aware of the graphs for the subcomponents of the graph (UI, API, e2e tests, etc.). In those graphs, we can put the fine details of those components, such as storing information about how migrations are performed in the database. The top level graph could contain domain knowledge that is relevant to all the graphs. This is the system of systems concept.'* ANTHONY'S FRAMING: *'instead of being peer-to-peer, this is more tier-to-tier. If peer-to-peer linking is 'horizontal', this idea is more 'vertical' between tiers… you could have a 'leadership' level that doesn't need to know every detail… a 'management' layer that knows more… a 'worker' graph that knows details. At each layer, it is probably the exchange of breadth for depth. In the military, we had 'strategic', 'operational', and 'tactical'.'* ═══ ⭐⭐ WHY VERTICAL IS NOT HORIZONTAL REUSED ═══ **HORIZONTAL is an INTERFACE.** Two designs meet at a contract; neither contains the other; the coordinate is *'I designed against your published surface at this hash'* (`cap:mirror-surface`). A mirror is a REFERENCE. **VERTICAL is a DECOMPOSITION.** The upper tier holds intent, the lower tier holds requirements decomposed FROM it, and delivery ROLLS UP — a containment-and-satisfaction relation with arithmetic attached. ⇒ **reflow2 HAS decomposition INSIDE a graph and mirroring ACROSS graphs. It does not have decomposition ACROSS graphs.** That is the gap, and the existing federation work does not close it. ═══ 🛑 MEASURED CORRECTION TO THE RECORD — the parent direction is NOT built ═══ `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs` asserts *'THE MECHANISM FOR THE PARENT DIRECTION ALREADY EXISTS… ANTICIPATED and BUILT, not missing.'* **Too strong:** 1. `report.rs` rolls delivery up via `decomposed_children` = `self.incoming(parent_id, DECOMPOSES)` (`graph.rs:1143`). 2. Reads are scoped to the bound `graph_id` and `create_edge` resolves BOTH endpoints in scope — a `DECOMPOSES` edge between two graphs cannot be created at all. 3. ⇒ **Nothing rolls up across a design boundary.** `cap:derived-completion` is verified WITHIN one graph. 4. Mirroring does not rescue it: `export_surface` publishes published Interfaces, the artifacts that SPECIFY/REALIZE them, published Requirements and the Project — **no Verifications.** Delivery = satisfied AND realized AND PASSING CHECK, so **the evidence is exactly the part that does not cross.** 📌 That node warns *'READ THE EXPORT, NOT THE SUMMARY'* after making this error once, then makes it again a paragraph later about a different mechanism. ═══ ⭐⭐ THE TIER FRAMING TURNS A KNOWN DEFECT INTO A WORSE ONE ═══ `req:decomposition-covers-its-parent`: reflow2 rolls delivery UP and **never checks that children COVER the parent** — a parent split into two children addressing a tenth reports DELIVERED once both close. Measured instance: reflow's monolith split into 01a–01f, `context_management` and `self_improvement` present in all six originals, absent from all seven children, **unnoticed for months**. 🛑 **'EXCHANGE OF BREADTH FOR DEPTH' IS THE MECHANISM THAT HIDES IT.** A decomposition by SUBJECT drops what belongs to no single subject; trading breadth for depth is that drop made deliberately, tier after tier. Inside one graph a reader sees both sides. **Across an authority boundary they cannot: the strategic tier sees `delivered` and is structurally unable to see what fell between the children** — and it is the tier least likely to look. ═══ 📌 WHAT THE DESIGN ALREADY HOLDS ═══ · `dec:nested-graphs` (ACCEPTED 2026-07-25) — a graph per OWNERSHIP boundary, `level`s inside; *a graph per system* rejected as a RULE because every seam costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check. **Alex's UI/API/e2e split is depth under one owner, so under today's rule it is ONE graph — which is exactly the rule his ask strains.** · **THE LEADERSHIP TIER IS ALREADY THERE, EXPRESSED HORIZONTALLY** — that decision calls `docs/org-scale-vision.md`'s *'one graph the whole company plans in'* a road not taken and replaces it with *'the CEO's objectives are one design that others MIRROR.'* Anthony's point is that a mirror may be the wrong shape, and the roll-up finding says he is right: mirroring gives visibility, not arithmetic. · `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs` — requirements already cross; the **Decision** cannot. Its unanswered question is this one in disguise: **is a mirrored Decision BINDING on the far side, or only VISIBLE?** Binding is what a tier means; visible is what a peer means. · `dec:idea-many-graphs-one-store`, `dec:idea-one-owner-many-projects` — both open, both the ownership rule strained by people with depth and no authority boundary. 🛑 MODELLING TRAP TO NAME BEFORE ANYONE BUILDS: `Component.level` (component → subsystem → system → system_of_systems → enterprise) is an **ASSEMBLY** ladder — *part of*. Strategic/operational/tactical is an **AUTHORITY and ABSTRACTION** ladder — a tactical design is not PART OF a strategic one, it REALIZES it. Reusing `level` conflates two relations, and `hierarchy_issues` already reads it the assembly way. 📌 UAF, CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: `dec:the-other-uaf-domains-wait-for-a-project-that-needs-them` names its re-ask trigger for the four DOMAINS (information, materiel, personnel, states), not for layering. **This note does not trigger it.** OPTIONS — SHAPE DEFERRED, and (b) is what Alex is asking for. (a) ANSWER WITH THE ACCEPTED RULE — one graph, `level`s, `cap:scoped-analysis`. Correct today; occurred to neither user. (b) ⭐ **ALEX'S ASK** — VERTICAL AS A FIRST-CLASS RELATION: a graph per tier, cross-graph decomposition, intent down and EVIDENCE up. Cost: cross-graph edges, or a mirror carrying verification state; reopens `create_edge`'s endpoint invariant, which is deliberate and well-argued. (c) VERTICAL AS MIRRORING, AS TODAY. Cheapest, already decided; the parent can compute nothing about its children. (d) TIERS INSIDE ONE GRAPH — an abstraction ladder distinct from `Component.level`, tiers as a projection. No separate ownership or write locks, which is most of what a tier split is for. (e) ⭐ **CHOSEN AS SEQUENCING, NOT AS SHAPE** — fix the coverage check first. 📌 ALEX'S OWN EXAMPLE IS STILL UNHOUSED: *'how migrations are performed in the database'* is not a requirement, capability or interface — operational know-how attached to a component, with nowhere to go today but an Artifact or a requirement's prose.		Captured under the brainstorm skill, sharpened by Anthony's vertical/horizontal framing, deferred as to shape on his word, and then narrowed again when he clarified that Alex means a graph per tier rather than levels or a view. That clarification is recorded on the options list itself rather than only in prose, because the re-ask trigger will bring someone back to this node months from now and 'options, none chosen' would hand them a blank field when the user has in fact stated one. The re-ask trigger follows the precedent `dec:the-other-uaf-domains-wait-for-a-project-that-needs-them` set, including naming what would make the deferral wrong. The measured correction to `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs` lives here rather than being edited into that node, because withdrawing another node's claim deserves its own visibility rather than a quiet overwrite.proposednothing
OPEN — reflow2's ten views all slice by ASPECT and none by ALTITUDE, so 'show me the top level' has no projection behind it (a SEPARATE need from tier graphs, and NOT a licence to hard-code the DoDAF catalogue)
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-14, extending Alex's system-of-systems note. HIS WORDS: *'the graph is the systems engineering 'object' and can have all vertical tiers. However, when a user requests, give me the 'top level management' view, the agent should be able to get the info from the graph and render the user the requested 'view'. I don't know all the DoDAF and UAF views, but there is probably something for 'management' or 'vision'.'* ⚠️ **CORRECTED TWICE WITHIN THE HOUR. BOTH CORRECTIONS ARE ON HIS WORD AND BOTH MATTER.** **CORRECTION 1 — this does not answer Alex.** The first version claimed it *'may dissolve half of the tier question'* and read Alex's UI/API/e2e case as an altitude-view problem. Anthony: *'I think my brother is more indicating that each tier is its own reflow2 graph that others are linked to vertically.'* Alex wants SEPARATE GRAPHS PER TIER — a storage question. **The altitude view neither answers nor replaces it.** They compose: a tier-split design still wants an altitude view inside each graph. · **ALTITUDE** — how much detail a reader is shown. A VIEW question. No new store, no seam. *This node.* · **OWNERSHIP / TIER** — separate graphs, vertically linked. A STORE question. *`dec:idea-a-top-level-graph-holds-what-the-component-graphs-share`, option (b).* 📌 Kept on the record because an agent reading only Alex's words could build the view, declare the ask satisfied, and leave the real thing unbuilt — which is what this node nearly did. **CORRECTION 2 — option (c) is CLOSED: the UAF/DoDAF catalogue does not belong in reflow2.** It originally proposed rendering CV-1/CV-2/CV-3/AV-1 as first-class outputs. Anthony: *'we purposefully did not define every UAF/DoDAF view as those are not appropriate for every design project AND reflow2 was meant as 'design anything' and 'build anything'… I left rendering the reflow2 graph to be able to store any design structure/content and left the agent the responsible party for 'rendering' the drawing.'* **The division is deliberate: the graph stores any structure, the AGENT draws — mermaid, HTML, markdown, whatever suits.** `req:design-anything` (ACCEPTED) is what forbids binding a design-anything tool to one discipline's catalogue. See `dec:idea-a-view-that-does-not-apply-is-said-so-before-it-is-drawn` for the doctrine in full and for the idea it produced. ═══ ✅ MEASURED: TEN VIEWS EXIST, ZERO SLICE BY ALTITUDE ═══ `tools/render_views.py` renders `functional`, `flows`, `structural`, `traceability`, `released`, `decisions`, `evolution`, `provenance`, `fielded`, `budgets` — held to `dec:views-are-projections` (*'renderer fill-ins are defects'*) and `cap:bl-40` (no-extrapolation). 🛑 **EVERY ONE IS AN ASPECT VIEW: the whole design through one lens. None answers *'show me less.'*** An altitude view trades depth for breadth by FILTERING what is shown — Anthony's *'exchange of breadth for depth'* done by the renderer instead of by a decomposition, and therefore **losing nothing**, since the detail stays in the graph. That is its one advantage over the tier-graph route, and it is not an argument against tier graphs, which exist for ownership reasons a view cannot supply. 📌 THE DoDAF MAPPING, KEPT AS CONTEXT AND NOT AS A BUILD TARGET (see correction 2): **CV-1 is titled 'Vision'** and is the leadership-facing view with no reflow2 equivalent; **AV-1** is the executive summary; CV-2 taxonomy and CV-3 phasing are largely derivable from `Capability` + containment + Epochs, which `view_evolution` and `view_released` already partly cover. ⚠️ The exact UAF abbreviations were NOT verified against the spec and are deliberately not asserted. **The useful reading is that the MATERIAL for a leadership view is already in the graph — not that reflow2 should ship named standard views.** ═══ THE HARD PART ═══ 🛑 **WHAT COMPUTES WHICH NODES ARE 'TOP LEVEL'?** An altitude view is only honest if the filter derives from something the design already records. Candidates, none chosen: `Requirement.designation` (`published` vs `internal` — an audience distinction that already exists, and the strongest candidate), `priority`, `concern`, KPP status, distance from the Project root, an explicit tier property. **A filter chosen by the renderer rather than derived from the graph is precisely the 'renderer fill-in' the doctrine calls a defect**, so this cannot be settled by taste. 🛑 MODELLING TRAP: `Component.level` (component → subsystem → system → system_of_systems → enterprise) is an **ASSEMBLY** ladder — *part of*. Management/vision altitude is an **ABSTRACTION** ladder. A subsystem is part of a system; a management view is not part of a worker view. Reusing `level` would make `hierarchy_issues` report nonsense. OPTIONS. (a) ALTITUDE VIEW DERIVED FROM AN EXISTING PROPERTY — most likely `designation`. Cheapest, no schema change, testable against the no-extrapolation standard. (b) AN EXPLICIT TIER PROPERTY, projected on. `req:a-vocabulary-distinction-proves-it-is-read` demands a computation read it, which this supplies. ⚠️ If tier GRAPHS are ever built, this property and that boundary must not disagree about what a tier is. (c) ~~RENDER THE NAMED DoDAF VIEWS AS FIRST-CLASS OUTPUTS~~ — **CLOSED on Anthony's word.** The catalogue belongs to the agent, not to reflow2. (d) LEAVE IT — an agent can answer 'show me the top level' conversationally from `graph_report`. Counter: unrepeatable between sessions. ⚠️ Note this is NOT the same as correction 2: leaving the DRAWING to the agent is doctrine, while leaving the FILTER to the agent's judgement is a renderer fill-in. The distinction is what separates this option from (a). 📌 RELATED AND SEPARATE: `dec:idea-document-generation` and `dec:idea-outward-docs-are-rendered-from-the-graph` ask what to DO with a rendered view; this asks whether the projection exists at all.		Captured under the brainstorm skill and corrected twice on Anthony's word within the hour — once for misreading Alex's ask as a rendering need, once for proposing that reflow2 ship the named DoDAF views. Both corrections are kept in the text rather than silently replacing it, following `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs`' precedent, because the two failure modes are worth seeing together: an agent that finds a cheaper adjacent problem and declares the original satisfied, and an agent that reaches for a familiar standard catalogue in a tool deliberately built not to have one. The second is the more likely to recur, since the catalogue is genuinely useful and the pull toward it feels like expertise rather than like a mistake. What survives both corrections is the measurement — ten aspect views, zero altitude views — and the open question of what could honestly compute the filter.proposednothing
OPEN — should reflow2 be able to tell an agent that a requested view does not apply to this design, given 'would rendering it require invention?' is the same question as 'is it applicable?'
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-14. HIS WORDS, restating settled doctrine first and then adding the new part: *'we purposefully did not define every UAF/DoDAF view as those are not appropriate for every design project AND reflow2 was meant as 'design anything' and 'build anything' type construct. This is why I left rendering the reflow2 graph to be able to store any design structure/content and left the agent the responsible party for 'rendering' the drawing. It'd be like if I requested you to render me an OV-1 of reflow2 right now — you'd refer to the graph and pull what you need; then you'd build me a mermaid diagram or some html file or markdown file to show what the OV-1 is. That being said, sometimes not every systems engineering view is applicable to a given design. Feel like the agent should be able to also say, 'an OV-1 isn't applicable for your design; are you sure you want me to generate?''* ═══ 📌 THE DOCTRINE THIS RESTS ON, RECORDED SO IT STOPS BEING RE-PROPOSED ═══ **THE UAF/DoDAF VIEW CATALOGUE IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN REFLOW2.** The division is: the GRAPH stores any design structure or content; the AGENT renders the drawing, in whatever medium suits — mermaid, HTML, markdown. Enumerating standard views inside reflow2 would bind a 'design anything' tool to one discipline's catalogue, and `req:design-anything` (ACCEPTED) is the requirement that forbids it. ⚠️ **A SESSION PROPOSED EXACTLY THAT AN HOUR EARLIER** — option (c) of `dec:idea-a-view-can-slice-by-altitude-not-only-by-aspect` suggested rendering CV-1/CV-2/CV-3/AV-1 as first-class outputs. **Closed on his word.** It is recorded here because the pull toward hard-coding a familiar catalogue is strong and will recur. ═══ ⭐⭐ THE FINDING: APPLICABILITY AND INVENTION ARE THE SAME QUESTION ═══ `dec:views-are-projections` already holds that **a view is a projection of the graph and renderer fill-ins are DEFECTS**; `cap:bl-40` holds SYNTHESIZE to a no-extrapolation standard. 🛑 **NOW NOTICE WHAT 'NOT APPLICABLE' ACTUALLY MEANS.** A view does not apply to a design precisely when the graph lacks the material that view projects from. And if the material is absent, **rendering it anyway REQUIRES the agent to invent the content** — which is the defect the doctrine already forbids. So: > *'Is this view applicable?'* and *'would drawing it force me to make things up?'* are **the same question asked at two different times.** ⇒ This is not a new principle. **It is the existing no-fill-in rule moved EARLIER — from a defect caught after the fact, to a question asked before the pen touches paper.** That reframing is what makes it worth building: the rule currently has no moment at which it is enforced, because the only party who could notice is the agent that is already mid-render and motivated to produce something. ⇒ AND IT MAKES APPLICABILITY COMPUTABLE RATHER THAN A JUDGEMENT. *'Does an OV-1 apply?'* is a matter of taste. *'Does this graph hold operational actors, activities and the exchanges between them, and how many?'* is a count. **The second is answerable by reflow2 without reflow2 ever knowing what an OV-1 is.** ═══ THE SHAPE THAT KEEPS THE CATALOGUE OUT ═══ The agent DECLARES the projection it intends to draw — the node types and edge types it will read. reflow2 answers with what it actually holds and what is absent. The agent then either renders, or says *'an OV-1 isn't applicable for your design; are you sure?'* **reflow2 never learns the view's name, so the catalogue stays with the agent and the counting stays with the graph.** That division is the same one `dec:three-party-checks` already sets: the LLM speaks, the graph counts, the human decides. ⚠️ AND IT MUST ASK, NEVER REFUSE. His wording is *'are you sure you want me to generate?'* — a warning with a way through, not a block. Consistent with `dec:ask-not-repair` and `dec:report-dont-judge`. A sparse view is sometimes exactly what the user wants to see; an empty OV-1 is itself a finding about the design. OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) LEAVE IT TO THE AGENT — status quo. It can already look at the graph and judge. Counter: unrepeatable between sessions, and the party judging is the one being asked to produce a deliverable, which is the weakest possible position for saying 'this cannot honestly be drawn'. (b) ⭐ REFLOW2 ANSWERS A DECLARED PROJECTION — the agent names node/edge types, reflow2 returns counts and absences. Keeps the catalogue out, makes the answer computable and repeatable. Counter: an agent can declare the wrong projection and get a confident answer to the wrong question. (c) A SERVED SKILL carries the discipline — a render-a-view skill whose steps include checking the material before drawing. Cheapest, and consistent with skills being where disciplines live. Counter: it is another instruction, and `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session` is the standing evidence that instructions lose to urgency. (d) HARD-CODE PER-VIEW APPLICABILITY RULES. **CLOSED on Anthony's word** — this is the catalogue-in-reflow2 route `req:design-anything` forbids. 🛑 THE LIMIT WORTH STATING: material presence is necessary but not sufficient. A view can be structurally renderable and still be the wrong instrument for the domain — an OV-1 of a machine shop might have actors and activities to draw and still be a category error. **Counting cannot see that; only the human can.** So (b) at its best reports *'here is what I hold and what I lack'*, and the applicability verdict stays with the person — which is the same honest division reflow2 uses everywhere else.		Captured under the brainstorm skill. Recorded separately from the altitude-view node because they are separately answerable: reflow2 could learn to report what a declared projection would find without ever gaining an altitude view, and vice versa. The reason this is worth a node rather than a note is the equivalence at its centre — applicability and invention turn out to be one question asked at two times — which converts a matter of taste into a count, and gives the existing no-fill-in doctrine the enforcement moment it currently lacks. Anthony's restatement of why the view catalogue is deliberately absent is recorded here too, because a session proposed hard-coding it an hour earlier and the pull toward a familiar standard catalogue will recur.proposednothing
OPEN — should reflow2 formalize agent-authored feedback written FOR another agent, and what exactly is gained by cutting the human out of the loop?
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-14, after relaying a Grok 4.6 feedback file from one of Alex's projects. HIS WORDS: *'This type of feedback is generated by the agent for a project via something like the statement of 'reflow2 is still a development project - please note any issues or gaps or opportunities to improve reflow2 at path/to/feedback.md'. Then the agent provides this feedback. It is probably more 'machine-to-machine' type feedback… we should probably formalize this feedback option within reflow2 with the specific direction of that the agent writing it can write it specifically for another agent - this is cutting out the human to provide specific feedback from one agent to another (you in this case), so it can probably be very efficient and remove any fluff that is needed when a human is in the loop.'* ═══ ⭐⭐ THE EVIDENCE FOR IT IS ALREADY IN: THE INFORMAL VERSION WORKED ═══ The file this idea came from produced **four independently reproduced defects** (`fact:agent-feedback-corroborated-2026-08-14`) — the near-duplicate guard firing on golden-thread siblings and across node types, `add_decision` unable to merge without resending the body, correct capture inflating loop debt, and `get_node` missing silently on a type with one instance. **A different agent, on a different model, on a different graph, hit four of them the same day without having read the file.** That yield came from an ad-hoc prompt with no format, no channel and no tooling. Formalising raises the yield of something already proven rather than betting on an untested idea. 😀 AND THE CAPTURE OF THIS VERY NODE SUPPLIED A SEVENTH INSTANCE OF ITS OWN HEADLINE DEFECT: creating this Decision was REFUSED as a near-duplicate of `fact:agent-feedback-corroborated-2026-08-14` — the TemporalFact recording that feedback, written two minutes earlier. A fact about what was reported and a decision about what channel should carry it are not the same write. ═══ 🛑 THE COUNTER, AND IT IS ABOUT WHICH HUMAN IS BEING CUT OUT ═══ **Two different humans are in this loop, and only one of them can be removed.** · **THE ROUTING HUMAN** — the person who currently has to read an agent's friction note, understand it, and relay it. Removing them is pure gain and is what Anthony is describing. · **THE CONSENTING HUMAN** — the person whose project the feedback was written inside. `report-friction` redacts the user's design content and **never files without asking**, and the Grok file honoured that unprompted: *'Per report-friction: do not open a public issue without asking. This file is the local log.'* ⚠️ **A channel that carries agent-authored feedback off the machine without that second human is an exfiltration path**, however good the intent. `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content` exists for exactly this, and the file shows the discipline working — *'Product/design content is summarized by type and count, not quoted.'* ⇒ THE HONEST FORM: **the agent WRITES freely for another agent; the human still decides whether it LEAVES.** Efficiency is gained in the authoring and the reading, never in the consent. ═══ 🛑 A SHARPER COUNTER TO 'REMOVE THE FLUFF' ═══ **What made that file valuable was not its brevity — it was that its claims were CHECKABLE.** Item 5 named the tool, the arguments and the observed result (`get_node({node_type: Project, id: 'proj:…'})` → `{node: null}`), so it could be re-run here in one call and confirmed on reflow2's own graph. Its neighbours that were only narrated could not be. ⚠️ **Optimising for compactness could delete precisely what made corroboration possible.** The right target for a machine-to-machine format is REPRODUCIBILITY, not terseness: tool name, arguments, observed result, expected result, and an honest *what I did not check*. The Grok file has all of those — including a *'Gaps (mine / process)'* section admitting it skipped `compare_designs` and guessed a Project id. **That self-reporting is not fluff, and it is the first thing a brevity-optimised format would drop.** 📌 IT ALSO SEPARATED CONFIRMED FROM UNCONFIRMED WITHOUT BEING ASKED. Its `get_instructions` truncation report did NOT reproduce here — the payload arrived complete — which is only discoverable because the report was specific enough to test. A format should make that distinction structural rather than leave it to the writer's conscience. OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) EXTEND `report-friction` WITH AN AGENT-TO-AGENT MODE — one skill, a second output shape aimed at a maintainer's agent rather than a maintainer. Cheapest, and it inherits redaction discipline already written and honoured in the field. (b) A NEW SERVED SKILL, leaving `report-friction` human-facing. Cleaner separation; two skills that must not drift apart. (c) A STRUCTURED FORMAT (fields, not prose) so the receiving agent can parse and triage rather than read. Highest leverage for the receiver. ⚠️ The four corroborated items were reproduced from PROSE that happened to name tools and arguments, so a schema helps only if it MANDATES exactly those fields. (d) A GRAPH NODE TYPE for feedback. 🛑 Blocked by a real constraint: the authoring agent works inside SOMEONE ELSE'S design, so the note cannot be a node in reflow2's graph without crossing a boundary. It must travel as a DOCUMENT — the same wall `dec:idea-a-top-level-graph-holds-what-the-component-graphs-share` hit, where nothing crosses between graphs but a published surface. (e) LEAVE IT AD-HOC — the prompt already works. Counter: it worked because Anthony happened to ask for it and happened to relay it. Nothing makes that repeatable, and the second and third user reports both arrived as email. 📌 THE CONSENT HALF IS ALREADY AN OPEN NODE, AND ALEX ASKED FOR IT HIMSELF: `dec:idea-feedback-collection-is-asked-once-and-recorded` — *'put in an update that asks me if I want to collect feedback and store my decision in the graph.'* **This is the CONTENT half of the same mechanism: his node decides whether feedback may travel, this one decides what it says and who it is written for.** Neither is built. ⚠️ THE STANDING REASON THIS MATTERS: every defect in the last two increments was found by a first-time user, by running two real projects at each other, or by an agent writing down what fought it — none by reading code, none by a gate.		Captured under the brainstorm skill. Two counters are recorded ahead of the options because both cut against the framing rather than against the idea, and an implementer reading only the proposal would miss them: 'cutting out the human' describes two different humans and only the routing one can go, and the value of the example file came from its reproducibility rather than its economy — so a format optimised for the stated goal of removing fluff would likely delete the self-reported process gaps and the tool-and-arguments detail that made four items checkable in a single session. Kept separate from `dec:idea-feedback-collection-is-asked-once-and-recorded` because that node asks whether feedback may be collected at all and this asks what it contains and who writes it for whom.proposedAgent-to-agent feedback is written for reproduction, not for brevity — and the human whose project it was written inside still decides whether it leaves
DECIDED — allocation is deferred to the last responsible moment: per-capability scope with a project default, and never allocating is a legitimate terminal state
✅ **DECIDED 2026-08-14 ON ANTHONY'S WORD, ON THE TWO SETTLED HALVES. The third sub-question is SPLIT OUT to `dec:idea-is-allocation-running-ahead-of-the-seams` (parked, trigger named) rather than left holding this one open.** THE IDEA, Anthony's words 2026-08-08: *'the allocation of functions to systems/services should be done as late as possible (agreeing that doing it at genesis is too early). I feel like doing it at the last possible moment before functional allocation to system/service is the right call.'* It answers a caution raised against `dec:idea-the-ility-chooses-the-allocation-graph`, which proposed asking at GENESIS what quality attribute a system is for: the objection was that at genesis you frequently do not know yet, and premature commitment costs as much as late discovery. His resolution keeps the question and moves WHEN it is asked — to the moment allocation must actually be committed. THE HOOK ALREADY EXISTS: `unallocated_capability` is already a detected gap, so 'capabilities exist, bound to nothing' is visible from graph state alone — the same state-not-history discipline `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` commits to. Nothing new needs remembering. **(a) PER-PROJECT OR PER-CAPABILITY — SETTLED 2026-08-08. PER-CAPABILITY SCOPE, PROJECT-LEVEL DEFAULT, RE-ASKED ONLY ON DIVERGENCE.** The schema already leans this way: DimensionAssessment attaches to ANY node, not to the Project, and a telemetry path and a config service in one system genuinely want different objectives. The recurrence worry — a mature design allocates continuously, so the moment repeats — is answered by machinery that already exists: an acknowledgement LAPSES when the shape it was accepted about changes, so the answer is recorded once and re-asked only when a new capability diverges. Recurring without being repetitive. ⚠️ Held most loosely of the three by the person who proposed it, and worth revisiting if the divergence test proves hard to state. **(b) IS 100% ALLOCATION AGAINST 0% SEAMS AN INVERSION — MOVED OUT 2026-08-14 to `dec:idea-is-allocation-running-ahead-of-the-seams`.** It is unanswerable from data the graph holds: 156 ALLOCATED_TO edges carry only `weight_basis`, nothing dates an allocation, and 1 of 320 ChangeEvents mentions one. Its trigger is 'allocation timing becomes recordable at all'. **Splitting it is the ruling: two settled halves should not read as undecided because a third is blocked on a substrate that does not exist.** **(c) A DESIGN THAT NEVER REACHES THE MOMENT — CLOSED 2026-08-08**, answered by doctrine that already existed. `maturity_report` deliberately refuses to say where a design SHOULD be, and its own output says a demonstrator *'may sit here forever and be right'*. So never allocating is a **LEGITIMATE TERMINAL STATE**, not an error or a stalled process. The only thing any future prompt owes is to be acknowledgeable like every other gap — which every gap already is. ⚠️ **COUNTER-ARGUMENT, RECORDED BESIDE THE RULING RATHER THAN ANSWERED BY IT, AND FLAGGED TO HIM BEFORE HE ACCEPTED:** the last-responsible-moment principle assumes deciding late costs less than deciding wrong, which holds only when deferral is free. Here it may not be — artifacts get written against an assumed structure long before anyone calls `allocate`. **If real files already embody a de facto allocation, then deferring the decision defers only the RECORD of it, and the graph arrives late to something the build already did.** That is the as-designed-versus-as-built gap `granularity_report` exists to surface, and it argues the trigger should watch **ARTIFACTS APPEARING** rather than the `allocate` call. Accepted with this open.		Revised under revise-design with a snapshot taken while all three sub-questions still read open (epoch:allocation-subquestions-narrowed, seq 289), so the state before the narrowing survives. Status stays `proposed` deliberately: two sub-questions closing does not settle the parent, and flipping it would assert a decision Anthony has not made. The most valuable thing added is not either answer but the finding under (b) — that the agreed method could not be executed, and why. A parked question with a stated trigger is recognisable when someone walks past the answer months later; a parked question with none is indistinguishable from a forgotten one, which is a distinction reflow2 cannot currently draw at all (detect_defects reports parked decisions as `orphan_node`, info severity, and two of the four outstanding structural defects are exactly that).acceptednothing
OPEN — should an acknowledged gap be able to declare a machine-checkable re-review trigger, rather than stating its retirement condition in prose?
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Nothing here is intent. Raised by an external agent-side field report, 2026-08-11 (fact:external-agent-side-report-2026-08-11, redacted). WHAT THEY OBSERVED. Several of their acknowledgements carried explicit retirement conditions written into the reason — of the shape 'revisit when the first implementation exists', 'replace this when that work is scheduled'. One of those conditions had been true for weeks and nothing surfaced it. `reviewed_gaps` says an acknowledgement is 'worth re-reading when the design shifts' and nothing detects the shift. Their line: acknowledgements are where gaps go to be forgotten SAFELY, and the safety decays silently. ⚠️ NARROWER THAN THEY WROTE, AND THE NARROWING IS THE POINT. Expiry machinery EXISTS: a review expires when the set of nodes it judged changes, and `req:set-scoped-acknowledgement-keys-on-its-rule` (accepted) already fixed the case where a set-scoped acknowledgement expired merely because the design grew. So this is NOT 'acknowledgements never expire'. It is that the trigger is always the same trigger — the affected set moved — and a human-stated condition ('when an artifact of this kind first appears') is invisible to it. Recording the narrow version matters, because the wide version reads as a defect in something that works. IDEAS, unranked: (a) A typed re-review trigger on the acknowledgement: a node type appearing, a count crossing zero, an edge arriving. Expressive, and it is a small query language nobody asked for — every one of those is a new thing to specify, validate and explain. (b) No new vocabulary: have `loop_status` flag acknowledgements older than N design-changes as re-review candidates. Crude, cheap, and it needs no condition to be stated correctly at write time — which matters, because the person acknowledging a gap is the least likely to predict what would falsify it. (c) Let the acknowledgement name the NODE TYPE it is waiting on, and nothing more. Covers the reported case exactly ('when the first artifact exists') at a fraction of (a)'s cost. (d) Nothing. `req:review-expires-when-what-it-judged-changes` is already proposed and unbuilt; finish that before adding a second expiry axis beside it. ⚠️ THE TRAP: a stated condition that is WRONG is worse than no condition, because it reads as watched. An acknowledgement saying 'revisit when X' that nothing evaluates is the same false-assurance shape as a `planned` verification silencing a gap — which this project already refuses. Whatever is offered must actually be evaluated, or must not be offered. 📌 SITS BESIDE `req:review-expires-when-what-it-judged-changes` (proposed): that one is about the trigger being too NARROW (only the set, not the content). This is about the trigger being SINGULAR. Same subsystem, different complaint, and they should be read together.		A real acknowledgement carried a condition that came true and nothing noticed. But expiry machinery exists and works on a different trigger, so the honest finding is that the trigger is singular rather than absent — and a stated-but-unevaluated condition would be a worse failure than the current silence, because it would read as watched.proposednothing
OPEN — should unplanned work take an IN-BETWEEN version (v0.25.1) so planned increments never renumber, instead of slipping them all up one?
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony thinking out loud 2026-08-08, immediately after `dec:an-unplanned-cut-slips-every-later-increment-by-one` was accepted and applied, and in direct response to the id-churn cost that applying it exposed. HIS WORDS: 'if we can't slip a version, just add the in-between version like v0.25.1 for the planned change, then preplanned versions can stay in place (their id stays the same) and we can add unplanned versions as v0.25.1 or v0.26.4 or whatever makes sense - I'm sure this has a drawback also as it probably doesn't fit when you should do a minor bump versus whatever the third decimal place is called.' (The third decimal is the PATCH number, semver's MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.) THE IDEA: an unplanned cut is numbered BETWEEN the planned ones rather than consuming one of them, so `epoch:v0260-planned` stays v0.26.0 forever, its id keeps matching its content, and nothing renumbers. WHAT IT SOLVES, and it is the real prize: the id churn is not merely reduced, it is ELIMINATED — no renaming, no risk to the snapshot history `dec:arrival-delta` reads plan movement from, and no ids that lie about their content. It also removes the cascade entirely: today's slip touched four epochs, and a scheme where planned numbers are stable touches none. THE DRAWBACK HE NAMED HIMSELF, AND IT IS REAL AND MEASURABLE ON TODAY'S CUT: patch is not a free slot. This project's CHANGELOG defines its own buckets — patch is 'bug fixes, doc fixes, tests, refactors, perf, and behavior changes that make a silent failure LOUD', minor is 'a change to the SHAPE of the tool surface (new/changed params, changed result shapes)'. v0.25.0 was MINOR by that table for exactly two reasons: `HealProposal.would_destroy` and `HealIssue.hubs`, both new result fields. Everything else in it was fixes. So v0.25.1 would have been WRONG for what actually shipped — by a hair, and the hair matters. THE HARM IS CONCRETE RATHER THAN PURIST, and the same table states it: patch means the consumer 'updates blindly; skills and calls unchanged'; minor means they 'may need to notice'. Numbering a shape change as a patch tells Alex he can update without looking when a result shape moved. That is a signal saying SAFE without having checked — the failure family this whole session kept finding. OTHER SHAPES, none chosen: (a) HYBRID — insert as a patch when the unplanned work genuinely IS a patch (the common case), slip only when it is genuinely minor (rarer). Keeps ids stable most of the time and keeps semver honest; costs two rules instead of one and a judgement at each cut, though that judgement is one the CHANGELOG table already forces. (b) DISSOLVE IT — name planned increments by CONTENT and assign the number at cut time from what actually shipped (`dec:idea-a-planned-increment-is-named-by-content-not-by-number`). Then neither slipping nor inserting is a problem, because no plan ever holds a number it can lose. This is the only option where the question stops existing rather than being answered. (c) REDEFINE THE BUCKETS — pre-1.0 semver gives latitude and the project has not made a stability commitment ('Major 1.0 — Deferred'), so it could declare that 0.x.y patch admits additive-but-non-breaking changes. Cheapest to write and the most expensive to be wrong about, since it weakens the one signal consumers act on blindly. (d) KEEP THE ACCEPTED RULE and pay the id cost, treating ids as birth numbers rather than delivery numbers. WORTH NOTING: (a) and (b) COMPOSE — content-named plans plus semver-honest numbering at cut time is arguably the same answer reached from two directions.		Recorded as an idea rather than as a change because Anthony was explicitly thinking out loud, offered the counter-argument himself in the same breath, and the accepted rule it revisits was settled minutes earlier. Nothing is superseded: `dec:an-unplanned-cut-slips-every-later-increment-by-one` stands and the slip has been applied. What makes this worth a node rather than a passing remark is that it is a genuine alternative to a rule with a known cost, and the cost is what prompted it — so a later session choosing between them needs both on the record, with the semver objection attached to the idea rather than lost in conversation.proposednothing
OPEN — should the backlog stop being a 581 KB markdown file and become graph nodes, and what is missing before it can?
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — Anthony, 2026-08-04: 'It's weak at holding what we learned about the tool while using it, because that lands in markdown by convention, and markdown doesn't get queried — it gets grepped, by someone who already knows what they're looking for. this needs to be solved. I wanted to stop using the BL, but it keeps growing as you say - instead, I wanted everything in the graph.' His preference is stated and is NOT recorded as settled: what 'everything in the graph' means mechanically is the open part. THE MEASUREMENT, taken 2026-08-04. `docs/backlog.md` is 3,350 lines / 581,031 bytes across 132 rows. Of the 8 rows filed in one session (BL-205..212), SIX are referenced by ZERO graph nodes. The file is not a registered Artifact, so `coverage_report` does not count it and no checksum tracks it. FOUR things were re-derived in that same session that were already written down somewhere: BL-205 (third rediscovery), `dec:export-once-per-pr` (accepted, invisible, violated and then re-announced as new), BL-70's alternatives family (nearly re-proposed), and dev_storyflow's hand-made doc-intent scope table (re-derived worse from filenames). THE FRAME IS ALREADY ACCEPTED AND THE BACKLOG VIOLATES IT. `dec:what-lives-where` states the rule: 'the design record should stop being PROSE YOU NAVIGATE and become A GRAPH YOU QUERY, with the prose kept as provenance hanging off the nodes it produced.' It carries a falsifiable test — 'IF REFLOW2 WORKS, STORYFLOW WOULD NOT HAVE NEEDED dev_storyflow… If a user still ends up splitting their repo to stay sane, reflow2 has not delivered what this decision claims.' THE SAME TEST GENERALISES AND REFLOW2 CURRENTLY FAILS IT ON ITSELF: if reflow2 works, reflow2 would not need a 581 KB markdown backlog. It is also the exact failure the dev_storyflow api-boss measured in that fleet's MEMORY.md — 'an index that must be read IN FULL to be useful has a hard ceiling', 20 KB against a 17 KB limit with everything past the line silently invisible. The backlog is 29 times that size. WHY IT HAS RESISTED THE OBVIOUS FIX — A BACKLOG ROW IS NOT ONE THING. Reading the eight rows from one session, they are at least four: (i) DEFECTS AGAINST SHIPPED CAPABILITIES (BL-205 loop_status too large, BL-206 the gate's truncated sweep, BL-208 the inert CI guard, BL-209 the blind orphan detector); (ii) UNBUILT WORK (BL-186 the folder driver, BL-211 genesis-from-a-folder); (iii) OPEN DESIGN QUESTIONS (BL-207's fix-shape fork); (iv) DISCOVERED LIMITS (BL-212, chronology cannot be recovered from a folder). Three of those four already have a home: unbuilt work is a Capability at `planned` behind a Requirement, an open question is a `proposed` Decision — which is what this very node is — and a discovered limit is a Constraint or DesignRule. ⭐ THE ONE THAT HAS NO HOME, AND IT IS THE LARGEST CATEGORY: a defect found by USING the tool. reflow2 has no way to say 'this capability is built, VERIFIED, and does not do what it claims.' `Verification` answers whether a check passes — and every one of BL-205/206/208/209 sat under a passing check. `DriftEvent` answers whether the code moved away from the design — and in all four cases the code and the design AGREED, and both were wrong. HEAL's issues are computed from graph shape, not recorded observations, so they vanish between runs. That absence is why these rows land in markdown: there is nothing to write them to. OPTIONS, none chosen. (a) ROUTE EACH ROW TO THE TYPE IT ALREADY IS and add no vocabulary. Cheapest, and it works for three categories of four. Counter: for the defect category it loses the finding — 'this is broken, here is the measurement, here is how it was found' becomes 'here is a need', which erases the evidence and reads as intent rather than as a bug. (b) A `Finding`/`Defect` NODE TYPE carrying claim, evidence, when observed, and what it bears on. Counter, and it is strong: this project has proposed a node type and WITHDRAWN it after measuring TWICE in one week (`Attestation` → `TemporalFact`, `Hazard` → `DesignRule` + `CONSTRAINS`), so the prior against new vocabulary is heavy — and `TemporalFact` ('a time-bounded assertion true only between two epochs') may already be the shape, since a defect is exactly 'this was true of the build from epoch X until the fix'. (c) EVERYTHING BECOMES A PROPOSED DECISION. Counter: 132 proposed Decisions would swamp `where-am-i` and the decision list, and most rows are not forks between real alternatives. (d) KEEP THE MARKDOWN BUT DERIVE IT FROM THE GRAPH rather than maintaining it by hand. In-house precedent exists and is unused for this: `dec:views-are-projections` ('a view is a projection of the graph; renderer fill-ins are defects') and `tools/render_views.py` already render DoDAF-flavoured views into docs/viewpoints.md. The backlog is simply not one of them. Counter: this solves RETRIEVAL and not CAPTURE — it only helps once the content is in the graph, so it composes with (a)/(b) rather than competing. (e) DO NOTHING AND ACCEPT THE COST, recorded so it is a choice rather than a default: the backlog is readable by a human today, and the re-derivation cost, while real, has been paid without anyone stopping work. --- ADDED 2026-08-04, ANTHONY ASKED WHAT A NODE AND AN EDGE CAN ACTUALLY HOLD. THE ANSWER IS THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES EVERY OPTION ABOVE, AND IT IS MEASURED. --- WHAT A NODE CAN HOLD. The schema's whole type system is `string` (170 declarations), `enum` (89), `float` (34), `bool` (10), `int` (7). There is NO dedicated text type and NO `max_length` anywhere in any schema file — `string` IS the narrative field and it is unbounded in practice: the `decision` property of this very node runs to several thousand characters without complaint. Every type carries at least one narrative-shaped field (`Decision.decision` + `.rationale`, `Requirement.statement`, `Capability.description`, `Component.purpose`), and Decision requires only `name` and `decision`. AND THE SCHEMA IS ADDITIVE: dynograph-core's own test is named `extra_properties_allowed` — 'Extra properties should be allowed (schema is additive)' — so a property the schema never declared is stored rather than refused. It validates the TYPES of declared properties and enforces the required ones; anything else passes through. WHAT AN EDGE CAN HOLD. More than assumed: 44 of the 60 edge types carry properties, across 46 distinct property names, and several are free text — `note`, `evidence`, `rationale`, `diff_summary`. SIXTEEN CARRY NOTHING, and they are all bookkeeping or temporal: AT_EPOCH, HAS_SNAPSHOT, VALID_FROM, VALID_TO, ABOUT_ENTITY, OCCURS_DURING, PERFORMED_IN, and — worth noting against (BL-212) — PRECEDES. The edge that would say 'this document came before that one' can carry no evidence for the claim. ⭐ THE STING, AND IT IS WHY THIS BELONGS ON THIS NODE RATHER THAN AS TRIVIA: ONLY 52 PROPERTIES IN THE ENTIRE SCHEMA ARE `fulltext: true`, and those are the only ones `search_design` indexes. The distribution is name 20 · description 12 · statement 5 · summary 3, then singletons: rationale, decision, purpose, question, evidence, intent, effects, design_intent, criteria, context_setter, answer, title. So `Decision.decision` IS indexed and — measured — `Decision.rationale` is NOT. Every 'why' written into a rationale field is stored and unsearchable. The same is true of any extra property invented under the additive rule: stored, not indexed, not returned by `describe_schema`, read by no report. That is this project's recurring declared-and-read-by-nothing shape one rung worse, because it is UNDECLARED and read by nothing. THE CONSEQUENCE FOR EVERY OPTION ABOVE: UNLIMITED PROSE IN A NODE IS GREP BY ANOTHER NAME. What makes the graph queryable rather than navigable is the `fulltext:` flag, the typed properties and the EDGES — not the narrative. Moving the backlog into nodes therefore helps only to the extent a row becomes STRUCTURE: which capability the defect bears on (an edge), what was measured (a typed property), whether it is still true (a status or a temporal bound), with the prose hanging off that as explanation rather than as the record. A row moved in as one long `description` rebuilds `backlog.md` inside the graph with worse ergonomics and no gain — and that failure would be invisible, because it would look like progress. AND IT PUTS A NUMBER ON THE DEPENDENCY WITH `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption`: with 52 lexically-indexed fields and no vector half, 'query the graph' today means ranked keyword search over names, descriptions and statements. Better than grep — cross-node, ranked, no filename needed — but the same KIND of retrieval. The ceiling on 'an agent can work from the graph alone' is set by that open question, so the two ideas should be weighed together rather than separately.
