Anthony, 2026-07-25, from work he has done: State Funerals for US Presidents (he worked President Bush's) — hundreds to thousands of people planning simultaneously, an echeloned plan (NORTHCOM OPLAN → JTF-NCR → each service → each unit), and events arriving during the run that the plan must react to in minutes. His words: 'using a common github repo may no longer work'. THE DECOMPOSITION THAT MAKES IT TRACTABLE IS ALREADY DECIDED: dec:nested-graphs (c) says a design is its own graph per ownership boundary, so a thousand planners are not a thousand writers on one store — they are ~100-200 graphs of 5-20 writers each, linked by mirrored published surfaces. Echelons own their plans; that is both the software answer and how the organisation actually works. FOUR ROADS for the tier itself. (a) NOTHING NEW — federation plus git, accepting minutes of latency; cheapest, and it fails only the react-in-near-real-time half. (b) ONE PROCESS PER GRAPH over streamable HTTP (rmcp has the transport, reflow2 serves stdio only), writes going to the store and the export DERIVED as the archival record; at federation scale the process-per-project cut already named in dec:central-host is also the natural sharding — one process per ownership boundary is one staff. (c) ONE SHARED MULTI-WRITER STORE, which means replacing single-writer RocksDB and owning consensus; most work, least alignment with a design that already shards by authority. (d) EVENT-SOURCED LOG plus materialised views — attractive because a plan IS a change history, expensive because every detector currently reads a materialised graph. WHAT BREAKS TODAY, in order: single-writer per graph (the six-seat outage of 2026-07-25 was this at tiny scale), the whole-document write path (769 KB for 606 nodes; a funeral federation is 10^5-10^6 nodes changing continuously), git-round-trip latency, nothing that pushes, no identity or authorization, and req:stale-seat-knows going from one bad afternoon to a systemic property.		Held as brainstorming because it is explicitly distant-future ('probably distant future') and because it challenges the PREMISE of two decisions rather than their reasoning — which is the honest thing to record, not to act on. dec:multi-writer-architecture chose repo-file-plus-merge on a rationale resting on concurrency being hypothetical; dec:central-host's rationale says outright that this tool 'does not need' simultaneity 'and may be harmed by it'. A thousand people replanning a state funeral under events is the named counter-case both were missing, and per dec:reopen-supersedes the move is a new decision point, never flipping those back. NOTE THE PART THAT NEEDS NO DECISION: the ownership boundary federation already draws is the natural AUTHORIZATION boundary — you write your echelon's graph and read your superior's published surface — so authz needs enforcement, not a new concept, and Interface.designation internal|published is already the read primitive. Also settled by inspection: ordering without a shared git history needs no global clock, because the same federation shape gives a total order WITHIN each boundary (the store, proved by the content-hash chain) and dated coordinates ACROSS boundaries (a mirror already carries whose design, which version, when) — exactly how echelons coordinate. Full reasoning in docs/planning-at-scale.md.proposednothing
OPEN — loop_status reports unsurfaced_gaps 0 before detect_gaps has ever run, so 'clean' and 'never scanned' are the same answer
RECORDED AS A MEASURED FIELD DEFECT PLUS AN OPEN QUESTION. Reported 2026-08-05 from the hxm_program session, item 4 of six. WHAT WAS OBSERVED, in the reporter's words: 'After the capture batch, `loop_status` reported `unsurfaced_gaps: 0` — but `detect_gaps` had never been run, and when it did run it found 3 REAL PHASE-LEVEL GAPS.' Their conclusion is the sentence worth keeping: 'AN AGENT THAT TRUSTS `clean: true` HAS NO REASON TO RUN THE DETECTOR.' ⭐ WHY THIS IS NOT SIMPLY A MISSING TIMESTAMP. `loop_status` is the call the SessionStart hook and the server instructions both push every session to run FIRST, described as 'the one cheap call that says what the coherence loop is owed'. It is the orientation surface. A false clean there does not mislead one report — it tells the agent the loop is settled at the exact moment the loop has not started. AND IT COLLIDES WITH AN ACCEPTED DECISION RATHER THAN JUST BEING AN OVERSIGHT. `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` is ACCEPTED: 'Loop debt is computed from graph state, never from run history' — with the stated reason that LOOKING IS NOT WRITING, so counting runs would reward bookkeeping. That ruling is right and it is exactly what produces this: a gap that has never been detected is not IN the state, so state-derived debt cannot see it. The defect is downstream of a correct decision, which is why it needs a decision rather than a patch. THIS IS THE THIRD INSTANCE OF ONE SHAPE IN A WEEK, AND THE PATTERN NOW HAS A NAME IN THIS PROJECT'S OWN RECORD: (BL-206), the coherence gate reporting OK over 20 artifacts it never swept; (BL-208), the export-lineage guard reporting nothing because a shallow checkout meant it could not see `HEAD~1`; and `dec:no-design-here-never-looked`, filed from the same report, where 'this directory has no design yet' was asserted without looking. The carried sentence from BL-208 was 'a guard whose no-op path is silent will eventually run nowhere and say so to nobody'. THIS IS THE READING-SURFACE VERSION: A COUNT THAT CANNOT DISTINGUISH ZERO FROM UNMEASURED READS AS ZERO. OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) THE REPORTER'S SUGGESTION — a `last_gap_scan` timestamp, or a `scanned: false` field. Cheap and directly answers it. Counter: a timestamp IS run history, which is what `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` deliberately excluded, so taking it means amending that decision rather than quietly contradicting it — and the amendment has to explain why THIS history is legitimate when run-counting was not. The distinguishing argument, if it is taken: recording that a detector RAN is not the same as crediting the agent for running it; one is a property of the reading, the other is a score. (b) MAKE THE ABSENCE STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN TEMPORAL — report `unsurfaced_gaps` as unknown until a scan has ever produced a gap-or-none result for the current graph revision, keyed on state rather than on time. Fits the accepted decision without amending it. Counter: needs a notion of 'the graph revision a scan covered', which does not exist. (c) NEVER REPORT A ZERO — say 'run detect_gaps' whenever the count is zero, whatever the cause. Crude, honest, costs nothing, and would have prevented the observed failure. Counter: it makes a genuinely clean design nag forever, which is how a signal gets trained to be ignored — the exact failure (BL-191) fixed for volatile artifacts. (d) LEAVE IT AND RELY ON THE STOP HOOK, which the reporter notes DID catch this ('the stop-hook nudge caught this — 'bookkeeping is not the loop' — which worked'). Counter: the hook fires at the END of a session, and the false clean is read at the START. NOT CHECKED, and it widens or narrows this considerably: whether the other zero-valued counters in `loop_status` have the same property — `unexamined_claims`, `unproven_capabilities`, `undispositioned_drift`, `unwritten_answers`. If they are all state-derived in the same way, this is one defect with five faces rather than one field.		Filed as its own node rather than a backlog row because the fix is not obvious and the obvious fix contradicts an accepted decision. `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` says debt is computed from state and never from run history, for a good stated reason; a `last_gap_scan` timestamp is run history. Whoever takes this has to either amend that decision with an argument for why recording a reading differs from scoring an agent, or find a state-shaped answer. A backlog row would have carried the symptom and lost the collision. The three-instance pattern is written out because this is the point at which it stops being a coincidence: two gates and now the orientation call, all reporting a confident absence they never measured. Naming it once, with the instances, is cheaper than finding it a fourth time. The unchecked item — whether the other four counters share the property — is stated because it decides whether this is one row or five, and nobody has looked.proposednothing
Loop debt is computed from graph state, never from run history
loop_status reports what the coherence loop is owed — anchored gaps never surfaced, questions waiting or answered-but-unwritten, structural defects, capabilities claiming realized/verified with no passing check, drift awaiting disposition, claims never examined — computed entirely from current graph state. reflow2 does not track when tools were run: phase nudges are excluded (guidance, not debt), and the write tools carry static loop_hint pointers at the next loop step in their own results.		From the StoryFlow fleet trial (BL-74): under operational load the agent kept bookkeeping via raw tools while the loop skills silently stopped — 'a design-discipline tool that depends on being remembered will lose to operational urgency every time; fire on a trigger, not on virtue.' Run-history ('no detect_gaps since Tuesday') is not honestly computable here: the core takes no clock, and looking-is-not-writing is doctrine — recording reads so observation could be tracked would make looking mutate the record. Outstanding debt is the state-based equivalent and the actionable truth regardless of who ran what when. The hint rides the tool result the agent already reads (zero extra round-trip to see it), and loop_status is the cheap computation a client hook can fire on its own events — rung a of the BL-74 ladder builds on exactly this call. Decided 2026-07-21.acceptedSay what the loop is owed, OPEN — loop_status reports unsurfaced_gaps 0 before detect_gaps has ever run, so 'clean' and 'never scanned' are the same answer
ACCEPTED 2026-08-06 — content_manifest and content_exists ANSWER when no store is configured; only content_put and content_get refuse
RECORDED AS AN OPEN QUESTION, NOT SETTLED. Surfaced by running impact-check on chg:content-path-no-default AFTER the edit rather than before — the blast radius named ifc:mcp-tools as a boundary crossing, which is exactly the 'changed one side of a contract' case that skill exists to catch. STILL OPEN. WHAT THE FIX DID. Removing `default_value` from `--content-path` makes the refusal in `ReflowService::content_store` reachable, which is correct for the WRITE path and is what ver:content-surface already claims. But all four content tools route through that same method (content_tools.rs:97, :129, :155, :185), so `content_manifest` and `content_exists` now refuse too. Before the fix, `content_manifest` on an unconfigured server ANSWERED — `entries: ()`, `total_bytes: 0`, `store_root: './reflow2-content'` — and that answer was worse than useless, because the root it named did not exist. So the fix is not a regression; the question is whether refusing is the RIGHT answer or merely a less-wrong one. THE CASE FOR REFUSING (what ships now): a manifest says 'whether the bytes are here', and with no store there is no 'here'. `req:no-silent-fallback` argues the same way for reads as for writes, and the refusal names the remedy. THE CASE FOR ANSWERING, and it is not weak: cap:content-manifest exists for the person 'handed the design ON ITS OWN', and its whole point is that `missing` names content the graph references and this checkout does not have — 'so a diagram that will not open is a named finding rather than a silent absence'. That reader has NO store by definition. Refusing tells them to configure one before they can be told what they are missing, which inverts the capability. The honest answer for them is every referenced hash listed under `missing`, `orphaned: ()`, and the store named as absent. `content_exists` has the same shape: it is documented as the cheap 'do I have everything?' call. WHY IT IS MOOT TODAY AND WILL NOT STAY MOOT: reflow2's own graph references ZERO content (136 Fragments, 0 with a `content_ref`), so both behaviours return the same information here. The distinction only bites once a design actually points at bytes — which is exactly when the person who needs it is the one who cannot answer it. Deciding it now costs nothing; discovering it then costs a user. BEARS ON req:the-store-is-reachable-from-a-session, which sits in the direct ring of this change. Whether 'reachable' means 'the tools are present and say what is wrong' or 'the store exists without anyone choosing where' is the requirement's own ambiguity, and it should be read before this is settled rather than after.		Resolved by Anthony 2026-08-06, taking the ANSWER branch: the reader cap:content-manifest exists for is 'someone handed the design ON ITS OWN', and that reader has no store by definition, so refusing them inverts the capability. Surfaced only because impact-check was run on chg:content-path-no-default and named ifc:mcp-tools as a boundary crossing — without it the refusal would have shipped on all four tools unnoticed, which is the value of that skill stated concretely rather than in principle. WHAT SHIPPED: DesignGraph::content_manifest now takes Option<&ContentStore>. With None, every referenced hash reports missing, orphaned is empty (no bytes exist to be unreferenced), total_bytes is 0, and store_root says '(no content store configured)' in words instead of naming a directory nobody chose. ReflowService::content_store_for_reading returns Option and is used by the two read tools; content_store (the refusing form) still backs content_put and content_get unchanged. WHY THE SPLIT IS PRINCIPLED RATHER THAN A COMPROMISE: req:no-silent-fallback forbids INVENTING a location, and neither path does that any more — the write refuses and names the remedy, the read reports absence as absence. The old behaviour violated it in the worst way, answering with a store_root of './reflow2-content' for a directory that existed nowhere. Both halves now say something true. PROVEN, not asserted: crates/reflow2-mcp/tests/tools.rs the_manifest_answers_without_a_store_while_writes_still_refuse holds all three behaviours in one case, deliberately beside a_server_with_no_content_store_says_so_instead_of_choosing_one so the pair reads as the contract. 70/70 tools tests and 15/15 core content tests pass; clippy -D warnings clean across both crates.acceptednothing
A bulk derivation is not a bulk accept, and it writes nothing until asked
release_includes_all derives a release's whole manifest from the design and writes it in one call, with `apply` defaulting to false so the derivation is reported before anything is written. Entries already in the manifest are reported as already_present and their frozen as_checksum is never recomputed.		BL-153 flagged the counterweight to state before building: dec:two-sided-accept and dec:ask-not-repair mean a bulk form must not become a silent one, and 'a batch of 144 acknowledgements with one reason is exactly the erosion those decisions exist to prevent'. Those decisions bound bulk DISPOSITIONS — a judgement taken about each item. No disposition is taken here: the graph is asked what the project contains and answers, and the one judgement a human still owns (which release ships it) is the argument the caller supplies. So the family does not apply, and a per-item disposition would be ceremony over a derivation. What DOES apply is the no-silent-write bar: hence apply defaults to false, matching reconcile_artifacts' record_events, because a call that packages a release is the one you most want to read before you run it. The frozen-checksum guard is the harder half — a derivation that recomputed every entry would rewrite the manifest of a shipped release each time the live drift baseline moved, silently and in bulk, which is the axis-Z sin the frozen copy exists to prevent.acceptedA release's manifest is derived from the design, not typed out
OPEN — is 'the same functions, structured as I would structure them NOW' a second kind of delta the graph should model?
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-02, thinking out loud after asking what a functional decomposition of reflow2 would be. Nothing here is intent; nothing has been promoted. THE DISTINCTION HE IS DRAWING, in his words: 'this is a different kind of delta from capability increments to more of breadboard design to production grade production design. it may involve keeping the same functions, but restructuring the design/packaging and/or which functions are allocated to which systems/services.' And the general form: 'knowing what I know now, would I have designed this the same way?' — which he says 'should almost be a reflow2 skill', and which applies to ANY design, not only reflow2's. EXPLICITLY NOT A REWRITE: 'I wasn't really saying to develop a reflow3. in fact, as the graph can support epochs and capability increments, we can evolve from the engineering mockup to full production grade morphing in the reflow2 graph for any design project.' TWO ORTHOGONAL AXES OF CHANGE, which is the load-bearing idea. (1) A CAPABILITY INCREMENT grows the function set — new requirements, new capabilities, delivered against a schedule. reflow2 models this well already: `DesignEpoch`, `SCHEDULED_FOR` with modality, `Release`/`INCLUDES`, and readiness gating on the increment. (2) A MATURITY RESTRUCTURING holds the function set INVARIANT and moves everything else — allocation, packaging, which functions live in which system or service, which seams are declared. reflow2 models this barely at all as a first-class thing, although the parts exist. THE PARTS THAT ALREADY EXIST, so this is assembly rather than invention: `ALLOCATED_TO` and `CONTAINS` already carry the allocation map that a restructuring moves; `evaluate_allocation` and `propose_allocation` already score and propose it; `dec:parallel-alternatives` plus `analyze_alternatives` already fork a design in SPACE (rather than time) and lay N variants side by side on the same measures; `compare_designs` already bands a difference into design content versus supporting layer; and `record_change` already snapshots a node's EDGES as well as its properties (BL-63), so a re-parenting is recoverable rather than lossy — which is what makes in-place evolution safe and is the technical reason a reflow3 is not needed. WHAT WOULD GIVE IT TEETH, and the part worth arguing about: a restructuring is SAFE EXACTLY WHEN FUNCTION IS PROVABLY PRESERVED, and that is computable rather than promised. The invariant is: no Capability added or removed, no SATISFIES edge changed — only `ALLOCATED_TO` / `CONTAINS` / Interface edges moved. `compare_designs` already reports at that granularity, so a skill could CERTIFY a restructuring rather than assert it. That is the difference between a refactor someone hopes is safe and one the graph checked, and it is the same move `dec:passing-is-verified` makes for tests. WHAT IS MISSING, three things, none of them large. (a) NO SKILL asks the question: of fifteen served skills, `revise-design` handles one node the user changed their mind about, `retire-from-design` handles removal, `check-health` finds structural DEFECTS (cycles, single points of failure, islands) — none asks whether the structure is the one you would CHOOSE now, which is a different question from whether it is broken. (b) NO VOCABULARY MARKS THE EPOCH AS A MATURITY STEP: `DesignEpoch.epoch_type` offers `baseline | revision | milestone | incident_response | release_cut`, and a restructuring is none of those; `ChangeEvent.change_type` offers `refactor`, which does not distinguish a code refactor from a design re-allocation. (c) NO MATURITY LADDER FOR THE DESIGN ITSELF: `ReadinessAssessment` (TRL/MRL 1-9) was built for the enabling TECHNOLOGIES an increment leans on, not for the design's own structural maturity — whether it should also apply to the design is an open question, and the hardware ladder Anthony named (breadboard, engineering mockup, EVT, DVT, PVT, pilot run, mass production) is the vocabulary he is reaching for. THE OBSERVATION THAT PROMPTED IT, measured rather than asserted: reflow2's own design carries EIGHT functional systems (`dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition`, accepted 2026-07-23) and exactly THREE Interfaces, none of which sits between two of those systems — while 51 `DEPENDS_ON` edges cross system boundaries against 22 that stay inside one, over 14 distinct system pairs, the two largest being coherence-loop to store and coherence-loop to vocabulary at 16 each. So the functional blocks are declared on the containment axis and their seams are not declared at all, which is what a MOSA reading would want first (`dec:mosa-conformance`, also proposed).		Recorded through the brainstorm skill because Anthony was working the idea through rather than deciding it, and explicitly withdrew the stronger reading (no reflow3). ANTHONY'S CLOSING GENERALISATION, 2026-08-02, and it is the most important sentence in the discussion because it changes what the whole thing IS: 'this is really a realization that probably all designs start immature (breadboard or engineering mockup) and then morph to a more refined structure. this allows reflow2 to build in how designs typically go where initially getting function right is the first objective, then you go towards getting the structure/packaging right. this is often iterative and organic.' THE CONSEQUENCE, which reframes every measurement taken today: reflow2's 51 undeclared cross-system dependencies are NOT technical debt and NOT a criticism of any decision — they are the expected state of a design that has been correctly prioritising function. A design at that point is ON the normal trajectory, not off it. Which means the thing reflow2 should learn is not 'detect bad structure' but 'know that this trajectory EXISTS and where a design is along it' — the same move `dec:readiness-is-an-observation-the-threshold-is-the-judgement` makes for technology maturity, applied to the design's own structure. A tool that reported undeclared seams as defects would be punishing correct early-phase work, which is exactly the failure `cap:coverage` avoids by refusing to be a score, and exactly what `sharpening.md` §2 calls accommodation if the design were then bent to silence it. WHAT THAT IMPLIES FOR THE VOCABULARY QUESTION, sharpening option (c) rather than answering it: if function-first-then-structure is the norm, a maturity ladder for the DESIGN is not a nice-to-have bolted onto readiness — it is the axis along which every design moves, and 'where am I on it' becomes a first-class question a design brain should answer. The counter-argument stays on the record beside it: a distinction earns its keep only when a computation reads it (`dec:edge-orthogonality`), so the ladder is worth vocabulary only if something computes position along it rather than merely labelling it. Kept as ONE question because the skill Anthony wants ('would I design it this way now?') is the human-facing form and the second delta type is what the graph needs to hold its answer. Options are prose rather than registered alternatives, deliberately, so it raises no `undecided_decision_point` while it is still a musing.proposedCertify that a restructuring preserved function, Report where the build does not separate what the design separates, Locate a design on the function-to-structure trajectory
The merge conflict case table: retain-and-ask on delete, edges symmetric with nodes, conflicts are Questions
The three-way merge (cap:merge-designs, dec:merge-three-way) resolves per node, per property, and per edge against the base by this case table. NODES/PROPERTIES: only one side changed a property -> take it; both changed it differently -> conflict. add/add (same id, no base) -> treated as modify/modify against an empty base: matching properties merge, each differing property is a conflict. delete/delete -> node gone, no conflict. delete/modify (one side removes the node, the other changes it) -> RETAIN-AND-ASK: the proposal keeps the modified node and raises a conflict asking the human to confirm the deletion or keep it, leaning toward keeping — deletion is the destructive side and must be re-justified, never the silent default (req:intent-preserved, retire-vs-delete). Symmetric in both directions. EDGES: first-class design content and get the identical three-way rule — one-sided add or remove -> take it; the same edge changed differently on both sides, or one side removes while the other changes it -> conflict; never silently drop an edge one side deliberately cut (req:no-silent-fallback). CONFLICT REPRESENTATION: a both-sides conflict is a Question node with source 'merge_conflict', a deterministic id (FNV over base + node/edge id + property, the existing gap-id normalization), carrying the base/ours/theirs values; it reuses the existing answer_question / open_questions machinery and writes nothing until dispositioned, and its normalized id is the key a later rerere rung (BL-80 #5) replays a recorded resolution against. No new node type — the schema stays 28.		User decided all three axes 2026-07-22, each the doctrine-aligned option, closing the sub-decisions dec:merge-three-way explicitly deferred. Retain-and-ask over a neutral conflict because losing a node is not symmetric with keeping it: req:intent-preserved and the retire-vs-delete distinction make a delete the move that must be justified, so the proposal keeps the node and asks rather than treating erasure as an equal default. Edges symmetric with nodes because they carry the golden thread — a lighter union-and-keep-wins rule would override a deliberate one-sided edge removal without asking, which is exactly the silent drop req:no-silent-fallback forbids; compare_designs already bands edge divergence, so the input is there. Reuse Question over a dedicated MergeConflict type for the recurring schema-minimalism reason (the vocabulary was already sufficient — same lesson as dec:certainty-derived and dec:component-verified-computed): the answer/open-questions machinery, the deterministic FNV gap-id normalization, and the human-decides routing all already exist, and reusing them makes the conflict rerere-ready for free (BL-80 #5) while keeping the schema at 28 node types. With this, the merge is fully specified — nothing left but the build and its verification.acceptedThree-way merge two divergent designs
rerere: record a conflict resolution content-keyed in the graph, replay it advisory-only
reflow2 records how a human resolved a merge conflict and offers it back when the same conflict recurs (git's rerere), on three axes the user decided. (1) STORAGE — in the graph, as an answered Question (source=merge_resolution) whose id IS the conflict's content fingerprint: reuses the answer_question/open_questions machinery, travels with the design in the export, no schema change (stays 28 node types) — exactly what dec:merge-conflict-semantics anticipated ('reuse Question; its normalized id is the key a later rerere rung replays against'). (2) BEHAVIOR — advisory: a recorded resolution is surfaced as a suggestion on the matching conflict, and the human still confirms (dec:report-dont-judge, dec:three-party-checks). apply_merge applies only what it is given; an opt-in use_recorded lets the human bulk-accept every recorded suggestion in one move (the confirmation is passing the flag), and apply refuses if any conflict still has neither an explicit nor a recorded decision. (3) KEY — content only: the fingerprint is over (property, base value, ours value, theirs value), independent of which node, so ONE resolution replays across ALL nodes with the identical conflict — this is git's model and what delivers the motivating BL-73 win (20 near-identical conflicts, 21 near-identical hand-resolutions → resolve the shape once). apply_merge records every applied property/edge-property resolution keyed by content, so the memory grows as you work.		User decided all three axes 2026-07-22, each the doctrine-aligned option. Content-only keying because it is the whole point: the BL-73 field pain was N near-identical conflicts across different nodes, and a per-node key would give near-zero reuse and miss exactly that case; content-only is git's proven model, and pairing it with advisory behavior keeps over-reach visible (the human sees each application). Advisory over auto-apply because the three-party doctrine puts the decision with the human — but the recorded suggestion plus a bulk-accept toggle kills the repetitive grind without silently resolving on the human's behalf. Reuse-Question over a new node type or a side cache is the recurring no-schema-change lesson AND keeps the memory inside the design that travels in the export (a side rr-cache would be a second source of truth that a teammate importing the design would not receive). Scoped in v1 to property and edge-property conflicts (a clear base/ours/theirs value triple, and the N-near-identical shape); node-type and delete/modify keys are deferred (no clean value triple), as is aging/pruning the memory. Extends cap:merge-designs; the conflict ids the merge already mints were built for exactly this (dec:merge-conflict-semantics).acceptedReuse a recorded conflict resolution (rerere)
Merge survivor is chosen by provenance, id breaks ties
When HEAL merges DUPLICATES-asserted nodes, the survivor is picked by provenance rank (authored > planned > imported > reconciled > inferred > healed); node id breaks ties. Pre-provenance graphs are unchanged.		User decided option 2 for BL-29 (2026-07-20): provenance is the closest thing the graph has to 'who asserted this and how deliberately'. Refinement from the 2026-07-20 self-adopt live session: a node with UNSET provenance defaults to authored, which made two genesis stubs tie against authored+verified survivors and nearly win on alphabetical id — set provenance explicitly on both sides before proposing a merge, and consider ranking unset below authored in a future revision.acceptedheal
The three-way merge takes explicit inputs over git's DAG, and reports a proposal it never auto-applies
The design merge is a three-way typed merge exposed as a core op (MCP tool + CLI flag), the write-side sibling of compare_designs. (1) Inputs are three explicit export documents — a common ancestor (base), ours, theirs; git supplies the base (git merge-base + the committed reflow2.json at that commit), so reflow2 does not build its own commit DAG for this rung. The multi-parent/ref layer that would let reflow2 find its own merge-base is deferred to BL-70/#3. (2) The algorithm is git's trivial-merge case table run per node and per property against the base over typed values, not lines: only one side changed a property -> take it; both sides changed it differently -> a structured conflict. (3) It produces a merge proposal — auto-resolved one-sided changes plus a list of both-sides conflicts rendered as Questions ('node X.prop Y: base=A, ours=B, theirs=C — which?') — and writes NOTHING to the graph. The human dispositions the conflict Questions, then an explicit apply commits the merge. Compare reports and never writes; merge does the same until the human has looked.		User decided both axes 2026-07-22, both the recommended option. Explicit-inputs-over-git because the exports are already git-committed (dec:repo-file-embedded) and git already tracks the merge-base — building a second DAG inside reflow2 would reimplement what git provides and contradicts 'export/import is the right-sized git bundle analogue' (BL-80's explicit do-NOT-import list). It keeps rung #1 shippable now and defers the ref/branch layer to where it belongs (BL-70). compare_designs already computes the typed per-property diff this consumes, so the input side is built. Report-a-proposal-never-auto-apply because a both-sides conflict IS a Question and the graph must not silently pick a side (dec:report-dont-judge, req:human-decides, req:no-silent-fallback); mirroring compare's read-only contract keeps the sibling honest, and the explicit apply is the disposition gate (dec:two-sided-accept's spirit — no silent write) without a staging area (BL-80 explicitly rejects the index). Typed per-node/per-property conflicts are strictly better than git's line markers — the key 'graph is not files' caveat. This specifies BL-12's merge problem: rung #1 (this algorithm over three documents) + #2 (the retained ancestor, here git's) = the L core of BL-12. Deferred to their own decisions: delete/modify and add/add conflict semantics (retire-vs-delete makes a delete meaningful, so delete/modify must go to the human, never auto-resolve), edge-merge banding, and the exact shape of the conflict Question.acceptedThree-way merge two divergent designs, merge
OPEN — should reflow2 report MOSA conformance, given it already computes most of the criteria?
UNDECIDED, RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING. Anthony, 2026-07-25, supplied the DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook (OUSD(R&E) Systems Engineering and Architecture, February 2025, Distribution A) and was explicit about the frame: 'just taking principles, concepts and ideas from this. not looking to implement mosa exactly over this document.' So this records what the guidebook's concepts illuminate about reflow2, not a plan to become a MOSA tool. THE DEFINITION IT GIVES: 'an acquisition and design approach consisting of a technical and business architecture that supports using system interfaces compliant with widely supported and consensus-based standards... A MOSA system structure allows for severable components to be incrementally added, removed, or replaced throughout the life cycle' (10 U.S.C. 4401, mandated for all DoD acquisition programs to the maximum extent practicable). ITS FIVE-STEP FRAMEWORK is a process, not a document: Plan, Modularize, Identify Interfaces, Define Interfaces, Standardize Interfaces — and reflow2 can already model a process rather than only a product (cap:model-process, Flow nodes), so the framework is expressible as a Flow whose steps the graph can be checked against. THE FINDING THAT MATTERS, from Table D-1 'MOSA Conformance Criteria and Verification Methods': most of what MOSA asks a program to demonstrate, reflow2 already computes for other reasons. Their MODULARITY criterion — 'encapsulated, cohesive, loosely coupled, and organized into functional categories' — is the Leiden modularity score, community detection and the god-component detector that graph_report already prints. Their MOSA OBJECTIVES criterion — 'demonstrate severable modular components' — is propagate_change: if the blast radius of a change inside a module stops at that module's interfaces the module is severable, and if it leaks past them the module is not modular whatever the architecture diagram says. That is severability as a COMPUTED property rather than an assertion, which is the same move dec:certainty-derived made for requirement status and cap:derived-completion made for delivery. Their MOSA MODULES criterion — 'implement minimal functions, are functionally independent, encapsulated, and traceable to requirements' — is the god-component detector plus the golden thread. Their LIFE CYCLE CHARACTERISTICS criterion — severable, replaceable, interoperable, allowing competition — is the severability computation plus the alternatives layer, where interchangeable suppliers behind one interface are exactly an analysis of alternatives. WHAT IS GENUINELY MISSING, and it is one vocabulary item and one check. (1) NOTHING MARKS AN INTERFACE AS KEY. MOSA's whole discipline turns on designating major/modular system interfaces and then holding them stable and open; reflow2 has Interface nodes, provides/consumes and SPECIFIES, but no way to say 'this one is the published boundary and that one is internal plumbing'. BL-45 found the identical hole from the opposite direction — external dependencies between reflow2 projects — and recorded it as 'nothing marks an Interface external-facing'. Two independent routes to one missing property is the strongest evidence this design has for a vocabulary addition. (2) NOTHING CHECKS STANDARDS COMPLIANCE, and the vocabulary for it is present and unused: DesignRule is defined as a chosen standard or convention with an `enforced` flag, and there are zero DesignRules in any graph — the same schema-present-practice-absent shape as the temporal axis and the KPP vocabulary before them. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded beside the idea rather than used to bury it: MOSA is domain vocabulary for defence acquisition, and req:design-anything says the vocabulary stays neutral. A MOSA conformance report is therefore a VIEW — a projection over computations that already exist, in the acquisition community's words — and not a set of new node types. Building it as a view keeps the core neutral (dec:views-are-projections) and any renderer fill-in remains a defect. If it were ever built as schema, reflow2 would have taken on one domain's language as its own, which is the thing it has refused since the beginning.		Recorded 2026-07-25 as brainstorming from the DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook Anthony supplied, on his framing: principles and concepts, not an implementation of MOSA. PROMOTED THE SAME DAY on his word ('let's promote both') into the two things the guidebook actually exposed as missing, both now accepted: req:key-interfaces (the design says which interfaces are the published boundaries, and computations read the distinction) and req:modularity-computed (severability and cohesion are computed from the graph, not asserted by the diagram). Both are GOVERNED_BY this decision. WHAT STAYS OPEN is the question this decision was opened on, and it is narrower now: whether reflow2 ships a MOSA-BRANDED report. The requirements are domain-neutral by construction — published boundary, severable part — so they can be built without answering it, and the acquisition community's words for the same criteria belong in a view over the computation rather than in the schema (dec:views-are-projections, req:design-anything). Deciding otherwise would adopt one domain's language as reflow2's own, which is the thing it has refused since the beginning. SEQUENCING, and it is not arbitrary: req:key-interfaces comes first because req:modularity-computed depends on it — severability is only checkable once the design knows where a boundary is. req:design-composes also links through published boundaries, so the same property serves the federation thread; that is the second independent route to it, after BL-45 found the identical hole from the system-of-systems side on 2026-07-20.proposedThe design says which interfaces are the published boundaries, and computations read that distinction, Modularity is computed from the design, not asserted by the architecture diagram
Many writers keep the repo file and merge on pull — no hosted service
DECIDED 2026-07-25: the design STAYS a graph-in-a-repo-file, and many writers are handled by merging on pull. No hosted service, no shared writable store. Each person's design lives at ./.reflow2/graph in their own checkout, git moves it, and genuinely overlapping work is resolved by the three-way merge that already exists — typed per-node and per-property against the common ancestor, with each conflict minted as a Question carrying a deterministic id, and recorded resolutions replayable across near-identical conflicts (rerere). THIS CONFIRMS dec:repo-file-embedded RATHER THAN SUPERSEDING IT. That is the outcome worth noting: this was the first field-sourced re-opening of a settled decision, triggered because dec:repo-file-embedded's own rationale said the concurrency argument was 'hypothetical while there is one writer' and fifteen developers made it concrete. The precondition genuinely changed, the decision was genuinely re-opened, and the original answer survived contact with the new evidence. A re-opening that ends where it started is not wasted — it converts an assumption into a tested position. WHAT WAS REJECTED AND WHY. A HOSTED SERVICE: rejected on cost against confirmed intent, not on taste. It contradicts req:persistence ('the graph lives at ./.reflow2/graph inside the consumer project, so the design travels with the repo') and req:invocation ('the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio, installed into a consumer project'), both accepted, so choosing it would have required retiring or revising confirmed intent rather than merely adding machinery. It also puts the design on a machine the user does not control, carries permanent operational burden, and breaks the session-transcript identity for everyone but the local user (a local path resolves for one person and silently misses for the rest). A HYBRID — hosted claims and presence over local designs: rejected as the weaker version of the same trade. It keeps req:persistence but strains req:invocation with a second surface to run, and buys live visibility that the claims layer can approximate without a server. WHAT THIS COMMITS TO BUILDING: the scoping primitive (BL-44 cluster claims) so two people do not collide in the first place, and merge-on-pull ergonomics. The honest weakness accepted with this choice: no live view of what others hold, so overlap surfaces at merge time rather than before it — which is exactly the trade git itself makes, and the one this project's users already understand.		Raised by the user and his brother, 2026-07-24, from a concrete scenario rather than speculation. This is the first field-sourced trigger to re-open a settled decision, and it is worth recording WHY it counts as one: dec:repo-file-embedded's own rationale reads 'the service's strongest argument (concurrency) is hypothetical while there is one writer.' Fifteen developers is that hypothesis arriving, so the decision is not being second-guessed — its stated precondition has changed. That is exactly the signal cap:revise-trigger is being built to surface automatically; here it arrived by conversation instead, which is itself evidence the trigger is worth building. Held proposed deliberately: the architecture question is upstream of every feature beneath it (req:concurrent-planning among them), and starting to build under an unmade decision is how a design acquires an architecture nobody chose. The counter-argument that belongs in the weighing, so it is not lost: reflow2's loop is built around asking a human and recording an attributable answer — deliberate, sequential, credited — and simultaneous editing may be the wrong shape for that product even where it is technically reachable. What the raised scenario actually asks for is non-colliding parallel work plus good merges, which may be reachable without a service at all.acceptedClaim a region of the design so two people do not collide in it, OPEN — is the per-user graph scope a convenience or a COMPARTMENT, and what must reflow2 promise (and refuse to promise) if designs are separated by clearance?, OPEN — does collaborating on a shared server cost the self-contained package, or does it only flip which way the default points?, Several people can plan against one design without colliding, What a session learns is written to the graph as it is learned, not summarized into a file on the way out
DECIDED — a graph per ownership boundary, levels inside each
DECIDED 2026-07-25 by Anthony: option (c), A GRAPH PER OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY WITH LEVELS INSIDE EACH. A design is its own graph when something at that level is separately OWNED, separately RELEASED, or separately SHARED — and a subtree of one graph otherwise. The hierarchy does not decide; authority does. That is the shape federated systems engineering actually uses, and it makes the split rule non-arbitrary: you can always answer 'why is this its own design?' with a name, a release train, or a recipient. WHAT FOLLOWS, and each is an obligation rather than a detail. (1) THE COORDINATE. Edges cannot cross stores because the schema validates both endpoints, so a link between designs is not an edge: the other side's published surface is MIRRORED into your graph as local nodes, and the mirror carries the coordinate — which design it came from, at what content hash, when. Your own components then PROVIDE and CONSUME the mirrored Interface with ordinary local edges, so the golden thread works unchanged and foreignness is a property of the NODE rather than of the link. Same reasoning as dec:fork-point-address: a coordinate resolved against a document, never a live ref layer. (2) ROLL-UP. A parent's view of a composed child must derive from the child's own evidence or a requirement satisfied inside the child fires unsatisfied in the parent forever — cap:derived-completion's computation one level up. (3) FRESHNESS. A mirror is a dated claim about a VERSION, so a newer surface with a different hash makes it stale and that must be detectable, never assumed current (the cap:freshness and confirmation-ledger shape). (4) THE SEAM. Two teams changing the boundary itself still collide, in the one place the merge machinery does not reach; the published-surface document is what they are actually negotiating over. THE ROADS NOT TAKEN, kept because req:roads-not-taken says they are part of the record. (a) ONE GRAPH, ZOOM BY LEVEL was not rejected — it was BUILT FIRST and remains correct for everything inside one ownership boundary; cap:scoped-analysis delivers it, and (c) is a superset rather than a replacement. What (a) alone could not do is give two owners separate write locks, separate release trains, or a way to share one part without sharing everything. (b) A GRAPH PER SYSTEM was rejected as a RULE, not as a possibility: a system that is separately owned still gets its own graph under (c), but depth alone stops being sufficient reason, because every seam costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check, and a three-level tower of graphs inside one team buys none of what those cost. THE TENSION THIS RESOLVES, and it should be resolved out loud: docs/org-scale-vision.md records the destination as 'one graph the whole company plans in'. Under (c) that is no longer the destination — an enterprise is many designs federated at ownership boundaries, and the CEO's objectives are one design that others mirror rather than one graph everyone writes into. That document now describes a road not taken and should say so.		Raised 2026-07-25 as brainstorming, because Anthony said plainly he was not convinced by the collaboration design and an unconvinced author is a finding rather than a disagreement to be argued down. Promoted to intent the same day, and COLLAPSED the same day on his word ('let's do (c) option'). THE SEQUENCE IS THE ARGUMENT for why this was worth holding open for a few hours rather than deciding immediately: option (a)'s scope filter was built FIRST precisely because it forecloses nothing, so by the time the decision was made there was working evidence about what per-level analysis actually feels like — and (a) turned out to be a subset of (c) rather than a rival to it. Deciding on day one would have been a guess; deciding after building the cheap half was a choice with evidence behind it. WHY (c) OVER (b), stated as the discriminator that survived from the brainstorm: every seam between designs costs a coordinate, an evidence roll-up and a freshness check, so a level earns its own graph only when it is separately owned, released or shared. A three-level tower of graphs inside one team pays all of that and buys none of it. (b) is not forbidden by this — a separately-owned system still gets its own design — it is that DEPTH stops being sufficient reason. WHAT THIS COSTS, recorded so nobody is surprised: docs/org-scale-vision.md's 'one graph the whole company plans in' is now a road not taken, and req:concurrent-planning's answer changes shape — ownership boundaries become the primary isolation mechanism, with the claims layer and the merge driver serving work INSIDE one boundary rather than across all of them. The first rung built on this decision is the coordinate (cap:mirror-surface): the other side's published surface mirrored as local nodes carrying which design, which hash, and when.acceptedCompose two designs by mirroring the other's published surface, coordinate and all, A team asks the detectors about its own part, and is told what it did not see, OPEN — should .mcp.json name SEVERAL graph_ids so one session reasons across reflow2 + flo2 + dynograph-foundation at once, and how does that sit against one-session-one-graph?, OPEN — how does a downstream owner levy a requirement on an upstream design they do not own? (Anthony leans: write-only-at-proposed, carried by git), OPEN — a published surface already carries designated REQUIREMENTS; should DECISIONS cross a design boundary too?, OPEN — should a project hold SEVERAL graph_ids in one store and operate on whichever the question needs, which is a linking mechanism nested-graphs never considered?, OPEN — where does the graph live when ONE PERSON works many interrelated projects, which is the case dec:nested-graphs' rule was not written for?, A system's design can be a unit of its own that composes with the designs around it
OPEN — 'this directory has no design yet' is asserted without looking, and it minted a THIRD graph on a repo that already had two
RECORDED AS A MEASURED FIELD DEFECT PLUS AN OPEN QUESTION. Reported 2026-08-05 from a real session on `hxm_program`, Anthony's own working repo at NSLS-II. Nothing here is settled. ⭐ WHAT HAPPENED, AND IT IS AN ACCIDENT THE TOOL CAUSED RATHER THAN FAILED TO PREVENT. A session rooted at the repo root was told 'this directory has no design yet' and offered only `reflow2_start_design`. TWO POPULATED GRAPHS EXISTED ONE AND TWO DIRECTORIES DOWN: ~/git_projects/hxm_program/.reflow2 37bbd9a6e0e75369 'hxm_program' minted 0.23.0 TODAY ~/git_projects/hxm_program/simulated_beamlines/.reflow2 8a9ce30fedd213e5 'simulated_beamlines' minted 0.17.0 ~/git_projects/hxm_program/simulated_beamlines/HEX/.reflow2 6771abb9b0683423 'HEX' minted 0.22.1 The user believed the design lived at `simulated_beamlines`. By the time that surfaced, the agent HAD ALREADY MINTED A NEW ROOT GRAPH. The reporter's own summary: 'One directory listing would have prevented the accidental third graph.' WHY THIS IS THE SEVERE ONE OF THE SIX FILED. Every other item in the report is friction — this one produced a WRONG ARTEFACT in the user's repository, silently, and the user did not learn of it until later. It is also the exact failure shape this project has been finding all week and naming in its own words: A GREEN OR CONFIDENT ANSWER FROM SOMETHING THAT NEVER LOOKED. `reflow2_check` reported OK over 20 artifacts it never swept ((BL-206)); the export-lineage guard reported nothing because it could not see `HEAD~1` ((BL-208)); `loop_status` reports `unsurfaced_gaps: 0` before `detect_gaps` has ever run (item 4 of this same report). 'No design here' is that sentence again, addressed to a person deciding whether to create one. AND IT IS WORSE THAN THE OTHERS IN ONE RESPECT: the other three report a state, and this one INVITES AN IRREVERSIBLE ACT on the strength of it. A design minted in the wrong place is not a bad reading; it is a fourth thing to reconcile. THE SECOND HALF, WHICH THE REPORT COUPLES TO IT: SESSION BINDING. 'The MCP server binds to the session's working directory. From a root-rooted session there is no way to write into the nested HEX graph — the user would have to open a session in that directory.' Verified against this repo's own `.mcp.json`: the launcher is passed `--graph-path ./.reflow2/graph`, a RELATIVE path with NO ANCESTOR WALK. So which design you are editing is decided by where your shell happened to be. Also reported: choosing the new root graph 'required a manual `/mcp` reconnect after `start_design`, because the running server predated the design and kept serving only `start_design`.' ⚠️ THIS FALSIFIES ADVICE GIVEN THE SAME DAY, and the correction belongs on the record next to it. Asked how to structure exactly these repos, this agent answered that a single graph needs no restructuring because `Artifact.location` is an opaque string and reflow2 performs no file IO — so one graph could register artifacts across sibling repos. TRUE OF ARTIFACT LOCATIONS AND FALSE OF THE THING THAT MATTERS: with cwd-binding and no ancestor walk, 'one graph' silently means 'every session must start at the repo root', and a session opened one directory down does not find it — it offers to mint another. The advice was given from the schema and the doctrine (`dec:install-once-per-machine`) without checking the launcher. THE SAME METHOD ERROR AS THE `export_surface` CORRECTION AN HOUR EARLIER: an absence asserted from a description rather than read from the code. OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) SCAN BEFORE OFFERING TO MINT — the reporter's own suggestion: 'no design here, but 2 exist below: (paths, labels). Use one of those, or really start fresh?' Cheapest, and it directly prevents the accident that occurred. Counter: reflow2 performs NO FILE IO by doctrine (`dec:agent-navigates-content`), so the scan cannot be reflow2's — it has to be the agent's, which makes this an instruction in the served surface rather than a tool, and instructions are weaker than a type system. That may be the honest answer rather than a weakness, but it should be chosen rather than defaulted to. (b) WALK ANCESTORS WHEN RESOLVING THE GRAPH PATH, the way git finds `.git`. Familiar and predictable; counter: it silently changes which design a session writes to based on cwd depth, which is the same class of surprise, and `--graph-path` is explicit today. (c) A GRAPH SELECTOR — 'design tools take an optional graph ref, defaulting to the nearest `.reflow2`' (reporter's 2a). The largest, and it is the one that would also answer the nested-write problem. Counter: it makes every tool call carry an ambient target, and this project has been careful that a claim without a seat is refused rather than guessed (`dec:stateless-seat-handle`). (d) HOT-LOAD THE FULL SURFACE AFTER `start_design` (reporter's 2b) — narrower, fixes only the reconnect papercut, and is independent of the rest. WHAT MUST NOT BE RE-DERIVED: `dec:install-once-per-machine` (the in-repo half is optional), `.mcp.json` passing a RELATIVE `--graph-path`, and the fact that three graphs of three different mint versions (0.17.0 / 0.22.1 / 0.23.0) now coexist in one repo with no stated compatibility policy — the report's item 6. NOT CHECKED: whether `reflow2_start_design` could refuse, rather than warn, when a `.reflow2` exists below it. Refusing is stronger than reporting and may be right for an act this hard to undo.		Filed from a first-hand field report on Anthony's real work rather than from self-host, which is the second time in one day that pointing reflow2 at something it did not author produced a finding self-host could not. That pattern is now three-for-three ((BL-199), (BL-213), this) and is the strongest standing argument for keeping external use in rotation. Recorded as its own node rather than as one of six backlog rows because it is categorically different from the other five: those are friction, this one CAUSED a wrong artefact in a user's repository and invited an irreversible act on the strength of an unchecked claim. Filing it beside 'version skew is a papercut' would flatten that. The falsified advice is written into the node deliberately. It was given today, confidently, from doctrine rather than from the launcher — and an agent reading this later needs to see that the one-graph recommendation rested on a fact nobody had checked, not just that it was incomplete.proposedOPEN — is a session pointed at a design by editing .mcp.json and reconnecting, or by a graph reference carried per call?
ACCEPTED 2026-08-06 (conditional) — a hosted reflow2 holds N single-writer stores in one process, one lock each; the directory stays the unit of a design
PROPOSED, NOT SETTLED. Submitted by @ajs from flo2 (docs/proposals/multi-graph-hosting.md, written against reflow2 0.24.0) as the concrete architectural answer to the hosting question that req:many-designs-one-service deliberately left open — that requirement's own statement says 'this is deliberately silent on where the designs live: one process per design and one holding many are both answers to it, and that is the hosting question, not this requirement.' This is that question being answered. THE ANSWER: one process opens, serves and closes SEVERAL design graphs at once, with each client session attached to exactly one — instead of the process binding one graph directory at startup and holding it for its whole life. TWO MISREADINGS KILLED EXPLICITLY, because both make the change sound far more dangerous than it is. (1) IT DOES NOT RELAX SINGLE-WRITER. RocksDB's exclusive lock is held PER DIRECTORY; nothing prevents one process holding many directories and many locks. Each design keeps exactly the single-writer guarantee it has today. The proposal is to hold N single-writer stores, not to make one store multi-writer. (2) IT IS NOT MANY DESIGNS INSIDE ONE STORE. graph_id already namespaces every stored key, so co-habiting is technically possible — and it is the wrong answer. THE ALTERNATIVE CONSIDERED AND REJECTED — many designs inside a single RocksDB store, relying on graph_id namespacing. Rejected because it would collapse the per-project directory the rest of reflow2 is built on: per-project export and the committed design document, backups and --import restore, the sidecar identity/version/sync files, the git merge driver, and the plain fact that a project's design lives under its own .reflow2/. It also makes identity.rs's silent failure mode — a design opened under the wrong id presents as EMPTY — considerably easier to hit. The gain is a smaller number of open RocksDB instances, which is a resource optimisation, not an architectural benefit. NOTE: this is the same shape as dec:idea-many-graphs-one-store, which Anthony raised as a brainstorm on 2026-08-05; this proposal answers it in the negative for the HOSTING case. WHY THIS IS SMALLER THAN IT SOUNDS — the groundwork is already in place, and this is the part worth reading before estimating. ReflowService.graph is already Arc> (crates/reflow2-mcp/src/service.rs:74), chosen precisely because several client sessions share one server (req:sessions-share-a-graph) — a registry of graphs is a map of things already shaped to be shared. Seats are already per-session not per-process (service.rs:88-93, req:seat-per-client). Per-session service instances already exist and already carry graph, graph_path and content_path (service.rs:2484-2492), so attaching a session to a CHOSEN graph is a change to where those fields come from, not to their existence. Identity is already out-of-band and per-store (crates/reflow2-core/src/identity.rs), designed to be read BEFORE the design is opened — exactly what a registry must do. HTTP already exists (--http and --serve-shared since v0.14.0). Opening is already a plain function call with no process-global state (DesignGraph::open_rocksdb, crates/reflow2-core/src/graph.rs:113). What binds the process to one graph is the CLI contract and the startup path in main.rs, not the core. WHAT ACTUALLY HAS TO CHANGE. (1) A graph registry with a lifecycle: a process-level map from graph key to open graph, carrying the metadata that currently rides on the service — graph_path, content_path, identity, and the write_gen counter the loop nudge reads (service.rs:94-99), all becoming per-graph. Opening must be on demand and BOUNDED: a cold open builds the full-text index and takes seconds on a large design (shared.rs allows 30 seconds), so the first request cannot be treated as cheap and concurrent first requests for the same graph must collapse into one open rather than racing. Eviction needs a policy — each open graph costs a RocksDB instance with its own block cache, file handles and tantivy index — so an idle timeout per graph (the existing --idle-timeout is per PROCESS) plus a cap on simultaneously open graphs, with a clear error at the cap rather than silent thrashing. (2) How a session says which graph it wants: today --graph-path, fixed for the process lifetime. SELECTION SHOULD BE BY graph_id, NOT BY PATH — a path is a property of the server's filesystem and leaks it to clients, while graph_id is the durable name the design already answers to; the registry maps id to path. Candidates in order of preference: an HTTP path prefix (/g//, visible in logs and routable by ordinary proxies), an MCP initialize parameter, or a tool call that attaches the session — the last is the worst, because it makes every session stateful in a way a reconnect silently loses and leaves a window in which a session is connected to nothing. (3) The rendezvous convention: shared.rs publishes a sidecar beside each store saying a server holds this graph and where it is, and the election is arbitrated by whichever spawned process wins the RocksDB lock — a convention that assumes one server per graph. A multi-graph server holds several stores and therefore several rendezvous claims, and should publish into EACH held graph's sidecar so an unrelated local session that opens that directory attaches rather than failing its open. (4) Not breaking the single-graph path: the overwhelmingly common case is one project, one directory, --graph-path, and it must keep working exactly as it does, including --only-if-present and the latent surface (main.rs:772) which is what makes reflow2 installable machine-wide without minting a store in every directory. THE CLEANEST FRAMING: single-graph mode is multi-graph mode with a registry of one, pre-populated at startup and with selection defaulted — NOT a second code path. (5) Commands that open the store directly: --import, --export and --stop-shared open it outside the server and currently instruct the user to stop the server first; with one server holding many graphs, 'stop the server' becomes a much more expensive instruction because it evicts every other project, so these should either route through the running server or grow a per-graph release. RISKS ACCEPTED WITH THIS SHAPE. Isolation regressions are silent and severe — a handler that reaches the wrong graph corrupts a design rather than erroring, which is why it is carried as its own requirement rather than as a note here. Resource exhaustion: N open graphs is N block caches and N tantivy indices, and without a cap a busy server degrades in a way that looks like reflow2 being slow. Failure blast radius grows: today a panic loses one project's session; serving fifty, it loses fifty. And flo2 becomes schedule-coupled to this work — under the per-project-process alternative flo2 could have been built entirely around an unchanged reflow2, and that coupling is being accepted deliberately.		Raised by @ajs from flo2's side of the seam, 2026-08-05, and it is the first time the hosting question has arrived with a concrete consumer behind it rather than as an architecture preference. WHY IT IS RECORDED HERE RATHER THAN AS A RE-OPENING OF dec:multi-writer-architecture: Anthony authorized re-opening that decision on 2026-08-05 ('yes, re-open it'), and per dec:reopen-supersedes a re-opening mints a NEW decision rather than flipping the accepted node — but that new decision ALREADY EXISTS as dec:central-host, whose own rationale says exactly this and cites the same rule. Minting a third node for the same seam would have been the duplicate HEAL later flags and somebody has to merge. So this records the concrete ANSWER and hangs it under dec:central-host, which holds the question. WHAT IS GENUINELY NEW HERE, and the reason this is not a rerun of the 2026-07-25 argument: dec:multi-writer-architecture rejected a hosted service on cost against confirmed intent — it contradicts req:persistence ('the graph lives at ./.reflow2/graph inside the consumer project, so the design travels with the repo') and req:invocation ('the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio'). Neither objection is answered by this proposal and both still stand for the LOCAL case. What changed is that flo2 is a hosted web app whose whole premise is that somebody who cannot clone a repository or run a CLI can still take part in designing something — and that premise is already accepted intent here, as req:design-reachable-without-the-repo. The proposal does not ask the local case to move; it asks for a second deployment shape alongside it, which is precisely what rule:no-foreclosure was written to keep reachable ('build nothing today that forecloses growing into a hosted, multi-user, multi-project service'). This is that rule being cashed in. THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded so nobody rediscovers it: dec:multi-writer-architecture's rejection of a hosted service turned partly on permanent operational burden and on putting the design on a machine the user does not control. A container image and a graph registry do not make either objection false — they make it somebody's job. The proposal is explicit that reflow2 has NO AUTHENTICATION OF ANY KIND today and that authorization is flo2's job at the layer in front; reflow2's obligation is only that a session bound to graph X cannot address graph Y. If that split is not stated and held, this decision quietly converts an accepted 'no hosted service' into a hosted service with no security story, which is the drift dec:reopen-supersedes exists to prevent. WHAT WAS CHECKED AND FOUND SOUND, recorded because it is the natural place to look and it is the wrong place: the export is NOT incomplete. Every node type created during a session appears in export_graph's output, including Question, ChangeEvent and Fragment, and adopt_on_import correctly preserves graph_id so a clone adopts the design's identity rather than minting a new one.acceptedOne process holds many designs: open on demand, bounded, evicted when idle, Designs live on mounted storage, and a store without its identity sidecar is refused rather than opened empty, A session names the design it wants by graph_id, and the server maps id to path, registry, A session bound to one design cannot read or write any other design in the same process — and this must be proven before multi-graph hosting ships
OPEN — retirement is two edge types and neither is consulted: which one survives?
UNDECIDED, and it is Anthony's call. The schema declares BOTH `SUPERSEDES` and `OBSOLETES` for the same relationship — one node retiring another on the record — and NEITHER is read by any computation. The choice is which one is the real vocabulary, and then making it mean something. Option A: keep `OBSOLETES` (the one the code and the retire-from-design skill already use) and delete `SUPERSEDES` from the schema and from docs/three-axes.md. Option B: keep `SUPERSEDES` (the one the schema's own doc comment describes as 'target retired on the record') and migrate the code. Option C: both survive with a stated distinction — but nobody has yet said what that distinction would be, and two words for one relationship is how a vocabulary rots.		FOUND BY THE SCHEMA SWEEP, 2026-07-28, and it is the `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` shape at edge level rather than property level. WHAT WAS MEASURED. `SUPERSEDES` has ZERO references in the entire Rust source: nothing creates it, nothing reads it. It is nonetheless documented in `nodes.rs` ('source supersedes target — target retired on the record') and named in `docs/three-axes.md` as part of what covers the time axis. `OBSOLETES` is the one actually in use — `collapse_decision` draws it when a chosen alternative retires the losers, and the retire-from-design skill instructs users to draw it for a capability or component with a successor. But `OBSOLETES` has NO READER either: grep across the whole core crate finds the constant, the one create site, and a doc comment. No rollup, detector or report consults it. WHAT THAT MEANS TODAY, stated exactly rather than dramatised: retiring something marks it and changes nothing downstream. A retired capability still counts in every rollup, still raises its gaps, still appears in delivery arithmetic. It is currently LATENT — reflow2's own design contains zero instances of either edge, so the retire path has never been exercised on this project — but the skill is actively telling users to draw an edge that has no effect, which is worse than an edge nobody knows about. WHY IT IS NOT JUST HOUSEKEEPING. `req:intent-preserved` ('the past is never overwritten') is the requirement retirement serves, and the retire-from-design skill exists precisely to force the question 'was this ever true?' — history retired on the record versus a mistake deleted. That whole discipline currently terminates in an edge nothing reads. Whichever edge survives, the deciding question is the same: what SHOULD consult it — delivery roll-up, the gap detectors, `graph_report`'s counts — and does a retired node stop counting, or count separately? DELIBERATELY LEFT `proposed`: this is a vocabulary choice with migration consequences for anyone who already drew either edge, and `dec:certainty-derived` forbids recording it as settled on the user's behalf.proposednothing
