No START-HERE document — orientation is a projection, and writing it down would be dev_storyflow in miniature
Anthony asked 2026-07-31 whether a 'start here' file or node should tell a newly-cloned agent what it needs to pick up where the last person left off — offered explicitly as an idea to explore, with the observation that reflow2 often already has something. It does, and the answer is: BUILD THE VIEW, NOT THE DOCUMENT. NO START-HERE FILE. Two recorded positions already forbid it, and neither is a stretch. `req:session-memory-in-graph`: 'a summary written at the end is the one a busy session never gets to, and an end-of-session digest is a retelling rather than a record.' And `dec:what-lives-where`'s whole storyflow lesson is prose-you-navigate losing to graph-you-query. A START-HERE.md is `dev_storyflow` in miniature — it would go stale, and STALENESS IN AN ORIENTATION DOCUMENT IS THE WORST PLACE FOR IT, because it is the first thing read and the reader has nothing yet to check it against. THE NEED IS REAL AND MOSTLY ALREADY DESIGNED. Three planned capabilities cover it between them: `cap:what-next` (which of the agreed things to do now, ranked so an unmade decision outranks the work waiting on it), `cap:onboarding` (where does a new piece of work belong, for someone who did not build the system), and `cap:session-memory` (what the last session learned, queryable rather than narrated). None needs a document; all three are projections, which is what `dec:views-are-projections` already says every view is. WHAT IS GENUINELY MISSING, and it belongs in `cap:what-next` rather than in a new thing: WHICH FEW DECISIONS SHAPE EVERYTHING ELSE. Neither what-next nor where-am-i answers it today, and it is what a newcomer actually needs — not the task list, but the handful of choices that explain why the rest looks as it does. EVIDENCE AGAINST URGENCY, recorded because it is the kind of thing that otherwise gets built on a feeling. `where-am-i` DID orient a fresh agent on this design earlier the same day: 627 nodes, roughly six calls, using `scan_nodes` with `brief: true` and reading six Decisions in full. It scales today because reads are bounded (`cap:bounded-reads`). The concern that it stops working is a FORECAST, not yet an observation — worth watching rather than pre-solving, and worth re-measuring when the answer changes rather than assuming it has. SO THE ORDER IS: build `cap:what-next`, whose blocker has already cleared, and add the shaping-decisions section to it. Do not add a fourth thing beside three planned ones that already answer the question.		Taken on the recommendation rather than the request, which is the point worth noting: the question was 'should we write a start-here document', and the honest answer was that the artefact would work against the reason the project exists. Anthony's own framing left room for that — 'maybe this isn't needed because an agent using reflow2 can already quickly know what a project is about' — and the measurement supports it. The more useful outcome was not the answer but what looking produced: `cap:what-next` states a prerequisite that has since been met, and nothing surfaced it. A capability that records its own blocking condition in prose has written a trigger that nothing fires. That is the same shape as every other declared-but-unread property this project keeps finding, and it is the argument for the shaping-decisions section being a COMPUTATION rather than another paragraph. The in-degree caveat is kept deliberately. The first version of the idea looked convincing because the top three results were genuinely load-bearing; the top result was not, and reporting the idea without that would have been reporting a demo rather than a measurement.acceptedSay what to work on next, as a projection with its reasoning shown
PROPOSED — where-am-i shows four ranked open decisions and one deliberately UNRANKED, and a rough ranking is explicitly good enough
PROPOSED, APPROVER `who:ajs`. His shape, 2026-08-10: *'maybe we do a top 4 and bottom 1 that always appears in the where-am-i?'* TWO CONSTRAINTS HE STATED IN THE SAME BREATH, AND BOTH LOWER THE BAR ON PURPOSE. (1) APPROXIMATION IS EXPLICITLY ACCEPTABLE: *'this doesn't have to be an exact 'what is the most pressing decision'. getting something in the general ballpark of what decisions I need to make or a rough 'top 5' is better than an equal set of 60+ decisions.'* THIS IS AN ACCEPTANCE CRITERION AND IT SHOULD BE READ AS ONE. It means the ranking need not be defensible item by item — only roughly right at the head — which disposes of the standing objection that every candidate signal is too noisy. A flat list of 83 is the baseline being beaten, and it is a low bar. RECORDED BECAUSE THE OPPOSITE INSTINCT IS THE DEFAULT ONE: this project's habit is to refuse to compute what it cannot compute honestly, and here the user has said in advance that rough is what he wants. (2) UNRANKED IS NOT DISCARDED: *'it is not like we are throwing the unmade decisions aside and saying 'these are not ranked well, therefore not important and we'll never make a decision on them'.'* Nothing leaves the pile by ranking low, and the display must not read as a shortlist of what matters. ⭐⭐ AND HE NAMED THE FLAW HIMSELF, WHICH IS WHY THE SHAPE HAS FIVE SLOTS AND NOT FOUR: *'which has a side effect of saying things not searched for are not important, which is not true.'* ⇒ THE BOTTOM SLOT IS THE EXPLORATION TERM, ARRIVED AT INDEPENDENTLY AND FROM THE OTHER DIRECTION. `dec:attention-is-measured-behaviourally-not-lexically` records, from the reinforcement-learning framing, that any attention ranking reinforces what has already been visited — so a node nothing surfaces is never read, never accumulates, and never rises, permanently; and that the standard remedies are an exploration term or optimistic initialisation. Anthony reached the same requirement from the user-experience side, before seeing that consequence applied. **THE TOP FOUR ARE EXPLOITATION AND THE BOTTOM ONE IS EXPLORATION.** A convergence from two independent directions is the strongest evidence this design gets that a property is real rather than clever. THE SUBTLETY THAT DECIDES WHETHER THE BOTTOM SLOT WORKS AT ALL: 'bottom 1' IS NOT A RANK, IT IS A HUGE TIE. Under any attention signal, everything never surfaced scores identically — measured 2026-08-10, 61 of 83 open decisions govern nothing and would sit in that tie under a consequence ranking too. So the slot needs a TIEBREAK, and the choice of tiebreak is the whole design: - DETERMINISTIC (always the same one) STARVES THE REST and is the failure mode dressed as a feature. - RANDOM among the never-touched is ε-greedy proper, and samples the set over time. - OLDEST-UNSEEN is random's better-behaved cousin: it guarantees coverage instead of merely expecting it, and it makes the slot's promise checkable. COVERAGE IS COMPUTABLE AND SHOULD BE STATED RATHER THAN FELT: one slot per orientation against 61 unranked items is 61 orientations to see them all once. That is months at any normal cadence. If that is too slow the answer is more slots or an oldest-first draw, and the number is the argument — not a preference. WHAT THIS SHAPE DOES NOT DEPEND ON, and why it can ship first: the slot structure is independent of HOW the top four are ranked. Any signal fills it — consequence (`dec:idea-a-critical-path-through-the-undecided`), attention (`dec:idea-what-gets-searched-repeatedly-is-becoming-important`), or the already-accepted rule in `req:what-next` that an unmade decision outranks the work waiting on it. IT IS THEREFORE BUILDABLE BEFORE EITHER OPEN QUESTION IS SETTLED, using whatever ranking exists, which makes it the smallest useful increment in this whole thread. TWO THINGS THE DISPLAY MUST SAY, given constraint (2): that the bottom slot is a DELIBERATE sample of the unranked and not the least important thing, and how many open decisions are not shown. A five-item list that silently stands for 83 is the false completeness `where-am-i` already forbids ('never report from a page as if it were the whole set'). OPEN, NOT SETTLED HERE: the tiebreak (random vs oldest-unseen); whether four is the right exploitation width; whether the ranking behind the top four is one merged score or two lists; and whether the same shape belongs in `loop_status` as well as `where-am-i`.		Anthony's shape, recorded as its own Decision rather than folded into either open ranking question because it is separable from both and shippable before either — the slot structure works with any ranking, including the one `req:what-next` already accepts. Folding it into a brainstorm node would bury the one piece of this thread that can be built now. The convergence is the part worth preserving. The exploration requirement was derived an hour earlier from the Q-table framing as a consequence nobody had asked for; Anthony proposed the bottom slot from the user-experience side without reference to it. Two independent derivations of the same property is stronger evidence than either, and a later session that finds only one of them would be free to drop it as over-engineering. The acceptance criterion is recorded as prominently as the shape because it cuts against this project's own reflex. reflow2 repeatedly refuses to compute what it cannot compute honestly — `dec:readiness-is-an-observation-the-threshold-is-the-judgement` is the canonical case. Here the user has pre-authorised a rough answer, and without that on the record the natural instinct is to refuse to rank at all and ship nothing.acceptedSay what to work on next, as a projection with its reasoning shown
What ATTACHES an Artifact is defined by excluding bookkeeping, not by listing the edges that count
PROPOSED, AWAITING ANTHONY'S WORD — the code is built and tested this way, but the rule shape is a judgement he should ratify. BL-176's fix could have taken either form. THE FORM NOT TAKEN: extend the inclusion list — count REALIZES plus DOCUMENTS plus SPECIFIES (plus PRODUCES incoming, plus SATISFIES) as attaching an Artifact. This is what the field report asked for and it would have closed the reported case. THE FORM TAKEN: invert it. An Artifact is an orphan when EVERY edge it carries, in either direction, is bookkeeping — INCLUDES from a Release, CHANGED from a ChangeEvent, YIELDED from a Fragment, AT_EPOCH. Anything else attaches. REASONING, and it is a generalisation of the bug rather than a preference: an inclusion list has to be extended every time the vocabulary grows, and until someone remembers, correctly-modelled work reads as a defect. That IS this bug — the list said REALIZES and the schema had since grown DOCUMENTS and SPECIFIES. BL-170 was the same shape from another direction, a hidden inclusion list making a region invisible, and BL-114 witnessed this same detector doing it twice in an unrelated repo. An exclusion list fails the other way: a new DESIGN edge counts as attachment the day it is added and needs no edit here, while only a new BOOKKEEPING edge needs a line. THE COUNTERWEIGHT THAT DEFINES THE RULE'S LIMIT: this is deliberately NOT the degree-zero rule the Decision arm of the same detector uses. Degree-zero was settled for Decisions by measurement and is right there — but almost every Artifact in a mature graph carries a Release INCLUDES edge, so degree-zero would silence orphan_node everywhere. The distinction is that bookkeeping edges are drawn by the machinery, not by anyone saying what the file is FOR. WHAT STILL FIRES, pinned by tests: an Artifact attached by nothing, and a document artifact with no DOCUMENTS edge — because BL-176 was explicit that this doc describes nothing either IS worth saying, so artifact_type must never be a free pass. THE HONEST LIMIT, and it is BL-199: reflow2's own graph goes 0 to 0 across this change and cannot demonstrate the fix, because all 139 of its artifacts carry REALIZES — including 32 of its 35 documents and specs, against the link-artifacts skill's own instruction. The evidence is the six new tests and the field measurement, never this graph. THE RISK OF THE CHOSEN FORM, stated so it is not discovered later: if a future bookkeeping edge type is added and nobody adds it here, it will silently count as attachment and quiet the detector for those nodes. That is the mirror of the failure being fixed, and it is accepted as the smaller one because bookkeeping edge types are added rarely and deliberately while design edge types are added often.		Recorded because the choice is invisible in the diff — both forms produce the same result on every case anyone has reported, and they differ only in how they FAIL as the vocabulary grows. A future maintainer reading `ARTIFACT_BOOKKEEPING` should find the reason it is an exclusion list rather than rediscovering the argument, and Anthony should get to overrule it while it is still cheap.proposedRepair structure
OWNED_BY is built: claims were shown insufficient, and ownership becomes its own edge
DECIDED AND BUILT 2026-08-09, Anthony's word, closing the condition dec:ownership-reads-claims-before-adding-an-edge set on 2026-08-08. THAT DECISION SAID: build the first cut from CLAIMS, and \'decide on OWNED_BY only after that is built and SHOWN TO BE INSUFFICIENT\'. Its rationale named the disqualifying evidence in advance — \'if claims turn out to model the wrong thing (they are TRANSIENT WORK-IN-HAND, while ownership is DURABLE and survives the session), that is a real distinction and the edge becomes justified on evidence rather than on anticipation.\' THE EVIDENCE ARRIVED AS DESCRIBED. dev_storyflow filed the distinction on 2026-08-09 and Anthony supplied the use case: \'there are areas of the design that are his and areas that are mine... it is probably durable, survives every session, and should never be released.\' Claims cannot carry that, operationally rather than theoretically: claim_region's own description says advisory and session-scoped, the parallel-work skill says release at checkout, and on a shared server a claim reads `unknown` rather than `live` and never expires on its own. Standing ownership claims would permanently drown the tool's actual job — showing who is ACTIVELY in your ground. ⭐ THE FRAMING THAT MADE IT LEGIBLE — reflow2 had two of the three WHO axes: AUTHORED_BY who WROTE this past tense · historical · never changes CLAIMS who is IN it RIGHT NOW transient · advisory · released at checkout OWNED_BY whose AREA this is durable · standing · never released AND THE REFRAME THAT DECIDED SCOPE: every earlier version of this ask was framed around an agent fleet, which invites \'that is exotica\'. Two people splitting a design is the ORDINARY case of collaborative design work. dev_storyflow retracted the general form of their own counter-argument on exactly this point — their objection (ownership in the graph duplicates their PROTOCOL.md matrix and would rot) \'is specific to an organisation that ALREADY writes ownership down. A pair of collaborators has no matrix.\' WHAT WAS BUILT: · OWNED_BY, `* → Contributor`, with `note` (what is actually owned, and any bound on it) and `since`. · DELIBERATELY NOT A TRACEABILITY EDGE — absent from structural_rule, the THIRD of a kind after AUTHORED_BY and CLAIMS. Owning something says who ANSWERS for it, not that a change to it changes them. A test asserts a Contributor never appears in a blast radius. · A served `owned_by` tool. · loop_status(contributor_id) now reports `gaps_on_owned_ground` — open gaps standing on that person's ground, each naming WHICH owned nodes it touches. `not_attributable` shrinks by exactly that many, so the more ownership a design records the less the tool has to say \'I cannot tell whose this is\'. Scoped `clean` now requires BOTH halves empty: a gap on your own ground is owed by you as surely as a decision you were asked to settle. ⚠️ WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT, and it is the restraint that matters: THE OWNERSHIP-ORPHAN DETECTOR. An unowned node raises NOTHING. dec:idea-detect-ownership-orphans holds that question open because of the fleet's strongest objection — in a 1,127-node graph most nodes legitimately have no owner (\'a Constraint about prose rendering is nobody's in the accountability sense\'), so a naive detector fires on the majority and becomes a signal trained to be ignored, while in a two-person project the design is mostly partitioned and the same detector is nearly silent. WHICH TYPES ARE OWNABLE looks like a per-project declaration rather than a fixed rule, and that is a design input nobody has supplied. THE ASYMMETRY IS THE POINT AND IS WORTH KEEPING: \'is this gap on ground you own?\' is a FACT the graph can answer. \'Should this have an owner?\' is a JUDGEMENT it cannot. The first shipped; the second did not. STAMP MOVED: a 61st edge type. The next release owes an upgrade note. Four separate count guards caught it — schema.rs, vocabulary.rs, the MCP tools test and smoke_mcp.py — which is the schema's own tripwire working exactly as intended.		Recorded as its own Decision rather than by editing dec:ownership-reads-claims-before-adding-an-edge, because that one is ACCEPTED and dec:reopen-supersedes is explicit that a settled choice is never un-accepted — a new decision supersedes it. This is not a reversal: it is that decision's own condition being met and its own build order being followed to its stated end. The restraint half is recorded here rather than only in the capability, because \'we built the edge and deliberately did not build the detector\' is the kind of thing a later session re-derives as an oversight unless the reasoning is on the record beside the choice.acceptedWhose AREA a node is, recorded durably and read where debt is reported

Where the publish/subscribe role lives: on the Interface, or on every node
OPEN — Anthony's word needed. Anthony described the role as an attribute of each NODE in an architecture (publish / subscribe / both / non_external). reflow2 already carries something very close: `Interface.designation` (internal | published), with PROVIDES and CONSUMES naming who stands on which side. So the question is whether the pairing role extends the Interface, or becomes a property every node type carries. ALTERNATIVES WEIGHED. (1) Extend `Interface.designation` — RECOMMENDED. (2) A role property on every node, Anthony's original shape: most general, lets any node participate in a seam; costs correctness, because a Component both publishes and subscribes so the value collapses to `both` and pairs with everything, and it adds a property to 28 node types for a case nothing currently needs. (3) Neither — keep pairing manual as mirror_surface does today and let compose_and_analyse surface a bad seam as an ordinary gap once a human has wired the two sides; cheapest, but leaves exactly the hand-wiring that made this idea worth having.		WHY THE INTERFACE. An Interface IS a boundary — it is the one node type whose entire reason for existing is to be the place two things meet, which is exactly what pairs. The publish side already exists there, is already exported by export_surface, and already withholds internals correctly. And a role is not intrinsic to a node: the same Component publishes one contract and subscribes to another, so a single role on the Component would be wrong about half the time. Anthony's `both` value is the tell — it is needed only because the attribute is sitting on the wrong noun. On an Interface, `both` is rare and meaningful (a genuinely bidirectional contract) rather than a shrug. WHAT MUST BE ADDED WHICHEVER WAY IT GOES, because this is the actual missing half: a way to declare what a design NEEDS from outside — a REQUIRED boundary — standing on its own, without the consumer first having modelled the provider's contract inside its own design. Concretely, a third value alongside `internal` and `published`, plus the matchable KEY Anthony named (an id and a description), which is what one design's `required` is matched against another's `published`. Without a key, pairing falls back to fuzzy name matching alone, and names are exactly what two organisations that never coordinated will have chosen differently. NOT SETTLED HERE: how a pair is recorded — an edge between the two Interfaces, or mirroring one into the other. MIRRORS already exists for the second; there is no edge type meaning 'these two boundaries are the same boundary seen from opposite sides', and adding one WOULD move the version stamp and lock out older reflow2 installs.acceptedPair two designs by complementary role, so the seam is computed rather than hand-wired
AoA alternatives are branch-by-file and live in design-space (CONTRADICTS), not time (epochs)
Parallel alternatives (an analysis of alternatives held open until a decision) are represented BRANCH-BY-FILE: each alternative is a separate exported design (a git branch's reflow2.json, or an export file), not a world-tag inside one live graph. This reuses everything BL-80 built — cross-branch comparison is compare_designs, collapsing the winner is merge_designs/apply_merge, retiring the loser is retire-from-design — so reflow2 owns almost no new branch machinery, consistent with the merge's 'git is the DAG' decision. Semantically, alternatives are design SPACE, not time: sibling alternatives coexist 'now' and CONTRADICT each other, held under a proposed Decision (the decision point) until it collapses — distinct from an epoch (EVOLVES_INTO, before->after). Forking is not advancing time; storage may still be a ref/epoch, but the semantic layer keeps 'the road not taken' apart from 'an earlier version' (BL-70's warning). v1 is the N-way AoA report (analyze_alternatives): measures per branch (graph_report snapshot — nodes, open gaps, allocation health, verification coverage) side by side, plus each branch's structural divergence from a named baseline (compare_designs). Rung 2 wires the decision point: a proposed Decision GOVERNS lightweight alternative pointers that CONTRADICT their siblings; collapsing accepts the Decision, merges the winner into the baseline, and retires the losers with their rationale.		User decided both axes 2026-07-22, each the recommended option. Branch-by-file over world-scope because BL-80 already built the comparison (compare_designs), the collapse (merge/apply_merge) and the retire machinery, so branch-by-file is the cheapest increment BL-70 itself named ('one exported graph per alternative plus a cross-export comparison report ... branch-by-file works today') and it is consistent with dec:merge-three-way's 'explicit inputs, git is the DAG'; world-scoping would bake world-awareness into every detector (possible_duplicate, allocation, SPOF, …) — a large invasive change for a simultaneous-in-one-graph benefit not yet needed, and BL-70 says branch-by-file 'teaches what the real scoping primitive must preserve' first. Space-over-time because an AoA holds both roads at once (design space, CONTRADICTS); reusing the epoch/PRECEDES time chain for branches (git's literal branch=commit-in-a-DAG, BL-80 #3) would make the road-not-taken indistinguishable from an earlier version — exactly the conflation BL-70 warns against. This is the fork/navigation substrate BL-81 (roads-not-taken) needs and shares the scoping primitive with BL-44 (cluster claims). Deferred: the decision-point pointer nodes + collapse wiring (rung 2), world-scoping if simultaneous in-graph AoA proves needed, and per-branch readiness scoring (BL-68).acceptedCompare parallel alternatives on the same measures (AoA), Hold and collapse a decision point (forkable alternatives)

Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: phase-coverage trial, BL-30.acceptedDetect gaps, Recover intent from test evidence, without letting the tests prove themselves, Whether intent has been delivered is computed from the golden thread, never asserted
OPEN — does reflow2 model scheduled time (H-hour, durations, critical path) as a first-class axis?
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. The one place the vocabulary genuinely strains against a plan. reflow2's temporal axis is DECISION time — DesignEpoch, Snapshot, valid_from/valid_to, ChangeEvent: 'when did we settle this, and what was in force then'. A plan needs EXECUTION time: H-hour and offsets from it, durations, windows, and a critical path computed from dependencies. Flow + PRECEDES + TRIGGERS gives ordering, not schedule. (a) ADD IT — scheduled instants/durations on Flow steps plus a computed critical path; the biggest vocabulary addition since the temporal axis, and it makes 'the timeline slipped' a computation rather than a note. (b) LEAVE IT OUT and reference an external schedule (MS Project, a synch matrix) from the graph; keeps reflow2 out of a crowded, well-solved problem, at the cost that the blast radius of a slip cannot be computed — which is exactly the thing worth having. (c) MINIMAL — offsets from a named reference event and durations, no calendar, no resource levelling, no Gantt: enough to compute what a slip breaks, not enough to be a scheduling tool. THE VOCABULARY CONSTRAINT EITHER WAY: no military or acquisition words enter the schema (req:design-anything, and the way dec:mosa-conformance was settled) — H-hour is a named reference event, not a schema noun.		Named as the honest gap while mapping a staff planning process onto the existing vocabulary, which otherwise carried it almost without strain: ALLOCATED_TO is troop-to-task, Interface plus PROVIDES/CONSUMES is a coordination point or transfer of authority, Decision plus register_alternative is COA development and comparison, Constraint is constraints and restraints with breach computed, Verification is a rehearsal or confirmation brief, and a FRAGO is a ChangeEvent with a computed blast radius. Recorded rather than acted on because (c) is a real design choice that turns on whether any computation would read it — the same test dec:exploratory-staging applies to brainstorm vocabulary — and because getting it wrong means either reimplementing MS Project badly or leaving the highest-value computation on the table. Detail in docs/planning-at-scale.md §1.proposednothing
DECIDED in the field — a session is pointed at a design by a PROJECT-SCOPED config override, and an absolute path must never enter a global config
DECIDED BY DOING IT, 2026-08-05, on `hxm_program`. This is `dec:how-a-session-is-pointed-at-a-design` option (a) — edit config, restart — CARRIED OUT AND VERIFIED, together with the constraint that makes it safe. ⭐ THE RULE THAT MATTERS, AND IT WAS MISSING FROM THE PROCEDURE THIS AGENT SUPPLIED: reflow2 is configured USER-GLOBALLY on this machine (`~/.claude.json` `mcpServers`, `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`) with a RELATIVE `--graph-path .reflow2/graph`. An absolute project path must go ONLY into PROJECT-SCOPED config — `~/.claude.json` under `projects('/ABS/PATH').mcpServers.reflow2`, or `claude mcp add reflow2 --scope local`. PUTTING AN ABSOLUTE PATH IN THE GLOBAL ENTRY WOULD POINT EVERY PROJECT ON THE MACHINE AT ONE PROJECT'S GRAPH. ⚠️ AND THAT IS EXACTLY WHAT THIS AGENT'S INSTRUCTIONS WOULD HAVE CAUSED. Asked for 'exact instructions', it produced a procedure saying 'edit every config that launches reflow2' and listed only REPO-LOCAL paths (`.mcp.json`, `opencode.json`, `.vscode/mcp.json`). THE ERROR WAS IN THE DERIVATION, NOT THE TYPING: the procedure was read out of `tools/reflow2_init.py`, which writes repo-local configs — and `reflow2_init.py` NEVER WRITES `~/.claude.json`, so it does not describe how this machine is actually set up. A generic answer was given to a specific question by reading the installer's INTENT instead of the machine's STATE. The user's own agent caught it and wrote the missing rule. THE VERIFIED PROCEDURE, as executed: (1) confirm the target store EXISTS and read its `graph.id.json` for the id and label — never point at a missing path, because that mints a new empty graph; (2) add the project-scoped override, changing ONLY `--graph-path` and preserving `--shared` and `--only-if-present`; (3) RESTART THE SESSION — a `/mcp` reconnect is not enough, because the stdio server survives it and project scope is read at session start — then confirm via `ps` that the process start time is after the edit and the command line shows the absolute path; (4) call `design_identity` and check the id and label against step 1, stopping before any write if they disagree. WHAT THIS AGENT DID NOT KNOW AND SHOULD HAVE: `--only-if-present` EXISTS AND IS ALREADY SHIPPED (`crates/reflow2-mcp/src/main.rs:76`, checked at `main.rs:772` against `latent::design_present`). It is why a graph-less directory only OFFERS `start_design` rather than silently minting. Nine proposed requirements considered and not accepted — seven dropped, two folded into one rule
Anthony's word, 2026-07-30, after asking for the open requirements to be strongly scrutinised: an unaccepted requirement that is not value-adding and only causes confusion should be retired as 'considered, but not accepted' rather than carried. NINE of twenty-six went. All are `dropped`, not deleted: the capture was real and the reasoning is worth keeping, so each keeps its full statement and a snapshot of its final state on the timeline (`epoch:prune-proposed`). DROPPED AS NOT VALUE-ADDING (7). `req:drift-rolls-up-to-a-score` and `req:framework-is-chosen-not-defaulted` — both record a DOUBT rather than a need, and say so in their own names: 'probably NOT from a single scalar' and 'a framework registry is probably the wrong fix'. A requirement that argues against its own mechanism is a Decision wearing the wrong hat. The live fact inside the second (`Project.domain` is written and never read) survives inside `req:defaults-do-not-assert`. `req:friction-has-a-baseline` and `req:friction-has-a-severity-bar` — measuring reflow2's own usability against a baseline, and a threshold at which friction becomes scheduled work. Both are backlog hygiene dressed as product requirements: the answer to unconverted friction reports is to act on them, not to model them. `req:context-is-a-modelled-quantity` — `cap:bounded-reads` already answers the acute version, where a read that would not fit says so and names what it withheld. What remained was design-time estimation, which the requirement's own text calls the weak half. `req:blocking-is-partial` — freezing drifted work while the rest proceeds. Nobody has been hurt by the all-or-nothing gate; speculative. `req:adopt-says-how-much-it-got` — REDUNDANT with `req:coverage-visible`, which is accepted and delivered by `cap:coverage`. FOLDED INTO `req:defaults-do-not-assert` (2). `req:edge-defaults-do-not-assert` and `req:functional-vocabulary-computes` restate one rule — node defaults, edge defaults and declared-but-unread vocabulary are the same defect: THE SCHEMA MUST NOT DECLARE WHAT NOTHING READS OR CHECKS. Their measured evidence is preserved inside the surviving requirement rather than lost with them. A CORRECTION MADE DURING EXECUTION, kept on the record because the reasoning that produced it was wrong in an instructive way. `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` was proposed for folding as the third member, on the grounds that it had exactly ONE edge and was 'an orphan in all but name'. That single edge was an incoming SATISFIES from `cap:supporting-is-not-conflict`, which is `realized` — the contradiction detector already reads `alignment`. So the requirement was not an orphan; it was DELIVERED, and its status had simply never moved off `proposed`. It is now `accepted`. Low edge count was read as low value, and for a requirement that has been built, edge count is exactly backwards: a delivered requirement needs only one edge, the one from the thing that delivered it. NOT TOUCHED, and worth recording why. The 2026-07-28 planning cluster — `req:epochs-can-be-planned`, `req:plans-move-honestly`, `req:version-combination-is-an-object`, `req:graph-indexes-snapshots` — are Anthony's own ideas, quoting him directly (the Black-Scholes analogy for plan volatility, 'in systems engineering, I think this would be 2 views of the same system'). They are structurally disconnected, but that means CAPTURED AND NEVER WIRED, not low value. The fix for those is to wire them, not to retire them. `req:assumptions-are-first-class` (ordinary risk practice) and `req:correspondence-rules-are-stateable` (ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010) likewise stand.		The prompt was his: 'if some of them are not value added and just cause confusion, then we don't have to do them — we can retire them as considered, but not accepted.' The test applied to each was whether the requirement would change what anyone BUILDS. A requirement that records a doubt does not; it records that a mechanism looked wrong, which is a Decision. A requirement that restates one already accepted does not; it splits one thread in two. A requirement that describes how the project should manage itself does not; it is process. What survived is everything with a code citation, a real incident, or a standing external practice behind it. TWO SIGNALS AGREED ON FOUR, and the fifth disagreement is the useful one. `req:framework-is-chosen-not-defaulted`, `req:functional-vocabulary-computes`, `req:friction-has-a-baseline` and `req:friction-has-a-severity-bar` each sat in a `disconnected_community` island AND on the retire list on their merits. But the same check listed four of Anthony's own ideas as islands, and `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` — nearly edgeless — turned out to be delivered. So structural isolation is evidence about WIRING and never about worth, in either direction: it over-accuses parked captures and it under-accuses delivered work whose thread is short. Checking the one edge before dropping it is what caught that, and the check cost one call. DROPPED, NOT DELETED, which is the retire-from-design skill's central distinction. These were genuinely considered — several were found by measurement. Deleting them would erase why the surviving rules are shaped as they are, and would let the same captures be re-made next quarter by someone who could not see they had been weighed. `dropped` also stops them raising `unsatisfied_requirement`, so the open list means what it says again.acceptedAdopting an existing system reports how much of it was actually recovered, Work that drifted can be frozen without freezing the work that did not, Context cost is MEASURED and budgeted, not estimated at design time, A default must not assert what nobody chose, Escalation from drift is computed — but probably NOT from a single scalar, Edge properties default like node properties do, and the sweep never looked at them, Project.domain is written and never read — but a framework registry is probably the wrong fix, Usability is measured against a baseline, so getting harder to use is detectable, Friction is classified and has a bar at which it becomes work, The functional vocabulary must compute something or not be declared
Reads surface loop debt only when it's real — option C (state-derived, orientation reads, fire-on-change)
RESOLVED 2026-07-24 on Anthony's word: OPTION C. A read carries a loop-debt pointer ONLY when loop_status would report real outstanding debt, and stays silent when the loop is clean — never the static-every-read of (B), which BL-90 already rejected as boilerplate the agent learns to skim. AXIS 2 resolved: the hint rides the orientation-shaped reads (graph_report, scan_nodes, search_design, get_node — what an agent runs to get its bearings), and fires only when the owed-set CHANGES since it was last surfaced (fire-on-change) — so it appears once when debt arises and stays quiet until the picture moves, which also bounds the per-read cost of computing what is owed. The read-side sibling of the write tools' loop_hint (dec:loop-status-state-not-history). Satisfies req:read-surfaces-debt; unbuilt until it lands in the MCP read tools' result path. Options weighed: (A) do nothing — SessionStart + Stop suffice; (B) static reminder on every read; (C, CHOSEN) state-derived conditional hint.		Leaning C on axis 1, for reasons already on the record. (B) is the failure mode the user explicitly rejected in BL-90 ('aggressive wording across ~90 tool descriptions — cancels out at that scale'): boilerplate on every return trains the agent to skim past it, and reads differ from writes in a way that makes static wrong here — a write always advances the loop (it creates debt, so a static 'next step' is always relevant, which is why the write-side loop_hint is static and accepted), whereas a read creates no debt, so a constant reminder is irrelevant most of the time and becomes noise. (C) respects dec:loop-status-state-not-history (debt is computed from current state, never remembered) and dec:anchored-first (a real, named problem outranks a generic nudge). (A) is the honest null option: the three existing triggers may already be enough, and the marginal value of C is specifically the mid-session read that SessionStart and Stop don't see. Axis 2 exists because loop_status is cheap but not free; the throttle is where C's cost is paid. Sibling of the write-side loop_hint; BL-74 family. A readiness forecast is a TemporalFact, because a forecast is not an observation
BL-68 vocabulary question 3, answered by Anthony 2026-08-01. A readiness FORECAST over time is carried as a `TemporalFact` series on the technology — 'TRL 3 valid from now, TRL 7 valid from epoch 2035' — rather than as a projected `DimensionObservation` per epoch. THE DECIDING ARGUMENT IS A FIELD NAME, and it is not pedantry: `DimensionObservation.observed_at` says OBSERVED, and nobody observed anything in 2035. Recording a projection as an observation is exactly the fiction (BL-157) was filed about — a record asserting something happened that did not — and it would sit inside the very machinery a roadmap is computed from, so the fiction would propagate rather than sit still. `TemporalFact` is already defined as 'a time-bounded assertion true only between two epochs', with VALID_FROM/VALID_TO and the property that any past state stays reconstructable; a readiness projection is literally that shape, so this reuses the vocabulary rather than bending a neighbouring one. TWO OBLIGATIONS THE SHAPE CARRIES, both of which must be built with it: the fact must MARK ITSELF as forecast rather than measured, because the whole value of the roadmap is that a reader can tell which epochs rest on evidence and which on projection; and it must carry CONFIDENCE THAT DECAYS WITH HORIZON, which `req:plans-move-honestly` already commits to for plans and which a ten-year TRL projection needs more than any plan does. WHAT THIS MAKES COMPUTABLE, which is BL-68's whole thesis: the epoch an increment can deliver on is the earliest epoch by which every enabling technology on its golden thread clears its stated threshold — and because the thread and the facts are both in the graph, the answer can NAME ITS REASON ('2036 because THIS component is TRL 3 today, projected 7 in 2035'), which is the legibility the row says real programs lacked.		Anthony's call, 2026-08-01. Chosen over the projected DimensionObservation, which was the cheaper option and would have reused the existing per-epoch drift trail and its queries — rejected on the `observed_at` argument above. Also chosen over deferring the question until the representation ships, which would have followed this project's own recurring lesson (reproduce on real data before designing the fix); taken now instead because the forecast is not a refinement of the representation but the thing that makes the roadmap compute FORWARD rather than confirm backward, so designing the representation without it would settle the easy half against a guess about the hard one. Pairs with dec:readiness-is-an-observation-the-threshold-is-the-judgement; neither is useful alone.acceptedReadiness gates an increment, and the roadmap says why, An epoch can be planned, not only recorded, The epoch an increment can deliver on is computed from readiness, not declared
Readiness is its own construct, and the gating threshold is stated — never defaulted
BL-68 vocabulary question 2, answered by Anthony 2026-08-01. TWO PARTS, and the second is the load-bearing one. REPRESENTATION: readiness gets its OWN construct — an integer level 1-9 with a kind (TRL/MRL) — not a value in the `dimension` enum. Three reasons, all from the schema rather than preference: `DimensionAssessment.score` is a float 0.0-1.0 documented as '0 = worst, 1 = best', so a 1-9 ladder can only enter it lossily (TRL 7 as 0.78 asserts a precision the ladder does not have); the `dimension` enum is a closed list of QUALITY AXES — reliability, maintainability, coupling — and readiness is not a quality of the design, it is a fact about the maturity of an enabling technology; and `maturity` is ALREADY in that enum meaning code maturity, so adding TRL beside it would put two different things under one word, which is the (BL-115) shape (two states rendering identically because the vocabulary has no word for one of them). THRESHOLD: the level at which readiness GATES is stated on the thing being gated, and reflow2 REFUSES to supply a default. An absent threshold reports as ungated; it is never assumed. THIS IS THE PART THAT KEEPS THE FEATURE INSIDE `dec:report-dont-judge`: a TRL is an OBSERVATION, so computing over it is detect_gaps-shaped rather than ranking-shaped and does not conflict with `dec:alternatives-unranked-forkable`'s rule that the human does credit assignment. But the threshold IS a judgement — 'TRL below 5 means not buildable yet' is a policy about risk appetite — and a default would let reflow2 silently decide buildability. THE PRECEDENT IS MEASURED, NOT ARGUED: `Interface.medium` defaulted to REST and thereby made two silent boundaries 'agree' on a value neither had chosen, which `ver:seam-incompatibility` caught and BL-129 fixed. A defaulted readiness threshold is the same defect with a bigger blast radius, because it would gate a roadmap.		Anthony's call, 2026-08-01, on the re-scoped BL-68 (PR #32) rather than on the row as filed in July. Chosen over adding `trl`/`mrl` to the dimension enum, which is cheaper and would have given the per-epoch forecast trail for free, and over a single project-wide threshold policy — rejected because it cannot express that a demonstrator tolerates TRL 4 while a fielded increment needs 8, which is exactly BL-68's own worked example (laser satellite refuelling: today's increment versus the ten-year one). Costs a schema change, so it pulls in the minor bump, the upgrade doc and the foundation-migration checklist.acceptedLocate a design on the function-to-structure trajectory, Readiness gates an increment, and the roadmap says why, An epoch can be planned, not only recorded, The epoch an increment can deliver on is computed from readiness, not declared
reflow2's own feedback documents are deleted once their content is in the graph — a policy for THIS repository, not a claim about how consumers should work
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-15, given after the capture was complete and after he had been shown the collision with `req:sources-are-kept-not-just-parsed`: 'for our own reflow2 set of feedback docs; once ingested, please remove (this is my policy just for the reflow2 design because I don't want documents accumulating and have to clean up some day — I want to keep a nice clean repo)'. DISTINCT FROM `rule:design-information-lives-in-the-graph-not-in-documents`, which the guard named: THE RULE SAYS WHAT MAY NOT BE STORED; THIS SAYS WHAT HAPPENS TO A DOCUMENT THAT ALREADY EXISTS ONCE IT HAS BEEN CAPTURED. A prohibition and a lifecycle step. It is also the OBSOLETES source the retirement needs — only an ACCEPTED DECISION withdraws anything from a design, and a DesignRule cannot play that part. SCOPE, DELIBERATELY NARROW — his own framing, twice: 'our own reflow2 set of feedback docs' and 'just for the reflow2 design'. This governs THIS repository's inbound feedback documents. It is NOT a product position, NOT advice to consumers, and NOT a general answer to where prose belongs. `dec:idea-can-the-graph-be-the-official-record-an-organisation-trusts` holds that larger question and stays open. THE CONDITION IS 'ONCE INGESTED', WHICH IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART. Removal is licensed by capture having HAPPENED, not by the rule existing. Both documents removed under this decision were captured first, item by item, into TemporalFacts, Decisions and Fragments carrying the reporters' words verbatim — and the un-distilled remainder stays recoverable from git history, so the deletion costs reconstruction detail rather than findings. ⚠️ WHAT THIS KNOWINGLY OVERRIDES, recorded rather than glossed: `req:sources-are-kept-not-just-parsed` is ACCEPTED and says ingest keeps the original corpus documents 'so the corpus becomes part of the design rather than an input consumed and discarded'. It was left accepted-and-unsatisfied on purpose when `cap:content-store` was discontinued (`dec:the-content-store-is-discontinued`, 2026-08-09), with a `design_artifacts` folder named as the replacement and still unbuilt. HE WAS SHOWN THAT COLLISION AND CHOSE REMOVAL ANYWAY. The requirement's status is his to move and has NOT been moved on his behalf; it stays accepted and unsatisfied, and this decision is the reason a later reader will find them pointing in opposite directions. WHY HE CHOSE IT, in his words from the same thread: documents 'get forgotten and hard to maintain'; a corpus 'piling up' is the fear (dev_storyflow's 900+ records now being read slowly); and 'documents are external and require grep to see contents… having in the graph is immediately searchable'. The backlog file that 'kept growing and growing' is the precedent he cites, on the record as `dec:backlog-is-retired`. MECHANICS: the Artifact nodes are RETIRED ON THE RECORD, not deleted. They keep their names, their checksums — the proof of exactly what was captured — and their Fragments and YIELDED edges, so every finding can still be traced to the document that produced it. OBSOLETES is drawn from this decision to each Artifact (`dec:idea-discontinued-is-a-first-class-state`).		Recorded as its own accepted Decision rather than merged into the rule after the guard named it: a prohibition on storing and a lifecycle step for what already exists are different acts, and only an accepted Decision can be the source of the OBSOLETES edge that retires the two Artifacts. Accepted on his explicit word given in this session; no status was moved on his behalf, and the requirement it overrides was deliberately left where it stands.acceptednothing
A cut fires when every REQUIRED item scheduled for the increment is delivered — the trigger is computed, not scheduled
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31: an increment is cut when every item scheduled for it with `modality: required` is DELIVERED. Nothing else gates the cut, and no calendar does. WHAT MAKES IT COMPUTABLE RATHER THAN A CONVENTION, and this is why it needs no new machinery: `SCHEDULED_FOR` already points at a `Release` as well as a `DesignEpoch` — the capability-increment axis beside the time axis, deliberately one edge type for both paired views — and `arrival_delta` already accepts either as its target. So the trigger IS `arrival_delta(release).missed_obligations == ()`. `missed_obligations` is exactly the set of `required` claims that did not land, and `required` was already defined as an obligation whose miss is a computed violation rather than a slip (`dec:schedule-is-an-edge-with-modality`). The trigger is therefore read off the same computation that reports the delta, not asserted beside it. EXPECTED items do NOT gate the cut. That is the whole point of the modality split: `expected` is a plan and may slip without stopping a release, `required` is an obligation and cannot. An increment with three expected items outstanding and no required ones is READY, and the outstanding three are reported rather than silently dropped. `outstanding` ITEMS ARE A QUESTION, NOT A BLOCKER. An item still pointed at the increment, undelivered, that nobody has moved or dropped is neither deferred nor discontinued, and at cut time it is the question `req:plans-move-honestly` says must be ASKED and never defaulted: does it slip to the next increment, or is it withdrawn? If it was `required`, the cut does not fire until that is answered — because answering it either delivers the item or moves it, and both change `missed_obligations`. REJECTED — A FIXED CADENCE (weekly, fortnightly). It cuts whether or not anything landed, and fails to cut when something did. `req:frictionless-update` asks for releases that are 'frequent and very minor, so updating is routine rather than an event', and a calendar delivers neither half: it produces empty releases in quiet weeks and holds finished work back in busy ones. FREQUENCY IS A PROPERTY OF HOW SMALL THE INCREMENTS ARE SCOPED, not of how often the trigger is checked — which puts the frequency dial where someone can actually turn it. REJECTED — ANY CONSUMER-VISIBLE CAPABILITY LANDING. Closest to `req:frictionless-update` in spirit and rejected on a specific inability: it cannot say 'these three things ship together'. A release whose trigger is 'anything shipped' cannot express an increment that is only coherent when complete, and this project has already shipped such a pair — planned epochs are meaningless without the schedule that populates them. WHAT THE TRIGGER DOES NOT DECIDE, deliberately: whether the increment is CORRECT. `req:released-eq-designed` (priority critical) and the CI gates are the quality bar; this is only the readiness signal. A green trigger on a red build is not a release, and nothing here overrides that.		Chosen from three put to Anthony, and the deciding argument is that this option is the only one already computable from what the design holds. The other two would each have needed a new mechanism — a schedule to run the cadence against, or a rule for what counts as consumer-visible — and both would have sat beside the graph asserting something the graph could not check. This one is read off `arrival_delta`, which shipped the same day, and it gives `modality: required` its second job: it already made a miss a computed violation, and now it also decides when a release is ready. A vocabulary distinction that two computations read is exactly what `dec:edge-orthogonality` says earns its keep. The cadence rejection is worth keeping in full, because 'release weekly' is the obvious answer and the reason it fails is not obvious: it optimises the wrong variable. `req:frictionless-update` wants updating to be cheap and routine, and the way to get that is small increments, not frequent checks of a large one.acceptedv0.19.0 — the planning axis runs forward: planned epochs, the satisfaction schedule, and the arrival delta
OPEN — the cut trigger is vacuously true when an increment requires nothing, so readiness must also demand at least one required item
PROPOSED, not accepted — this refines `dec:release-trigger`, which is Anthony's word, and per `dec:reopen-supersedes` a settled choice is re-opened by minting a new Decision rather than by editing the accepted one. THE HOLE, found by pointing the machinery at itself within minutes of recording the trigger. `dec:release-trigger` says a cut fires when every item scheduled `required` is delivered, computed as `arrival_delta(release).missed_obligations == ()`. That predicate is VACUOUSLY TRUE when the increment has no `required` items at all — so an increment promising nothing reads as ready, and so does a completely empty one. MEASURED, not reasoned: `rel:v0200` was created carrying exactly one `expected` capability (`cap:changelog-view`, unbuilt, reporting `outstanding`) and zero required ones. `arrival_delta` returned `missed_obligations: ()`, which under the trigger as written means READY TO CUT — a release whose entire content is one thing nobody has built. WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: this is the EMPTY-RELEASE failure that `dec:release-trigger` used to REJECT the fixed-cadence option ('it cuts whether or not anything landed'), arriving through the chosen option's own back door. The argument against the alternative applies to the choice, which is the shape worth naming — a rejection reason that was never checked against the thing it was arguing for. PROPOSED FIX, one clause: readiness requires AT LEAST ONE item scheduled `required`, AND all of them delivered. `missed_obligations == () AND required_count > 0`. `expected` items still do not gate the cut — that half of the trigger is untouched and correct. WHAT THE FIX ALSO BUYS: it makes 'this increment has been scoped' a precondition of cutting it. An increment with no required items has not had the question 'what must ship for this to mean anything?' asked of it, and the trigger should not answer a question nobody put. NOT PROPOSED, deliberately: requiring that every scheduled item be delivered. That would collapse the modality distinction the schedule exists to carry, and make an increment hostage to its most speculative entry. NOTE ON PROVENANCE: `rel:v0200` and the `cap:changelog-view` schedule against it were created BY THE AGENT as a forward-roadmap placeholder to exercise the increment axis, not on Anthony's instruction — he asked only for this increment to be modelled as v0.19.0. It should be confirmed or dropped on his word. It has already earned its keep by surfacing this hole.		Recorded rather than fixed, because `dec:release-trigger` carries Anthony's signature and amending it silently would be the forgery `dec:certainty-derived` forbids for requirement status — the same rule one node type over. Worth keeping for the method as much as the content: the hole was not found by reading the decision back, it was found by MODELLING A SECOND INCREMENT and asking the tool. The first increment (`rel:v0190`) is fully required and fully delivered, so it exercises only the case where the predicate is meaningfully true; nothing about it could have exposed a vacuous one. A single well-formed example proves a rule works and cannot show where it does not apply.acceptedWhat was planned against what arrived, computed and never stored
Re-opening a settled choice mints a new Decision that obsoletes the old one; the accepted Decision is never un-accepted
When a past decision is re-opened to take a different road, the original Decision stays `accepted` untouched, and a NEW `proposed` Decision is created that OBSOLETES it and holds the alternatives (including the road originally taken, now a sibling rather than the incumbent). The decision-point machinery already built (register_alternative / alternatives_for / collapse_decision, and the undecided_decision_point gap) applies unchanged to the new node, because it is a genuinely open choice. The record therefore shows both that the question was settled and that it was later re-asked, with the reasoning of each visible in its own node.		User decided 2026-07-24. THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVE: flip the original Decision's status back to `proposed` and hang the new alternatives on it — simpler, and reuses the existing node. Rejected because it overwrites the fact that the choice was ever settled: a reader of the graph afterwards sees an open question and cannot tell it was once answered, or when, or on what grounds. That is the ADR failure mode this whole system was built against (dec:two-sided-accept, 'silent drift-accept does not exist'), and it would make the strongest evidence for re-opening — that we chose X, lived with it, and the trials found the hole — the very thing the re-opening erases. Snapshots would in principle preserve it, but only if one was taken, which makes the integrity of the record contingent on remembering a second step. Superseding is unconditional. It also composes with the existing vocabulary rather than straining it: OBSOLETES already means 'retired on the record, not deleted' (the retire-from-design exit), and the new node's own `alternatives` obituary is written by collapse_decision when the re-opened choice closes, so the second decision documents the first without rewriting it.acceptedHold and re-fork a decision's unchosen alternatives, Surface when a settled road may be worth re-opening
The graph lives as a repo file, embedded — not a service
RocksDB directory beside the repo, exports as the durable, diffable record.		The service's strongest argument (concurrency) is hypothetical while there is one writer; it would put the user's design on a machine they do not control and is permanent operational cost. Reopening conditions are written down. Decided 2026-07-18 (surface-plan.md); BL-12/BL-15 carry the consequences.acceptedExport and import a design
The confirmation ledger reports claim history, never judges a claim
Per capability: drifting / confirmed / unexamined, with the disposition counts visible.		Five design_holds claims with zero design edits is the erosion signature and the ledger makes it legible — but judging a specific claim false is semantic, and a deterministic detector would fire on every stable design with cosmetic churn (the unexpected_coupling lesson). Upgrade to rmcp 3.0.1 now, as a one-line bound change, and measure what it costs rather than reasoning about it
Take rmcp 3.0.1 on Anthony's direct word ('I want to upgrade to rmcp v3.0.1'), replacing the `rmcp = '2'` pin. The entire code change is one generic bound in `serve_http`: rmcp v3 narrowed `StreamableHttpService::new` from `S: Service` to `S: ServerHandler`, because the sessionless transport builds a handler per REQUEST and must ask it for `get_info` and the tool list with no session having cached them. Both surfaces that come through that door — the real service and the degraded one — already implement `ServerHandler` via `#(tool_handler)`, so nothing was lost. NOT chosen: staying on rmcp 2 until the seat question is answered. The upgrade and the seat fix are separable, and holding a working dependency bump hostage to an open design decision would have left reflow2 on a pinned major with no evidence about what actually breaks.		The v3.0.0 notes list eight breaking-change areas — sessionless Streamable HTTP, stateless lifecycle, subscriptions, MRTR response enums on `call_tool`/`get_prompt`/`read_resource`, the tasks API, split metadata types, OAuth, MSRV 1.88 — and exactly one of them reached reflow2's code. The `#(tool)`/`#(tool_router)`/`#(tool_handler)` macros absorbed the MRTR enum change entirely, MSRV 1.88 is under this workspace's 1.94, and the OAuth, tasks and subscription surfaces are ones reflow2 never touched. All 118 toolsnaps match, so the served tool surface did not move. THE PART THAT MATTERED WAS NOT IN THE DIFF. Every gate stayed green, and that green was misleading: every one of reflow2's own test clients negotiates `2025-06-18`, `2025-11-25` or `2024-11-05`, and `ProtocolVersion::LATEST` in rmcp 3.0.1 is still `V_2025_11_25`. Nothing in the suite speaks `2026-07-28`, so nothing exercised the sessionless path that the whole requirement is about. This is the same failure shape as row 3AX-3 in the coverage matrix the day before: a green tick only as wide as the case its evidence exercises. Measured instead, with `tools/stateless_seat_probe.py` — one client, two `claim_region` calls, count the distinct seats. stdio: one seat. HTTP at 2025-06-18: one seat. HTTP at 2026-07-28: TWO seats, one per request. So `req:seat-per-client` is intact on every transport in use today and broken on exactly one that nothing uses yet, which is why this is a deadline and not an outage — Claude Code and grok build both connect over stdio. There is no configuration that avoids it: `StreamableHttpServerConfig::legacy_session_mode` is documented to apply only to protocol versions below 2026-07-28, and requests negotiating that version 'are always served statelessly regardless of this setting'. The CLIENT chooses the version, so reflow2 cannot decline on its behalf; it can only decide what identity means once the choice is made.acceptedmain.rs, Reachable from another machine, but only on purpose
The trust boundary having one caller makes ingest an articulation point — accepted, and the fix is the second caller
ACCEPT the single_point_of_failure finding on cmp:ingest rather than add redundancy. The topology it reports is true: cmp:sanitize is reached only through cmp:ingest today, because INGEST is the only path by which foreign text currently enters the graph, so every route to the trust boundary runs through one component.		Recorded because the finding appeared the moment the sanitizer landed (2026-07-25) and would otherwise be re-litigated every session, and because the suggested fix is the wrong shape here: `add_redundancy` is coherent for a running part that can fail over, and a second copy of a pure text filter would be duplication, not resilience. What WILL dissolve it is already named in the module docs and in cap:sanitize-ingress — the import path. `import_graph` deliberately does not rewrite the document it is handed (an export's content is its identity), so the next rung is detect-and-report on import, and when that lands the boundary has two callers and the articulation point is gone honestly. Deliberately NOT done: wiring cmp:export or cmp:graph to cmp:sanitize now to quiet the detector, because that would be an edge the code does not have — the same fabrication dec:ask-not-repair forbids of a heuristic. Joins the five accepted SPOFs under the BL-93 disposition: loop_status will not call the structural set clean, and that is expected.acceptedingest
OPEN — how the satisfaction schedule records ARE / EXPECTED / REQUIRED-BY
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony's distillation (2026-07-28) is that the roadmap is a SATISFACTION SCHEDULE — requirements mapped to the epoch or increment where they are satisfied — and his own verbs carry three modalities: requirements 'ARE satisfied' in epoch 1, 'are EXPECTED to be satisfied' in increment 3, KPP 1 'is REQUIRED to be satisfied' by epoch 27. THE OBSERVATION THAT MATTERS MOST: the three do not want the same treatment, and one of them must not be stored at all. ARE SATISFIED — must be COMPUTED, never recorded. `req:completion-computed` is accepted and says whether intent has been delivered is computed from the golden thread and never asserted. A stored 'requirement A was satisfied at epoch 1' would be exactly the assertion that requirement forbids, and it would rot the moment the thread moved. The backward direction already works; it needs a way to ask 'as of epoch N', not a place to write the answer. EXPECTED TO BE SATISFIED — the vocabulary already exists. `ANTICIPATES` is declared from `*` to `*` with a `confidence` float 0.0–1.0 and the hint 'Source plans for or foreshadows a future target need.' `req:plans-move-honestly` already named it as the hook. So `req:X --ANTICIPATES(confidence)--> epoch:3` may be the whole mechanism, with confidence decaying by horizon per the Black-Scholes framing. REQUIRED TO BE SATISFIED BY — different in kind, not degree. Missing an EXPECTED date is a surprise to record; missing a REQUIRED date is a VIOLATION to compute. This is the scheduling face of a KPP: `req:inviolable-intent` already computes content violations, and this would give it a deadline dimension. Open whether that is a distinct edge type, or `ANTICIPATES` with a binding flag — and the honest test is the one this project keeps applying: which one lets a computation read it without inventing a value nobody set. WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING, having looked: less than the requirement's ambition suggests. The capability view's forward half is expressible today (`Release.status: planned`). The schedule edge exists (`ANTICIPATES` with confidence). What does not exist is (1) a `DesignEpoch.epoch_type` value meaning 'has not happened yet', (2) any reader of `ANTICIPATES` — it is declared and nothing computes over it, which is `req:defaults-do-not-assert`'s sibling defect of declared-but-unread vocabulary, and (3) an ARRIVAL operation: someone must be able to say an epoch arrived, at which point the planned-versus-delivered delta is computed and the pin recorded. Arrival is where the three requirements meet: it is when a planned epoch stops being a claim (`req:epochs-can-be-planned`), acquires a git pin (`req:graph-indexes-snapshots`), and produces the delta between what was planned and what landed (`req:plans-move-honestly`). It is also the natural moment for `cap:changelog-view` to render, since the changelog between two arrivals is the same delta in prose.		Anthony's atom, recorded in his own verbs because the three modalities are carried by the verbs and would be lost in a paraphrase. The 'ARE satisfied must not be stored' point is the one worth not losing: it is the difference between a roadmap that reports and a roadmap that claims, and this design already has an accepted requirement forbidding the second. Everything else here is options; that one is a constraint the existing design imposes on any shape chosen.proposednothing
The satisfaction schedule is an edge carrying modality, not an overloaded pin and not a node
A new edge type SCHEDULED_FOR runs from Requirement or Capability to a DesignEpoch or a Release, carrying a `modality` property with values `expected` (a plan) and `required` (an obligation whose miss at arrival is a computed violation — the scheduling face of a KPP). One edge type serves both of the paired views: epochs for the time axis, releases for the capability-increment axis. Chosen by Anthony 2026-07-30 over two rejected alternatives.		REJECTED: overloading AT_EPOCH. It is declared `from: '*'` to DesignEpoch and its extraction hint says a Snapshot or ChangeEvent is pinned to the epoch it BELONGS TO. Adding schedule semantics would give one edge type two unrelated meanings — belongs-to and due-at — over a wildcard source, so nothing could tell them apart. That is the exact shape of the wrong-direction edge found on 2026-07-30: an edge that reads correctly and is still undetectably wrong, because no second contradicting fact exists to make its error computable. REJECTED: a Commitment/Schedule node. Heavier, and justified only if a scheduled claim must carry rationale, owner or confidence as first-class fields. It does not today, and confidence in particular should be MEASURED from arrival history rather than authored (dec:arrival-delta). CHOSEN, and why the edge: modality is a property of the RELATIONSHIP between an item and a moment, not of either endpoint — the same capability can be `expected` at one epoch and `required` by another, so putting it on either node would collapse that. It also leaves 3470 existing edges untouched. THE ABSENT THIRD MODALITY IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART: Anthony's three verbs are ARE satisfied, EXPECTED to be satisfied, and REQUIRED to be satisfied by — but `achieved` is deliberately NOT a value here. dec:arrival-delta and req:completion-computed already settle that delivery is computed from the golden thread and never asserted; storing it as a schedule modality would create a second source of truth that can disagree with the first, and a plan that records its own success is the plan lying about itself.acceptedThe graph answers as-of-epoch-n itself, without a git lookup, A requirement or capability can be scheduled against the moment it is due
The satisfaction schedule is a traceability edge — WHAT→WHEN, the same shape as ALLOCATED_TO's WHAT→WHERE
PROPOSED — built, because the defect was live and the fix has an exact precedent in the same table; the SHAPE awaits Anthony's word, the way `dec:snapshot-id-per-revision` did. `SCHEDULED_FOR` joins `structural_rule` as `(forward: Downstream, backward: Upstream)`. From a Capability or Requirement, walking out to the moment it is due reaches a commitment DOWNSTREAM of it — a changed capability moves the increment it was promised to; walking back from an increment reaches what was promised into it. Identical to `ALLOCATED_TO`'s WHAT→WHERE, one axis over: WHAT→WHEN. WHAT WAS BROKEN. `structural_rule` is the table that decides what counts as a traceability edge, and `is_traceability_edge` is read by BOTH `propagate` and `structure` so the impact walk and the topology analysis agree on what 'connected' means. `SCHEDULED_FOR` was never added to it. So the satisfaction schedule validated, stored and queried perfectly while every traversal stepped over it: impact never reached an increment, and a Release wired only by its schedule was a DISCONNECTED ISLAND. THIS IS THE `INCLUDES` BUG, RECURRED, and the previous instance is documented three lines above the fix in the same file: *'Absent from this table, every Release+Environment pair was a disconnected island in the design network — found modelling v0.4.0, fixed for v0.5.0.'* Twice now a new edge type has reached a `Release` without anyone asking whether the impact table should know about it. HOW IT SURFACED, which is the part worth keeping: not by review, but by MODELLING A RELEASE FORWARD from the plan rather than backward from a cut. Every previous Release was recorded after the fact and wired with `INCLUDES`, which is in the table; `rel:v0190` is the first modelled from its schedule, and `disconnected_community` fired on it the moment it existed. The gap had been latent since `SCHEDULED_FOR` shipped and nothing could have found it, because no design had yet used the edge in the way that exposes it. THE STANDING WEAKNESS THIS NAMES, and it is not fixed here: nothing checks that a new edge type was CONSIDERED for `structural_rule`. The table is a silent opt-in — an omission compiles, validates, passes every test, and simply makes traversals quieter. Two instances in one file is a pattern, and the honest fix is a check that every edge type is either listed or explicitly recorded as deliberately excluded (`SPECIFIES`, `DOCUMENTS` and the temporal bookkeeping are excluded ON PURPOSE and the comment says so — so the vocabulary for saying 'not this one' already exists, it is just not enforced). MUTATION-CHECKED: remove the `SCHEDULED_FOR` arm and `a_changed_capability_reaches_the_increment_it_was_promised_to` fails, and nothing else does.		Built rather than parked because the defect was not hypothetical — it was firing on `rel:v0190` in the live design, and the alternative on offer was `generate_bridge`, i.e. inventing an edge to hide a missing rule. That would have papered over the finding with exactly the kind of fill-in `dec:views-are-projections` calls a defect. The direction was read off the precedent rather than chosen: `INCLUDES` had already settled that a Release is downstream of its contents ('the contents are the source of truth, the release a downstream packaging of them'), and a schedule is the same relation before the fact instead of after it. Left PROPOSED because whether a schedule should propagate impact at all is a real design question — it widens every blast radius that touches a scheduled item — and that is Anthony's call, not something to settle by having fixed it.proposedA requirement or capability can be scheduled against the moment it is due
The single MCP service is an accepted single point of failure
cmp:service is the sole bridge between the reflow2-mcp subsystem and both the core and the kit, and it stays that way. The single_point_of_failure warning on it is accepted as intentional, not resolved by adding redundancy.		req:invocation mandates one reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio as the entire user-facing surface; a redundant second service would contradict that 'one door' design and buys nothing while there is a single local writer (dec:repo-file-embedded). Articulation-point analysis of the component/interface dependency graph (2026-07-21 self-host review) confirms cmp:service is a genuine cut vertex — removing it disconnects the MCP surface — so the finding is true, and the right disposition is to accept it rather than fix it. Contrast cmp:flow, flagged by the same detector but NOT a cut vertex (BL-69). Redundancy is the wrong fix; this SPOF is the architecture working as intended.acceptedservice
A descriptive design stays on acknowledgement for now — the vocabulary waits for a second instance, and the trigger is named
SETTLED ON ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-16: HOLD — take option (c), acknowledgement, and build NOTHING yet. `acknowledge_gap` with a reason remains the answer for a design that describes something already running. No new status value, no new project-level field. ⚠️ THIS IS A DEFERRAL WITH A NAMED TRIGGER, NOT A REJECTION. Reopen — as a new Decision superseding this one — when EITHER holds: 1. a SECOND design turns up that is descriptive end-to-end (one observation in one domain is what is on the table today), or 2. acknowledgement VOLUME becomes the complaint rather than the vocabulary — i.e. someone reports the count of acknowledgements, not the wrongness of the words. Recorded so a later session does not read a settled decision as a closed subject.		THE CASE IS REAL AND WAS NOT DISPUTED. Modelling the three branches of the US federal government, `Capability.status` is wrong on every rung: `planned` is false for a thing running since 1789, and `realized` means AN ARTIFACT REALIZES IT when there are no artifacts and never will be, because the implementation is not that project's to build. `build_without_verification` and `design_without_build` fire on a design that is complete and correct for its phase. WHY IT WAS STILL HELD — one reason, and it is the load-bearing one: MOST REAL DESIGNS ARE BOTH. This project's own recorded operating context is brownfield and continual — the ~10-year-old bluesky stack at Brookhaven NSLS-II is partly as-built and partly proposed, and several organisations carry competing partially-built designs. A project-level flag says ONE thing about a design with TWO halves. The honest shape is therefore a project-level default PLUS a per-capability override — which is options (a) and (b) TOGETHER, more schema surface than either alone, on the strength of a SINGLE observation in a SINGLE domain. ⭐ AND THE PROJECT'S OWN METHOD ARGUES FOR WAITING. The decision text's own 'not established' line reads: whether descriptive models are a niche worth schema surface, or the first of many. The operating context argues they are not niche — but that is an ARGUMENT, not a MEASUREMENT, and distrusting exactly that gap is this project's standing habit. The increment's repeated lesson is that defects are found by real users and by running two real projects at each other, never by reasoning forward from one report. WHAT (c) COSTS, stated plainly so the deferral is not mistaken for free: the condition is PERMANENT rather than situational, so this is an unbounded number of acknowledgements for one fact about the project — and the design cannot TELL a reader it is descriptive; only the acknowledgement reasons can, one at a time. That cost is real, it is tedium rather than falsehood, and tedium is a far cheaper problem than wrong schema. WHAT THE RULING PRESERVES FOR WHOEVER BUILDS IT LATER, because these were the sharp parts and would be expensive to rediscover: - IT MUST BE ITS OWN FIELD, NOT A `set_project_mode` VALUE. `set_project_mode` today means 'how much may a machine change this' and gates exactly one thing — whether `apply_heal` applies or proposes. 'What this design IS' is an ORTHOGONAL axis. That field's description was already corrected once in plain language for promising a breadth the code did not implement; overloading it would repeat precisely that over-promise. - (b) BEATS (a) ON ERGONOMICS where they compete: a project-level statement is said once, where a status value is restated per capability — 38 times for the model in question, with nothing detecting a half-and-half design. - (d) — folding it into the `adopt` skill — was judged a DIFFERENT case rather than a harder instance: `adopt` recovers a design from something you CAN point a checksum at, and this subject is real but has no artifacts at all. RAISED BY the US-government genesis session, 2026-08-15 (item 4), which graded it MEDIUM for descriptive models and cosmetic for greenfield software, and which reached the right diagnosis without needing the fix.acceptednothing
A REALIZES edge says whether anyone checked the file against the rule — and `unchecked` is the default, so the silence becomes countable
SETTLED (b) ON ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-16. REALIZES gains `conformance: unchecked | reviewed | verified`, DEFAULTING TO `unchecked`. A matching checksum keeps meaning only 'the file has not moved'; whether anyone confirmed the file still does what the Requirement says becomes a thing the graph states rather than a thing a reader must remember to doubt. THE DELIVERABLE IS THE COUNT, not the ceremony. '412 of 460 realizing edges were never checked against their requirement' is a sentence this design cannot say today, and it is what the property is for. A computation must READ it (`dec:edge-orthogonality`), so the property ships with the report that reads it or it does not ship. (d) — raising it as a gap — is DEFERRED, not rejected, and becomes cheap once the data exists.		THE EVIDENCE CAME FROM OUTSIDE, WHICH IS WHY IT COUNTS. A Requirement said the calendar day is the person's CIVIL date, not UTC. The realizing check-in used the ISO date of `createdAt`, which is UTC. The Capability said `realized`. The artifact's checksum matched its baseline, so `reconcile_artifacts` was silent. EVERY SIGNAL IN THE GRAPH WAS GREEN AND THE CODE DID NOT DO WHAT THE REQUIREMENT SAID — and THE USER FOUND IT IN THE PRODUCT. Alex's Grok session, 2026-08-14, item 5, judged the deepest of its fourteen. THE SHAPE: REALIZES carries `completeness` and the Artifact carries a checksum. Between them they answer whether the file has MOVED since we looked. They do not answer, and cannot, whether it still IMPLEMENTS the property the Requirement states. Nothing distinguishes A FILE THAT WAS CHECKED AGAINST THE RULE from A FILE THAT WAS MERELY HASHED, and the two produce identical reports. WHY THIS IS NOT A DETECTOR: reflow2 reads a DESIGN, never a running system, and judging whether code implements a civil-date rule is program analysis it deliberately stays out of (`dec:agent-navigates-content` keeps it out of file IO entirely). So every candidate was about RECORDING what is known, never computing it. ⭐ WHY (b) BEAT (a) — document the hole — AND THIS IS THE GENERAL PRINCIPLE, not a preference: A DOCUMENTED HOLE IS SOMETHING A READER MUST REMEMBER; A DEFAULT OF `unchecked` IS SOMETHING THE GRAPH SAYS OUT LOUD, EVERY TIME, WITH NOBODY REMEMBERING ANYTHING. That is the same move made twice already this month and both times it was right: #200 stopped INJECTING a default nobody chose, and #213 started REPORTING the property nobody declared. Make the absence visible rather than implied. WHY (c) LOST — lean on a Verification that names the PROPERTY rather than the file. Killed by its own evidence: HIS SESSION HAD A PASSING UNIT VERIFICATION AND SHIPPED THE BUG ANYWAY. A check that does not say what it covers changes nothing. WHY (d) IS DEFERRED RATHER THAN REJECTED — surface it in the gap list. It is the strongest answer eventually and the wrong one FIRST: every REALIZES edge starts at `unchecked`, so a gap per edge is instant noise on a large design — and noise is exactly the failure just fixed in `loop_status` by `req:the-loop-can-say-what-this-session-owes`. Build (b) now; (d) costs almost nothing afterwards because the data will already be there. ⚠️ THE HONEST LIMIT OF (b), recorded so nobody later mistakes it for a guarantee: its value depends on people actually moving edges OFF `unchecked`, and NOTHING FORCES THAT.
