It may simply relocate the silence. What it does do unconditionally is make the silence COUNTABLE, and a number is something the loop can report and a person can act on where a documented caveat is not. RELATED AND NOT REOPENED: `req:completion-computed` (delivery is computed from the thread, never asserted) and `cap:independent-evidence`. The tension this decision resolves is that completion is computed from EDGES, and an edge asserting realization was exactly the thing nobody checked. ALSO WEIGHED: the same session marked two Capabilities `realized` on unit tests before a user had clicked through, and named that as its own error. `realized` vs `verified` ALREADY EXISTS in the capability lifecycle — so part of this was a missing PROMPT rather than a missing concept, which is why (a) was a genuine contender rather than a straw man.acceptednothing
A Verification MAY verify a Constraint — a check that measures whether a limit holds is a real modelling need, and Project stays out
SETTLED ON ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-15: 'allow VERIFIES → Constraint'. OPTION (a) of the four below. WHAT WAS BUILT, the same day: `schema/verify.yaml`'s `to:` list becomes `(Capability, Requirement, Artifact, Component, DesignRule, Constraint)`. The schema is compiled in via `include_str!`, so the rebuild carries it. PROVEN THROUGH THE PATH THAT WAS ACTUALLY BROKEN — the importer, not a unit assertion. A document holding `VERIFIES ver:latency_gate -> con:latency` now imports (exit 0, '2 node(s) and 1 edge(s)'). ⭐ AND THE COUNTERWEIGHT RAN IN THE SAME BREATH: a document holding `VERIFIES -> Project` is STILL REFUSED, with the same precise message. THE LIST DISCRIMINATES; IT WAS NOT QUIETLY WIDENED. Pinned by `crates/reflow2-core/tests/verifies_reaches_a_constraint.rs`, 2 cases, MUTATION-CHECKED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: removing `Constraint` fails the case and leaves the counterweight passing; restoring the pre-2026-08-08 `to: \'*\'` passes the case and FAILS THE COUNTERWEIGHT — which is what proves the counterweight is doing work rather than agreeing for free. ⚠️ PROJECT IS DELIBERATELY STILL OUT, AND DEV_STORYFLOW'S EXPORT THEREFORE STILL WILL NOT IMPORT. Their file carries TWO illegal edges — one Constraint, one Project — and only the Constraint half was ruled on. A Verification that verifies a whole Project reads as a modelling slip rather than a need, but nobody has decided, and this decision deliberately does not decide it for them. Their backup remains unrestorable until either that edge is migrated by them or Project is admitted here. WHY (a) OVER THE OTHERS: (b) migrating the edge away would reshape a real design to satisfy a validator, which is the failure `rule:never_shape_a_field_to_satisfy_an_instrument` names and which their own reporter warned against — 'the question should be asked before anyone deletes data to satisfy a validator'. (c) re-deriving across every known graph settles this instance without settling the rule, and can still be done later. (d) restoring the wildcard discards the reason the enumeration was added, which is recorded in the file and was a real gain: it made 'which of my rules have no detector?' an askable question. THE ORIGINAL QUESTION, PRESERVED so a later reader sees what was weighed: A Constraint is 'a limit or rule the design MUST respect' — a latency budget, a mass cap, 'no PII leaves the device'. Asking whether a limit HOLDS is the most natural thing anyone would want to check about it, and it is exactly what `budget_report` answers arithmetically for the numeric case. A Verification is how this design records that something was CHECKED. Refusing to connect them said a limit may be stated and computed but never independently verified. AND THE ASYMMETRY WAS ODD ON ITS FACE: `DesignRule` was already in the list, and `unverified_enforced_rule` exists precisely so a gate-blocking rule owes a passing check. A Constraint is the DesignRule's sibling — the imposed limit beside the chosen one — and nothing in the schema explained why they were split. HOW IT AROSE: `ver:side_e_slo_gate_unwired_2026_08_09` VERIFIES `con:side_e_perf_slos_are_enforced_nowhere` in dev_storyflow — a check measuring whether a performance constraint is actually enforced. The 2026-08-08 narrowing of `VERIFIES` from `*` to an enumeration derived its list from a census that found five types at 95/27/13/2/1 edges and MISSED TWO CARRYING ONE EDGE EACH. See `fact:defect-a-schema-narrowing-orphaned-live-edges-and-no-export-is-ever-imported`. NOT SETTLED BY THIS, and left open on purpose: whether `Project` belongs; whether the list should be re-derived across all three known designs; and whether any detector should READ the new edge — admitting it makes the claim expressible, and nothing yet computes anything from it.		Recorded as his ruling rather than as an agent's fix because it is a schema change with real data on both sides: the wrong answer either destroys a legitimate edge or admits everything. He chose the option that repairs the design without touching anyone's data. The Project half was deliberately NOT bundled with it — the reporter who found both asked for them to be judged separately, and folding them together would have settled a second question nobody put.acceptednothing
OPEN — should `propagate_change` seed from a DriftEvent, so the honest modelling and the useful tooling stop pointing at different node types?
RECORDED SO THE CHOICE IS MADE DELIBERATELY RATHER THAN BY DEFAULT. Anthony approved bundling `record_was_incorrect` into the schema increment (2026-08-09); this node exists so that adding the enum value does not silently foreclose the better fix, which may make it unnecessary. THE OBSERVATION THAT STARTED IT, dragon Boss (`cca98fbf`, dev_storyflow, 2026-08-09), correcting an edge that asserted a runtime dependency the code never had: *'the ChangeEvent hint itself says DriftEvent is the design-vs-reality construct, BUT `propagate_change` takes a ChangeEvent, so recording it as drift would have cost me the impact check.'* And the conclusion, which is the part worth keeping: **'the honest modelling and the useful tooling point at different node types, and I chose the tooling.'** THAT IS A TOOL SHAPING THE RECORD. A caller who wants a blast radius must record their finding as a ChangeEvent whether or not it is one, because that is the only node type `propagate_change` accepts. So the ledger fills with design-evolution entries that are actually drift observations — and no detector can tell them apart afterwards, because by then they are the same type. --- OPTION A — ADD `record_was_incorrect` TO ChangeEvent (the approved path) --- FOR: cheap, certain, and read — `changelog_view` buckets on `change_type`, so the value does work immediately. Bundled into a schema-clustered increment, its stamp cost is shared. AGAINST: it grows ChangeEvent to cover a case the schema already says belongs elsewhere. `ChangeEvent`'s own hint calls itself 'the design-evolution log; DISTINCT from DriftEvent, which records design-vs-reality divergence rather than intended change' — and a record that was wrong from the start is divergence, not intended change. So A makes the ledger MORE expressive and the type boundary LESS true. --- OPTION B — TEACH `propagate_change` TO SEED FROM A DriftEvent --- FOR: fixes the cause rather than the symptom. `DriftEvent` already exists and already means exactly this; nothing new is declared, so `dec:edge-orthogonality`'s test is satisfied without growing vocabulary. It would also remove the incentive that currently mis-types every drift finding somebody wanted a blast radius for. AGAINST: a real piece of design work, not a one-line enum addition — the propagation walk starts from what a ChangeEvent CHANGED, and a DriftEvent's equivalent anchor has to be defined rather than assumed. Unknown whether it moves the stamp. --- OPTION C — BOTH --- They are not exclusive: A gives the ledger a truthful value for corrections that ARE design evolution; B gives drift findings their impact check without lying about their type. FOR: the two solve different halves. AGAINST: doing A first removes most of the pain, which is exactly how B never gets built. ⚠️ WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN: A ships, the pain goes away, and B is never revisited — leaving the tool still shaping the record for every future drift finding. This node is the guard against that, and it should be read before `req:the-ledger-can-say-the-record-was-wrong` is built. NOTHING IS PROMOTED. Anthony has approved the bundling of A, not a choice between A and B.		Minted alongside Anthony's approval to bundle the enum value, precisely because approving A is not the same as rejecting B, and an unrecorded alternative is one nobody argues with later. The evidence is a consumer's account of choosing the wrong node type on purpose because the right one lost them a tool — which is a stronger signal than a feature request, since it shows the surface changing what people record rather than merely what they can express.proposednothing
A lost identity sidecar is caught by what the filesystem can see, because the store cannot be asked what designs it holds
On a durable open, refuse when the identity sidecar is absent AND the store directory already held data AND the legacy probe finds no design under the old shared id. 'Already held data' is answered BEFORE the store is opened, from the filesystem alone: a `.sst` file, or a non-empty write-ahead log. Opening creates the directory, so the evidence exists for exactly one line. All three prior behaviours are unchanged — a sidecar that is present is read (and still refused if unreadable), a genuinely fresh store still mints, and a pre-identity graph under the shared id is still adopted.		THE CHECK THIS REPLACES IS ONE WE CANNOT WRITE. The honest question is 'does this store hold a design under ANY id', and it cannot be asked: graph_id namespaces every stored key and dynograph-storage exposes no enumeration of ids — count_nodes(graph_id, type) requires the very id you are trying to discover. dynograph-storage is pinned by git tag v0.12.0 in the workspace Cargo.toml, so acquiring that scan means a change to another repository, a new tag, and a bump here. That is a real option and it is the BETTER fix; it is not this fix. 'The store already held data, and it is not the legacy design' answers the same question from outside, with nothing but read_dir. It is a PROXY, and the ways it is wrong are worth stating rather than discovering: a store created and opened but never written, whose sidecar is then lost, is refused though nothing is at stake — the refusal names how to proceed, and the alternative (minting over a live design) is unbounded, so the tie breaks toward refusing. A store whose data files were deleted while the directory survived would not be caught, which is not a case a mis-scoped mount produces. WHY A PROXY NOW BEATS THE REAL CHECK LATER. cap:hosted-state-on-a-volume is BUILT, not planned — art:dockerfile realizes it — and it already ships knowing this exact failure. Dockerfile:78-82 says so in capitals: a store opened without its identity sidecar 'finds nothing and PRESENTS AS AN EMPTY DESIGN, reporting nothing wrong', and mounting `.../graph` rather than its parent 'is a plausible-looking mistake that silently loses a project. MOUNT THE PARENT.' The mitigation for a known silent-data-loss path was a comment addressed to the one person who cannot read it: the operator gets no error, because there is no error. The capability's own statement already says the required behaviour is to refuse. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, so nobody reads more into a green check: it does not RECOVER the design. The store still holds it, under an id nothing can now name. Recovery needs the sidecar restored from backup, or the scan above — at which point the id could be read back off the store and the refusal could become self-healing. That is the follow-on this defers, and the reason to prefer the foundation change eventually rather than instead. The asymmetry it removes was already visible in the code: an UNREADABLE sidecar was refused with 'reflow2 will not guess', while an ABSENT one minted silently — and absent is the likelier of the two on a mounted volume.acceptedDesigns live on mounted storage, and a store without its identity sidecar is refused rather than opened empty
OPEN — do the skills come from the server instead of being copied into the project?
THE HARD CONSTRAINT FIRST, because it rules out the literal proposal: no harness discovers skills from an MCP server. Claude Code, OpenCode and Copilot read `.claude/skills/`, Grok CLI reads `.grok/skills/` (docs/skills/README.md), and a skill that is not in one of those directories is not a skill — it is a file nobody loads. So 'reference something in the MCP to discover all those skills' cannot be honoured as harness-native skills today. What CAN be honoured is the substance: nothing in the project changes after setup, and updates ride the package. FOUR PIECES, separable, in increasing cost. (1) SERVER INSTRUCTIONS — already how reflow2 delivers its loop doctrine (the paragraph in every session's context comes from the server, versioned with the binary, zero repo files). The catalogue of skills, one line each, belongs here: that is exactly what a skill's frontmatter description does, and it is what makes progressive disclosure work. (2) A `reflow2_skill(name)` TOOL returning the body on demand, with `list_skills` alongside. Works in EVERY MCP client including Grok, needs no filesystem copy, and always matches the binary. (3) MCP PROMPTS — reflow2 declares only `enable_tools()`; adding `enable_prompts()` would serve the command-shaped skills as `/mcp__reflow2__` slash commands with zero files in the repo. Claude-Code-shaped, so it complements (2) rather than replacing it. (4) LOCAL OVERRIDE — a skill present in the project's own `.claude/skills/` wins over the served one, so customisation survives and the served set is a default rather than a cage. WHAT THE PROJECT WOULD STILL HOLD after all four: the pointer paragraph, `.mcp.json` (and the other harnesses' formats), `.reflow2/` and its gitignore line. That is his brother's proposal exactly.		Feedback from Anthony's brother, 2026-07-25, and it names the same failure shape reflow2 keeps finding in itself: a COPY drifts, and the fix is to remove the copying rather than to refresh it better — the same reasoning that retired the fleet's mint-race guard in dec:identity-out-of-band, and the same one behind computed-not-remembered everywhere else in this project. The evidence is already on the record: the installer's docstring concedes that the kit freezes while reflow2 moves, and reflow2's OWN kit manifest went four releases stale with nothing noticing. THE HONEST COST, recorded beside the idea: a harness-native skill is auto-matched by the harness from its description without the agent being asked, and a served skill is not — the agent has to know to call for it. Moving skills to the server therefore trades the harness's own progressive disclosure for freshness, and the mitigation (the catalogue in the server instructions) is a hand-built version of what the harness does for free. That trade is the decision, and it is worth putting to both brothers rather than assuming: one of them is the consumer whose repo churns, the other is the one who would maintain two delivery paths.acceptedServe the skills AND the working instructions from the binary, so a project holds only a pointer, After setup, a project never has to change again for reflow2 to move
Snapshot identity is per revision, but only when a revision actually happened
Option (a) from req:snapshot-per-revision-not-per-epoch, in a form that keeps existing ids stable. The FIRST capture of a node in an epoch keeps the id `snap:{epoch}:{node}` exactly as before. A genuine SECOND revision in the same epoch appends `:r2`, `:r3`, so HAS_SNAPSHOT becomes one-to-many precisely when history requires it and not before. An IDENTICAL re-capture returns the existing snapshot instead of minting a duplicate — compared against the TAIL of the chain and nothing earlier. A ceiling of 64 distinct snapshots per (epoch, node) errors rather than growing history quietly, and is checked only when a new capture is actually needed, so an idempotent retry against a full chain still succeeds. NOT chosen: (b) refusing a second record_change in one epoch, and (c) keeping one snapshot per epoch and making the second call a no-op.		Truest to req:intent-preserved, which is the requirement this bug violated — (c) preserves the original but still discards the intermediate, which is losing history on purpose rather than by accident, and (b) pushes epoch hygiene onto the caller when an epoch is meant to bound a round of WORK, not a single edit. The first-capture id is left unsuffixed because existing graphs and committed exports carry those ids and a test pins one; suffixing everything would have rewritten history to fix a bug about not rewriting history. Idempotence on an unchanged re-capture is the mirror of the bug being fixed: snapshotting a node that has not moved is a no-op, not a new version, and minting one would make the history claim edits that never happened. It also keeps record_change safe to retry. TAIL-ONLY COMPARISON, and it is the load-bearing detail. A node edited A -> B -> A inside one epoch has three genuine revisions. Comparing against ANY earlier snapshot would match the first A-capture and hand it back for the third, recording two — hiding an edit that DID happen. That is the same class of loss as the overwrite this fixes, just quieter, and it would have shipped as a half-fix. Matching only the tail also keeps the `:rN` order readable as the order the revisions occurred in, which is the only ordering a reader has: every snapshot in an epoch is pinned to that one epoch and carries no sequence of its own. The 64 ceiling is a signal, not a storage limit: a node revised that many times inside one epoch means the epoch has stopped bounding anything, and the error says so. RECORDED AT `proposed`: the requirement itself said the shape of the fix was a choice and none of the options was obviously right. Anthony directed the work be finished, not this particular shape — so the shape is on the record awaiting his word, and reopening it supersedes rather than un-accepts (dec:reopen-supersedes).proposedRecord a change, A second revision of a node in one epoch must not overwrite the first snapshot
A seat is minted on request and carried as a tool argument, and a claim without one is refused rather than guessed
CHOSEN BY ANTHONY, 2026-07-30: option (a), mint-and-carry, with the refusal from (d) as its backstop. Decided but NOT YET BUILT. The shape. A tool mints a seat and returns it; the client passes it on the calls that care (`claim_region`, `release_claim`, the stale-seat check). `ClaimReq.seat` already accepts one, documented today as 'pass your own only if you have a durable handle for the session (a fleet worker name); it is a name, never a lock' — so the argument exists and what is missing is the minting and the discipline around it. This is transport-independent by construction: it works identically on stdio, on legacy Streamable HTTP and on the sessionless transport, where today identity is inherited from whatever the transport happened to do and quietly differs between them. THE BACKSTOP IS THE LOAD-BEARING HALF. Option (a) alone has a quiet failure mode: an agent that forgets the handle silently gets fresh-seat-per-request behaviour again, which is the exact bug being fixed, reintroduced by omission. So when a claim-family call arrives on a sessionless transport WITHOUT a seat argument, it is REFUSED by name, saying what would have worked — never served by minting a per-request seat and reporting success. That is `req:no-silent-fallback` applied to identity, and it is what makes the option safe rather than merely correct when used correctly. NOT CHOSEN, on the record. (b) Derive the seat from what a stateless request already carries — rmcp reconstructs a `ClientInfo` per request via `peer_info_for_stateless_request` — rejected because nothing in those headers is guaranteed stable or unique per client, so it trades a loud missing parameter for a quiet wrong answer. (c) One seat per server PROCESS on the sessionless transport — rejected because it is precisely the regression `req:seat-per-client` was written against, `claim_report` telling six sessions they are each other. (d) Refusing the claim family on sessionless HTTP outright — kept as (a)'s backstop rather than as the whole answer, because as the whole answer it makes `cap:remote-sessions` conditional on a protocol version and narrows what reflow2 offers.		Anthony's word, given 2026-07-30 when the four options and their costs were put to him. The requirement itself (`req:seat-identity-survives-stateless-mcp`) named this as the open part — 'deciding how a client obtains and carries the handle without making every tool call carry a parameter no human should have to think about' — so this closes the fork the requirement opened rather than inventing a new one. Why the backstop decided it. The three rejected options each fail quietly: (b) returns a wrong seat, (c) returns a shared one, and bare (a) returns a fresh one — and in all three cases the call SUCCEEDS. This design's standing objection to that shape is recorded in `req:no-silent-fallback` and was the reason `ver:stateless-seat` exists at all: the original bug was not that seats were wrong but that nothing said so. A refusal is the only branch that cannot rot silently. Composes with `dec:identity-out-of-band`, which already holds that names are assigned with zero coordination rather than derived from shared state — a server-minted handle is that principle one layer up. It also matches where the MCP 2026-07-28 revision itself points: 'servers that need cross-call state use explicit, server-minted handles passed as ordinary tool arguments.' Not urgent, and the measurement says why: `tools/stateless_seat_probe.py` reports one seat per client on stdio and on HTTP at 2025-06-18, `proxy.rs` pins 2025-06-18 on both handshakes so shared and remote mode are unaffected, and rmcp's `ProtocolVersion::LATEST` is still `V_2025_11_25`. It becomes urgent the moment an external client negotiates 2026-07-28 against a shared `--http` server. WHEN IT LANDS: `ver:stateless-seat` flips to passing on its own evidence, `tools/stateless_seat_probe.py` exits zero and is worth promoting from a baseline to a CI gate, and `decision:ack:350d55cf9c8c3247` — the acknowledgement holding the failing check acceptable — should be WITHDRAWN rather than left standing.acceptedA seat is minted on request and carried by the caller, and a claim that cannot name one is refused, Seat identity must not rest on protocol-level MCP sessions, which the 2026-07-28 spec removes
The epoch chain is backfilled from shipped releases only — real tags, or nothing
Every epoch on the retrospective chain corresponds to a real shipped release with a real git tag and date (v0.4.0 through v0.10.1), plus the pre-existing genesis and post-v0.5.0-hardening epochs. Each Decision is anchored to the epoch of the earliest release whose committed export actually contains it — evidence from the repo, not reconstruction from memory. Each Release is pinned to its own epoch. Epochs before v0.9.0 carry no checksum, because their exports predate the hash chain; they say so in their description rather than claiming one. Going forward, an epoch is cut as work happens so nothing needs backfilling again.		User decided 2026-07-24 among three options. THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVES: (a) forward-only — anchor from today and leave the past alone. Rejected because all 34 existing decisions are the ones actually worth re-opening; a fork layer that can only fork decisions made after it was built is a fork layer with nothing to fork. (b) full reconstruction — invent an epoch per work session across the whole history and synthesize the missing snapshots. Rejected because most of those boundaries are guesses, and a fabricated epoch is worse than an absent one: it looks like evidence. Release tags are the natural resolution because they are the only points in this project's history that are independently attested (a tag, a date, a published binary, a committed export), and because 'the design as of the release that shipped it' is the question a fork actually asks. The cost is deliberately accepted: the 9 founding decisions anchor to v0.4.0, the earliest tag carrying an export, which is their earliest EVIDENCE rather than their origin — recorded as such in that epoch's description instead of being silently presented as the date they were made. FOUND WHILE DOING THIS: reflow2's own temporal axis was nearly unused — zero Snapshots, 8 of 42 ChangeEvents pinned, no Decision anchored at all, the chain stopped four days back — because add_change_event (cheap, epoch-free) had been used throughout where record_change (pins and snapshots) was meant. The fork layer's foundation was missing, not merely its ref layer.acceptedtemporal
The authority detector binds on what is settled from here, not on the 121 settled nodes that predate it
GRANDFATHER IT. The check owed by rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word applies only to nodes that reach a settled state AFTER a recorded cutoff. Everything settled before the cutoff is out of its scope permanently, and is NOT backfilled. Anthony, 2026-08-11, answering the question put to him as gap:9d265ef455a2e245 / question:9d265ef455a2e245. THE MEASUREMENT THAT MADE THIS A QUESTION AT ALL, taken before it was asked rather than after: accepted Decisions (excluding `decision:ack:` review records) 105, of which 50 carry any AUTHORED_BY, 47 to who:ajs Requirements moved off `proposed` 109, of which 43 carry any AUTHORED_BY, 36 to who:ajs TOTAL SETTLED 214, of which 93 carry any AUTHORED_BY, 83 to who:ajs So 121 of 214 settled nodes carry nobody's name. Every one of them moved on the owner's word — the word simply was never recorded as an edge. A check written to the letter of the spec would therefore have gone red against 57% of the settled design on the day it landed, and NONE of those would have been violations. ⭐ THIS IS THE SIBLING CLAUSE'S TRAP, ONE RULE OVER, AND IT WAS NOT NAMED IN THE SPEC. rule:a-design-is-named-by-an-id-not-a-path is advisory for exactly this reason, in its own words: 'an honest detector would fail against the entire existing tool surface on the day it was written, and the only ways to make it green would be to block every build or to attach a check that proves nothing.' The authority rule's detector spec listed ONE precondition (resolve the forked owner identity) and missed this one. The fork is now resolved — 6 Contributors, `ctr:anthony` gone, `who:ajs` sole owner identity — so the FIRST precondition is met and this is what was underneath it. WHY FORWARD-ONLY IS THE ANSWER AND NOT A CONCESSION. The threat the rule was made enforced against is an AGENT WRITING IN THE OWNER'S VOICE (rule text, 2026-08-09: 'what one person needs protection from is not another person; it is an agent writing in his voice'). That threat is entirely prospective. The 121 are not that threat; they are bookkeeping that predates the rule. A check scoped to them would be measuring conformance to a convention that did not exist when they were written — the same error as dec:reopen-supersedes' '7 of 14 obsoleted-but-accepted', which turned out to be measuring conformance and not deviation. WHAT WAS REJECTED AND WHY, recorded so neither is re-litigated: (1) BACKFILL THE 121, then enforce across everything. Rejected. It would record the owner's approval 121 times on nodes no agent can individually evidence, and it makes the check green BY CONSTRUCTION — which is precisely the green-washing cap:governance-proposal's own description forbids ('never attach a verification to close the finding, because a graph node green-washes exactly like a document'). The attribution would be defensible in aggregate and unevidenced one by one, which is the worst combination: queryable and unfounded. dev_storyflow's finding ⑮ is the same shape — edges that are queryable and wrong are strictly worse than prose that is honestly informal. (2) FLIP THE RULE BACK TO ADVISORY. Rejected. It reverses the owner's explicit 2026-08-09 answer ('stop the build') to buy nothing but a closed gap, and it would leave this project with zero enforced rules that actually enforce. ⚠️ THE MECHANISM IS A REAL DESIGN CHOICE INSIDE THIS DECISION, NOT A FREE ONE. A Decision carries NO TIMESTAMP (the same limit that stops what_next scoring staleness), so 'after the cutoff' cannot key on a date. It must key on the design's own time axis — a DesignEpoch, or the ChangeEvent boundary at which the detector lands — which is what req:graph-indexes-snapshots exists to make answerable without a git lookup. The cutoff epoch is to be recorded WHEN THE DETECTOR IS BUILT, not now: minting it in advance would date the rule to a moment nothing enforced. WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO. It does not close gap:9d265ef455a2e245. That gap is unverified_enforced_rule and needs a PASSING Verification, and no check exists yet — the gap stays open as honest debt, and acknowledging it here would be recording a judgement the owner did not make. It also says nothing about rule:bl-41, the OTHER enforced rule with no detector (gap:b5ca966a38d7f372), which is a different problem: a rule about LLM behaviour that graph state may not be able to detect at all, and the first real customer for req:a-rule-says-whether-it-can-be-checked-at-all. 📌 THIS DECISION IS THE FIRST NODE BORN COMPLIANT WITH THE RULE IT SHAPES — settled only on the owner's word, and carrying an AUTHORED_BY approver edge to who:ajs recording that word at the moment it was given.		The rule was made enforced to stop an agent settling intent in the owner's voice — a prospective threat. The 121 unattributed settled nodes are not that threat; they are bookkeeping predating the rule, and 121 of 214 means an unscoped check would go red on history rather than on violations. Backfilling would make the check green by construction on evidence no agent holds; reverting to advisory would discard the owner's explicit answer. Forward-only is the only option that leaves the check meaning something on the day it lands.acceptedDesign intent moves only on the owner's word — an agent may propose anything and settle nothing
The content store is discontinued — built, shipped, correct, and used zero times
DECIDED AND DONE 2026-08-09, Anthony's word: \'let's discontinue the content store.\' Supersedes dec:where-content-lives, dec:what-lives-where, dec:content-store-implementation, dec:content-manifest and dec:content-growth-is-bounded-by-what-not-by-size. ⭐ THE EVIDENCE WAS USAGE, MEASURED IN EVERY PROJECT THAT HAS IT — reflow2's own design: no --content-path configured, no .reflow2/content directory, and 0 of 148 Fragments carrying a content_ref. flo2: no content path. dev_storyflow: no content directory. THREE PROJECTS, ZERO USE, on a feature that is built, tested and documented. HIS ARGUMENT, in his words: the bytes cannot fully live in a repo because it would become a huge object rapidly; dev_storyflow's 700+ documents have been ingested and \'those documents are no longer really needed\'; better to put important design artifacts directly in the git repo in something like a design_artifacts folder; it is another feature that must be maintained; and in flo2 the blob could reach terabytes needing backup, security and per-project separation. AND AN ARGUMENT NOBODY HAD MADE: dec:where-content-lives settled on a content-addressed store whose blobs are COMMITTED TO GIT. Git is already a content-addressed store. The design was a content-addressed layer inside a content-addressed system, and the dedup and integrity hash it provided were both things git already gives anything committed. AND A FOUNDING MOTIVATION THAT DID NOT SURVIVE: the store was partly built to make sessions \'stateful\' by holding transcripts. cap:session-memory already rejected that mechanism in its own text — \'a pointer to a 3 MB transcript is a RECEIPT, not documentation: leaning on it recreates the markdown problem one level down.\' Its actual design needs no store: takeaways as first-class graph content, the transcript a Fragment carrying a session UUID. See dec:idea-is-session-context-already-in-the-graph. WHAT WAS REMOVED: content_put / content_get / content_exists / content_manifest, crates/reflow2-core/src/content.rs, crates/reflow2-mcp/src/tools/content_tools.rs, the --content-path flag, both test files, and the loop nudge's session-artifacts advisory (which told sessions to content_put a rendering). ⚠️ TWO ACCEPTED REQUIREMENTS ARE NOW UNSATISFIED ON PURPOSE, AND THAT IS THE HONEST STATE RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT. Both are Anthony's own words from 2026-07-31 and the store was their answer: · req:agent-artifacts-are-captured — \'in many sessions, the agent will create artifacts... having all these artifacts automatically stored in the reflow2 blob storage would be great.\' · req:sources-are-kept-not-just-parsed — ingest keeps the original corpus documents, so the corpus becomes part of the design rather than an input consumed and discarded. He was shown both in the impact check and chose to KEEP THEM OPEN AND UNANSWERED rather than drop them or claim a replacement. The design_artifacts folder is the intended answer and is UNBUILT, so recording it as satisfied would be fiction. detect_gaps will now ask about them, and that question is the retirement working rather than a bug. THREE OTHER REQUIREMENTS EXISTED ONLY BECAUSE THE STORE DID and go quiet with it: req:the-store-is-reachable-from-a-session (a surface for it), req:export-says-what-it-cannot-carry (a warning about pointers the export cannot carry), and req:content-reaches-every-seat. Their statuses are Anthony's to move; nothing was changed on his behalf. ⚠️ AND THE REPLACEMENT RESTS ON THE SCHEMA'S WEAKEST JOIN, stated so it is not discovered later: a design_artifacts folder puts the weight on Artifact.location and Fragment.title, which is the field dev_storyflow filed FOUR defects about on this same day — unvalidated paths, a literal ellipsis matching nothing, title-vs-source ambiguity, and no way to ask \'is this path already in the graph?\'. That is an argument for fixing `location` before leaning on it, not against the plan. RETIRED ON THE RECORD, NOT DELETED (retire-from-design, Path A). The capability, its verifications and its artifacts keep their nodes and their history; the ChangeEvent carrying change_type `deprecation` is the marker, because Capability.status has no terminal value — which is exactly dec:idea-does-a-capability-need-a-cancelled-state, still open and still Anthony's, and this is now its first real instance.		Recorded as a new Decision rather than by editing the five it supersedes, per dec:reopen-supersedes: an accepted decision is never un-accepted, a later one obsoletes it. The two unsatisfied requirements are named in the decision itself rather than left to be inferred from a gap report, because \'we removed the thing that answered your stated need\' is the part a later reader most needs and the part a tidy graph would hide.acceptednothing
The MCP surface is split by transport rather than given a new medium — one Interface was describing two boundaries
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-13, choosing between four options put to him: SPLIT `ifc:mcp-tools` into its stdio and streamable-HTTP transports rather than add `json_rpc` to the `medium` enum. THE PROBLEM AS IT HAD STOOD SINCE 2026-07-28. `ifc:mcp-tools` claimed `medium: REST`, which was never chosen — it was the schema default before `unspecified` replaced it (`req:seam-incompatibility`), and reflow2's own three boundaries all said REST while being a Rust library API, a document format and an MCP tool surface. The correction was blocked on a genuine vocabulary question and was RAISED FOR HIM RATHER THAN GUESSED, because inventing schema vocabulary is a design decision. ⭐ THE DIAGNOSIS THAT DISSOLVED THE QUESTION: the node's own `endpoint` field already said it — *'a stdio pipe to a launched process, OR the address given to `--http`'*. **One Interface was describing two boundaries.** They differ in more than medium: the HTTP one can be reached remotely, sit behind a gateway and terminate TLS; the stdio one can do none of those, and has no transport to secure at all. WHAT THE SPLIT COST AND WHAT IT AVOIDED: · NO SCHEMA CHANGE, so no new enum value. That matters more than it looks: **enum values are not counted by the version stamp** (it counts node and edge TYPES), so adding one is a compatibility event nothing can detect — the stamp-blindness pattern this design has recorded four instances of already. · Existing vocabulary suffices for the half that has an answer: `cli` is exactly right for a launched process spoken to on its stdin/stdout. · Four live edges to consider and three `CHANGED` history edges left where they were. 🛑 IT QUARANTINES THE PROBLEM RATHER THAN SOLVING IT, AND THAT WAS SAID BEFORE HE CHOSE. `ifc:mcp-tools-http` still has NO correct enum value and stays `unspecified` rather than taking a wrong one. `medium` is a pairing-key axis where `unspecified` reads as UNKNOWN and never as agreement, **so that boundary cannot pair with anything until the vocabulary question is settled.** Adding `json_rpc` remains open and untaken. ═══ MEASURED IMMEDIATELY AFTER, AND IT VINDICATES THE CUT ═══ `seam_report` against flo2's `ifc:reflow2-design-api`, run on both halves: ifc:mcp-tools-http agreed 3 · incompatible 1 · unstated 4 incompatible: transport_security ours none / theirs tls unstated: medium ours (none) / theirs REST ifc:mcp-tools agreed 3 · incompatible 2 · unstated 3 incompatible: medium ours cli / theirs REST incompatible: transport_security ours none / theirs tls ⇒ **THE SPLIT MADE THE CHECK ABLE TO TELL THE TWO APART.** The stdio boundary now says loudly, on `medium`, that it is NOT the thing flo2 means — flo2's spec reads *'MCP carried over HTTP, as reflow2 already serves with --http / --serve-shared'*. Before the split a single node would have paired with flo2 ambiguously and carried the TLS finding on the wrong boundary. 📌 AND IT SHARPENS THE OPEN TLS QUESTION. `fact:reflow2-flo2-seam-measured-2026-08-13` recorded two readings of the `transport_security` disagreement: (a) a segment artefact, flo2 terminating TLS at its own edge, or (b) a real assumption gap. On a stdio pipe (a) was arguable, because there is no transport to secure. On the HTTP boundary it is not: that really is plain HTTP with no TLS while flo2 says `tls`. **(b) is now the more likely reading**, and resolving it still needs flo2's side, which was deliberately not written to. WHAT REMAINS OPEN: whether the `medium` enum should gain `json_rpc` at all. This decision settles only that the surface is two boundaries.		Recorded as its own accepted Decision rather than by quietly editing the interface, because the interface's spec had carried this as an OPEN question raised for Anthony since 2026-07-28 and the record should show both that it was asked and how it was settled (`dec:reopen-supersedes`' principle). The load-bearing point is that the question dissolved rather than being answered: the node's own `endpoint` field already described two boundaries, so the missing enum value was a symptom of a modelling error, not a vocabulary gap. Splitting needed no schema change and avoided adding an enum value that the version stamp cannot see. It is recorded as a partial settlement on purpose. The stdio half now has a correct value (`cli`); the HTTP half has none and stays `unspecified`, which means it cannot pair on medium with anything — including flo2 — until `json_rpc` or an equivalent is decided. That cost was stated before the choice was made rather than discovered afterwards. Measured the same minute: pairing both halves against flo2 shows the stdio boundary now incompatible on `medium` (correctly — flo2 means the HTTP one) and the HTTP boundary carrying exactly one real disagreement. The split is what let the check tell them apart.acceptednothing
DEFERRED — whether reflow2 models information, materiel, personnel and state is a SCOPE question, and the re-ask trigger is named rather than left to memory
ANTHONY, 2026-08-10, answering four gaps as one: req:vocabulary-covers-information, -materiel, -personnel and -states are DEFERRED as a class. WHY AS A CLASS. They are one question wearing four hats — does reflow2 model the other UAF domains, or is it deliberately scoped to function and structure? Answering them piecemeal would decide the scope by accident, four times, without anyone noticing they were the same decision. They came from Anthony UAF/DoDAF background (user-se-background-viewpoint-doctrine), so they are real vocabulary a systems engineer expects, not speculative additions. DEFERRED IS NOT DECLINED. Each is a coherent requirement and none was argued down. What is missing is a PROJECT THAT NEEDS THEM: reflow2 own design has no materiel, no personnel beyond Contributor, and no behavioural state machine, so building the vocabulary now would be declaring types nothing reads — which req:functional-vocabulary-computes forbids in as many words, and which dec:idea-detect-vocabulary-that-nothing-reaches exists to detect. THE RE-ASK TRIGGER, NAMED SO DEFERRED CANNOT DEGRADE INTO NEVER ASKED AGAIN (the shape dec:the-telemetry-kpp-question-waits-for-flo2 set): re-open when a design reflow2 is actually pointed at needs one of them. Concretely — a project with physical parts to sustain (materiel), an organisation with roles performing activities (personnel), a protocol or device with modelled behavioural states (states), or a data contract whose entities and attributes must cross an interface (information). The bluesky/NSLS-II work is the likeliest source of the last two. WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS WRONG: if a consumer hits one of these and works around it in prose rather than asking, the deferral will look correct while costing exactly what it was meant to avoid. That is unobservable from inside this design, which is the honest limit of this decision.		not recordedacceptedWhat crosses an interface is modellable — data entities, their attributes and their relationships, Physical resources are modellable — supply, sparing, maintenance and consumption, which `Resource` does not mean, People are modellable inside the design, not only around it — organisation, role, and who performs a function, Behavioural state and its transitions are modellable, distinct from lifecycle status
The registry ROOT is the tenant boundary — listing stays unfiltered, and reflow2 still authenticates nothing
DECIDED 2026-08-12, Anthony's word, on the question the registry raised the moment it existed: WHO MAY LIST WHICH DESIGNS. ⚠️ THIS IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM THE ONE ALREADY ANSWERED, and conflating them is the trap. `req:a-session-cannot-address-another-design` and `ver:a-session-cannot-name-another-design` settle ADDRESSING — can a session open a design it was not given? (No: refused by name, and a path is not an alternative route in.) This settles EXISTENCE — may a session learn a design is there at all? **A design can be perfectly isolated and still leak the list**, and for a hosted service the customer list is often the most sensitive thing it holds. THE TWO CASES PULL OPPOSITE WAYS, AND BOTH ARE REAL. - ONE OWNER, MANY PROJECTS. Anthony holds reflow2, flo2, dynograph-foundation, dev_storyflow. He WANTS a session to list them and pick, and asked for exactly that on 2026-08-05: 'can a reflow2 tool be to simply return all graph_ids to the agent and the agent then can choose whichever graph_id the user specifies?' — captured inside the ACCEPTED `req:a-session-chooses-its-design`. - MANY TENANTS, ONE SERVER. flo2's hosted case. A session working on one customer's project must not learn that another customer EXISTS. DECIDED: **THE REGISTRY'S ROOT IS THE TENANT BOUNDARY.** `Registry::discover(root)` reads what is under that root and nothing else; `graph_ids()` stays unfiltered and lists exactly that. An operator serving many tenants gives each its own root. Isolation is then a property of WHAT IS THERE rather than of a check on who is asking. WHY, and the first reason is the one that rules out the alternative on principle rather than on effort: 1. **REFLOW2 HAS NO AUTHENTICATION AND IS NOT GETTING ANY.** Stated in the design and printed on the container image label: 'NO AUTHENTICATION — deploy on a private network behind a gateway that authenticates.' A filtered listing REQUIRES knowing who is asking, so building one means reflow2 growing an identity system it has explicitly refused. That is not a cost, it is a contradiction. 2. **IT IS FREE.** The root is already a parameter of `Registry::discover`. This is a deployment shape, not code. 3. **IT IS THE BOUNDARY THAT ALREADY WORKS.** `a_real_design_outside_the_root_is_refused_like_any_other` proves a design genuinely present elsewhere on the machine is refused IDENTICALLY to one invented. The root is already the isolation boundary; making it the tenant boundary is the same mechanism, not a new one. 4. ⭐ **IT IS ALREADY THE RECOMMENDED ANSWER TO A DIFFERENT QUESTION.** flo2's blast-radius section holds '(a) Partition. Shard graphs across several reflow2 processes so a crash loses a subset' and adds 'this is why it belongs with #1 — it is a property of the registry's routing, not a layer above it', with the warning that designing them apart means designing the first one twice. **Partitioning gives tenant isolation and blast-radius containment from ONE decision.** WHAT WAS REJECTED, and why, so nobody re-proposes it: - A FILTERED LISTING (one registry, trimmed per caller). Rejected on (1): it needs identity reflow2 does not have and will not acquire. - NO LISTING AT ALL (you may only attach to an id you were handed). Safe, and it breaks `req:a-session-chooses-its-design` — which is ACCEPTED and whose whole first half is discovering what exists before choosing. - LIST EVERYTHING AND TRUST THE OPERATOR TO SCOPE IT. This is what shipped, and it is what this decision RATIFIES rather than changes — but only once the root is NAMED as the boundary. Undecided, the same code reads as an oversight; decided, it is the mechanism. WHAT IT COSTS, honestly: a root (and likely a process) per tenant is more resource-hungry than one shared server, and it pushes 'which tenant is this?' up to flo2's gateway. That is where it already belongs — flo2's own boundary list says 'Authentication and authorization, entirely' is flo2's job, and its only obligation on reflow2 is that a session bound to one graph cannot address another, which is now tested. ⇒ WHAT THIS SETTLES FOR THE TRANSPORT (`cap:select-graph-by-id`, still `in_progress`): **the registry routes WITHIN a root and never across one.** A selection surface — the preferred HTTP path prefix `/g//` — resolves against the root that server was given, and there is no cross-root operation to design. The security property is decided BEFORE the surface is built rather than retrofitted onto it, which is what flo2's tracker warns about: 'a handler that reaches the wrong graph corrupts a design rather than erroring, so this wants property tests, not examples.' 📌 NOT SETTLED HERE: whether one PROCESS may hold several roots. `dec:one-process-many-stores` (accepted, conditional) is about a process holding N stores; this is about what one REGISTRY offers. If a process ever serves two roots, the per-root boundary still holds and the routing question is separate.		Anthony chose this over a filtered listing and over refusing to list at all, after the registry made the question live rather than theoretical. The load-bearing reason is that a filter would require reflow2 to know who is asking — an identity system the design has twice refused in writing — whereas the root is already a parameter, is already the isolation boundary the registry tests prove, and is the same partitioning that flo2's blast-radius section independently recommends. One decision covers tenant isolation and blast radius, which is what that section asked for when it said to decide them together rather than twice.acceptedA session names the design it wants by graph_id, and the server maps id to path
Artifact.granularity and .volatility declare no schema default — the safe reading is supplied by the reader, so absence stays honest
Remove `default:` from `Artifact.granularity` and `Artifact.volatility` in schema/build.yaml. Nothing else: no code change, no backfill, no change to the content hash, no tolerance added to the round-trip gate.		Anthony's word, 2026-08-15, choosing a FOURTH option over the three music_graph proposed in F23 — and this settles F23 and the round-trip gate's behaviour as ONE decision, which was his framing before it was anyone's analysis. THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDED IT: the safe reading already lives in the reader. coverage.rs:209 reads granularity with `.unwrap_or('atomic')`; drift.rs:436 reads volatility with `.unwrap_or('stable')`. Those are the only two readers. So the schema default was redundant with the code — it changed no report's verdict, and its only observable effect was to write an intent nobody expressed onto every Artifact at import. Proven by the counterweights, which are the point: the two absence cases in tests/artifact_intent.rs (`graph_with(None)`, `graph_with_granularity(None)`) passed BEFORE this change because the schema injected the value and pass AFTER it because the reader supplies it, unchanged either way. WHY NOT THEIR THREE. (a) backfill on import and open — migrates a store once, but writes values nobody chose into every consumer store permanently, which is the exact erosion cap:defaults-are-not-serialized exists to prevent. (b) exclude default-valued properties from the content hash — their own preference, and the one route this design has already argued CANNOT work: absence would come to mean 'nobody said OR somebody chose the default', the distinction lost in the act of protecting it, and it would weaken the hash for the 71 properties that legitimately keep defaults. (c) have --import print what it defaulted — leaves the gate red and the restore broken, and only makes the blocked commit self-explanatory. ⚠️ IT REVERSES A DELIBERATE KEEP, and that is the honest cost. BL-198 removed ten of 81 defaults on 2026-08-10 and KEPT these two, on the reasoning that `stable` is the safe reading. That reasoning was correct and is untouched; what is new is the measurement that the reader already holds it. The reflex being corrected is the same one BL-198 named from the other side — there it was 'single-valued means informationless', wrong three times in ten; here it is 'the safe reading must be stored', wrong because storing it converts a fallback into an assertion. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: nothing already written moves. reflow2's own Artifacts keep their values, so its export does not churn and its own round trip stays clean. It does not address F24 (the latent surface never re-probes after a CLI restore), which sits on the same restore path and is a separate defect.acceptedAn artifact declares what it stands for and how its content behaves, so a report can tell two opposite states apart, A property nobody chose is not stored, so absence means nobody said
The recoverability clause is withdrawn; the rest of the stranded-server defect stands
Where fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server and fact:correction-stranded-server-is-recoverable-without-a-reconnect disagree, THE CORRECTION STANDS: a session stranded by the deleted-inode spawn failure IS recoverable in place, by starting a replacement daemon by hand from the on-disk path. The original node's remaining claims — the spawn failure itself, its cause in current_exe() resolving a deleted inode, and its misleading 'check the server log' advice — are unaffected and still hold.		Recorded because detect_defects reported the CONTRADICTS edge as an unresolved contradiction, and it was right to: two facts about the same failure disagreed, and nothing said which a reader should act on. Left alone, the next stranded session finds both and has no way to choose — which is worse than either claim alone, because the expensive answer ('unrecoverable, restart the session') is the one written with more authority. WHY THE CORRECTION WINS ON EVIDENCE RATHER THAN ON RECENCY: it was established by execution on 2026-08-08 — the failure was hit, the recovery run, and a dozen subsequent tool calls succeeded in the same session with no reconnect. The original clause was inherited from a session handoff and reasoned from the spawn path, never tested; the node's own evidence field says the diagnosis was 'recorded ... as worth filing and still unfiled'. A measured claim beats a reasoned one about the same mechanism. THE DISTINCTION THAT MAKES BOTH NODES TRUE ONCE THIS IS APPLIED: the dead inode blocks the client from CREATING a daemon, not from FINDING one. Attaching is a separate act, and any daemon started by any means satisfies the lookup. So the original is right about spawn and wrong about the session. NOT DONE HERE, deliberately: the original node's statement is left intact rather than edited. Its wrong clause is now answered on the record instead of erased, which keeps visible that reflow2's own graph carried a confident untested claim for a day — the same failure class the design keeps finding elsewhere, and worth being able to point at.acceptedfact:correction-stranded-server-is-recoverable-without-a-reconnect, fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server
DEFERRED — whether a telemetry content leak is inviolable cannot be answered until flo2 has real users, and the trigger is named rather than left to memory
ASKED AND DEFERRED, 2026-08-09. Anthony was put the consequence question for `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content`: if flo2 ran at 1,000 users and one telemetry payload turned out to have carried a customer's node id or search query, would that sink the effort or would he fix it and move on? HIS ANSWER: **too early to say — flo2 isn't real yet.** THAT IS A TRUE ANSWER AND IT IS RECORDED AS ONE. The requirement stands exactly as captured, at `proposed`, unpromoted and undowngraded. What is deferred is only whether it is INVIOLABLE — a KPP, ranked above every ordinary gap and owing a binding to the parts that could spend it. WHY IT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN SIMPLY NOT ACTED ON: the kpp-proposal skill's own instruction is to write down a non-yes, because the same signals will otherwise make the next session ask again, and *being asked the same question twice is how someone learns the tool is not listening*. This node is that record. ⭐ THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THIS AND A DECLINE, which is the reason it is worth its own node: a DECLINE means the need is tradeable and the question is closed. A DEFERRAL means the question is LIVE and currently unanswerable — criticality is a claim about consequence, and the consequences here (customer trust, an accusation, a contract) do not exist yet because the customers do not. Nobody can honestly rate the severity of a breach against users who are hypothetical. === THE TRIGGER, NAMED SO IT DOES NOT DEPEND ON ANYBODY REMEMBERING === RE-ASK WHEN ANY OF THESE IS TRUE: - flo2 has real users who are not Anthony or Alex — the first outside tenant is the moment the consequence becomes real. - flo2 acquires a stated privacy posture, terms of service, or any promise made to a user about their data. A promise made externally is a commitment the design should already be holding. - Anyone begins BUILDING the telemetry emitter. The threshold has to exist before the thing that could breach it, or the binding is retrofitted onto a shipped surface. ⚠️ AND THE ORDER MATTERS: `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content` is buildable NOW and does not wait for this. The structural guarantee it asks for — a payload schema whose every field is enum-valued or numeric, hence structurally incapable of carrying a design — is the right shape whether or not the threshold is ever declared inviolable. Deferring the KPP question must not be read as deferring the requirement. 📌 WHAT IS ALSO NOT DEFERRED, because it is decidable today and independently: usage counts may justify OPTIMISING a hot tool and may NOT, alone, justify CUTTING a cold one. `dec:bl-155` already measured that reflow2 cannot tell \'unused\' from \'unreachable\', and a removal decided on counts would delete exactly the capabilities that were never surfaced.		Recorded per the kpp-proposal skill, which requires writing down a non-yes so the question is not re-litigated — but recorded as a DEFERRAL rather than the decline the skill's step 6 describes, because Anthony's answer was that the question is unanswerable yet rather than that the need is tradeable. The named trigger is the part that does the work: without it, \'too early\' degrades into \'never asked again\', which is the failure mode a decline at least records honestly.acceptedUsage telemetry carries the verb and never the object — what was called, never what it was called on
OPEN — 'documents to graph entities' is TWO problems, and the failing one is reading the graph back, not getting content into it
RECORDED AS A REFRAME PLUS A MEASUREMENT, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-04, stating the root question that unifies the dev_storyflow corpus and the reflow2-dogfooding threads: 'how do we transition documents to graph entities? whether that is a huge corpus of documents in dev_storyflow or getting away from using documents in reflow2, it is how do we make decisions based on graph content, not documents.' Nothing here is settled. THE SPLIT. (IN) documents become graph entities — ingest_step, provenance Fragments, the content store, cross-document convergence. Partly built, and every remaining piece is scheduled across epoch:v0240-planned..v0280-planned. (OUT) a person or agent DECIDES from graph content instead of from a document. Almost nothing is scheduled. The whole increment plan is capture, detection, seams and write-surface. ⭐ THE MEASUREMENT, AND ALL OF IT IS FIRST-HAND FROM ONE SESSION ON 2026-08-04 RATHER THAN RECALLED. `reviewed_gaps` returned 130,922 CHARACTERS and could not be read at all — it was written to a file and queried with `jq`. That is the tool answering 'what have we already decided to accept', which is a decision-making read, and it was unusable AS a read. It joins: `loop_status` at 72,886 characters until (BL-205) fixed it the day before, and it is the call the SessionStart hook and the server instructions both call 'the one cheap call'; `describe_schema` on ONE node type at ~30 KB ((BL-142)); and `scan_nodes` on 241 Decisions, where the where-am-i skill's own guidance forced reading names only and confessing that exactly one had been read in full. Add the standing limit: 52 properties are `fulltext: true` and `Decision.rationale` is not one of them. THEY ARE ALL ONE DEFECT: A READ THAT RETURNS EVERYTHING IT KNOWS INSTEAD OF WHAT WAS ASKED. The graph holds the content correctly. It cannot serve it back at the size it now holds. That is neither a vocabulary problem nor an ingest problem, which is why every framing so far has missed it — `dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph` reasoned about what a node can HOLD, and the binding constraint is what a read can RETURN. THE CONSEQUENCE THAT SHOULD NOT BE SOFTENED: TODAY A DOCUMENT BEATS THE GRAPH FOR MAKING A DECISION, AND IT IS A FAIR FIGHT THE GRAPH LOSES. A document can be skimmed, searched with ctrl-F, and read end to end. The graph offers 130 KB or a list of names. Reaching for the markdown is therefore RATIONAL BEHAVIOUR RESPONDING TO A REAL DIFFERENCE, not a bad habit to be disciplined out of, and no improvement to capture changes it. THE SHAPE OF AN ANSWER, offered because the in-house precedent is already built and shipped rather than as advocacy: the transition is not documents → graph, it is DOCUMENTS → GRAPH → DERIVED DOCUMENTS. `cap:changelog-view` ('a changelog is a derivable view of the graph's own delta') shipped in v0.20.0 and CHANGELOG.md is generated today; `dec:views-are-projections` is accepted; `tools/render_views.py` is 44 KB of renderer producing docs/viewpoints.md and has existed since 2026-07-19. The renderer, the doctrine and the proof all exist — the backlog simply is not one of its views. This also explains why option (d) on `dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph` kept losing: it was judged as a RIVAL to the capture options when it is the OUT half of the same answer, and that node already half-saw it ('solves RETRIEVAL and not CAPTURE — it composes with (a)/(b) rather than competing'). ⭐ THE TEST THIS YIELDS, AND IT IS ANTHONY'S OWN DELETION INSTINCT MADE SAFE. He asked: 'should I delete the documents and force us to use the reflow2 graph?' Deletion is the right TEST and the wrong COMMITMENT. The test is: CAN YOU DELETE THIS DOCUMENT AND REGENERATE IT FROM THE GRAPH? Yes → the graph is the source and the document was a view. No → the document is still the source, and WHAT CANNOT BE REGENERATED IS PRECISELY WHAT THE GRAPH IS MISSING. Run it per document, never on the repo at once, and regenerate BEFORE deleting so nothing is ever at risk. Where each stands today, assessed 2026-08-04: CHANGELOG.md PASSES (already derived); docs/viewpoints.md PASSES; COORD.md's in-progress table passes the day `claim_region` is used for real, because the computation exists and is served (`dec:coord-board-in-graph`); docs/backlog.md FAILS, and the rows that cannot regenerate are the exact statement of what vocabulary is absent; AGENTS.md FAILS PERMANENTLY AND CORRECTLY, because an agent reads it before it knows reflow2 exists. That last row is why this is not a march toward zero documents — it is a march toward zero documents that are SOURCES, and the test says which is which instead of leaving it to taste. FOR A CORPUS THE TEST POINTS THE OTHER WAY. Source documents cannot be regenerated and must not be — `req:sources-are-kept-not-just-parsed` says so. The test applies instead to the READING: after ingest, can 'what did I want to build, and what of it exists' be answered without opening a document? A no means the ingest landed prose rather than structure, which is exactly what the 52-fulltext-properties limit predicts for rows imported as long descriptions. WHAT IS NOT DECIDED HERE. Whether the OUT half is a v0.24.0 obligation, its own increment, or a discipline applied to every read as it is touched. Which reads to fix first, and by what rule — `reviewed_gaps` is the loudest but `scan_nodes` on a mature type may be the most consequential. Whether 'answer-shaped rather than type-shaped' needs new tools or bounded forms of the existing ones. And whether the backlog renderer is a `render_views.py` view, a served tool, or neither. --- COUNTED 2026-08-04, SAME SESSION. The item left unverified above is now closed, and it answers the bug-list-or-increment question against the cheaper reading. --- ⭐ OF 33 COLLECTION-RETURNING READ TOOLS ON THE SERVED SURFACE, EXACTLY THREE LET THE CALLER BOUND THE RESULT, AND ONLY ONE CAN PAGE. Counted over `crates/reflow2-mcp/src/tools/*.rs` (144 tool functions across 12 modules). The 33 are: alternatives_for, budget_report, changelog_view, claim_report, confirmation_ledger, content_manifest, coverage_report, describe_schema, detect_defects, detect_gaps, dimension_drifts, evidence_report, export_graph, export_surface, find_tools, flow_report, granularity_report, graph_report, graph_report_markdown, hierarchy_issues, ility_report, loop_status, maturity_report, open_questions, readiness_report, recall_resolutions, release_report, reviewed_defects, reviewed_gaps, scan_nodes, seam_report, search_design, surprising_connections. The three bounded: `scan_nodes` (limit + offset + next_offset + capped_by — the only real paging), `search_design` (limit, no offset), `find_tools` (limit with a default). The only other `limit` in the tool surface is `Constraint.limit`, a domain property, not a bound. SO IT IS AN INCREMENT, NOT A BUG LIST — the guess of 'four' was low by an order of magnitude. TWO HONEST QUALIFIERS THAT KEEP THE NUMBER FROM BEING OVERSTATED. (i) Not all 30 are broken today: several bound themselves internally rather than by parameter — `loop_status` became a digest under (BL-205), and `graph_report_markdown` is a summary by construction. The claim is that the CALLER cannot bound them, not that all thirty are unreadable now. (ii) Because none of them share a paging mechanism, each fix is bespoke. That is the real cost, and it is the argument for treating this as one increment with a common shape rather than as thirty separate rows — which is exactly how (BL-205) was filed and fixed, alone, one tool at a time, three days ago. THE SHAPE THIS SUGGESTS, not chosen: `scan_nodes` already solved this problem completely — `total` against `returned`, `omitted`, `next_offset`, `capped_by`, and a payload budget so a cap is never silent but never a surprise. It is an in-house pattern, tested, and adopted by exactly one tool. Generalising it is a smaller design question than inventing one.		Recorded because the measurement is perishable in the exact way this project keeps rediscovering: 'reviewed_gaps returned 130,922 characters' becomes 'reads felt big once' within a session or two, and then the next reader re-derives it or, worse, does not. The numbers are first-hand from a single sitting and are written down so the next session argues from them. Kept as its own node rather than appended to `dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph` because it CONTRADICTS that node's framing rather than extending it. That node asks what a node and an edge can hold and concludes the answer turns on how much of a row becomes structure; this one says the binding constraint is downstream of that entirely — a perfectly structured graph nobody can read back is still a graph nobody decides from. Folding the correction into the node it corrects would hide it. Deliberately does NOT register alternatives, so this stays a question rather than becoming a fork the loop asks Anthony to choose between. AMENDED the same session: the item this node named as unchecked was checked, and the answer (3 of 33, one pager) moved it from a bug list to an increment. Recorded as an amendment with the prior state snapshotted rather than as a fresh node, because the unchecked and checked forms are the same claim at two confidence levels — and the fact that naming the hole is what got it filled within the hour is worth the record.acceptednothing
The LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides
Every capability is designed as a check one party places on another; none does another's job.		The parties are not interchangeable: the LLM cannot be trusted with arithmetic, memory or its own confidence; the graph cannot judge meaning; the human cannot remember everything or notice slow drift. The deterministic core computes, the graph carries claims and their audit trail, questions route judgment to the human. docs/partnership.md maps each known LLM failure mode to its mechanism. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam).acceptedRecord a change, Detect gaps, A rule the project follows is captured with its consequence stated, not inherited from a default, Notice when a stated need is really a KPP, and ask, Notice the requirement nobody wrote down, Judge whether a requirement is well formed, and say which part a machine can judge, Ask the user a plain question
Silent drift-accept does not exist
set_artifact_checksum requires a disposition: design_holds (a dated claim) or design_updated (naming the design-side ChangeEvent, linked to the artifact).		'Accept the file, leave the design alone, say nothing' is how a design erodes into fiction over N legitimate fix cycles while reporting zero gaps — the failure that sank the original reflow. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: erosion trials, BL-33.acceptedRecord a change, Say which way the design and the build have diverged, and bring the design back up, Reconcile against what was built
A check older than its code is a freshness FACT, not a gap
DECIDED on Anthony's word, 2026-07-26: 'go with freshness fact on the confirmation ledger (always visible, never nagging)'. The alternative was a gap source — asked once through gap_to_prompt, acknowledgeable, and appearing in detect_gaps until answered. Rejected for the reason the ledger's own module doc already gives about signals: a stale-looking check is a STANDING PROPERTY of a claim rather than an event, it would fire on every legitimate refactor as readily as on a real hole, and an open list that can never reach zero gets skimmed — which is precisely the failure the gap workflow exists to prevent (the BL-23 lesson: when a detector punishes correct work, the answer is a different question, not a tuned threshold). As a ledger fact it is visible every time somebody asks how a claim stands, and it nags nobody.		Prompted by a real miss the same day. cap:degraded-surface was `verified` with a passing check, and that check drove stdio only; adding the HTTP transport widened what 'the server explains its own absence' had to mean, without widening anything that tested it. reflow2 reported zero gaps throughout, and it was right to — nothing it knew was false. But it HAD the evidence: art:main drifted twice (chg:shared-sessions, chg:remote-sessions) while art:test-degraded-server never moved, and Verification.last_run_at is written by verify.rs and read by nothing anywhere in the core. Same shape this project keeps finding — a field declared, written, and consulted by no computation (the temporal axis before BL-70, the whole inviolable-intent vocabulary before BL-96): the higher-yield question is what the core already does that nothing can reach. Deliberately NOT the wider question of measuring what a check actually covers, which is unknowable from the graph and belongs to BL-95.acceptedSay whether a check is older than what it checks
A view is a projection of the graph; renderer fill-ins are defects
Renderers may only emit what the graph states; everything else is confessed as a finding.		UAF/DoDAF doctrine from the author: the graph stores all design detail, the agent only renders viewpoints. If rendering requires extrapolation, something is missing inside reflow2 — almost always.
