The repo holds what the design PRODUCED; the content store holds what INFORMED it — and storyflow is the case that proves why
Anthony's rule, 2026-07-31, drawing the line the content store needs and nothing had yet stated. THE TEST, in his words: 'the actual implemented design of something or its artifacts' stays NATIVE IN THE REPO. Everything that INFLUENCED the design without being its output goes in the CONTENT STORE. NATIVE IN THE REPO — the codebase reflow2 helps build, and anything that gets compiled, tested, shipped or read by a consumer. It is versioned, diffed and reviewed as code always has been; reflow2 changes nothing about it. A README or an ADR that ships WITH the product also stays native, because it is a product-facing artefact rather than an input — the rule is about role, not about whether something is prose. IN THE CONTENT STORE — a markdown file a user wrote describing a design aspect, a corpus of decision notes, a whiteboard photograph, a session transcript, a diagram an agent drew to explain a choice. These informed what got built and are not themselves the thing built. THE EVIDENCE, AND IT IS WHY REFLOW2 EXISTS. storyflow began as one repo holding the codebase AND every markdown file recording Anthony's design decisions — now 900+ documents. Two costs, and the second is the one that matters: (1) NAVIGATION. The repo was a mess: design notes and source interleaved, and neither easy to move through. (2) RETRIEVAL, which is the deeper failure. In his words: 'whenever I started implementing design, I had to remember where in those 900+ design documents something actually was' — they were not all in one folder, not consistently labelled, not structured so you could work out where anything lived. And worse: 'some of my design choices were spread across multiple documents', so even finding the right document was not finding the answer. THE WORKAROUND TAKEN: a two-repo split — `storyflow` for the codebase, `dev_storyflow` for the design corpus (979 notes as of the 2026-07-20 adopt trial). It works, and it fixes exactly ONE of the two problems. WHY THAT MAKES IT THE MOTIVATING CASE RATHER THAN THE SOLUTION. Separating the documents cures the mess and does NOTHING for retrieval. You still have to remember where a decision lives; a choice spread across five documents is still spread across five documents, now in a tidier folder. reflow2's claim is that the design record should stop being PROSE YOU NAVIGATE and become A GRAPH YOU QUERY, with the prose kept as provenance hanging off the nodes it produced. The content store is therefore NOT a neater `dev_storyflow`: the document goes to the store, what it SAID becomes nodes, and asking 'where was this decided' becomes a query rather than an act of memory. AND IT IS WHY CROSS-DOCUMENT IDENTITY IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN A NICETY. 'Spread across multiple documents' is precisely the case `req:corpus-ingest` was written for — the same thing named in forty specifications converging on ONE node with several provenance Fragments rather than forty near-duplicates. Anthony's 900 documents are the corpus that requirement describes, and this is the experience that motivates it. THE FALSIFIABLE FORM, worth stating because it is checkable rather than rhetorical: IF REFLOW2 WORKS, STORYFLOW WOULD NOT HAVE NEEDED `dev_storyflow`. One repo, code native, the design in the graph, the sources in the store. If a user still ends up splitting their repo to stay sane, reflow2 has not delivered what this decision claims.		Recorded because the content store shipped without anyone stating what belongs in it, and a store with no placement rule fills up with whatever the first person guessed — after which the rule is set by accident. The storyflow history is the valuable half rather than the rule. The rule alone reads as tidiness; the history says what tidiness is worth and where it stops helping. A user who had already tried the obvious fix, at real scale, and found it solved half the problem is much better evidence than an argument, and it is evidence from the author's own working life rather than a hypothetical. The falsifiable form is deliberate. This project keeps finding declared properties nothing checks (`dec:edge-orthogonality`'s rule that a distinction earns its keep only if a computation reads it), and a doctrine about what goes where is exactly the kind of claim that can sit unexamined for a year. 'Would storyflow have needed a second repo?' is a question someone can actually answer later.acceptedStore bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash, The backlog is retired: every open row becomes the node type it already was, and docs/backlog.md is deleted rather than derived, OPEN — should the backlog stop being a 581 KB markdown file and become graph nodes, and what is missing before it can?, OPEN — 'documents to graph entities' is TWO problems, and the failing one is reading the graph back, not getting content into it, Ingest keeps the source documents, not only what it extracted from them
OPEN — what identifies an arrived epoch's snapshot: a tag, a commit, or the export's own content hash?
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. For an epoch or increment that has ARRIVED there IS a past to point at, so the question is only which handle the graph stores. Three candidates, and they answer different questions rather than competing. (a) GIT TAG (`epoch/2026-Q4`, `v0.18.0`). Human-readable, already the in-repo precedent — `rel:v0180` lives in the graph, tag `v0.18.0` lives in git, and nobody greps tags to learn what shipped. Cost: a tag is mutable and deletable, so a pin can quietly stop meaning what it meant. (b) COMMIT SHA. Immutable and exact. Cost: opaque to a person, and says nothing about which repo it is in — useless on its own in a multi-repo ecosystem. (c) THE EXPORT'S OWN `content_hash`. Every export already carries one, and `prev_content_hash` already chains them, so reflow2 HAS a version history of the design that owes git nothing. The same design exported on any machine hashes the same, which git cannot say of a commit. Cost: a hash identifies but does not LOCATE — you cannot fetch a document from its hash. THE SHAPE THIS SUGGESTS: `content_hash` is the IDENTITY and the git ref is the ADDRESS. They answer 'is this the same design?' and 'where do I get it?', which are different questions, and storing both makes a third thing computable for free — if the tag later points at a commit whose export hashes differently, the pin has drifted, and that is exactly the kind of finding reflow2 exists to make rather than to suffer. A SEPARATE QUESTION, and the one that decides how much is even needed: DOES REFLOW2 CREATE GIT REFS, OR ONLY RECORD THEM? Measured while thinking this through — reflow2 shells out to git NOWHERE. The merge driver is invoked BY git, never the reverse. So recording-only would preserve a property the tool currently has completely: it takes no clock, and it would take no VCS either. It could print the command it would have run. Creating tags would also mean write access to repos reflow2 does not own, which in an ecosystem of coupled repos is a different tool. MULTI-REPO: one epoch does not pin one ref, it pins a SET — one per design — which is `req:version-combination-is-an-object`, already the recorded dependency of `req:epochs-can-be-planned`. So the pin is a version combination, not a string.		Anthony's question (2026-07-30): how the mechanics of using git to capture snapshots would actually work. Recorded as options because he asked to think it through, not to be handed an answer. The `content_hash` option is worth flagging because it was not in the original framing and it is already built: exports have carried `content_hash` and `prev_content_hash` since the lineage chain landed, and the gate already fails when the chain is broken. If identity is what is wanted, most of it exists.proposednothing
Content lives in a content-addressed store behind object_store, local backend, COMMITTED to the repo
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31. Both earlier states are preserved: the original four-way fork at `snap:epoch:arrival-delta:dec:where-content-lives`, the object_store amendment at `…:r2`. THREE PARTS, all his word: 1. ADOPT `object_store` (Apache Arrow, originally InfluxData), LOCAL FILESYSTEM ONLY. The `fs` backend is a default feature and `InMemory` needs no feature at all; `aws`/`azure`/`gcp` stay OFF, which keeps `reqwest` and the crypto providers out of the tree. Cloud backends remain one configuration change away with no rework, because the whole point of the crate is that the backend is a runtime detail — so this is the smallest useful slice rather than a narrowing. 2. BLOBS ARE COMMITTED TO THE REPO. Chosen because it is the only option where the bytes are DISTRIBUTED BY THE SAME MECHANISM AS THE DESIGN: clone and you have everything, nothing to configure, nothing to be down, nothing to fall out of step. Every alternative is a second distribution channel, and a second channel is a second thing someone can skip — after which they see a design with holes in it and cannot tell. That is the failure `req:content-reaches-every-seat` exists to prevent. ACCEPTED COSTS, named rather than glossed: repo weight, and git handles binary churn poorly. Text — markdown, mermaid, HTML — diffs and compresses well and is most of what this will hold; raster images are the real risk and are the thing to watch first. 3. THE STORE LIVES IN `reflow2-mcp`, THE POINTER IN `reflow2-core`. Forced by a property worth keeping rather than chosen for taste: `object_store` is async and `fs` pulls tokio, while `reflow2-core` is deliberately synchronous — measured 2026-07-31, its entire dependency list is dynograph-{core,storage,graph,resolution,vector}, serde, serde_json, sha2, with no tokio, no async, no futures. So the core holds the CONTENT HASH, which is sync, deterministic and in-memory-testable, and `reflow2-mcp` does the I/O with the tokio it already carries through rmcp and hyper. Same split as `coverage_report`: the core computes, the surface touches the world. WHAT MUST HOLD, unchanged by the answers: the pointer is a CONTENT HASH and never a path (`cap:session-memory` already recorded what a path costs — it 'resolves for one person on one machine and silently misses for everyone on a shared graph'), and an unresolvable pointer FAILS LOUD and names itself (`req:no-silent-fallback`). Content addressing also keeps this reversible: because a blob can be verified wherever it came from, moving to a different distribution mechanism later changes how bytes are fetched and nothing about what the graph says. STILL TO CHECK AT BUILD TIME, not decided away: `object_store`'s MSRV against the workspace's 1.94, and its transitive tree with cloud features off MEASURED rather than assumed. Per `dec:design-dependencies-declared` the dependency is DECLARED with its version and the features taken by name — a new crate in this tree is a recorded reliance, not a line in a Cargo.toml. AND ONE THING DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN: what bounds repo growth. A size cap that refuses oversized blobs loudly was offered and not taken, so nothing currently stops a large binary landing in the history where it cannot be removed without rewriting it. That is the first thing to revisit if the repo starts to hurt, and it is cheaper to add before there is history than after.		Settled in one pass because Anthony's research had already dissolved the hard part: once `object_store` makes the backend runtime configuration, 'which storage' stops being an architectural commitment and only the git question remains — and that one turned out not to be about repo weight at all, but about whether the bytes travel the way the design already travels. The placement was not a preference. It came from measuring `reflow2-core`'s dependency list and finding it genuinely free of async, which makes 'put the store in the core' a decision to spend a property the crate has kept deliberately for a convenience it does not need. Reading the manifest answered in a minute what an argument about layering would not have settled at all. The open item on repo growth is recorded rather than decided because the honest answer depends on evidence nobody has yet: what actually gets stored. A cap chosen now would be a number invented to feel safe — the asserting default `req:defaults-do-not-assert` exists to prevent — while a cap chosen after a month of real blobs would be measured. The cost of waiting is that git history is unforgiving, and that is exactly why it is named here rather than left to be discovered.acceptedStore bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash, The graph holds pointers; a content store holds the bytes — narrative, transcripts, diagrams and drawings travel WITH the design
The schedule lives in the graph and is queried; nothing is snapshotted into git
CHOSEN BY ANTHONY, 2026-07-30: 'yes, promote this intent.' Option (d) of the brainstorm; the roads not taken are kept below. THE DECISION. A design's forward-looking schedule — which capabilities and requirements are expected at which epoch or increment — lives in the graph and is reached by QUESTION, not by document. His acceptance test, in his words: 'what capabilities are due to be released in epoch 5' and 'what didn't we achieve that we were supposed to in increment 10?' Nothing is written into git as an epoch snapshot: no epoch branch, no per-epoch file, no rendered roadmap held as a record. 'Let the agent/user figure out how to render the snapshot' — rendering is an OUTPUT, produced on demand and thrown away, never the record. WHERE GIT KEEPS A REAL JOB, and it is narrower than the original idea: an ARRIVED epoch corresponds to real commits in real repos, so 'what was actually deployed at epoch 3' pins a version combination (`req:version-combination-is-an-object`). Forward-looking plans describe GRAPH content and stay in the graph; backward-looking arrivals describe CODE and pin code. The information is in git either way, because the schedule lives in the graph and the graph is exported to `docs/design/reflow2.json` on every commit. ROADS NOT TAKEN, kept because they were genuinely considered. (a) EPOCH BRANCHES — his own original mechanism, 2026-07-28: 'epoch branches: project_x:epoch_1 captures what we expect the graph to look like at epoch_1.' A branch is the only place you can look at a future design whole, which is a real virtue. Not taken: checking out a branch normally makes the whole REPO reflect that state and there is no future code to reflect; a full export is 1.6 MB, so N epochs is N × 1.6 MB of near-identical JSON rewritten on every replan; branches invite merge semantics that do not apply; and a branch pointer moves silently, which is exactly what `req:plans-move-honestly` must be able to see. (b) A FILE PER EPOCH ON MAIN — my recommendation, and NOT TAKEN BECAUSE IT WAS WRONG rather than merely less good. Its selling point was that `git log -p` on the file would give the plan's revision history for free. But the schedule lives in the committed export, which already has git history and its own `prev_content_hash` chain — so the property existed and the file was an artifact added to obtain something the design already had. That is the shape this project keeps finding in other designs, found here in my own advice. (c) RENDER TO FILES — the generated form of (b), carrying the same redundancy plus a staleness obligation. THE ARGUMENT THAT DECIDED IT. Both of his questions are QUESTIONS, not documents: a query answers them directly, while a file answers them only if someone rendered the right one at the right moment. And every materialised artifact acquires a staleness problem the moment the graph moves — `docs/design/reflow2.json` has a gate for it, `dataflow.html` has a check for it, and `docs/loop-model.json` demonstrated the failure the same day by becoming permanently unreproducible. Not materialising is the only way to have no drift at all. MY EARLIER OBJECTION DID NOT HOLD, recorded because it was argued at length before being withdrawn: I claimed graph-only breaks readability for someone not running reflow2 (`req:design-reachable-without-the-repo`). It does not — the schedule is in the committed export, so it is reachable, merely not pretty, and prettiness is what on-demand rendering is for.		Anthony's idea, Anthony's lean, and Anthony's word to promote it. `req:graph-indexes-snapshots` was reworded on the same word, because it described indexing git refs and that is no longer what it means; its original text is preserved at `snap:epoch:planning-axis-intent:req:graph-indexes-snapshots`. Worth keeping: the option that won is the one that ADDS NOTHING. No new file, no new branch, no new format, and — per the requirement it satisfies — largely no new storage, since epochs, Snapshots capturing incoming edges, and `compare_designs` already exist. The two rejected options both proposed materialising something, and both were arguing for a property the committed export already provides. Also worth keeping, because it is a pattern rather than an incident: the file-per-epoch recommendation was mine, argued confidently, and wrong for the reason this project most often finds things wrong — it added a mechanism to obtain a property that already existed. Anthony's instinct to strip it back was better than my proposal to build it.acceptedThe graph answers 'as of epoch n' itself — a design's own time axis is not a git lookup
OPEN — is notification computed from the blast radius, or subscribed to?
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. When a plan moves during execution — 'the motorcade slips thirty minutes' — somebody has to be told, and the question is who decides that. (a) SUBSCRIPTION, the way every coordination tool works: you join a channel, or somebody remembers to include you on the distribution. Cheap, familiar, and it fails one way every time — the person who most needed to know was not on the list, and nobody finds out until it matters. (b) DERIVED FROM THE BLAST RADIUS: propagate_from already returns who a change impacts, including which published boundaries it crosses, so the owners of the impacted regions ARE the distribution. Nobody maintains a list, nobody is spammed with changes that cannot touch them, and when the plan changes shape the distribution changes with it for free. (c) BOTH — derived by default, with an explicit watch for people who want a region they do not own. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT TO (b), recorded beside it: a blast radius is only as good as the edges that exist, so an unrecorded dependency means a silent non-notification — which is the same failure as (a), reached by a different route, and arguably harder to notice because the mechanism looks principled. The mitigation is that a missing edge is already what detect_gaps hunts, so the honesty debt has an owner.		This is the most distinctive idea in the 1000-planner exploration and the strongest reason reflow2 would belong in that problem rather than a chat tool with a plan attached: a FRAGO is a ChangeEvent whose blast radius is computed, and 'who does this break' is a question reflow2 already answers. It is the same shape as every other answer in this project — computed, not remembered — and it inherits the honesty rules, so a notification would have to say what changed, what it impacts and what is now unresolved, never 'the plan was updated'. Kept separate from dec:live-tier because the mechanism choice is separable: (b) is worth building for a single team on the repo-file architecture, with no hosting at all, the moment anyone wants it.proposedThe loop can answer what this design owes a NAMED PERSON, not only what it owes in total

THAT IS FALSE. That capability is PLANNED, NOT BUILT. Expiry is keyed on the gap id, which hashes the affected node IDS — so a review expires when the affected SET changes membership and NEVER when the affected nodes change CONTENT. This review therefore does NOT self-expire. If the capability is reworded, someone must revisit this judgement BY HAND. *** AND IT WAS PROVEN LIVE, WITHIN THE HOUR, ON THIS VERY ACKNOWLEDGEMENT. *** Later in the same session Anthony asked for the recommendation-with-options behaviour to be cemented, and cap:gap-carries-a-reading was substantially rewritten: renamed, given three shape obligations and a language rule, and its check rewritten with two new negative assertions. That is precisely the failure cap:review-expires-on-content exists to fix — in its own words, 'a review outliving the wording it reviewed is worse than no review, because it reads as a human having agreed to something they never saw' — reproduced by the very sentence asserting it could not happen. That is not a UX preference — a design brain whose entire loop is ask-the-human-and-record-the-decision cannot let a second person's word enter as the first person's, which is dec:certainty-derived's forgery rule applied across people instead of across time, and it means the machinery this needs is the Question/answer surface plus Contributor attribution that already exist, not a second write path. Worth noting for whoever builds it: the cheapest form of this requires no service at all — a read-only export shared as a file is already 'reach without write', and the proposals could ride back as a design export that the owner merges. The requirement is HIS OWN idea, captured the same day; accepting this gap parks the MODELLING question, not the intent. WHAT BLOCKS IT IS A REAL VOCABULARY PROBLEM, FOUND BY CHECKING AND RECORDED SO NOBODY RE-DERIVES IT. The first answer given was 'reflow2 already has the vocabulary — model the release procedure as a Flow'. THAT IS WRONG AS THE SCHEMA STANDS: PART_OF_FLOW is declared Capability -> Flow and accepts nothing else, so a Flow's steps must be Capabilities. 'Bump the version in three files' is a chore, not a capability. Modelling seven release chores as seven Capabilities would put fake entries into the very set that coverage_report and the verification counts range over — 100 real capabilities plus seven chores makes every one of those reports quietly wrong, permanently. The correction is recorded here rather than edited over the earlier claim. SO THE OPEN QUESTION IS ONE LEVEL DOWN, AND IT IS GENUINE: is a procedure step a first-class design object, or is it documentation the design POINTS AT? Making it first-class means widening PART_OF_FLOW to accept a step type — which MOVES THE STAMP and locks every older reflow2 out of the design, so it is a release-shaped decision, not a side edit. Pointing at it instead means writing the procedure as a document in the content store (which now exists) and referencing it from the Project — cheap, no schema change, but an agent reads prose rather than querying steps, which is most of what was asked for. WHY NOT NOW: v0.20.0 was deliberately scoped to cap:changelog-view ALONE, and a schema change is not a side quest to slip in beside it. Nothing is lost by waiting — the requirement holds the reasoning and the derivability argument, and the seven recovered steps are written down outside the graph in the meantime. THE ONE THING NOT TO DO is build it as a Flow of invented Capabilities to make this note go away. That would trade a visible open question for a silently wrong metric, which is the exact trade req:no-silent-fallback exists to forbid. THE EVIDENCE STANDS AND IS NOT WEAKENED BY THE PARK: cutting v0.19.0 required reconstructing seven steps from `git show v0.18.0` plus a grep, and at least two of them — that an upgrade doc is owed ONLY when the schema stamp moves, and that the release manifest must be exhaustive with nothing computing it — were discoverable only from a past commit message.acceptedA design records how its project actually ships

The four SEMANTIC criteria cannot be unit-tested for correctness — a test asserting 'this vague requirement was flagged' only proves the fixture was flagged — so what must be pinned there is the GUARD: a quality complaint never edits a requirement, never changes its status, and is surfaced as a question rather than a verdict. ACKNOWLEDGED UNDER PROTEST, and the protest is the point: this contradiction IS resolved, and the detector cannot see it. dec:the-stranded-server-correction-stands is accepted, is edged GOVERNED_BY from both endpoints, and states exactly which clause of the older fact is withdrawn and why. That is precisely what the check-health skill says makes a contradiction go away ('two nodes joined by CONTRADICTS with no resolving Decision') and what every such issue's own suggested_fix_type asks for ('generate_decision'). It changed nothing: detect_defects returned the identical issue id afterwards. The detector reads the edge and never looks for the Decision — recorded as fact:defect-a-contradiction-cannot-be-resolved-only-acknowledged. So this acknowledgement is a WORKAROUND for a reflow2 defect, not a judgement that the disagreement is acceptable. It is chosen over the only alternative — deleting the CONTRADICTS edge — because deleting it would erase that reflow2's own graph carried a confident, untested claim for a day, and that history is worth more than a clean defect list. WHEN THE DETECTOR IS FIXED, this acknowledgement should be withdrawn (withdraw_defect_acknowledgement) rather than left standing, or the graph will record a resolved contradiction as a tolerated one forever.acceptedfact:correction-stranded-server-is-recoverable-without-a-reconnect, fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server

  epoch_planned_read_half["PLANNED — 'The graph can be READ at the size it has reached.' The OUT half. THE MEASUREMENT THAT FORCED IT: of 33 collection-returning read tools, THREE let the caller bound the result and only scan_nodes can page; reviewed_gaps returned 130,922 characters and had to be read with jq. Today a document BEATS the graph for making a decision, and that is a fair fight the graph loses — so no capture improvement is worth anything until this lands. CONTENTS: BL-194 open_questions all-clear; BL-192 enums name legal values; BL-195 the bridge a ruling forbids; BL-201 wire or retire Requirement.concern; BL-203 an unexercised type is visible; generalise scan_nodes' envelope (total/returned/omitted/next_offset/capped_by + payload budget) to the other 30 tools, since it already solved this and was adopted by exactly one; dec:gap-reporting-when-most-intent-is-unbuilt (accepted), because 300 captured ideas produce 300 identical gaps. JOINED 2026-08-08 from dev_storyflow: scan_nodes has no status filter and get_node returns no edges, which cost a lane its stated bound — and a filtered count MUST name its predicate, or it becomes the fifth number in their four-counts report. BL-205 is DONE (shipped early in #70). NO VERSION NUMBER BY DESIGN (dec:idea-a-planned-increment-is-named-by-content-not-by-number): the number is assigned at the cut from what actually ships. release_cut		BL-124: exclude review records from the design network. An acknowledgement Decision is wired GOVERNED_BY into everything it acknowledges, so it joined the island it acknowledged and made disconnected_community permanently unclosable. Fixed at design_network() rather than at the defect-id hash because it has three consumers. MEASURED on reflow2's own graph: 125 review records carrying 610 edges; four of the eight most central nodes were acknowledgements and are now none, with real components rising (rel:v0170 +75%, cmp:detect +41%); and surprising_connections went 16 to 32 — the bookkeeping edges were SUPPRESSING half the real surprises by tying communities together, which is the opposite of the predicted pollution. (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), BL-125: canonicalise the checksum on BOTH sides of the drift comparison, not only on the way in. The property and its honest `unspecified` default already existed and the foundation exemption already worked — only the door was missing, so a user following add_interface then set_interface_spec left every boundary unspecified and collected false single-point-of-failure warnings for shared libraries, having done exactly what the tools invited. Put on set_interface_spec rather than add_interface because it is part of what a consumer must AGREE with, which is that tool's subject, and the seam checker already compares it. release_cut		A Decision reachable from NOTHING is now reported by orphan_node, graded by status. Found 2026-08-01 by running check-health and detect-and-ask on reflow2's own design, getting a clean bill from every detector — detect_defects 0, hierarchy_issues 0, dimension_drifts 0, propose_heal 0 operations — and then counting zero-degree nodes by hand: `dec:sanitize-spof-accepted`, an ACCEPTED single-point-of-failure disposition, had no edges at all and was the only one of five such dispositions not linked to what it disposes. `disconnected_community` structurally cannot see it, because it reports clusters of >=2 and a node joined to nothing is never a cluster. IT IS WORSE THAN UNTIDY: a Decision with no edges cannot be reached by propagation so it never enters an impact analysis, and a disposition specifically can never EXPIRE, because expiry is computed from the affected set (`ver:reviewed-defects`) — a conditional judgement silently becomes permanent. THE RULE IS DEGREE-ZERO AND THAT WAS SETTLED BY MEASUREMENT, NOT TASTE, against my own stated recommendation. The tempting narrow form — an accepted Decision with no incoming GOVERNED_BY — was measured on reflow2's own design and fires on SIX, five of which have degree 1-3: connected, merely not through that one edge type. That is BL-42's shape exactly, where this same detector reported a well-connected Capability missing one named link, became 20 of 31 defects, and had to be cut back to a single rule. Degree-zero fires on ONE and is self-limiting: any edge at all silences it. Review records (`decision:ack:`) are excluded because `structure.rs` already keeps them out of the design network as judgements ABOUT the design rather than structure (`ver:acknowledgement-not-structure`), and all twelve of reflow2's own are `accepted` by construction. Measured after the fix on the real design: 1 warning and 2 info across 1225 nodes, and the two info are proposed decision points, which is a legitimate state. Mutation-checked three ways. (ChangeEvent: new_feature), BL-111: the nudge's 'fires once' promise is computed rather than merely stated — an atomic claim, so a duplicate hook registration is harmless instead of doubling the message (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), BL-141(b): a cycle running only through library/data contracts, with no real DEPENDS_ON hop, drops from Critical to Warning. Downgraded, never silenced — the finding keeps its place, affected set, suggested fix and explanation. (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), BL-141(b): four new cases of 19 — the file-format round trip is a Warning, the same shape over REST stays Critical, one real DEPENDS_ON edge keeps it Critical, and an unspecified medium never earns the downgrade. (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), BL-153 fix shapes (1) and (3): the bulk forms, and the tool surface that carries them (ChangeEvent: new_feature), BL-153: the release manifest becomes derivable, and the two files that carry it move with it (ChangeEvent: new_feature), BL-157 + BL-158: the ledger gains a word for 'nothing moved' — a first baseline is recorded as a first baseline, and a clean reconcile records what it confirmed (ChangeEvent: new_feature), BL-159: the two records of the build-gate contract are now cross-checked by the build. AGENTS.md's 'A change is done when all of these are clean' block and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` were two hand-kept records of one contract, and following the documented one exactly still produced a red build (PR #27). `skill_lint.py` now fails if a `cargo`/`python3` gate in ci.yml appears in NEITHER the block nor the blockquote that names deliberate omissions, if a listed command is spelled differently from the way CI runs it, or if either list names a gate CI has stopped running. FOUR CHECKS RATHER THAN THE ROW'S ONE, and the extra one is the load-bearing one: the row proposed COVERAGE only, but the defect that filed BL-159 was a FLAGS difference on a gate that WAS listed (`-p reflow2-core` clippy lacking `-D warnings`), which coverage alone cannot see — so identity and fidelity are checked separately. THE SPLIT THAT KEEPS IT HONEST is BL-160's threshold lesson again: the lint OBSERVES (is this ci.yml line a gate at all — mechanical, in code), the document JUDGES (does it belong in the everyday local subset — in AGENTS.md, where a human reads it). FOUND ON DAY ONE, which is the payoff: `cargo test -p reflow2-core --no-default-features` and `test_check_doc_versions` were in ci.yml and in neither list. The second is the trap the design anticipated — `check_doc_versions` is a substring of `test_check_doc_versions`, so a substring match would have reported the second as already covered; matching is exact on the script stem. THE CHECK CAUGHT A DEFECT IN ITSELF on its own commit: scanning the whole blockquote read the backticked words `cargo` and `python3` out of the new paragraph describing the lint and reported them as gates CI had stopped running. REPORTED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: reverting the first-paragraph scoping ALONE leaves every check green, because the runner-word exclusion covers today's prose — the two are not redundant in general, and the scoping is pinned on synthetic text where the redundancy cannot hide it. (ChangeEvent: new_feature), BL-160: a registered checksum's LENGTH is a dialect too, and the compensation lived in the wrong layer. reflow2's own designs register `hexdigest()(:16)` (build_design_graph.py) while an honest caller running `sha256sum` supplies all 64, and `reconcile_artifacts` compared STRINGS — so a full sweep of a provably clean tree reported 51 phantom drifts in the same minute `reflow2_check.py` said 'OK — design and build agree'. The gate was right for the wrong reason: it carried a Python workaround truncating the observation to the registered length, which no other consumer had. This is BL-125 in a second form and takes the same verdict — a false red on a gate whose whole job is to be believed is worse than no gate. `artifact::checksums_agree` now answers it in the core for every consumer, on BOTH the drift comparison and `set_artifact_checksum`'s would-move-the-baseline guard (the half that would have failed a BL-157 bulk sweep on every short-registered artifact), and the Python workaround is DELETED rather than duplicated by the next consumer. Required is a real PREFIX relationship, never truncate-both-to-N, and it applies to the `sha256:` dialect only. MEASURED ON THE REAL DESIGN: 109 artifacts, 51 truncated baselines, all 51 now unchanged, and the only 4 drifts are the files this change edited. Corrects a belief the design itself had recorded — chg:accept-e52b527aba651ac4 says a full-length registration is 'harmless, since reconcile truncates the observation to the registered dialect'; reconcile never did, the gate did. (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), BL-161: the loop nudge was corrupting the tally it judges from — a non-atomic write plus an error-swallowing read let one concurrent hook wipe the session's record, so a session that consulted the graph constantly was told at Stop that it never had (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), BL-163: the impact-check trigger keys on a ChangeEvent's PRESENCE where it means its PRECEDENCE — no op set counts propagate_change at all, so recording the change AFTER the edit satisfies the trigger that exists to catch recording the change after the edit (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), BL-68 part (1): readiness becomes a GATING score with a forecast — a ReadinessAssessment construct (TRL/MRL, 1-9), a GATED_ON edge carrying the stated threshold, and TemporalFact gaining basis + confidence so a forecast marks itself as a projection rather than an observation (ChangeEvent: new_feature), FIRST baseline, not an accepted change. art:detect was registered with no checksum, so the most central file in the design — realizing cap:detect, cap:kpp, cap:aggregate-gap-keying, cap:release-pinned-to-time and cmp:detect — could never report drift, and reconcile_artifacts reported it as `no_baseline` rather than clean. Found twice on 2026-08-01 by two independent routes the same hour: an exhaustive reconcile sweep (106 of 107 unchanged, this one uncheckable) and the new derived release manifest, which named it as the sole entry in without_checksum. The file content is unchanged by this session; only the baseline is being established. `design_holds` is the honest available answer and it is an imperfect fit — the disposition vocabulary assumes there WAS a baseline, and establishing a first one is a different act from accepting a move. Filed as friction rather than worked around silently. The skill's method — size a model by contracts and capabilities, never by an LOC ratio — is unchanged. Anthony chose re-running tools/reflow2_init.py over acknowledge_gap; it overwrote nothing (ten edited skill mirrors kept, all three MCP configs left alone) and check_kit_manifest.py then exited 0 with 10 notes and no findings. RECORDED AFTER THE EDIT, and that is the point of writing it down: the snapshot pinned beside this event holds the NEW (passing) state, so the prior `failing` value survives only in this text. revise-design step 2 — snapshot BEFORE editing — was skipped, because reconcile_verification was called with record_events at its default of false: it reported the divergence ('recorded as failing, the run reported passed') to the session and wrote nothing. Without this event the graph would say `passing` with no trace it ever said otherwise, and answering what-changed-when-and-why would need git archaeology — which is the test revise-design sets and the thing req:the-past-is-never-overwritten exists to prevent. The drift itself lives in gitignored local state under .reflow2/, so no commit can fix it and no CI can see it: this check can catch a stale kit, but only a person at the machine can clear one. release_cut		Clippy collapsible_if: the contributor-existence guard became a let-chain. Behaviour identical, 1055 tests unchanged. NO DESIGN MEANING. Fifth instance of hashing before the last edit in one session — and the third distinct mechanism: fmt after the work (twice), and now a REQUIRED CLIPPY FIX after the work. The pattern is not carelessness about hashing; it is that every mandatory gate runs AFTER the code looks finished, so 'finished' is never the moment to hash. Hash immediately before the export, after every gate has run. (ChangeEvent: refactor), First baseline for the detector owed by rule:per-design-state-is-never-a-process-global becoming enforced. Hashed after the file was final and after the negative control was reverted — the artifact-checksum mistake this project has made three times is hashing before the last edit. (ChangeEvent: baseline_established), First baseline for the v0.27.0 upgrade note, written because the schema stamp moved (60 to 61 edge types, OWNED_BY added). Nothing moved; this is a new file getting its first hash. (ChangeEvent: baseline_established), loop_status's served description trimmed from 2039 to under the 1500-char budget skill_lint enforces. Behaviour and parameters unchanged; every clause that survived is load-bearing (the approver discriminator, only-assignment-is-attributed, scoped-clean, the refusal on an unknown id). NO DESIGN MEANING. Worth recording as a real constraint rather than a nuisance: a served tool description is a BUDGETED surface, so a change that explains itself well in a commit message still has to earn its space in the description an agent reads at call time — and skill_lint is what enforces that, caught in CI after three local gates had already passed. (ChangeEvent: refactor), reflow2.toml's own version string moved 0.26.1 to 0.27.0 as step 1 of the release cut. The design meaning of a cut lives in rel:v0270 and epoch:v0270, not in a version string, so the design holds unchanged. This drift is expected on EVERY cut: reflow2.toml is the only registered artifact the version bump touches (Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and AGENTS.md are not registered). (ChangeEvent: refactor), rustfmt reflowed the file after the first baseline was taken; behaviour is unchanged and all three tests still pass. NO DESIGN MEANING. Caught by the CI design-coherence gate, not by me — and it is the fourth instance of the same self-inflicted error: HASHING BEFORE THE LAST EDIT. The specific trap here is new and worth naming: `cargo fmt --check` is a CI gate, so running fmt is a REQUIRED step that happens AFTER the work looks finished, which puts a file mutation after the natural moment to hash. The rule that actually holds is hash last, after fmt, immediately before the export. (ChangeEvent: refactor), v0.27.0 — ownership arrives, the content store leaves, and governance is integrated rather than split (Release)

milestone		BL-198 step 1 landed by REMOVING `default:` from ten properties, not by changing code. The route changed on a measurement: `default:` in the schema YAML is not documentation — dynograph-core applies it at WRITE time (schema.rs:507 inserts any missing property that declares one), which is where 3,207 stored values across 59% of the design came from. So export-side suppression could never have worked — the store cannot tell a chosen value from an injected one — and the real fix is one YAML token per property. FORWARD-ONLY: nodes already written keep what they hold, so the export does not churn and compare_designs sees nothing; the phantom-diff cost this epoch was scoped around does not arise on this route at all. TEN of 81 removed, 71 kept, and the RATIO is the finding: three mechanically-obvious candidates turned out to be meaningful and were kept on evidence. revision		A Decision OBSOLETES what it withdrew, and four computations now read it: the three capability detectors fall silent and delivery stops counting a discontinued capability as a satisfier. NO SCHEMA CHANGE — OBSOLETES is already `* -> *` and putting the DECISION at the source dissolves the successor problem that made this look like it needed new vocabulary. Only an ACCEPTED decision discontinues anything. The cascade is deliberate: the requirement a withdrawn capability served drops back to unsatisfied and is asked about again. DeliveryCoverage gains `satisfied_only_by_discontinued` so the numbers say why they moved rather than shrinking silently. Applied to the content store, whose capability had read `realized` with a `passing` check for two days after its code was deleted. Gives OBSOLETES its first reader, which is what dec:one-retire-edge has been asking for since July. Anthony 2026-08-11: 'reflow2's own rules shouldn't be tracked by hand, but by some governance rules.' CORRECTION TO AN EARLIER CLAIM IN THE SAME SESSION: the export rule was NOT unwired — req:the-export-is-serialised-rather-than-socially-enforced is accepted and fully traced through art:check and ver:gate-suite. What was missing is that the policy existed only as a requirement on the SOFTWARE (the gate must detect a severed chain) and never as a convention binding a CONTRIBUTOR, so unverified_enforced_rule — which scans DesignRules — could not see it. `enforced: true` records that breaking it already stops the build, measured twice today; the consequence question was NOT put to Anthony and the rule says so. The new Verification is narrower than ver:gate-suite on purpose: the gate makes several distinct guarantees and one check standing for all of them cannot say which clause still works. That measurement, taken BEFORE any code was written, produced MIN_MODELLED_RATIO: absence of a recorded consumer is only informative where recording one is the design's habit, so below half the list is WITHHELD and the ratio itself is the finding. THE FINDING BEHIND IT: `provenance::last_synced` was written by two paths (export_graph, import_graph) and read by exactly one (inside export_graph) — so the design knew a shared record had moved at the first moment of a session and said nothing until the write, hours later. FIXES A REAL DEFECT FOUND WHILE BUILDING IT: `sync::assess_overwrite` computed its comparison from `effective_content_hash`, which TRUSTS the content_hash a document states about itself and computes one only when absent — so a record edited by anything but export_graph (a merge, a hand-fix) kept its old stamp, BOTH fast paths returned Clear, and the stale-seat refusal went quiet in exactly the case req:stale-seat-knows exists to catch. On the export path that is silent data loss: the write would delete the other person's work. Now computed from content, with the discrepancy itself reported as `stamp_disagrees`. v0.28.0 cut — 21 PRs since v0.27.0 and no schema move. Three new served tools (what_next, consumption_report, sync_status) and three behaviour changes a consumer will feel: search-before-you-add now REFUSES a near-duplicate create across five capture tools, HEAL stopped offering fabricated repairs, and a refused enum names its legal values.
release_cut		DEFECT, found and fixed 2026-08-12: tools/export_via_binary.py MATERIALIZED 182 property values nobody chose, and shipped them in a release. It imports the source document into a FRESH temp graph, and import runs every node through schema validation, which INSERTS any declared property the node omits (dynograph schema.rs). So 91 Artifacts that honestly carried no `granularity`/`volatility` came back out asserting `atomic`/`stable`. Measured across the record: 81 of 172 artifacts carried granularity through PR #155 (exported via the live server), then 172 of 172 in v0.28.0 and PR #157, both exported through this tool. THIS IS fact:bl-198's DEFECT REINTRODUCED BY THE TOOL BUILT TO FIX THE STAMP, and its cost arrived exactly as BL-198 predicted: compare_designs against the live graph reported 91 phantom changes, the same instrument that has twice produced a false data-loss claim here. NOTHING WAS LOST — the live store was always correct; the RECORD over-asserted. AND THE TOOL CANNOT REPAIR ITS OWN DAMAGE: after the round trip nothing can tell an injected value from a chosen one, which is BL-198's whole point. So the fix is two-part. (1) The record is re-exported DIRECTLY from the real store with the new binary, which gives the correct stamp AND changes no property — the temp graph was only ever needed because the running server held the lock, so freeing the lock removes the need for the round trip entirely. (2) The tool now DIFFS what it wrote against its source and reports every (node_type, property) it materialized, refusing to be silent about it; it cannot undo the injection, so it names it and tells the caller to export directly instead. (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), The v0.28.0 version bump. reflow2.toml is a registered artifact, so step 1 of a release cut always drifts it. NO DESIGN MEANING MOVES: what a cut means lives in the Release node and its epoch, not in a version string. Accepted BEFORE release_includes_all is applied, so the manifest freezes the shipped value rather than the pre-bump one — the recorded order does this after and pays a gate failure plus a second export for it. FOUND BY RUNNING THE TOOL TWICE, 2026-08-12: a second mirror of the SAME design collided with its own first — 12 of 13 ids refused as collisions, mirrored_edges 0, mirror_content_hash null — leaving the stale node in place with the host edge still pointing at it while `mirrors` reported the OLD pin. So the staleness register read FRESH after a failed refresh, which is worse than never refreshing. THE QUESTION SETTLED FIRST: what happens to a host edge whose foreign target is gone from the new surface? A refused refresh changes NOTHING and the pin does not advance, which is the lie the whole fix is about. release_cut		Adds the materialization guard: the tool now diffs what it wrote against its source and names every (node_type, property) the round trip invented, because it CANNOT undo the injection - after the round trip nothing tells an injected value from a chosen one. THE DESIGN ALREADY SAID THIS (fact:bl-198); only the tool was wrong, hence design_holds. See chg:the-export-round-trip-injected-defaults. (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), DEFECT, found and fixed 2026-08-12: tools/export_via_binary.py MATERIALIZED 182 property values nobody chose, and shipped them in a release. It imports the source document into a FRESH temp graph, and import runs every node through schema validation, which INSERTS any declared property the node omits (dynograph schema.rs). So 91 Artifacts that honestly carried no `granularity`/`volatility` came back out asserting `atomic`/`stable`. Measured across the record: 81 of 172 artifacts carried granularity through PR #155 (exported via the live server), then 172 of 172 in v0.28.0 and PR #157, both exported through this tool. THIS IS fact:bl-198's DEFECT REINTRODUCED BY THE TOOL BUILT TO FIX THE STAMP, and its cost arrived exactly as BL-198 predicted: compare_designs against the live graph reported 91 phantom changes, the same instrument that has twice produced a false data-loss claim here. NOTHING WAS LOST — the live store was always correct; the RECORD over-asserted. AND THE TOOL CANNOT REPAIR ITS OWN DAMAGE: after the round trip nothing can tell an injected value from a chosen one, which is BL-198's whole point. So the fix is two-part. (1) The record is re-exported DIRECTLY from the real store with the new binary, which gives the correct stamp AND changes no property — the temp graph was only ever needed because the running server held the lock, so freeing the lock removes the need for the round trip entirely. (2) The tool now DIFFS what it wrote against its source and reports every (node_type, property) it materialized, refusing to be silent about it; it cannot undo the injection, so it names it and tells the caller to export directly instead. release_cut		A discontinued node now SAYS SO to whoever reads it — `scan_nodes` and `get_node` carry a derived `discontinued`, because all four of the existing readers were computations and none was a READ. FOUND BY BEING WRONG IN FRONT OF THE OWNER, 2026-08-12: `cap:content-store` was discontinued 2026-08-09 on Anthony's word (`dec:the-content-store-is-discontinued`, accepted, OBSOLETES drawn correctly) and its code deleted — yet a brief scan returned `{'node_id':'cap:content-store','status':'realized'}` with nothing marking the retirement. A session read that, believed the store was live and missing only a surface, and RECOMMENDED HE BUILD A SURFACE FOR A FEATURE HE HAD PERSONALLY REMOVED THREE DAYS EARLIER. He caught it himself and challenged the diagnosis, which was also wrong: the first explanation blamed `Capability.status` having no terminal value, when the mechanism `dec:idea-discontinued-is-a-first-class-state` settled needs no status at all. THE ACTUAL DEFECT is narrow — `is_discontinued` was `pub(crate)` and every caller was a computation (three capability detectors, consumption, delivery arithmetic, the report). All correct, all silent to a reader. Same class as `get_node` answering a bare `null` for an unknown TYPE: a fact the server HOLDS and declines to give. FIX: `is_discontinued` made `pub`; both read tools decorate every node with `discontinued`, PRESENT AND FALSE on live nodes so 'not withdrawn' and 'this build does not report withdrawal' cannot share an answer; both served descriptions now say the stored `status` records what was BUILT and does not move on withdrawal, so filtering a list on `status` alone counts things that no longer exist. DERIVED ON EVERY READ, NEVER WRITTEN BACK — so a reader and a detector cannot disagree, and `dec:idea-does-a-capability-need-a-cancelled-state` (open, marked, Anthony's) is not settled by implementation. 8 tests written first, 5 of 5 mutations killed. ONE CLAIM LEFT UNPINNED AND LABELLED AS SUCH: decoration happens before the payload size is measured so the budget stays honest, and reversing those two lines kills no test — catching it needs a graph within ~22 bytes per node of the scan budget. Toolsnaps regenerated: exactly 2 of 149 changed. (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), A fresh install now names the shareable design record, and the settings merge stops reformatting somebody else's file — both from Alex's first run on a real work project (ChangeEvent: test_failure_fix), Anthony accepted req:linking-two-projects-is-a-served-process on its wording, after being shown the ten steps and three flagged judgement calls (ChangeEvent: scope_change), One Interface was describing two boundaries — the MCP surface split into its stdio and HTTP transports, on Anthony's word, rather than adding a protocol to the medium enum (ChangeEvent: scope_change), The content-store retirement now OBSOLETES everything its own text says it removed, not just one capability of five. FOUND WITHIN MINUTES OF SHIPPING THE READER FIX, 2026-08-12, and BY that fix: with `discontinued` finally visible on a read, `cap:content-manifest` came back `realized / discontinued:false` for a tool that no longer exists. `dec:the-content-store-is-discontinued` (accepted 2026-08-09) names its casualties explicitly — 'content_put / content_get / content_exists / CONTENT_MANIFEST, content.rs, content_tools.rs, the --content-path flag, and BOTH TEST FILES' — but its OBSOLETES edges reached `cap:content-store` and the five Decisions it supersedes, and nothing else. THE RECORD CONTRADICTED ITSELF: the prose said removed, the structure said live. FOUR NODES WERE STRANDED, AND THE TWO WORST ARE VERIFICATIONS. `ver:content-store` and `ver:content-surface` both read `passing`, last_run_at 2026-07-31, for test files deleted on 2026-08-09 — a PASSING CHECK IS THE STRONGEST CLAIM THIS SYSTEM MAKES, and both were attached to nothing while sitting inside the 138-passing count the graph report shows. `cap:content-manifest` (realized) and `cap:session-artifacts` (VERIFIED, and its whole mechanism was content_put) were the other two. THIS RECORDS AN EXISTING DECISION RATHER THAN MAKING A NEW ONE — Anthony's word 2026-08-12, 'go ahead and draw the edges', given after being shown that it moves delivery arithmetic, silences three detectors on those nodes, and changes the confirmed/passing counts. He was asked precisely because this project treats those numbers carefully; the edges make the structure agree with prose he had already accepted. ⭐ THE GENERALISABLE PART, and the reason this is worth reading later: A RETIREMENT IS DRAWN ONE EDGE AT A TIME WHILE THE THING BEING RETIRED IS A CLUSTER — a capability, its siblings, its verifications, its artifacts. Nothing checks that a discontinuation covers everything its own decision text names, and nothing did here. That gap is why four nodes sat wrong for three days with every gate green, and it is a candidate detector: a Decision whose text names removals that carry no OBSOLETES.
